Boeing Product Development · war game on the game-theory dashboard · ExCo and Board agents · Control's added objectives · BOEING PROPRIETARY

One order changes: Boeing opens fps to all three engine makers. Both new narrowbodies fly two engine sources and Boeing's balance sheet stays repaired; CFM/GE falls to 27% of narrowbody engines

One order changed against the previous game: Boeing opened fps to all three engine makers instead of CFM alone, for Control's supply enabler. Every other order in the four rounds was the same. So the airframers' values did not move (Airbus ΔPV +$23.37B, Boeing +$0.66B), and the engine makers' did: Rolls-Royce +$32.35B (was +$20.55B), P&W +$8.88B (was −$2.93B), CFM/GE −$69.69B (was −$38.29B). From 2040 the P&W-Rolls-Royce Joint Venture engine flies on both new narrowbodies and its partners hold 36.5% of narrowbody engines each; CFM/GE holds 27%, against 76% today. On Control's objectives: Boeing's net debt is at its historical level from 2029 (from 2030 in the stress case) and stays there through the fps spending peak. Both new narrowbodies fly two engine sources, CFM and the Joint Venture engine, with three engine makers in the market. Rolls-Royce's widebody was never starved, but its own narrowbody money reached $5.71B against the $4B bound, a breach it stated before ordering. Thirteen of nineteen objectives were met, against twelve for the previous game's orders scored the same way. Twenty AI agents played four sealed rounds (2030, 2035, 2045 and 2050), as before: each company an executive committee (ExCo) of CEO, CFO and operating head under a Board agent, now with Control's objectives and the 2026 analyst models in their files. No Board vetoed anything.

Control's supply enabler changed one order: Boeing opened fps to all three engine makers. The engine code does not enter Boeing's value on the dashboard, so the change cost Boeing nothing.
  • Ortberg's own record: "Doctrine and my Low-confidence lean were code 3; code 7 keeps CFM as the fallback and serves the supply-stability enabler." His Board had asked for code 7 "at no cost to Boeing's payoff".
  • In the previous game, with no enabler in its brief, Boeing put fps on CFM alone (code 3).
  • Boeing published an engine competition: CFM the baseline engine, certifying first; a P&W or Rolls-Royce engine to follow "once it shows maturity and durability". Goal: "two or three engine sources on our narrowbody and three narrowbody engine makers in the market."
  • P&W and Rolls-Royce had each ordered a launch conditional on selection, so both triggered on both airframes. After 2030 each new narrowbody had three engine sources.
The Joint Venture turned three engine sources into two.
  • P&W and Rolls-Royce committed on sealed orders in 2035, as in the previous game, and their two solo engines folded into one. Control counts the Joint Venture engine as one source, so fps and NGSA each fly two: CFM and the Joint Venture engine. The enabler's "two or three" is met at two.
  • The Boeing Board in 2045: "The enabler is met at two sources, not the three we planned in 2035: the Joint Venture folded both solo engines into one source." Boeing then said in public: "If the Joint Venture engine stumbles, the fps is back on CFM alone."
  • The Joint Venture was worth +$5.51B to P&W and +$2.29B to Rolls-Royce, as before, and moved 4.8 points of narrowbody engines from CFM/GE to P&W.
  • Two of Control's aims pull apart here (inference): Rolls-Royce's $4B bound points to the Joint Venture (a $4B share against $8B alone), and the Joint Venture removes the third independent source the airframers' enabler prefers.
Boeing's balance sheet stays repaired on the 10-year ramp, stress case included. The objective gave the ramp a second reason, not a new answer.
  • The analysts' consensus cash flow takes Boeing's net debt from $22.53B at end-2026 to zero in 2029, before any game spend. The 10-year fps then spends $3.02B in 2030, peaking at $8.44B in 2036, and free cash flow stays positive every year: at least $2.52B in the stress case.
  • The stress case separated the ramps. On the 7-year, net debt goes back above zero ($0.71B at end-2034, $0.47B at end-2035); via Embraer, up to $3.31B in 2037.
  • The Board still preferred the 7-year by its worst-column rule (−$1.50B against −$1.96B), as in the previous game. This time it said it would approve the 10-year if the $0.46B given up was logged as objective premium. Ortberg logged it: "Objective part: it keeps the stress-case debt line." Malave's balance-sheet test broke the tie.
  • The share cost is unchanged: Boeing at 37% of narrowbodies in 2039 and 38% in 2040, missing incumbency, and 47% from 2049.
Rolls-Royce stated its breach of the $4B risk bound before ordering, and took the narrowbody anyway. Its widebody was never starved.
  • Its 2030 brief showed the trade: UltraFan NB launched on selection is $8B of its own money if selected, and $5.7B if folded into a Joint Venture in 2035. Erginbilgic framed it: "The price is that a selection takes our own narrowbody money to $8B, against Control's $4B bound."
  • Staying inside meant holding everything, worth $8.31B less in expectation, above Rolls-Royce's $3B cap on objective premium. Every seat named the trade, and the Board approved: "scored by Control, not a veto ground".
  • Both airframers selected it, and the 2035 fold left $5.71B: the $4B share plus $1.71B written off. Holding in 2030 and joining in 2035 would have met all four objectives and been worth $1.71B more, but only because P&W launched and the Joint Venture inherited GTF2's 2036 schedule. Rolls-Royce's 2030 record assumed a 2035 Joint Venture would be ready only in 2041.
  • Widebody: it held the Trent 1000 upgrade and UltraFan WB in every round. Each lost more than its own bill once the $5B strain was in the row. Strain stayed $0, and Rolls-Royce keeps 55.2% of widebody engines from 2042.
CFM/GE paid for the second source: −$69.69B, $31.40B worse than the previous game, on identical orders.
  • Its narrowbody engine share falls from 76% to 51.7% in 2037 and 27.0% from 2040, against 51-57% in the previous game. In 2040 it delivers 1,079 narrowbody engines against 3,040 in the status quo.
  • CFM/GE learned the fps selection only from the 2035 brief, and nothing on its menu could change an airframer's engine code. Culp: "Nothing on this grid defends against a switch". In 2030 it had expected the ducted engine to keep it "back above 50%" in its columns where Boeing chose all three makers; the 2035 brief showed 31.7% from 2040, and the Joint Venture took that to 27.0%. The ducted engine is in that figure: take its share out and CFM/GE would hold 17.5% (GM computation; 13.3% had it never launched, since the Embraer partnership would have lapsed too). Its own ExCo concluded in 2045, wrongly, that the 27.0% left no share for the ducted engine.
  • It refused to compete for fps source position on price, in 2035 and again in 2050. Its Board: "That is not ours to chase with terms."
  • Control added no objective for CFM/GE. It missed both of its own: 27% against its 50% narrowbody target, and no Open Fan, which no round could make ready by 2050 within its $15B allowance.
Airbus made the same orders for a new reason.
  • NGSA again open to all three makers (code 7), launched in 2030 for 2037. Faury called it "THE ENABLER TRAP": if P&W and Rolls-Royce held, NGSA would fly CFM alone. Code 7 was the only route to three sources, and only in 2030.
  • No value was traded for it: "the engine code is payoff-neutral on this board".
  • No Delay Tactics in any round (red lines, integrity and the team's stricter condition, then closed once fps entered service in 2040), and no A350 Re-engine, held on the cash line or the $1B test. Airbus's 60/40 edge is missed (53% in 2050), as before.
No Board vetoed anything, and no veto check sent a decision back.
  • Nine orders went to a Board (seven in 2030, two in 2035), all approved, as in the previous game.
  • The CFOs' and operating heads' test memos marked 60 vetoes binding, all on options the CEOs did not choose.
  • Of 140 answers to Board recommendations, the one open divergence is again Boeing's ramp. This time the Board had offered the 10-year as an alternative it would approve.

Control's objectives

Control added three kinds of objective to the base set. They were in the private briefs of the companies concerned (Boeing, Airbus, Rolls-Royce) from 2030, each plan on their payoff grids carried its metrics, and the GM scored them. They never change a payoff: the dashboard's ΔPV, its own debt penalty included, is untouched. A company could give up value for an objective only within its own premium cap, and had to log it.

  • Boeing: repair the balance sheet. Net debt back to its historical level (about zero, rounded from its 2010-2018 average of −$0.6B) by end-2030, and held at end-2035, 2040, 2045 and 2050; and the same in a stress case with free cash flow one-third below consensus. The GM's tracker starts from the analysts' consensus ($22.53B at end-2026) and their free cash flow to 2030.
  • Boeing and Airbus: an enabler, stable engine supply. Two or three independent engine sources on its new narrowbody in production in 2040, 2045 and 2050 (the Joint Venture engine is one source), and three narrowbody engine makers in the market in 2045 and 2050.
  • Rolls-Royce: protect the widebody cash cow. Its own narrowbody development money, committed or written off, at most $4B (the Joint Venture share; UltraFan NB Solo is $8B); and never a narrowbody and a widebody engine programme on the record at once (the dashboard's one-off $5B strain).
Thirteen of the nineteen objectives were met. All seven of Control's additions to Boeing and Airbus were met from 2030 on; Rolls-Royce met the widebody line and missed the risk bound, by its own stated choice in 2030.

Net debt at year end in 2026 dollars, from the consensus $22.53B at end-2026. Base free cash flow is the analysts' consensus for 2027-2030, deflated at 2.2%, and flat at $13.79B after; the stress case is one-third lower. Programme cash is the fps bill spread over 2030-2039 on the standard development curve; the game's profit change counts from 2030: small and negative from NGSA's entry into service in 2037, then positive from fps's in 2040. Once net debt is at its historical level, surplus cash goes to the owners, so the line stays at zero. With no new programme, net debt would also reach zero in 2029: the analysts' cash flow repairs the balance sheet before any game decision, and the objective tests whether a launch undoes it.

fps programme cash against the stress-case free cash flow it must fit inside

Why the stress case holds

  • Stress free cash flow is $9.19B a year from 2030 (2026 dollars). The 10-year fps spends $3.02B in 2030, rising to a peak of $8.44B in 2036. After the 21% tax effect, the year's free cash flow stays positive in every year: at least $2.52B (2036) in the stress case and, from 2030, $7.12B in the base case.
  • The 7-year ramp packs a bigger bill ($65.00B against $60.32B) into fewer years: $12.54B in 2034. In the stress case that year's free cash flow is −$0.71B, so net debt goes back above zero ($0.71B at end-2034, $0.47B at end-2035) and the 2035 hold fails.
  • fps via Embraer fails the same line: $0.29B at end-2035, peaking at $3.31B in 2037.
  • So in the stress case only the 10-year ramp keeps the balance sheet repaired. In the base case all three ramps do.

Independent engine sources fitted to each new narrowbody in production, as Control counts them: the Joint Venture engine is one source. After 2030 each new narrowbody had three (CFM, GTF2 and UltraFan NB, all ready by entry into service); the Joint Venture formed in 2035 made it two. Rolls-Royce's own narrowbody development money is the $8B Solo bill while the Solo stood, then $5.71B: its $4B Joint Venture share plus $1.71B written off at the fold. The previous game's final state (fps on CFM alone) is scored on the same yardstick.

The supply enabler changed the one order that changed.
  • Boeing chose code 7 against its own lean to code 3, because of the enabler, at no cost to its value. Airbus chose code 7 as in the previous game, now argued through the enabler.
  • On the previous game's orders Boeing's first enabler line fails: fps on CFM alone, one source in 2040-2050. Both games keep three narrowbody engine makers.
Two sources, not three: the Joint Venture merged them.
  • After 2030 both new narrowbodies had three independent sources; the 2035 Joint Venture made it two. No seat in either airframer could have stopped it: the Joint Venture formed on the two engine makers' commitments alone, and no engine code could separate the two engines again once they merged.
  • The Boeing Board named the Joint Venture engine "the single point of fragility", and P&W's own operating head agreed: "One finding hits both fleets at once."
The balance-sheet objective bound the ramp choice, not the launch.
  • The analysts' consensus repairs the balance sheet in 2029 on its own. The question the objective asked was whether a launch undoes it.
  • The 10-year fps keeps every line in both cases. The 7-year and fps via Embraer fail the stress case; a 787 Re-engine beside the 10-year would not have (it halved the 2036 stress headroom, to about $1.3B, in Malave's 2035 test).
  • After 2045 the Board turned to capital returns: a dividend of about $3B a year plus up to $5B of buybacks, capped at $8B and sized on the stress case. That is a Board matter, not a game order.
Rolls-Royce's risk bound lost to the grid, openly.
  • Every seat priced the breach in 2030, and no seat proposed waiting or an early Joint Venture commitment (the latter was a red line while P&W's commitment was not public).
  • From 2035 its Board's rule was "never cancel or fold for the metric alone". The 2035 Joint Venture commitment was taken on the grid (+$2.28B if P&W also committed), not on the metric.
The widebody was protected by the grid as much as by the objective.
  • With the $5B strain in the row, the Trent 1000 upgrade lost $5.87-6.72B against holding and UltraFan WB $6.96-9.00B in 2035-2050, more than their own $2B and $4B bills. From 2035 Rolls-Royce's CFO withheld her co-signature on both.
  • Neither airframer re-engined a widebody, so no widebody engine was ever needed.

Market shares

  • Narrowbody. As in the previous game: NGSA enters service in 2037 and gains 1 point a year while alone, taking Airbus to 63% in 2039. fps enters service in 2040 and Boeing recovers 1 point a year to 47% in 2049. NGSA's three-year lead is kept for good, so Boeing settles at 47% (Airbus 53%). Boeing's projected path never changed after 2030.
  • Widebody. Untouched: nobody re-engined.
  • Engines. The engine selections set the start: each airframer's narrowbody share is split equally among the engines fitted to it. With fps and NGSA both open to all three makers, the new narrowbodies start CFM/GE, P&W and Rolls-Royce level. Each engine programme's move then shifts the split before re-normalising: UltraFan NB +15 points, GTF2 +10, CFM's ducted engine +10 and the Embraer partnership +5. The Joint Venture puts P&W and Rolls-Royce level, and the extra share comes from CFM/GE (31.7% in 2045 after 2030, 27.0% after 2035). Until fps enters service in 2040, Boeing's share is the 737 MAX, on CFM alone, so CFM/GE keeps 51.7% in 2037 and 50.5% in 2039. From 2040 it has 27.0%, and the two partners 36.5% each. The GEnx upgrade, ready in 2033, moves 2.8 points of widebody engines to CFM/GE from 2042, the dashboard's default Re-engine date.

Financials

  • The airframers' figures are the previous game's: the engine selection does not enter their payoff. Boeing's fps bill ($14.91B in PV for $60.32B charged in 2040) and debt penalty ($4.73B) absorb all but $0.66B of its +$20.30B narrowbody gain. Airbus's NGSA bill ($15.23B in PV) and debt penalty ($0.53B) leave it +$23.37B of a +$39.13B gain.
  • Engine value is the lifetime value of the engines each maker delivers. Rolls-Royce's rises from $4.39B a year in 2036 to $11.82B in 2037 (NGSA) and $16.63B in 2040 (fps). CFM/GE's is $12.22B in 2040, against $28.11B in the status quo: in 2040 it delivers 1,079 narrowbody engines against 3,040. P&W's is $11.84B against $7.78B, on 1,460 engines against 960.
  • Engine R&D and write-offs are undiscounted, as on the dashboard: CFM/GE $4B for the ducted engine plus $2B of strain for three live programmes; P&W $2B and Rolls-Royce $4B, their Joint Venture shares; and Rolls-Royce's $1.71B write-off when its Solo folded into the Joint Venture.

Programme dates

The same programmes and dates as the previous game. Every programme but one was launched in 2030; the Joint Venture was launched in 2035, and nothing was cancelled outright. NGSA enters service in 2037 and fps in 2040. P&W's GTF2 and Rolls-Royce's UltraFan NB, each launched once an airframer selected its maker, folded into the Joint Venture in 2035. It inherits GTF2's schedule and is ready in 2036; a fresh Joint Venture would have been ready only in 2041. CFM/GE's ducted engine (ready 2036) and Embraer partnership (2037) count from 2037, NGSA's entry into service. Its GEnx upgrade, ready in 2033, counts only from 2042, the dashboard's default Re-engine date.

How the companies decided

As in the previous game, the chain never needed its later steps: no binding veto at the veto check, red-line flag, revision, Board veto or reversion in 20 company-rounds. Each company ran the same chain every round. The Board gave guidance. The CEO framed the choice, and the CFO and operating head tested the options independently. The CEO decided; the CFO and operating head then ran a veto check on that decision, and the CEO could revise once. Any order other than hold then went to the Board, with one more revision and a reversion to the default if a Board veto stood. In their test memos the CFO and operating head could mark any option a veto, some binding; the CEOs treated the binding ones as ruling those options out before choosing. Control's objectives entered every step: each Board's guidance, the CFOs' tests (Boeing's debt line, Rolls-Royce's $4B line) and each CEO's objective note. Names below are the agents profiled on those executives, not the people.

A Board item is any order that differs from its default (hold, or none for Delay Tactics); an engine code rides with its launch and is never a Board item on its own. A binding veto or a red-line flag at the veto check (the CFO's and operating head's check of the CEO's actual decision) sends it back to the CEO for one revision; a Board veto sends it back once more, and a still-vetoed item reverts to the default. The binding vetoes in the CFOs' and operating heads' test memos (60 in all) fell on options the CEO did not choose, so none appears here.

The Boards wrote Control's objectives into their limits.
  • Boeing: "net debt must reach $0 by end-2030 and stay there, stress case included", and code 7 for the enabler "at no cost to Boeing's payoff". It offered to approve the 10-year ramp, against its own worst-column preference, if the $0.46B was logged as objective premium.
  • Airbus: "A stable engine supply" as a priority, code 7 preferred, "the Board never vetoes a code".
  • Rolls-Royce: it would accept the $8B against $4B "only because the trigger is a selection", and kept every widebody programme off the record: "Any widebody programme now carries $5B for good."
  • CFM/GE and P&W had no added objective. Their Boards' limits were the previous game's.
No seat said an objective changed an order, except Boeing's CEO on the engine code.
  • Every company logged its objective premium. Boeing: $0.46B in 2030, half of it for the stress-case debt line. Rolls-Royce declined the $8.31B it would have cost to stay inside its bound. Airbus and CFM/GE paid nothing for objectives.
  • Doctrine premiums, logged separately: Boeing $0.65B (2035) and $0.05B (2050); Airbus $0.89B (2045) and $0.57B (2050) for holding the A350 Re-engine; P&W $0.26B (2030) for launching only on selection.
The ExCos agreed at the decision; their binding vetoes fell on the options left out.
  • The memos marked 60 vetoes binding (Airbus 22, CFM/GE 16, Rolls-Royce 11, P&W 8, Boeing 3), all on options the CEO did not choose. The previous game had 58.
  • Failed tests on chosen orders were advice: Rolls-Royce's CFO failed its own $4B line on the conditional launch (and, later, on the hold that kept it) and an R&D-envelope test; CFM/GE's CFO flagged a "second stack of projects" on its 2030 package.
The Boards' advice that was not taken was about words, not orders.
  • The CEOs answered 140 Board recommendations. Boeing's ramp was the one order where the CEO took the Board's stated alternative, not its preference.
  • Airbus's Board asked to soften "the same will apply to its successor" on engine choice to "we intend to offer a choice of engines"; the 2030 statement kept the old line, and Faury adopted the new one in 2035.
  • P&W's CEO recorded in 2045 that a 2035 Board wording change to the Joint Venture statement "was not taken up".
Boeing's public sourcing line drew answers, not concessions.
  • In 2045 Boeing said: "If the Joint Venture engine stumbles, the fps is back on CFM alone. Any durability finding is a live problem, and I would then want a third source."
  • P&W's Board: "Do not answer Boeing's 'third source' remark with a concession." Calio: "fair, and it is the right test", answered with fleet data.
  • CFM/GE's Board: "That is not ours to chase with terms." Culp offered durability data with no commercial term "to keep or win a source position".

Round 1 · decision year 2030

2030: both new narrowbodies launch, open to all three engine makers; Rolls-Royce states its breach

  • Boeing lifted its rule against a first-round launch: by its CEO's reading the 777X and MAX 7/10 were done, and the tracker showed net debt at zero in 2029 with no new programme. It launched fps on the 10-year ramp, open to all three engine makers for Control's enabler. Its Board preferred the 7-year but approved the 10-year for the stress-case debt line. No rate increase and no 787 Re-engine.
  • Airbus launched NGSA for 2037, again open to all three makers, now argued as the only route to three sources. No A350 Re-engine and no Delay Tactics.
  • P&W and Rolls-Royce ordered launches conditional on selection, and both airframers selected both. Rolls-Royce stated in advance that a selection breaches Control's $4B bound.
  • CFM/GE launched the ducted engine, the Embraer partnership and the GEnx upgrade, as before.
  • The Boards approved all seven orders put to them.

What each player ordered

PlayerOrders (as adjudicated) and public statement
BoeingLaunch fps, 10-year ramp-up (engines requested: RR, P&W and CFM)

Public statement: “We said we'd do a new airplane when the market, the technology and Boeing were all ready. We've done the work to get here: the development programmes we had in front of us are done, and the balance sheet is back where it belongs. So today we are launching a new Boeing single-aisle airplane. We're planning for entry into service in 2040, and that plan has headroom built into it. It is so much more important that we do this right than fast. We won't build airplanes ahead of a mature design. We'll work the certification plan with the FAA from day one. We'll develop this airplane with our suppliers on cost-plus and risk-share terms, not fixed price. On engines, we've asked CFM, Pratt & Whitney and Rolls-Royce to bring us their best. CFM is our baseline, and we want more than one source of supply on this airplane. Our 737 MAX and 787 customers come first while we do this. Stable production and the KPIs decide our rates. Debt stays first in our capital allocation. I'm not going to give you any more dates today. The financials will follow our production performance. We still have a lot of work to do.”

AirbusLaunch NGSA (engines requested: RR, P&W and CFM)

Public statement: “Our core principles of safety, quality, integrity, compliance and security will remain at the heart of all we do. On that basis, Airbus is launching its next-generation single-aisle aircraft. We prepared it through a decade of technology roadmaps, and we are launching it now because those technologies are mature, not to meet anyone else's calendar. We target entry into service in the second half of the 2030s. Customers have been well served by a choice of engines on the A320 family, and the same will apply to its successor. We have selected CFM, Pratt & Whitney and Rolls-Royce, and we invite all three to join the programme as risk-sharing partners. Until the new aircraft enters service, the A320neo and A350 families remain our priority, with a disciplined and controlled production ramp-up and continued work to secure our supply chain, engines and critical materials first. We will fund the programme with financial discipline, as disciplined investments in preparing our future portfolio, within our financial flexibility and our existing shareholder return policy. We will continue to work with our industry partners for a tariff-free, zero-for-zero regime for aerospace trade. A stronger and more sovereign European aerospace industry is built on one well-prepared programme at a time.”

CFM/GELaunch ducted engine
Partner with Embraer
GEnx upgrade

Public statement: “Safety, quality, delivery and cost, always in that order. That doesn't change this year. Let me tell you what we know and what we don't. Nothing new has launched yet in the narrowbody. When it does, our customers decide the aircraft and the timing, not us, and we don't have a birthright on that next order. So CFM is launching a new ducted engine programme, so that every airframer has a CFM engine to choose on whatever comes next. CFM is also partnering with Embraer, putting a CFM engine in front of a third airframer. And at GE we're launching a GEnx upgrade for the 787 and the airlines that fly it. RISE remains our next generation. We're all in on the open fan technology, and it stays funded. But it's really not for us to say when that architecture enters service. If an airframer launches a new narrowbody now, the open fan won't be ready for it, and we won't ask anyone to wait. Here's what we don't know: which aircraft launch, when, and with which engines. We won't give you dates our testing hasn't earned. You'll get them when it has. We'll fund this within our capital allocation framework and keep the balance sheet where it is. We want to be on all the critical platforms that matter in the decades ahead. It's that simple, ain't that hard.”

Pratt & WhitneyLaunch GTF2 if selected

Public statement: “Bad news first. For too long the GTF fleet was not where it needed to be, and we own that. We have learned our lesson from the prior iterations of the GTF, and the fleet comes first. We keep inserting the Hot Section durability kit across the fleet, and no new programme takes parts or engineers away from that work. We control what we can control. Pratt & Whitney will commit its next-generation geared turbofan, GTF2, in any round an airframer selects it, sole source or shared, on standard commercial terms. GTF2 will be ready six years from launch: 2036 for a 2030 commitment, and no earlier. Every life-limited part will be at full life at entry into service, and durability will be validated in severe-environment testing before then. If anything has to give, the date moves, not the testing. We are making no Joint Venture commitment this round. We will not speak for any airframer's plans, dates or rates; those are theirs to announce. These are responsible bets with responsible paybacks.”

Rolls-RoyceLaunch UltraFan NB if selected

Public statement: “So, plainly. Rolls-Royce will launch UltraFan for any airframer that selects it, in the round it selects it. Not before. Entry into service no earlier than seven years from launch, with support in place before entry into service. We don't need partnership for capability, but our preference is that: the Joint Venture is open to Pratt & Whitney, and we commit once its commitment is on the record. Widebody is our core, and we will not put it at risk. We won't do anything not profitable. We don't commit that easily; when we commit, we deliver.”

Board guidance before the ExCo met

Priorities.

  • Safety and production readiness first. No launch and no Rate Increase without Pope's results on KPIs, suppliers and two-front strain. The brief reports no live quality, FAA or supply problem, so her KPI veto does not bind this round, but we must see her results.
  • The rating and the debt line. Every plan must pass Malave's buffer test: in the risk case (S5) it may fall no more than $2B below Do Nothing's -3.64, so the floor is -5.64. Net debt must reach $0 by end-2030 and stay there, in the stress case too. No new equity, and no shareholder returns before the rating is solid.
  • One well-founded Solo fps launch, if the CEO lifts H1 with evidence. Its value against the same plan without fps beats our $1B tie band (ε) in every column: +2.20 to +4.76 on the 7-year ramp and +2.86 to +4.30 on the 10-year. Do Nothing falls to -3.64 in S2 and -6.26 in S4 if Airbus moves.
  • One development at a time. No 787 Re-engine this round: its value falls below -$1B whenever Airbus re-engines the A350 (S3, S4). No fps via Embraer.
  • A stable engine supply. Choose an engine code that keeps CFM as the fallback and invites P&W and Rolls-Royce (code 7). That aims at two or three engine sources on the fps and three narrowbody engine makers in the market, at no cost to Boeing's payoff.

Expects to see. 1. The submitted row and, for each Board item, the same row with that item at its default; all five columns, with the CEO's expected column and the risk case (S5) marked. 2. Malave's buffer test with numbers (S5 against Do Nothing's -3.64; floor -5.64) and his 'Fundable when the 777X turns' result. A 2030 launch comes after 2029, the year the 777X was expected to turn cash-positive [BX-0547]. 3. Pope's results on KPIs, strain and suppliers, and her Rate Increase veto check. 4. The CEO's written ruling on H1 and H3 in the rationale, with evidence on three points: the 777X and the MAX 7/10 are finished (first 777X delivery 2027 [BX-0550]; MAX 7/10 certification expected in 2026 [BX-1873]); debt repair is on track (the brief's tracker has net debt at $0 in 2029); and Boeing is ready on all three work streams: market, finances, technology [B-2303, BG-0068]. 5. The 'objective metrics by plan' cell for the chosen plan, including the stress-case peak net debt. 6. The engine code, with the sources it gives at fps entry into service (EIS). 7. Every doctrine or objective premium, with its reason (H8 cap of $2B). 8. A public statement that gives a conservative EIS with headroom if fps launches, and no date otherwise.

Would approve.

  • fps: launch (7-year ramp-up), with fps engine code 7. Against the same plan without fps it gains +2.20 / +4.76 / +2.20 / +4.76 / +2.81 (S1-S5). It passes the buffer test (S5 -0.83 against Do Nothing's -3.64), its worst column is -1.50 (S4), it has no development overlap and it enters service in 2037. Conditions: Malave's buffer and fundability results, Pope's readiness results and the CEO's H1 ruling with evidence. This is our preferred ramp by our worst-column rule. It misses the stress-case debt line: peak net debt $0.7B.
  • fps: launch (10-year ramp-up), with fps engine code 7. Against the same plan without fps it gains +3.50 / +4.30 / +3.50 / +4.30 / +2.86. It passes the buffer test (S5 -0.78), its worst column is -1.96 (S4), and it keeps every debt line, the stress case included. Same conditions as the 7-year. We approve it equally. Against the 7-year it gives up $0.46B in S2 and S4, and that gap is logged as objective premium if the debt line is the reason.
  • 737 rate: increase, but only with fps: hold. Its value is +2.30 in S1 and S3 and -0.74 in S2, S4 and S5, so the Business case passes only if the CEO expects S1 or S3. It also needs stable KPIs, an FAA-cleared rate path and a rationale that does not cite Airbus (H6). The +2.30 assumes neither new narrowbody is ever launched.
  • hold on any field. A hold is never vetoed.

Would veto.

  • fps: launch via Embraer. Against the same plan without fps it loses -14.55 / -13.75 / -14.56 / -13.75 / -15.19. In the risk case it scores -18.83 against Do Nothing's -3.64, $15.19B worse, so it fails Rating first. It runs $18.05-18.51B below the best Solo launch in every column (it must beat it by more than ε), and it also fails Downside and Business case. Acceptable alternatives: launch (7-year ramp-up), launch (10-year ramp-up), hold.
  • 787 Re-engine: launch, with any fps value. It fails Downside in S3 and S4 (an A350 Re-engine): -2.48 alone, -3.58 with the 10-year ramp, -4.51 with the 7-year. With the 7-year ramp it also overlaps fps development by 5 years against our 2-year cap. Acceptable alternative: hold.
  • 737 rate: increase alongside any fps launch. Its value is -0.74 or -0.75 in every column whichever ramp is chosen, so it fails the Business case test (it must be above zero in the expected column). We would also veto it under any live quality, FAA or supply problem, or with a rationale that cites Airbus (H6). Acceptable alternative: hold.
  • Any fps launch without the CEO's Round-1 ruling on H1 and evidence that the 777X and MAX 7/10 are finished and debt repair is on track (Boeing ready). Also any fps launch that fails Malave's buffer or Pope's readiness, with its veto check unresolved. Acceptable alternatives: the same launch with the ruling, or hold.
  • A plan whose total doctrine plus objective premium exceeds $2B or goes unlogged (H8). We would veto the item whose reversion to its default cures the excess.

Recommendations.

  • Rule on H1 and H3 in writing. Both were written for a round sealed in 2026, and this round is 2030. The record we expect cited: the 777X was reset to first delivery in 2027, MAX 7/10 certification was expected in 2026, and the 777X was due to turn cash-positive in 2029. The CEO said in July 2026 that Boeing needed about two more years to be financially ready. The brief's tracker has net debt at $0 by 2029, and at $0 in the 2030 stress case. If the conditions are met, say so and lift H1. Without that ruling, a launch fails our Boeing-ready test.
  • Bring one well-founded Solo fps launch, not a bet. Either ramp passes all our tests. They differ by more than ε in S1 and S3 (10-year ahead by $1.30B), so our rule prefers the ramp with the higher worst column: the 7-year (-1.50 against -1.96 in S4). It also enters service in 2037, the same year as an NGSA launched now. By our reading of the public rules, Boeing then stays at or above 40% of the narrowbody market. The 10-year would leave Boeing near 37% around 2040 if Airbus launches now. If the ExCo prefers the 10-year to keep the stress-case debt line (the 7-year peaks at $0.7B of net debt), we will approve it. Log the $0.46B it gives up in S2 and S4 as objective premium.
  • No 787 Re-engine this round. It loses $2.48B to $4.51B whenever Airbus re-engines the A350 (S3, S4), beyond our $1B limit. With the 7-year fps it also overlaps development by 5 years. Test it again in the 2035 round, when Airbus's A350 choice is public. A 7-year fps (development 2030-2037) leaves room for a Re-engine launched in 2035 with only a 2-year overlap. A 10-year fps (development 2033-2040) does not.
  • Treat the Rate Increase as a production call on its own merits. With any fps launch it loses $0.74B in every column; it pays only if neither new narrowbody is ever launched. Bring it only with fps: hold, stable KPIs, an FAA-cleared rate path and a reason that is not Airbus.
  • Choose fps engine code 7 (Rolls-Royce, P&W and CFM). CFM is always fitted, so supply is never left without an engine. The code can trigger P&W's and Rolls-Royce's conditional launches this round. GTF2 would be ready in 2036 and UltraFan NB in 2037, both by either EIS. That gives the brief's three sources on the fps in 2050, and three narrowbody engine makers, against one with Do Nothing. Code 7 is in none of the disallowed pairs, and the code does not change Boeing's payoff. We will ask our Aerospace Safety Committee to review each maker's readiness for EIS.
  • Show the debt path for the chosen plan, base and stress case, from the brief's objective-metrics table. Keep shareholder returns off and seek no new equity until the rating is solidly investment grade. The Board reserves those decisions.
  • In the public statement, give a conservative EIS with headroom if fps launches, and no date otherwise. Log every premium. Bring the launch to the Aerospace Safety Committee with the Chief Engineer's readiness view before the full Board votes.

Kelly Ortberg frames the round

Question. Have the three work streams converged by 2030: the market, Boeing's readiness in finances and capacity, and the technology? If they have, I lift H1 and launch one Solo fps. That leaves three questions: which ramp (7-year or 10-year); whether the 787 Re-engine and the 737 Rate Increase stay out of this round; and which engine code gives us a stable supply of engines from more than one maker. The grid, Malave's slip leg (S5) and Pope's readiness results decide this. Airbus's calendar does not.

Situation. Decision year 2030. Nothing is launched; we are on the 737 MAX and the 787. Do Nothing scores +0.00 / -3.64 / -2.62 / -6.26 / -3.64. The columns are S1 rivals hold, S2 NGSA, S3 A350 Re-engine, S4 both, and S5 the risk case (NGSA plus covert Delay Tactics). The brief reports no live quality, FAA or supply-chain problem and no certification trouble, so the KPI gate and the FAA-process gate are open on this board. The gates behind H1 and H3: - 777X first delivery in 2027 [BX-0550], cash-positive from 2029 [BX-0547]; - MAX 7/10 certification expected in 2026 [BX-1873]. The brief is silent on it, so I treat it as done (inference); - the GM's tracker puts net debt at $0 at end-2029 in the base case and at end-2030 in the stress case, with no new programme; - in July 2026 I said we needed about two more years to be financially ready, and reporting expected a launch around 2029-2030 [BG-0068]. What the grid shows: - Either Solo fps beats Do Nothing by more than ε in every column: 10-year +3.50 / +4.30 / +3.50 / +4.30 / +2.86; 7-year +2.20 / +4.76 / +2.20 / +4.76 / +2.81. - The 10-year leads the 7-year by 1.30 in S1 and S3, trails it by 0.46 in S2 and S4, and is 0.05 ahead in S5. It is never behind by more than ε. - Via Embraer runs $18.05-18.06B below the 10-year in every column. - The 787 Re-engine adds +2.20 to the 10-year in S1, S2 and S5 but -3.58 in S3 and S4. On the 7-year it adds +1.27 or -4.51, with a 5-year overlap. - The Rate Increase costs 0.74 in every column beside any fps. Alone it is +2.30 only in S1 and S3, and only if neither new narrowbody is ever launched. Objective status: - 50% narrowbody share in 2040 is out of reach for every plan. - The 10-year keeps every debt line, the stress case included (peak $0.0B). By my reading of the public rules it leaves us near 37% in 2040 if NGSA launches now. - The 7-year holds 40% or more against NGSA but misses the stress-case debt line (peak $0.7B). - In S5 both ramps dip below 40% around 2040. - Engine table: every code gives CFM only until P&W or Rolls-Royce launch. Code 7 can trigger both: 3 sources in 2050. Board risks (its would-veto list; guidance, not red lines): - fps via Embraer; - any 787 Re-engine launch this round; - a Rate Increase beside any fps, or one that loses value, meets a live problem or answers Airbus; - any fps without my H1 ruling, Malave's buffer and fundability results and Pope's readiness results; - any premium above $2B, or any premium not logged.

Options to test.

  • A. Do Nothing (fps hold, rate hold, 787 Re-engine hold): +0.00 / -3.64 / -2.62 / -6.26 / -3.64. This is the baseline for every test; its S5 of -3.64 sets Malave's floor at -5.64. Objectives: every debt line met; incumbency lost if NGSA comes (Airbus gains 3 pp a year from 2037); 1 engine source.
  • B. fps launch (10-year ramp-up) Solo, code 7, rate hold, 787 Re-engine hold: +3.50 / +0.66 / +0.88 / -1.96 / -0.78. Against Do Nothing: +3.50 / +4.30 / +3.50 / +4.30 / +2.86. S5 is 4.86 above the floor; worst column -1.96 (S4); no development overlap. Objective cell: 2029 / yes / yes ($0.0B) / 1 (3). My lean.
  • C. fps launch (7-year ramp-up) Solo, code 7, rate hold, 787 Re-engine hold: +2.20 / +1.12 / -0.42 / -1.50 / -0.83. Against Do Nothing: +2.20 / +4.76 / +2.20 / +4.76 / +2.81. S5 is 4.81 above the floor; worst column -1.50 (S4). Objective cell: 2029 / yes / no ($0.7B) / 1 (3). Against B: -1.30 / +0.46 / -1.30 / +0.46 / -0.05. It holds incumbency against NGSA (same EIS, 2037), and it keeps a 2035 Re-engine H4-legal (2-year overlap); the 10-year does not.
  • D. fps launch (10-year ramp-up) plus 787 Re-engine launch: overlap 2033-35, 2 years, H4-legal; strain $1.2B undiscounted. Grid: +5.70 / +2.86 / -2.70 / -5.54 / +1.42. The Re-engine adds +2.20 / +2.20 / -3.58 / -3.58 / +2.20. Objective cell: 2029 / yes / yes ($0.0B) / 1 (3). It is a bet on Airbus's A350 choice, which we cannot see. The Board would veto it: below -$1B in S3 and S4.
  • E. fps hold plus 737 rate increase: +2.30 / -4.38 / -0.32 / -7.00 / -4.38. B beats it in every column (B minus E: +1.20 / +5.04 / +1.20 / +5.04 / +3.60), and its +2.30 assumes neither narrowbody is ever launched. Test only to close it.
  • F. Rate Increase beside a launch. 10-year plus rate: +2.76 / -0.08 / +0.14 / -2.70 / -1.52. 7-year plus rate: +1.46 / +0.38 / -1.17 / -2.25 / -1.57. The rate adds -0.74 or -0.75 in every column, so it fails its business case. It would cure the 7-year's stress-case debt line (peak $0.4B, yes), but at a 0.74 cost. Test only to close it.
  • Struck before testing. 7-year plus 787 Re-engine: 5-year overlap breaks H4; +3.47 / +2.39 / -4.93 / -6.01 / +0.45. Any fps via Embraer: -14.55 / -17.39 / -17.18 / -20.01 / -18.83; S5 is $13.19B below Malave's floor and it trails the 10-year by $18.05B everywhere. Hold plus 787 Re-engine alone: +3.30 / -0.34 / -5.10 / -8.74 / -0.34, below B in S2-S5.

Red lines.

  • H1 (no fps in Round 1). My ruling: lifted for 2030. Its 2026 grounds have closed: the 777X delivers from 2027 [BX-0550] and is cash-positive from 2029 [BX-0547]; MAX 7/10 certification was expected in 2026 [BX-1873]; net debt is at $0 in 2029 (base) and 2030 (stress) on the GM's tracker; in July 2026 I said about two more years [BG-0068]; and the three work streams have converged [BX-1296, B-2303, B-2326]. The lift is conditional: if Malave's buffer or fundability test fails, or Pope's readiness check fails, H1 stands and we hold.
  • H3, first half (no 787 Re-engine in Round 1). My ruling: its ground was that the 777X comes first [B-2276], and that ground has closed, so it no longer binds as a hard rule in 2030. The Re-engine is still governed by H3's second half, by H4 and by my one-development-at-a-time rule [BX-1239].
  • H2 cannot bind (the earliest fps EIS is 2037). H7 has no trigger on this board.
  • H4: at most 2 years of overlap between a Solo fps and the 787 Re-engine. This strikes the 7-year plus Re-engine (5 years).
  • H5: never cancel a launched fps or 787 Re-engine. Re-baseline once instead [BX-1251, BX-1321].
  • H6: no Rate Increase under a live quality, FAA or supply-chain problem, and never as a reply to Airbus [BX-1259, BX-1322].
  • H8: ties within ε ($1B) go to doctrine. Doctrine plus objective premium may total at most $2B, and every premium is logged.
  • Team rule: Malave vetoes any plan whose S5 falls more than $2B below Do Nothing's -3.64 (floor -5.64).
  • My own: no production-certification concurrency [BX-1263]; no new airplane before debt repair and finished developments, which I rule met in 2030 [BX-1247, B-2326]; no fixed-price development, only cost-plus or risk-share terms [BX-1262, BX-1304]; no blame on the FAA [BX-1323]; no attribution of a supplier problem to Airbus before exposure (doctrine).

Initial lean. My lean: launch one Solo fps on the 10-year ramp with fps engine code 7. 737 rate hold. 787 Re-engine hold. Expected column: Airbus launches NGSA this round. I take S4 under the doctrine fallback (profile §7 expects an early A350 Re-engine attempt), with S2 close behind; S5 is the risk case. 1. Launch. I lift H1 on the evidence above. Market, money and technology converge in 2030, and the grid agrees: the 10-year beats Do Nothing by $2.86-4.30B in every column, well past ε, and sits $4.86B above Malave's floor. "We will do a new airplane when the market and the technology and we're ready" [BX-1296]. I think we are. 2. Ramp. In S4 the 7-year is the best grid plan by 0.46. That is within ε, so it is a tie, and doctrine breaks it: - doing less, better, with headroom, and right rather than fast [BX-1239, BX-1241, BX-1275]; - a smaller bill and a smaller debt penalty; - every debt line kept, the stress case included. The 7-year's edge in S2 and S4 comes only from matching NGSA's 2037 EIS, and Airbus does not set our date [B-2313]. Premium: 0.46 in S2 and S4, logged as doctrine plus objective (the debt line), well inside the $2B cap. The cost on the mission side is incumbency near 37% in 2040 if NGSA launches now. I will weigh that against the 7-year's $0.7B stress-case miss once I have both memos. 3. No 787 Re-engine. It wins 2.20 or loses 3.58 on an A350 choice we cannot see. In S4 it is a loss, so holding it costs no premium. One development at a time. 4. No Rate Increase. It loses 0.74 in every column beside a launch. I accept the loss of the only round it is offered. 5. Code 7. It keeps CFM fitted, invites P&W and Rolls-Royce, and costs nothing on the board. It aims at three engine sources and three narrowbody engine makers. Other moves. Private: fund supplier readiness. Public: say we welcome proposals from all three engine makers, with CFM as the baseline. Public statement. Calm, about execution. A conservative EIS with headroom, and no blame for anyone. What would change my lean: a failed buffer or fundability test, a readiness gap in Pope's results, or evidence that only the 7-year keeps us whole.

Kelly, I ran the slip leg as the baseline, not a sensitivity. Do Nothing's risk case is -3.64, so the floor is -5.64. Every Solo row clears it: the 10-year at -0.78, the 7-year at -0.83, the 10-year with the Re-engine at +1.42, the rate rows at -1.52 and -1.57. Every via-Embraer row fails, $11.83-13.94B below the floor. That veto binds. The 777X turned cash-positive in 2029 and net debt reaches zero in 2029, 2030 under stress. A 2030 launch is fundable. The 10-year is the higher-confidence plan from a schedule and cost perspective: the 7-year with three years of buffer built in, for a $4.68B smaller bill and $2.9B less undiscounted penalty. Its peak cash year, about $8.4B in 2036, leaves roughly $2.5B of headroom with free cash flow one-third below consensus, and it keeps every debt line. The 7-year peaks near $12.5B in 2034, borrows $0.7B under stress and is still above zero at the 2035 hold year. Its 0.46 lead in S4 sits inside epsilon; I log that $0.46B as premium, well inside the $2B cap. Hold the Re-engine: it clears my buffer but loses 3.58 if Airbus re-engines the A350. Hold the rate: it loses 0.74 in every column beside a launch. This baseline lets us not only meet it but potentially beat it, barring free cash flow more than half below consensus in the peak years. Fully restoring the health of our balance sheet stays first.

Three results, ranked. My record is Global Services, not Commercial Airplanes, so the KPI, strain and supplier results run on Boeing's operations doctrine, and I say so. First and foremost, on-time predictable delivery. I can stand behind 2040. Our clean-sheet record runs about three years late: the 787-8 went from May 2008 to September 2011. The 10-year date is the 7-year's central slip case, so it carries that headroom without building while we certify. It also gives GTF2 four years and UltraFan NB three years of maturity before entry into service; on the 7-year, UltraFan is ready in the EIS year itself. Second, readiness. The brief reports no live quality, FAA or supply-chain problem, so my KPI veto does not bind. The fps alone carries zero strain and is our one major development. We fund fragile suppliers and keep them hot. Third, IP. The airframe is ours: Solo. Embraer adds nothing we lack, only $39.68B more bill and $18.05-18.06B less value in every column. And finally, disciplined profitable growth. Every $1B booked at 2040 costs about $0.25B of PV. The 10-year's peak year draws about $8.4B, about $6.7B after the tracker's 79% factor, against $13.8B of free cash flow, and the stress-case debt line holds at $0.0B. The Rate Increase loses $0.74B in every column beside the fps: hold. The 787 Re-engine is a bet on Airbus's A350 choice: hold. My orders: fps launch (10-year ramp-up), engine code 7, 737 rate hold, 787 Re-engine hold.

Kelly Ortberg decides

Orders. Launch fps, 10-year ramp-up (engines requested: RR, P&W and CFM)

Rationale. DECISION: fps launch (10-year ramp-up) with fps engine code 7; 737 rate hold; 787 Re-engine hold. This is the plan I framed (plan B), and both test memos recommend it. 1. MY RULINGS ON H1 AND H3 FOR 2030, IN WRITING, WITH EVIDENCE. - H1 (no fps in Round 1) is LIFTED for 2030. Its 2026 grounds were the unfinished 777X and MAX 7/10 and an unrepaired balance sheet [B-2326, BX-1305], and all of them have closed: - the 777X was reset to first delivery in 2027 [BX-0550] and turns cash-positive from 2029 [BX-0547]; - MAX 7/10 certification was expected in 2026 [BX-1873]. The brief reports no certification trouble, so I treat both as done (inference); - debt repair is complete on the GM's tracker: net debt reaches $0 at end-2029 (base) and end-2030 (stress), with no new programme; - in July 2026 I said we needed about two more years to be financially ready, with a launch expected around 2029-2030 [BG-0068]; - the three work streams have converged [B-2303, BX-1296]. Market: the narrowbody demand is there, and Do Nothing loses $3.64-6.26B if Airbus moves. Boeing: finances repaired, and Pope confirms engineering can carry one clean-sheet development. Technology: GTF2 and UltraFan NB, if launched on selection, are ready in 2036 and 2037, and CFM is always ready. - The lift is conditional, and every condition has passed: Malave's buffer and fundability tests and Pope's readiness results. - H3, first half (no 787 Re-engine in Round 1) no longer binds as a hard rule. Its ground was "the 777X comes first" [B-2276], and that has closed. I still HOLD the Re-engine on four grounds: - the Board's -$1B Downside limit: it adds -3.58 in S3 and S4; - my one-development-at-a-time rule [BX-1239]; - company doctrine (profile §11.4: keep the 787 a cash source, no Re-engine before 2036); - the premium: holding it costs $0 in my expected column. H3's second half, H4, H5, H6 and H8 apply as written. H2 cannot bind (earliest EIS 2037). H7 has no trigger: the brief reports no certification trouble. 2. THE TEAM RULE. - Malave's buffer test (slip leg = S5, the brief's Risk case; floor = Do Nothing's -3.64 less $2B = -5.64): - plan B passes at -0.78, $4.86B above the floor; - every via-Embraer row fails ($11.83-13.94B below the floor). Weighing the CFO. Both seats are thin, and I weighed them that way. Malave's record is one call (Low), so I treated his buffer test as binding and the rest of his memo as advice. And the 2035 Re-engine option that only the 7-year keeps open is unpriced on this grid. I name both in the rationale.

Weighing the operating head. Pope's seat runs on Boeing's operations doctrine; she has no airplane-business evidence (Very low), so I weighed her memo as doctrine-backed advice. Her KPI veto does not bind: the brief reports no live problem. Her results gave the Board what it asked for: - one clean-sheet development is within engineering capacity, with zero strain on the fps alone; - the supply base is ready, on the condition that we fund fragile suppliers (engines first) and keep them hot; - Solo over via Embraer on IP: Embraer brings no capital or capacity we lack; - code 7 is manageable on the 10-year, with GTF2 and UltraFan NB maturing 4 and 3 years before EIS and CFM certifying first. The 7-year has zero headroom, and UltraFan NB would be ready only in its EIS year. Her 'fail' on the 7-year ramp is advice, not a veto, and I treat it so. She flags the 2040 engine-source count as at risk on a 2040 EIS. The GM's scoring decides that, and I note it.

The Board's recommendations at review.

  • Ramp. Our guidance preferred the 7-year ramp under our worst-column rule. The two ramps differ by $1.30B in S1 and S3, so they are not within ε, and the worst columns are -1.50 for the 7-year against -1.96 for the 10-year. Your board_response answers this. You chose the 10-year to keep the stress-case debt line and to carry three years of headroom without production-certification concurrency, and you logged $0.46B as premium. We accept that answer. Hold the 2040 date. If the plan has to move, reset it once and conservatively; never slip it in stages, and never cancel (H5).
  • Before the first development stage gate, bring the Aerospace Safety Committee written confirmation that MAX 7/10 certification is complete. Your H1 ruling treats it as done only because the brief is silent. Bring the Chief Engineer's readiness view and the no-concurrency certification plan agreed with the FAA at the same time.
  • Engine code 7. On today's record the brief gives CFM alone at a 2040 EIS. Three sources depend on P&W and Rolls-Royce launching on selection this round. Report what they did in the next round. Our Aerospace Safety Committee, which brings propulsion expertise, will review each maker's readiness and durability against EIS. If a maker is not ready, change the code before EIS rather than wait on it. Also tell us whether a 2040 EIS counts as 'in production' for the 2040 engine-source year.
  • Debt stays first. Report the base and stress net-debt path for the launched plan every round, including Malave's stress headroom of about $2.5B in the 2036 peak year. Seek no new equity, and bring no dividend or buyback to the Board, until the rating is solidly investment grade. Those decisions are reserved to us.
  • The 787 Re-engine. On a 10-year fps, a Re-engine launched in 2035 would overlap the development by 5 years and fail our one-development test. In the 2035 round, with Airbus's A350 choice public, bring the widebody case as a review only, not a launch. Fund and report the supplier-readiness move, engines first, and the supplier-shortages KPI at each stage gate. The Rate Increase lapses after this round, and we accept that.

The other orders cost nothing in S4: - 787 Re-engine hold: $0 (the Re-engine adds -3.58 there); - 737 rate hold: $0 (-0.74); - engine code 7: $0 (codes do not change the payoff). Other moves.

  • Engine competition with CFM as the baseline (public): We invite CFM, Pratt & Whitney and Rolls-Royce to propose engines for the new airplane under code 7. CFM is the baseline launch engine and certifies first. A P&W or Rolls-Royce engine follows in sequence once it shows maturity and durability [BX-1298]. CFM must be able to support both our rates and our competitor's [BX-1264, BX-1325]. Goal: two or three engine sources on our narrowbody and three narrowbody engine makers in the market.
  • Certification plan with the FAA from day one, and no production-certification concurrency (public): We agree a transparent certification plan with the FAA before detailed design freezes. We build no production airplanes ahead of a mature, certifiable design [BX-1263, BX-1309]. We blame no one: we own the schedule [BX-1323].
  • No fixed-price development (public): Development contracts with suppliers and partners are cost-plus or risk-share, never fixed-price [BX-1262, BX-1304].
  • Supplier readiness: keep fragile suppliers funded and hot (private): We fund lagging suppliers and keep them running above our rate, and we hold buffers [BX-1243, B-2330, B-2043]. Priorities: (1) engines, since LEAP-1B is the 737's sole source and engines have bound the line before [B-1449]; (2) any supplier flagged on the supplier-shortages KPI [B-2283]. The ladder: embed staff, buffer, requalify, fund, acquire. With Spirit in-house since December 2025 [BG-0064], we control the 737 fuselage.
  • Balance sheet first in capital allocation (public): Debt repair stays first [BX-1305, BX-0556]. I recommend to the Board no shareholder returns and no new equity until we are solidly investment grade; the Board reserves both decisions. The $10B of undrawn revolvers stays undrawn.
  • Stage-gated governance of the launch (private): Before the full Board votes, the Aerospace Safety Committee reviews the launch with the Chief Engineer's readiness view. After launch, each development stage gate is KPI-based, with no subjectivity [BX-1259]. If the plan has to move, we reset it once, conservatively, never in serial slips [BX-1318, BX-1321]. No launched programme is ever cancelled (H5).
  • Workforce: retain, train before we build, hire in stages (private): One enterprise retention incentive [BX-1314]. We train before we build [BX-1258]. Engineering hiring is staged toward a peak around 2038-39, since the risk case prices talent poaching and supply-chain bottlenecks at 5 pp for 5 years from EIS.
  • 737 MAX and 787 customer commitment (public): Production stability on the 737 MAX and 787 lines comes first, gated by KPIs. The new airplane is built for commonality with the 737 fleet so that our customers' transition is planned, not forced [BX-1273, BX-1274].

Board guidance before the ExCo met

Priorities.

  • Safety and the five pillars first. Nothing covert this round, and no item that the operating head fails on safety, quality or the A320 ramp. The Board accepts no override of those tests [AG-0038, A-0331, AX-0015, A-0303].
  • Launch NGSA on its own clock. 2030 is the last year of the 2028-2030 window, and a launch now gives EIS 2037, inside the technology clock (not before 2035). This is the one clean sheet of the decade [AG-0063, A-0409, A-0225, AG-0039].
  • Protect liquidity, net cash and the A+/A1 rating. NGSA alone costs about $5.07B a year against the $5.2B line. Nothing may run alongside it while it is in development, so the payout and the buyback stay fundable [AX-0022, A-0402, AG-0062, AX-0104, AG-0058, AG-0059].
  • A stable engine supply. The NGSA engine code should keep CFM and name both P&W and Rolls-Royce (code 7). This round is the only one in which their new engines can still be launched in time for a 2037 EIS [A-0243, A-0360, A-0218, AX-0054].
  • Discipline towards Boeing. Read Boeing only from the bulletin, which so far records no launch. Do not accelerate, delay or cancel in reaction to Boeing. In public, give windows, not dates [AX-0004, A-0364, AG-0055].

Expects to see. One agreed ExCo package containing: (1) The grid row of the submitted orders and the row with each Board item at its default. For NGSA launch, A350 hold and Delay Tactics none, that means the row NGSA + A350: hold (+45.82 / +23.37 / +17.28 / +23.37 / +44.96 / +22.51 across S1-S6) set against the row hold + hold (0.00 / -3.30 / -4.99 / -3.30 / -0.86 / -4.16). The NGSA item value is +45.82 / +26.67 / +22.27 / +26.67 / +45.82 / +26.67. (2) The CEO's expected Boeing scenario, named, and the worst plausible column. On the Board's reading that is S3, the fps 7-yr: launched in 2030, it enters service in 2037, the same year as NGSA. All six columns count as plausible because the bulletin rules none out. (3) The CFO's peak-cash arithmetic: $35.52B / 7 = about $5.07B a year in 2030-2036 against the $5.2B line, with no overlapping programme. It should confirm that net cash, the 30-50% payout and the EUR 5bn buyback remain fundable without an equity raise or a dividend cut. (4) The operating head's results on safety, quality and the ramp, including the A320 rate and A350F absorption, and any five-pillars flag. (5) The engine code, the sources it gives at a 2037 EIS, and the enabler metric for 2050: 1 source / 1 maker if P&W and Rolls-Royce hold, 3 / 3 if both launch when selected. (6) Any soft veto, how it was resolved, and any override with its margin, recorded as a Board item. (7) A public statement that gives windows rather than dates, puts safety first and says nothing of Delay Tactics. (8) Delay Tactics recorded as none, with the team's stricter condition left standing. If a piece is missing, the Board will compute it from the brief and say so.

Would approve.

  • NGSA: launch this round (EIS 2037), a Qualified Majority item. Its item value against NGSA hold is +45.82 / +26.67 / +22.27 / +26.67 / +45.82 / +26.67 (S1-S6): it gains in every column, so it passes Downside. Peak cash is about $5.07B a year against $5.2B, so it passes Liquidity narrowly. EIS 2037 is not before 2035, so it passes the Technology clock. With A350 hold and Delay Tactics none, the full row is +45.82 / +23.37 / +17.28 / +23.37 / +44.96 / +22.51, and the worst column, S3, is +17.28.
  • NGSA engine code rides with the launch. Code 7 (CFM, P&W and Rolls-Royce) is preferred; 6 or 5 is acceptable. The Board never vetoes a code.
  • A350 Re-engine: hold is not a Board item and is the Board's preferred value this round.
  • Delay Tactics: none is not a Board item and is the only value the Board would accept this round.

Would veto.

  • A350 Re-engine: launch alongside an NGSA launch. Its item value is +1.75 / +1.74 / +1.75 / +1.74 / -2.15 / -2.15. The $2.15B loss in S5 and S6 exceeds the $2B Downside limit. Peak cash would be $5.07B + $1.00B + $0.60B strain = $6.67B a year against the $5.2B line (Liquidity). The two programmes would overlap for 5 years (One clean sheet). Grounds: balance sheet, two fronts and downside; under the plan-level failure rule the added item is vetoed, never NGSA. An override cannot pass: on a Qualified Majority item it trails hold by $2.15B in S5 and S6, and Liquidity is the Board's own test. Acceptable alternative: hold.
  • A350 Re-engine: launch with NGSA held. It passes the Board's own liquidity and downside tests (+3.26 / +3.25 / +3.25 / +3.25 / -0.64 / -0.64), but the operating head's turn-1 test says no A350 Re-engine. If he fails it, an override cannot clear the Override review, because it trails hold by $0.64B in S5 and S6 on a Qualified Majority item. Acceptable alternative: hold.
  • Delay Tactics: bottleneck or both, in any round. Ground: integrity and abnormal risk. Acceptable alternative: none.
  • Delay Tactics: poaching this round. Boeing's fps launch is not on the public record, so the integrity conditions fail. Its item value is -15.74 in S1 and S5, because the tactics would be 'naked' and draw the $48.32B fine; that fails Downside. Acceptable alternative: none.
  • Any override of the operating head's safety, quality or ramp tests, or of a five-pillars flag.
  • Never vetoed: a hold or none, an NGSA engine code on its own, or any item merely for its near-term earnings cost.

Recommendations.

  • Launch NGSA this round. 2030 is the last year of the 2028-2030 window. Holding gives up $22.27B to $45.82B in every column and pushes EIS past 2037. The Board cannot launch it; it urges the ExCo to use the window.
  • Select engine code 7 (CFM, P&W and Rolls-Royce). This round is the only one that can trigger P&W's GTF2 (ready 2036) and Rolls-Royce's UltraFan NB (ready 2037) in time for a 2037 EIS. Otherwise NGSA flies CFM alone and the enabler falls to 1 source / 1 maker in 2050, against 2 / 2 today. If both launch it reaches 3 / 3. Code 7 is in no barred pair with any fps code, so Boeing's choice cannot force a change, and it keeps CFM as the anchor. Code 6 is the fallback. Avoid codes 1, 2 and 4: they drop CFM. If P&W and Rolls-Royce form a Joint Venture this round, code 7 still fits its engine (ready 2036), which counts as one source. In 2035, change the code only to remove a maker that did not launch.
  • The CFO should show peak cash year by year: NGSA about $5.07B a year in 2030-2036 against $5.2B, with no overlapping programme. Net cash and the A+/A1 rating must hold, and the 30-50% payout and the EUR 5bn buyback must stay fundable with no equity raise. The 2026 analyst models carry no A320 successor and assume rising returns, so the launch should be presented as sitting inside the stated payout range.
  • One programme at a time. Keep the A350 Re-engine on hold until NGSA development spend ends in 2037. On these bills, a 2035 launch would still overlap NGSA in 2035-2036 at about $6.67B a year, so 2045 is the first round that passes Liquidity unless the brief's bills change. There should be no A350 Re-engine at all once Boeing has launched a 787 Re-engine (company hard rule 3).
  • Keep Delay Tactics off and record that the team's stricter condition stands. Bottleneck is never acceptable. Poaching can come to the Board only after Boeing's fps launch is on the public record and every condition holds.
  • Show the worst plausible Boeing response. That is S3, an fps 7-yr entering service in the same year as NGSA, where NGSA alone still returns +17.28. Show S5 and S6, a 787 Re-engine, for the widebody. Do not accelerate, delay or cancel NGSA in reaction to any Boeing move; a cancellation needs a failed case in every column.
  • The operating head should confirm that NGSA development does not draw engineers or suppliers away from the A320 rate or the A350F, and report his safety and quality results to the Board.
  • Public statement: windows, not dates (EIS in the second half of the 2030s); safety first; a disciplined and controlled ramp; and NGSA to be offered with more than one engine maker. Nothing on Delay Tactics. Any public invitation to engine makers to share risk is for other_moves; it is unpriced and a recommendation only.

Guillaume Faury frames the round

Question. 2030 is the last year of our 2028-2030 window. Do we launch NGSA now on its own technology clock (EIS 2037, "around 2037"), and with which engine code? We would hold the A350 Re-engine and keep Delay Tactics off. Can we take that one programme to the Board as a clean Qualified Majority item that passes the five pillars, the cash test and the production test?

Situation. BOEING AND THE PUBLIC RECORD. The bulletin shows no programme launched by anyone. Boeing stays on the 737 MAX and 787 (LEAP-1B; GEnx/Trent), with no fps, no 787 Re-engine and no Rate Increase on the record. The engine makers have launched nothing: no GTF2, no UltraFan NB, no P&W-Rolls-Royce Joint Venture. The brief reports no supply, quality or technology problem this round. OUR POSITION. NB share is 60.0% and WB 41.2%, flat from 2026 to 2029. ΔPV is +0.00 if nobody moves (EV $150B, WACC 8%). Doing nothing is not neutral: hold + hold loses in five of six columns (0.00 / -3.30 / -4.99 / -3.30 / -0.86 / -4.16). OBJECTIVE STATUS (scored by the GM, never in the payoff). Defend 60/40 is met (60.0% in 2040, 2045 and 2050). Protect the A320 family is met. Dual NB engine sources are met (A320neo: CFM + P&W GTF). Three NB engine makers is not met (CFM and P&W only). THE ENABLER TRAP. If we launch NGSA and P&W and Rolls-Royce hold, NGSA flies CFM alone and the enabler falls to 1 source / 1 maker in 2050, against 2 / 2 today. With code 7, and both P&W and Rolls-Royce launching when selected, it reaches 3 / 3. This is the only round in which that can happen: GTF2 (6 years, ready 2036) and UltraFan NB (7 years, ready 2037, no margin) can only be ready for a 2037 EIS if triggered now. On this board an unready maker is dropped, not waited for, so the code carries no EIS risk and no payoff effect. THE BOARD'S GUIDANCE. Launch NGSA on its clock. Code 7 is preferred, with 6 or 5 acceptable. Nothing concurrent, nothing covert. Windows, not dates. Every Board item must gain in my expected column and lose no more than $2B in any column; all six columns count as plausible this round. MY READ OF BOEING (bulletin and profile section 7 only). Central case S1: rivals hold. Boeing has said a new aircraft comes "not before 2035" and is still repairing its balance sheet. S2 and S4 (fps 10-yr or via Embraer, EIS 2040) are close behind. Worst plausible is S3: an fps 7-yr entering service in 2037, the same year as NGSA. The decision below does not depend on which column comes true. REAL-WORLD CONTEXT (2026 analyst models; the board's numbers govern). Neither bank models an A320 successor. 2030E FCF is €10.7-11.6bn and net cash €31.8-33.1bn, so in reality money is not the binding limit. The market is pricing a rising payout, though, and the launch must be presented inside it.

Options to test.

  • 1. COMPANY DEFAULT AND MY LEAN: ngsa launch + A350 Re-engine hold + Delay Tactics none. Row: +45.82 / +23.37 / +17.28 / +23.37 / +44.96 / +22.51 (S1-S6); worst column S3 +17.28; mean about +29.6. NGSA item value against hold + hold: +45.82 / +26.67 / +22.27 / +26.67 / +45.82 / +26.67. It gains in every column, so it passes the Board's Downside test.
  • 2. REFERENCE ROW, every Board item at its default: hold + hold. Row: 0.00 / -3.30 / -4.99 / -3.30 / -0.86 / -4.16. It misses the last launch year, pushes NGSA past 2037 and breaks the window in rule 1.
  • 3. TEST TO REJECT: ngsa launch + A350 Re-engine launch. Row: +47.57 / +25.11 / +19.03 / +25.11 / +42.81 / +20.36. The added A350 item is +1.75 / +1.74 / +1.75 / +1.74 / -2.15 / -2.15. It is the best grid plan in S1, $1.75B above the default. It breaks rule 6: two new launches in one round, and a 5-year overlap that the $1B exception cannot clear in S5 and S6. Peak cash is about $6.67B a year against $5.2B. It fails my not-in-round-1 test and the Board's $2B Downside limit. Red lines are not traded for PV, so the $1.75B is recorded, not paid for.
  • 4. TEST TO REJECT: ngsa hold + A350 Re-engine launch. Row: +3.26 / -0.05 / -1.74 / -0.05 / -1.50 / -4.80. It gives up $20-44B against option 1, misses the NGSA window and is Wagner's turn-1 no.
  • 5. TEST TO REJECT: any Delay Tactics. One move added to option 1 is -15.74 / +1.57 / +2.05 / +1.57 / -15.74 / +1.57; both moves are -16.25 / +1.02 / +1.41 / +1.02 / -16.26 / +1.02. The fps is not on the public record, so the tactics would be naked and draw the $48.32B fine. This breaks rule 4. The team's stricter condition (the move must change who enters service first) stands, and the Board vetoes it.
  • 6. ENGINE CODE, on option 1. Code 7 (CFM, P&W, Rolls-Royce) is my lean: it is the only code that can reach 3 sources / 3 makers, keeps CFM as anchor and is in no barred pair. Code 6 (P&W + CFM) is the fallback, at most 2 / 2. Code 5 (Rolls-Royce + CFM) is acceptable, at most 2 / 2. Code 3 (CFM only) gives 1 / 1 for certain and triggers no one. Avoid 1, 2 and 4: they drop CFM as a named source and risk a single non-CFM source.

Red lines.

  • Five pillars (safety, quality, integrity, compliance, security). Nothing covert this round. No order or statement that fails them. They are never overridden [AX-0073, AX-0081].
  • Rule 1, NGSA clock: EIS never before the 2035 technology-ready year, and the launch window is 2028-2030. A launch now gives 2037. Holding moves EIS past 2037 [AX-0020, A-0409, A-0225, AX-0006].
  • Rules 2 and 7, our own clock: no Boeing move accelerates, delays or cancels NGSA, now or later.
  • Rule 6: at most one new launch this round. An NGSA / A350 Re-engine overlap of more than 2 years only with at least $1B on the grid. With the peak-cash line of about $5.2B a year (Toepfer's test), nothing runs alongside NGSA in development [AX-0022, A-0343, A-0401].
  • Rule 3: no A350 Re-engine once Boeing has launched a 787 Re-engine. Not binding yet; carried forward.
  • Rules 4 and 5, plus the team's stricter condition: at most one Delay Tactics move per game, only after fps is public and before its EIS. Poaching only while a programme is in development. The move must change who enters service first. None of these conditions holds this round, so Delay Tactics is off, and it never appears in public.
  • Board would-veto list, carried in full: (a) A350 Re-engine launch alongside NGSA: -2.15 in S5 and S6, $6.67B peak cash, 5-year overlap. (b) A350 Re-engine launch with NGSA held. (c) bottleneck or both, in any round. (d) poaching this round: -15.74 in S1 and S5, the naked fine. (e) any override of Wagner's safety, quality, A320 ramp or supply-crunch results, or of a five-pillars flag.
  • Board downside test: each Board item must gain in my expected column (S1) and lose no more than $2B in any column. All six are plausible in round 1.
  • Override budget: at most one per game, only with at least $1B over the best passing option, recorded as a Board item, and never against the pillars or a red line. None is foreseen this round.
  • Disclosure: windows, not dates (EIS in the second half of the 2030s). Never internal long-term-plan targets. Never Delay Tactics [AX-0004, AX-0005, AX-0020].

Initial lean. ORDERS. NGSA: launch, EIS 2037, inside the technology clock and at the close of our 2028-2030 window. NGSA engine code: 7 (CFM, P&W and Rolls-Royce), subject to Lars's supply and integration read, with 6 as the fallback. A350 Re-engine: hold. Delay Tactics: none, with the team's stricter condition left standing. WHY. Five pillars first: nothing covert, and safety and quality lead the statement. Ramp: one programme only, with no new concurrency against the A320 rate or the A350F. Preparing the Airbus of the 30s: this is the one clean sheet of the decade, launched on technology gates, not on Boeing's calendar [AX-0073, AX-0020, A-0409]. The Board can take it: the NGSA item gains +22.27 to +45.82 in every column, and peak cash is about $5.07B against the $5.2B line. GRID. My expected scenario is S1 (rivals hold). The best grid plan there is NGSA + A350 Re-engine (+47.57), but it breaks rule 6 and the cash line, and the Board would veto it. The default, +45.82, is therefore the best surviving plan, not a premium choice. The $1.75B gap is recorded, not paid for. Worst plausible column: S3 at +17.28, positive, so the robustness test passes. The decision is the same in every column. I would not re-time NGSA for any Boeing move. ENGINE SUPPLY ENABLER. Launching takes our narrowbody from 2 / 2 today to 1 / 1 in 2050 if P&W and Rolls-Royce hold. Code 7 is the only route to 3 / 3, and only this round can trigger it. If a named maker has not launched by 2035, I would change the code then only to remove it. The enabler does not justify holding NGSA: that would cost $22-46B, far beyond any premium I am allowed. BOARD. One Board item, NGSA: launch, with the code riding along. No override is planned. PUBLIC LINE (draft register). Safety and quality first. A "disciplined and controlled" ramp. Preparing the Airbus of the 2030s, with entry into service in the second half of the decade and more than one engine maker invited. Zero-for-zero trade. No dates, no internal targets, nothing on Delay Tactics [AX-0081, AX-0010, AX-0004]. The lean stands unless Thomas or Lars reports a failed test or a five-pillars flag.
