Guillaume Faury decides

Orders. Launch NGSA (engines requested: RR, P&W and CFM)

Rationale. QUESTION. 2030 is the last year of the 2028-2030 launch window. Do we launch NGSA on its technology clock, alone, with an engine code that rebuilds our engine-supply base, as one clean Board item? STEP 1: DELETE RED LINES AND FIVE-PILLARS FAILURES. - All six Delay Tactics rows are deleted under rule 4. Boeing has not launched fps on the public record, so any move would be naked and draw the $48.32B fine. 'both' is a second move. bottleneck is an integrity flag. Toepfer and Wagner both fail them, and the Board would veto them. - NGSA + A350 Re-engine (+47.57 / +25.11 / +19.03 / +25.11 / +42.81 / +20.36) is deleted under rule 6. It is two new launches in one round with a 5-year overlap, and the $1B exception fails in S5 and S6 (-2.15). STEP 2: SURVIVORS AGAINST THE TWO TESTS. - NGSA hold + A350 hold (0.00 / -3.30 / -4.99 / -3.30 / -0.86 / -4.16) fails both. Toepfer's robustness test fails, Wagner's production-readiness test fails because the plan misses the window, and my NGSA clock test fails. - NGSA hold + A350 Re-engine (+3.26 / -0.05 / -1.74 / -0.05 / -1.50 / -4.80) also fails both: Toepfer's robustness test (worst column S6 at -4.80) and Wagner's A350F/Spirit-absorption and production-readiness tests. - NGSA launch + A350 hold + Delay Tactics none (+45.82 / +23.37 / +17.28 / +23.37 / +44.96 / +22.51) passes every test of both men. It is the only survivor, and it is also the company default. STEP 3: CHOICE. - Expected scenario: S1, rivals hold. In S1 the best grid plan is the deleted NGSA + A350 Re-engine row, $1.75B above the default. A red line is not traded for PV, so that gap is recorded, not paid for. The survivor is chosen. - No other survivor lies within $1B, so the tie-breaks do not apply. The plan already scores on all five of them: no early EIS, no concurrency, the last possible capex start inside the window, EIS 2037 holding within 2035-2037, and one Board item. - Robustness: the worst plausible column is S3 (fps 7-yr, EIS 2037, the same year as NGSA) at +17.28, positive. The decision is identical in every column. Nothing here is timed around Boeing. STEP 4: OVERRIDES. None. No soft veto stands against the chosen plan. The override budget (one per game) is untouched. ENGINE CODE: 7 (CFM, P&W, Rolls-Royce). This is Wagner's supply recommendation, taken as my agent file directs, and the Board's preferred code. - It keeps CFM as the anchor and appears in no barred pair, so Boeing's code choice cannot force a change. - It is the only code that can reach 3 sources / 3 makers in 2050. Without it, or if both makers hold, NGSA flies CFM alone (1 / 1). - Only this round can trigger GTF2 (ready 2036) and UltraFan NB (ready 2037) in time for entry into service. - On this board an unready maker is dropped, so the code carries no EIS risk and no payoff effect. - Unpriced load: three engine integrations and certifications. It is mitigated by certifying in sequence with CFM first and by reviewing the code in 2035, only to remove a maker that has not launched or is off track. BOARD-GATE LINE (one item: NGSA: launch, Qualified Majority; the engine code rides with it). - Five pillars: pass. Nothing is covert and no flag was raised by Toepfer (Internal Control) or by Wagner. - Toepfer's test: pass. Peak programme cash is $35.52B / 7 = $5.07B a year in 2030-2036 against $5.2B, with $0.13B headroom and no concurrent programme. Net cash and the A+/A1 rating hold with no new debt or equity. On the 2030 run-rate the payout stays inside 30-50%. On the board's books the $35.52B lands at EIS in 2037, and that charge is reported beside the cash view. - Wagner's test: pass. Safety and quality pass, the A320 ramp shield passes, A350F absorption is untouched, and overlap and strain are both zero. - Grid ΔPV: the item against hold is +45.82 / +26.67 / +22.27 / +26.67 / +45.82 / +26.67, a gain in every column. The plan row is +45.82 / +23.37 / +17.28 / +23.37 / +44.96 / +22.51, worst column S3 at +17.28. - The item clears the Board's downside test (no loss in any column against a $2B limit), its liquidity test and its technology-clock test (EIS 2037, not before 2035). - A350 Re-engine hold and Delay Tactics none are defaults, not items. DELAY TACTICS: none. The team's stricter condition (the move must change who enters service first) stands. I do not set it aside. Delay Tactics will never appear in any public line. A350 RE-ENGINE: on hold. - Wagner's capacity test would first pass in 2035, at the 2-year overlap limit. - Toepfer's peak-cash line moves the first passing round to 2045 on these bills (a 2035 launch runs at $6.67B a year in 2035-2036). - It never comes after a 787 Re-engine (rule 3). RECORD. Ordering principle in my framing: pillars, then ramp, then preparing the Airbus of the 30s, then whether the Board can take it [AX-0073, AX-0081, AX-0020, A-0409, AX-0026, AX-0010, AX-0054]. Confidence in my decision style is Low; the procedure follows the team rule and profile.md §9.

The NGSA item against hold gains +22.27 to +45.82 in every column, well inside the Board's $2B downside limit [AX-0022]. Overlap and the one-launch rule (rule 6): pass, with one launch and zero overlap [A-0343, A-0401]. Fine exposure, second move and poaching do not apply, since no move is ordered. Faury records that the team's stricter Delay Tactics condition stands. Five pillars: no flag. The supply-security move is limited to our own ramp. The trade advocacy and the risk-sharing invitation are public and unpriced. I could defend all of it to the Audit Committee [AX-0073, AX-0106]. Overrides: none used and none needed, so the one-per-game budget is untouched. One Board item: NGSA: launch, by Qualified Majority [AX-0026, AG-0049]. My conditions are carried into the decision: - shareholder returns stay inside the 30-50% payout range, at the lower end if ramp cash does not arrive; - the $35.52B charge at the 2037 EIS is reported beside the cash view; - no long-term-plan targets are disclosed [AX-0005]; - the public statement goes to the Board with the package [AX-0004]. Watch items, not vetoes: with $0.13B of headroom, any added programme cash in 2030-2036 needs a fresh peak-cash test. NGSA alone fails if its bill goes above $36.4B, FCF falls below €4.61bn, or the rate drops below $1.068 per €. On the engine code I defer to Lars Wagner. It does not change our payoff on the board.

Lars Wagner (operating head): concurs

Veto check, round 1 (2030). Lars Wagner, CEO Commercial Aircraft. My tests are derived from my role, not from my own record, so confidence is Very low. I concur. The orders match my recommendation exactly: ngsa launch, NGSA engine code 7, A350 Re-engine hold, Delay Tactics none. How the orders fare on my tests: - Five pillars and quality: pass. Every order is public and nothing is covert. The statement opens with safety and quality and gives a window for entry into service, not a date. The brief reports no quality event. - A320 ramp shield: pass. 2030 is after the end-2027 rate date. NB deliveries are flat at 1,200 a year (60.0%), and the brief reports no ramp or supply problem. - Engineering capacity: pass. NGSA is the only programme, so overlap is 0 years and strain is $0. - Production readiness: pass. 2030 is the last year of the 2028-2030 window. EIS is 2037, after the 2035 technology-ready year. - A350F and Spirit absorption: pass. A350 Re-engine is on hold, so nothing competes with the A350F or the Spirit A350 work packages. - Supply crunch, engine maturity slip and Boeing Rate Increase: not applicable. The brief reports none of them. Company red lines: no breach. - Rule 1: EIS 2037 is not before 2035. - Rule 4: no Delay Tactics move is ordered. - Rule 5: no poaching is ordered. - Rule 6: there is one new launch this round and no overlap. Overrides. None was used and none was needed, so the one-per-game override is still unused. No Delay Tactics move was ordered, and Faury records that the team's stricter condition stands. Engine code 7: my recommendation, adopted. CFM stays the anchor, and code 7 is in no barred pair under rules.md. Only this round can trigger P&W GTF2 (ready 2036) and Rolls-Royce UltraFan NB (ready 2037, no margin) in time for NGSA. If both launch, we have 3 engine sources and 3 makers in 2050. If both hold, NGSA flies CFM alone, with 1 source and 1 maker in 2050. The three mitigations I asked for are in other_moves: - certify the engines one after another, with CFM first; - review the code in 2035, only to remove a maker that has not launched or is off track, and never in reaction to Boeing; - secure supply for our own ramp only, not aimed at any rival's supply chain. One wording note, not a veto. The public line "the same will apply to its successor", on engine choice, only holds if P&W or Rolls-Royce actually launch an engine. If both hold, NGSA has one engine source. To protect the credibility of what we say in public, I would soften it to "we intend to offer a choice of engines" before release. This is Faury's call, and it does not touch safety, quality or the five pillars. Evidence: AX-0073, AX-0054, AX-0082, AX-0060, A-0441, A-0225, A-0366, A-0243, A-0360.

Board review

ngsalaunch (NGSA engine code 7: CFM, P&W and Rolls-Royce)approveThe Board approves this Qualified Majority item, a programme launch above EUR 800m, on the following record. The Board checked the brief's grid itself. - Unresolved objection: pass. Both veto checks concur, neither reports a red-line breach, there are no overrides and there is no revision. Wagner's wording note is not a veto. - Override review: not engaged. No override was used. - Liquidity and rating: pass, narrowly. $35.52B / 7 = $5.07B a year in 2030-2036 against the $5.2B line (EUR 4,753m at $1.10), with $0.13B of headroom and nothing running alongside. No new debt and no equity raise. - One clean sheet: pass. One launch this round, with zero overlap and zero strain. - Technology clock: pass. EIS 2030 + 7 = 2037, not before 2035, in the last year of the 2028-2030 window. - Downside: pass. The item value (the 'NGSA + A350: hold' row minus 'hold + hold') is +45.82 / +26.67 / +22.27 / +26.67 / +45.82 / +26.67 across S1-S6. It gains in the CEO's expected column, S1, and in every column the bulletin leaves open. The plan's worst column is S3 at +17.28. - Integrity: pass. Nothing is covert and Delay Tactics are none. - Safety and ramp: pass. Wagner passes the five pillars, quality, the A320 ramp shield, production readiness and A350F/Spirit absorption, and reports no supply crunch. - Returns kept fundable: passes through Liquidity. The Board approves the one Board item: NGSA: launch in 2030 with engine code 7, by Qualified Majority. EIS 2037 respects the technology clock and uses the last year of the window. On the brief's grid the item gains in every column (+22.27 to +45.82), so it clears the Downside test. Peak cash is $5.07B against the $5.2B line, a pass but a narrow one. The ExCo raises no objection, uses no override and has no safety, quality or ramp failure on record. A350 hold and Delay Tactics none are defaults and are not reviewed. The Board's main caution is the balance sheet. The headroom is $0.13B, and on the FY2025 base the dividend would draw on net cash. The Board therefore asks for a net-cash bridge and for the payout guardrail to be confirmed. It also asks that the engine-choice line be softened to 'we intend to offer a choice of engines'.

The Board's recommendations at review.

  • Liquidity has only $0.13B of headroom. Any programme cash added in 2030-2036, of whatever kind, must come back to the Board with a fresh year-by-year peak-cash test. The CFO's break-evens should be watched at each round and reported when crossed: an NGSA bill above $36.4B, FCF below EUR 4.61bn, or a rate below $1.068 per EUR.
  • The CFO flags that, on the FY2025 base, the dividend would draw about $2.45B a year from net cash, which would exhaust $13.4B within the development years. Before the 2035 round the Board asks for: - a net-cash bridge for 2030-2036 that includes the dividend, on both the FY2025 base and the 2030 run-rate; - confirmation of the payout guardrail (lower end of the 30-50% range if ramp cash does not arrive, no equity raise, no new return policy); - the effect of the single $35.52B charge at the 2037 EIS on reported earnings and on the payout base. Refundable advances, state support and risk-sharing are upside and are never assumed in the case.
  • Public statement: the Board supports Wagner's note. Replace 'the same will apply to its successor' with 'we intend to offer a choice of engines'. A second source depends on decisions by P&W and Rolls-Royce that Airbus does not control. Keep entry into service as 'the second half of the 2030s', with no dates or internal targets and nothing on Delay Tactics. The engine-maker invitation remains an unpriced, public other_move.
  • Engine supply: - Keep code 7, with CFM as the anchor and certifying first, and the other makers certified in sequence. - Review the code in 2035 only to remove a maker that has not launched or is off track for 2037, never in reaction to Boeing. - If neither P&W nor Rolls-Royce launches this round, NGSA will be single-source in 2050 (1 source / 1 maker). The ExCo should then report in 2035 how supply resilience is protected, without trading PV. - Wagner should report the integration and certification load of up to three engines at the Board's twice-yearly safety review.
  • Securing our own supply (in-house work packages, titanium, rare earths) must stay confined to Airbus's own ramp and never become a first claim aimed at a rival's supply chain. The Board asks that the Ethics, Compliance and Sustainability Committee be informed of these moves.
  • One programme at a time: keep the A350 Re-engine on hold. On these bills, a 2035 launch overlaps NGSA in 2035-2036 at about $6.67B a year and fails Liquidity, so 2045 is the first passing round. Bring it back only with fresh peak-cash arithmetic if the bills change, and never after a Boeing 787 Re-engine.
  • Delay Tactics stay off, and the team's stricter condition stands. Bottleneck and both are never acceptable. Poaching may come to the Board only once Boeing's fps launch is on the public record, fps is not in service, NGSA is in development, and every integrity condition holds.
  • Reaction discipline: NGSA stays on its own clock. It is not to be accelerated, delayed or cancelled for any Boeing move. A cancellation would need continuing to lose at least $1B against cancelling in every plausible column. In 2035, read Boeing only from the bulletin, and show the worst plausible column again together with the 60/40 path by column.

Final

Orders (as adjudicated). Launch NGSA (engines requested: RR, P&W and CFM)

Expected scenario. S1: rivals hold. Boeing has said a new aircraft comes 'not before 2035' and is still repairing its balance sheet, and the bulletin records no launch. S2 and S4 (fps 10-yr or via Embraer, EIS 2040) are close behind. The worst plausible column is S3 (fps 7-yr, EIS 2037, the same year as NGSA), where the plan still returns +17.28. The order is the same in every column.

Best grid plan in that scenario. NGSA + A350 Re-engine at +47.57 in S1. It is deleted for a company red line: rule 6, two new launches in one round with a 5-year overlap and -2.15 in S5 and S6. It also fails Toepfer's peak-cash test ($6.67B vs $5.2B) and Wagner's capacity and A350F tests, and the Board would veto it. The best surviving plan is NGSA + A350: hold + Delay Tactics none at +45.82 in S1. That is the company default and the plan ordered. Premium paid: +0.00 $B. No premium is paid. The only higher row in S1 (NGSA + A350 Re-engine, +$1.75B) breaks red-line rule 6 and is deleted before the doctrine-default comparison, so the $1.75B is recorded, not paid as a premium. The chosen plan is the best surviving plan in every column bar the deleted ones. No PV is traded for the briefing goal or the engine-supply enabler: the engine code is payoff-neutral on this board, and holding NGSA to keep 2 / 2 engine sources would cost $22.27-45.82B, far beyond any premium allowed.

Answers to the Board.

  • Launch NGSA this round (last year of the 2028-2030 window). Taken up. NGSA: launch in 2030, EIS 2037, inside the technology clock. This is the one Board item, by Qualified Majority. The item value against hold is +45.82 / +26.67 / +22.27 / +26.67 / +45.82 / +26.67, a gain in every column. Both Toepfer and Wagner pass it.
  • Select engine code 7 (CFM, P&W and Rolls-Royce); code 6 as fallback; avoid 1, 2 and 4; in 2035 change the code only to remove a maker that did not launch. Taken up. Code 7 rides with the launch, matching Wagner's supply recommendation. CFM is the anchor and certifies first. The enabler stands at 1 source / 1 maker in 2050 if P&W and Rolls-Royce hold, and 3 / 3 if both launch when selected; a Joint Venture engine (ready 2036) would count as one source. The 2035 review will only remove a maker that has not launched or is off track, never in reaction to Boeing. Code 6 is not needed now.
  • CFO to show peak cash year by year; net cash, A+/A1, the 30-50% payout and the EUR 5bn buyback fundable with no equity raise; present the launch inside the stated payout range. Taken up. Toepfer's paper: - Peak cash is $5.07B a year in each year 2030-2036 against $5.2B (one year's FCF at an assumed $1.10), with $0.13B of headroom and nothing concurrent. - No new debt or equity, so the rating is not pressed. - On the 2030 run-rate the payout stays inside 30-50%. The buyback runs in 2026-2029, before the spend. - On the FY2025 base the dividend would draw on net cash, so I adopt his guardrail: the lower end of the payout range if ramp cash does not arrive. - The $35.52B charge at the 2037 EIS is reported beside the cash view. - Public wording: 'disciplined investments in preparing our future portfolio', with no new return policy.
  • One programme at a time: A350 Re-engine on hold until NGSA development spend ends; 2045 first passing round on these bills; none after a 787 Re-engine. Taken up. A350 Re-engine: hold. Toepfer confirms that a 2035 launch would run at $6.67B a year in 2035-2036, so 2045 is the first round that passes Liquidity on these bills. Wagner's capacity test would pass 2035 at the 2-year limit, but the cash line governs. Rule 3 (no A350 Re-engine after a 787 Re-engine) is carried forward.
  • Keep Delay Tactics off and record that the team's stricter condition stands; bottleneck never; poaching only after fps is public and every condition holds. Taken up. Delay Tactics: none. The team's stricter condition stands, and I do not set it aside. bottleneck and both are excluded for good. Poaching would come to the Board only after an fps launch is on the public record and before its entry into service, as a single move while NGSA is in development.
  • Show the worst plausible Boeing response (S3) and S5/S6 for the widebody; do not accelerate, delay or cancel NGSA in reaction to Boeing. Taken up. The worst plausible column is S3 (fps 7-yr, same EIS 2037), where the plan returns +17.28. S5 gives +44.96 and S6 +22.51. The order is identical in every column. NGSA stays on its own clock: no acceleration, delay or cancellation in reaction to any Boeing move, and no cancellation without a failed case in every column (rules 2 and 7).
  • Operating head to confirm NGSA does not draw engineers or suppliers from the A320 rate or the A350F, and report safety and quality results. Taken up. Wagner reports passes on five pillars and quality, the A320 ramp shield, engineering capacity (zero overlap, zero strain), production readiness and A350F/Spirit absorption, with no five-pillars flag. His one unpriced concern, the load of integrating three engines, is handled by sequential certification and the 2035 code review.
  • Public statement: windows, not dates; safety first; disciplined and controlled ramp; NGSA offered with more than one engine maker; nothing on Delay Tactics; risk-sharing invitation as other_moves. Taken up. The statement: - opens with the five pillars; - gives entry into service as 'the second half of the 2030s'; - keeps the A320neo and A350 on a disciplined and controlled ramp-up; - names CFM, P&W and Rolls-Royce (engine selections are public in any case); - states zero-for-zero trade. It discloses no internal targets and says nothing of Delay Tactics. The risk-sharing invitation is listed in other_moves as public and unpriced.

Objective. The briefing goal (Defend the 60/40 edge; Protect the A320 family; Enabler: stable engine supply) is scored by the GM and does not change the payoff. No PV was traded for it. Defend 60/40. Met today. With NGSA launched it is met in S1 and S5: NGSA alone gains 3 pp a year from 2037, to the cap. My reading of rules.md, not tabulated in the brief, for the fps columns: - S2, S4 and S6 (fps EIS 2040): NGSA leads by 3 years, which points to roughly 53% in the long run. 2040 holds above 60%, but 2045 and 2050 fall below. - S3 (same EIS): we drift toward 50%. - In every fps column, holding NGSA does worse, so the launch is also the plan that best defends the edge. Protect the A320 family. Met in every column: nothing moves before 2037 and no Rate Increase is on record. Enabler, dual or triple sources. Met today (CFM + P&W GTF). With NGSA it falls to 1 / 1 in 2050 if P&W and Rolls-Royce hold, and rises to 3 / 3 if both launch when selected. Code 7 is the only code that can reach 3 / 3, and this is the only round in which it can be triggered. Enabler, three narrowbody makers. Not met today. It becomes met only if Rolls-Royce brings an NB engine (UltraFan NB, or the Joint Venture engine) that is ready by 2037. Code 7 plus the public risk-sharing invitation is the most I can do without trading PV.

Predictions. Boeing in 2030: most likely holds (S1, about 45%). Next most likely is an fps 10-yr or via Embraer (S2/S4, about 30% together), then an fps 7-yr (S3, about 10%) and a 787 Re-engine with or without fps (S5/S6, about 15%). A 737 Rate Increase is possible but would not change our programmes. Probability-weighted ΔPV on these weights is about +33.9B; in S1 it is +45.82B. P&W: likely to answer our selection with GTF2 launch if selected, ready 2036 with one year of margin, so that it keeps its place on our narrowbody. A Joint Venture commitment with Rolls-Royce is possible. Rolls-Royce: less certain. UltraFan NB launched now has zero margin to a 2037 entry into service. It may prefer the Joint Venture (ready 2036, counted as one source) or stay on widebody moves. CFM: likely to launch a ducted engine or rely on a LEAP derivative. It is fitted on NGSA either way. Board: approves NGSA: launch by Qualified Majority with code 7, and vetoes nothing in this package. 2035 bulletin: NGSA in development with engine-ready dates published. At the 2035 round the code is reviewed only to remove a maker that has not launched. NGSA is not re-timed for any Boeing move. The A350 Re-engine stays on hold on current bills (first passing round 2045, never after a 787 Re-engine).

Expected ΔPV. +45.82 $B (GM valuation after the round: +23.37 $B)

Other moves.

  • Public invitation to engine makers to share risk on NGSA (public): Airbus has selected CFM, Pratt & Whitney and Rolls-Royce (code 7) and invites all three to bring a new narrowbody engine to NGSA as risk-sharing partners, with entry into service in the second half of the 2030s. This supports the enabler (dual or triple sources, three narrowbody engine makers). It is unpriced, and it is a recommendation only, as the Board noted.
  • Secure our own supply for the A320 family ramp (public): Continue to bring critical work packages in-house and to de-risk titanium and rare earths for our own production system [AX-0060, AX-0061, AX-0062, AX-0063]. This is aimed only at our own disciplined and controlled ramp-up. It is not aimed at any rival's supply chain.
  • Certify NGSA engines in sequence, with CFM as the anchor (private): This is Wagner's mitigation for the unpriced load of integrating three engines. CFM integrates and certifies first, and the other makers follow in sequence, as on the A320neo. Shared engineering teams are protected for the A320 rate and A350F absorption.
  • Engine-code review at the 2035 round (private): Keep code 7 unless the 2035 bulletin shows that P&W or Rolls-Royce has not launched, or has an engine that is off track for a 2037 entry into service. In that case, remove that maker only. The change is never made in reaction to Boeing.
  • Payout guardrail during NGSA development (private): This is Toepfer's condition. Shareholder returns stay inside the stated 30-50% payout range, with no equity raise. If ramp cash stays near the FY2025 level, returns are kept at the lower end of the range in 2030-2036 rather than drawing on net cash. The $35.52B programme charge at entry into service is reported beside the cash view. No internal long-term-plan targets are disclosed.
  • Zero-for-zero trade advocacy through industry coalitions (public): Keep working with industry partners, Boeing included, for a tariff-free aerospace trade regime [AX-0088, AX-0046].

Board guidance before the ExCo met

Priorities.

  • Safety, quality, delivery and cost, in that order [CG-0009, CX-0658]. We will not fund a launch while Ali has a safety or durability flag the CEO has not resolved. Any Ducted must answer Culp's own red line of at least 20% better fuel burn, since a ducted engine gets 'less than half' the open fan's gain [CX-0217, CX-0183]. The CEO must strike or rebut it in the rationale, and durability is not traded for fuel burn [CX-0208].
  • Keep every new narrowbody on a CFM engine, but only with risk that is paid for [CG-0017, CX-0493]. Against Do Nothing, a defensive Ducted is worth +$8.4B to +$10.9B in every column where an airframer launches (S2-S5). If none launches (S1) it costs at most its $4B bill, and in S6 it costs -0.49.
  • Keep RISE whole as technology and make it a product only on an airframer path [CX-0469, CX-0205, CG-0065]. An Open Fan launched in 2030 is ready in 2045, the same year as one launched in 2035. In every column but S1 it waits, at -$16B to -$58B against Do Nothing. The product decision belongs to the 2035 round, the last round that can still meet 'ready by 2050'.
  • Protect the A-range rating and the payout floor [CG-0022, CX-0645, CG-0063]. New R&D and strain this round should stay within about $2.5B a year; Ducted + Embraer + GEnx comes to about $1.0B a year. Premiums stay at or below $2.0B this round, and the one RISE allowance stays unspent.
  • State Safran's consent on every CFM order: Ducted, Open Fan, Embraer and Lobby [CX-0184, CX-0160, CG-0066]. GEnx is GE alone and needs no consent.

Expects to see. For each Board item we want the following. (1) expected_scenario (S1-S6) and weights for all six columns in predictions. The bulletin rules out no column; without weights we use equal weights. (2) The submitted row and the row with that item at its default, column by column, including against Do Nothing in the expected column and the worst column. Default Embraer together with the Ducted, because it needs the engine. (3) Ghai's tests with numbers. The Ducted's $4B over 6 years is about $0.67B a year, plus about $0.33B a year of strain if Embraer or GEnx rides with it. We also want any Ghai veto and Culp's answer to it, on evidence. (4) Ali's ready years against the first new narrowbody's entry: Ducted 2036 against NGSA or a 7-year fps in 2037 and a 10-year fps in 2040; Open Fan not before 2045. We also want any safety or durability flag from Ali, in his memo or his veto-check note, and the cross-functional answer to it. (5) Culp's 20% fuel-burn red line struck or rebutted in the rationale for any Ducted. (6) The Safran gate for each ducted, Open Fan, Embraer partnership and emissions lobbying order, with a reason why Safran would agree. (7) The hard-rule-3 trigger named for any Ducted. Here that is the grid's slot-taking columns, S3 (code 2) and S6 (codes 1 and 2), because no rival engine is on the record. (8) premium in dollars against the best plan in the expected column. Any RISE allowance must be stated separately in premium_reason; we expect none this round. (9) Every override with its evidence. (10) A public statement that names no rival, blames no one, gives no Open Fan entry before 2045, no untested Ducted date and no CFM price talk without Safran.

Would approve.

  • ducted engine: launch if the expected column is one where an airframer launches (S2-S5). Item value against Do Nothing on its own: S2 +10.17, S3 +10.17, S4 +8.43, S5 +10.88. In Ducted + Embraer + GEnx, with Embraer defaulted alongside: +10.61, +13.05, +10.17, +12.85. All are above the $1B margin. The downside is bounded at its bill: S1 -4.00 against a $4B bill, or -6.00 against $6B with the strain; S6 -0.49 or -1.38. If the CEO expects S1, the Ducted can still pass under hard rule 3 through S3, where a rival takes CFM's slot (+10.17 or +13.05), provided the weighted item value is at least zero. With equal weights it is +5.86 or +6.55; the hedge holds while the chance that no airframer launches this round stays below about 0.7 (alone) or 0.66 (in the package). The premium cap still applies; see would_veto. Timing: launched now, it is ready in 2036, before the earliest new narrowbody entry in 2037. Launched in 2035, it would be ready in 2041. CFM parity rule: a defence that keeps both airframers on CFM fits joint practice, so we assume consent.
  • Embraer partnership: launch, only with the Ducted launched this round and an expected column in S2-S5. Net of the $2B strain it adds (Ducted + Embraer against Ducted): S2 +0.43, S3 +2.87, S4 +1.74, S5 +1.97. When GEnx shares the strain: +2.44, +4.88, +3.73, +3.97. The downside is bounded: the worst is -2.00 in S1, against a $2B bill. CFM parity rule: a CFM engine offered to a third airframer fits 'serve every airframer', so we assume consent (inference); a stated sentence is welcome.
  • GEnx: GEnx upgrade or GEnx investment; the two are identical on the board. On its own it is worth +0.77 to +0.78 in every column, with no strain. Alongside Ducted + Embraer it is also +0.77 to +0.78, because that pair already carries the strain. It is GE alone, so there is no Safran gate. It sits below our real threshold, and we review it with the package.
  • The package Ducted + Partner Embraer + GEnx upgrade. It is the grid's best plan in S2 (-20.69), S3 (-71.86), S4 (-50.10) and S5 (-48.96), so the premium is nil in those columns. It carries one $2B strain charge and about $1.0B a year of R&D and strain over six years, well within the payout floor.
  • hold on any field: we never veto it. GEnx alone is the best plan in both S1 (+0.78) and S6 (-104.23).

Would veto.

  • Open Fan: launch this round, alone or in any combination. Item value against Do Nothing: S1 -8.00, S2 -57.60, S3 -35.40, S4 -41.46, S5 -51.84, S6 -16.07, against an $8B bill. Alongside the Ducted it adds -10.00 to -62.08. It fails the bounded-downside test and airframer-path test (a) in five plausible columns. The RISE allowance cannot carry an Open Fan the grid shows waiting, because our time horizon is 3. A 2030 launch also gains nothing over 2035, since both are ready in 2045. Grounds: no airframer path and unbounded downside.
  • emissions lobbying: launch without a live Open Fan: on its own it does nothing for $1B plus strain. If the Open Fan is vetoed, Lobby falls with it. Even with the Open Fan, Open Fan + Lobby is -11.00 to -40.76 against Do Nothing.
  • ducted engine: launch in any of four cases. (a) The expected column is S1 or S6 and the CEO names no slot-taking column with a weighted item value of at least zero. (b) The declared premium exceeds the $2.0B cap: if the CEO expects S1, the package gives up $6.00B against GEnx alone, or $4.78B for the Ducted alone, so the case must rest on stated weights in which it is the best plan, not on an S1 expectation. (c) Culp's 20% fuel-burn red line, or an Ali durability or date flag, stands unanswered. (d) Its value depends on a ready year earlier than 2036.
  • Embraer partnership: launch with no new CFM engine launched this round or already live. It also fails with an expected column of S1, where it is -2.00, or 0.00 with GEnx, which is not above zero. It fails in S6 without GEnx (-0.89). If Embraer is vetoed, a GEnx order beside a lone Ducted goes with it.
  • genx alongside a single other project, either the Ducted alone or the Open Fan alone. It scores -1.22 to -1.23 in every column, because it triggers the $2B strain.

Recommendations.

  • Safety first. Put Ali's readiness and durability review of any Ducted in the package, with test evidence behind the 2036 ready year. Have Culp strike or rebut his 20% fuel-burn red line in the rationale. We read a hard-rule-3 Ducted as a defence of the installed base; GE's next-generation engine stays RISE. No durability may be traded for fuel burn.
  • Delivery and timing. If you expect an airframer to launch this round, launch the Ducted now rather than in 2035. Launched now, it is ready in 2036, against an NGSA or a 7-year fps entering service in 2037 and a 10-year fps in 2040; a 2035 launch would not be ready until 2041. Say in the rationale why now rather than after the 2035 bulletin.
  • Put the expected column and weights for all six columns in predictions. Show each Board item against Do Nothing in the expected column and the worst column. On equal weights the Ducted package is worth +6.55 and the Ducted alone +5.86; tell us if your airframer reading differs.
  • Keep RISE funded as technology and bring the product decision to the 2035 round. A 2035 launch is still ready in 2045, and the bulletin will show by then whether any narrowbody can enter service earlier. If an airframer launches this round, say plainly that the Open Fan would wait and that 'ready by 2050' is out of reach on our tests, rather than stretching them. Keep the one RISE allowance unspent.
  • Cost and capital. Add a second or third project only where the grid pays the $2B strain: Embraer and GEnx together with the Ducted, never GEnx beside a lone Ducted. State every premium in dollars against the best plan in the expected column, with the RISE allowance shown separately. Keep the payout at no less than 70% of free cash flow; the package needs about $1.0B a year against about $2.5B of room. As real-world context, neither partner's analyst model carries a next engine, so tell us whether the Ducted would come out of buybacks and what Safran funds.
  • CFM parity rule. Name the Safran gate for each narrowbody order, with the reason Safran would agree. For a defensive Ducted, the reason is that it keeps both airframers on CFM. For Embraer, it is a CFM engine for a third airframer. The record shows no Safran position, so do not assert one.
  • Public statement: name no rival, blame no one, make no CFM price talk without Safran, give no Open Fan entry before 2045, and give no Ducted date that testing does not support.

Larry Culp frames the round

Question. What game are we playing, and how do we win? [CX-0467] The game is the installed base on the next narrowbody, not share for its own sake. "Our major economics happen in and around the first and second" shop visit [CX-0422], and "we're not going for share" [CX-0493]. Nothing has launched, and "we don't have a birthright on that next order" [CX-0564]. Both new narrowbodies (fps and NGSA) are open this round, and orders are sealed and simultaneous, so any threat that lands this round has to be met this round. We win by doing three things. First, keep every new narrowbody on a CFM engine, with risk that is paid for. Second, keep the 787 on GEnx. Third, keep RISE whole as technology until an airframer wants it as a product [CX-0469, CX-0205]. So the question for this room is this. Do we launch a defensive Ducted now, ready in 2036 ahead of a 2037 entry, and do Partner Embraer and the GEnx upgrade ride with it under one strain charge? Or do we take GEnx alone and wait for the 2035 bulletin?

Situation. PUBLIC RECORD, 2030. No programme has launched; everyone flies today's products (737 MAX, 787, A320neo, A350; LEAP, GTF, GEnx, Trent). Shares were flat over 2026-29: - NB airframes: Boeing 40%, Airbus 60%. - NB engines: CFM 76%, P&W 24%, RR 0%. LEAP is sole source on the 737 and shares the A320neo with the GTF. - WB engines: GEnx 42%, Trent 58%. No rival new NB engine is launched, committed or selected, and no Joint Venture commitment is on the record. STILL OPEN. - fps: the 7-year version enters service in 2037; the 10-year version and the Embraer route in 2040. - NGSA: enters service in 2037. - Both widebody Re-engines: enter service 5 years after launch. OUR POSITION. - ΔPV is +0.00 if nobody moves. EV $160B, debt $35B. - Objective, NB at least 50% in 2040, 2045 and 2050: met today at 76%. It is at risk only in the columns where a rival takes our slot (S3, S6). - Objective, Open Fan launched and ready by 2050: not met. Only a launch by the 2035 round can still meet it, since launch + 10 must be 2050 or earlier. GRID READING. - Hold loses -32.07 (S2) to -105.01 (S6) in every column where an airframer launches, because a new airframe splits our sole-source 737 slot and our A320neo slot. - S3 (NGSA, code 2) and S6 (codes 1, 2) are the columns where a rival selection takes CFM's slot. That is the hard-rule-3 trigger on the grid, since no rival engine is on the record. - Best plan by column: GEnx alone in S1 (+0.78) and S6 (-104.23); Ducted + Partner Embraer + GEnx in S2 to S5 (-20.69, -71.86, -50.10, -48.96). - Every Open Fan row loses -8.00 to -57.60 against hold. BOARD GUIDANCE (non-binding, labelled as such). The Board would VETO: - an Open Fan this round in any combination: it waits in every launch column, and a 2030 launch is ready in 2045, the same year as a 2035 launch; - Lobby without a live Open Fan; - GEnx beside a single other project (-1.22, strain); - Partner Embraer with no new CFM engine, or with S1 as the expected column; - a Ducted if any of these holds: (a) S1 or S6 is expected and no slot-taking column is named at a weighted value of zero or better; (b) the premium is over $2.0B; (c) my 20% line, or an Ali durability or date flag, stands unanswered; (d) its value rests on a ready year before 2036. It would APPROVE a defensive Ducted, alone or as Ducted + Embraer + GEnx, when the expected column is S2 to S5 or my weights carry it. In return it wants: - weights for all six columns; - Ali's ready years against the first new NB entry; - the Safran gate for each order; - the 70% payout kept whole; - new R&D plus strain of about $1.0B a year; - the RISE allowance unspent; - a public statement with no rival named, no blame, no Open Fan entry before 2045, no untested Ducted date and no price talk.

Options to test.

  • Row A, hold everything (Do Nothing, LEAP derivative; the reference row). By column S1-S6: 0.00 / -32.07 / -85.68 / -61.04 / -62.58 / -105.01.
  • Row B, GEnx upgrade alone. By column: +0.78 / -31.30 / -84.91 / -60.27 / -61.81 / -104.23. That is +0.77 to +0.78 against hold everywhere. GE alone. It is the best plan in S1 and S6, and the fallback if the Ducted fails a test.
  • Row C, Ducted alone. By column: -4.00 / -21.90 / -75.51 / -52.61 / -51.70 / -105.50. Against hold: -4.00, +10.17, +10.17, +8.43, +10.88, -0.49. S1 costs the whole $4B bill. In S2 it sits $1.21B below the best plan.
  • Row D, Ducted + Partner Embraer + GEnx upgrade (one $2B strain charge). By column: -5.22 / -20.69 / -71.86 / -50.10 / -48.96 / -105.61. Against GEnx alone: -6.00, +10.61, +13.05, +10.17, +12.85, -1.38. Against Ducted alone: -1.22, +1.21, +3.65, +2.51, +2.74, -0.11. It is the best grid plan in S2 to S5.

  • Weighted check. On equal weights: Row D -50.41, C -51.87, B -56.96, A -57.73. On my preliminary weights (S1 .30, S2 .25, S3 .10, S4 .10, S5 .15, S6 .10): D -36.84, C -37.79, B -41.80, A -42.58. D's edge over C is only +0.95 there, inside the $1B ε, so the tie-break decides it. Both Ducted rows fall below GEnx alone once P(S1) passes about 0.60, with the rest spread evenly.
  • Timing check, which the grid cannot price. A Ducted launched now is ready in 2036; launched in 2035 it is ready in 2041. Ghai to size what waiting costs in the launch columns, and the salvage from a 2035 cancel (write-off of $4B x 5/6 = $3.33B).
  • Rows excluded unless a memo changes them, each recorded with its reason: - Ducted + GEnx: -1.22 against Ducted alone in every column, from the strain. - Open Fan: -8.00 to -57.60 against hold. - Open Fan + Lobby: -11.00 to -40.76. - Ducted + Open Fan: -14.00 to -51.20. - Lobby alone: does nothing. The Open Fan rows break H2, and the Board guidance would veto them.

Red lines.

  • Safety, quality, delivery and cost, always in that order [CX-0658]. No launch while a safety or durability flag from Ali stands unresolved by a cross-functional answer [CX-0012].
  • H1: never refuse an airframer and never lock one out. The LEAP derivative is an offer, and we want to be on all the critical platforms [CX-0587, CX-0185].
  • H2: never press an airframer into the Open Fan wait [CX-0205]. No Open Fan launch while a new NB can enter service before it is ready. Any airframe launched in 2030 enters service in 2037-2040, and the Open Fan is not ready before 2045. The one exception is the declared RISE allowance, and I do not plan to touch it this round.
  • H3: a Ducted only as a defence, never as the next-generation product [CX-0217, CX-0183]. The trigger has to be named: here it is the grid's slot-taking columns, S3 and S6.
  • H5: never cancel RISE for cost while an airframer may want it [CX-0174, CX-0398].
  • H6 (applied through Ali's test): no date without test evidence [CX-0009]. No untested Ducted date in public, and no Open Fan entry before 2045.
  • H7: the Safran gate on every CFM narrowbody order (Ducted, Open Fan, Embraer, Lobby) [CX-0184, CX-0166]. GEnx is GE alone.
  • H8: no public blame and no comment on rivals [CX-0625, CX-0580].
  • H9: doctrine plus objective premium at most $2.0B this round and $4.0B for the game. One RISE allowance of up to $15B, declared in full against the best non-RISE plan.
  • My line: a next engine needs at least a 20% fuel-burn improvement [CX-0217]. It binds RISE as the next generation. A defensive Ducted is not offered as the next generation (it gets 'less than half' the open fan's gain [CX-0183]), so the line does not bar it. I will rebut it in the rationale and never call the Ducted next-generation.
  • My line: durability is not traded for fuel burn [CX-0208].

Initial lean. This is a lean, not a decision; your memos decide it. OPEN FAN: HOLD. RISE stays whole and funded as technology, with no cancel [CX-0214, CX-0174]. A 2030 launch is ready no sooner than a 2035 launch (both 2045) and waits in every launch column. The product call belongs to the 2035 round, the last one that can meet 'ready by 2050'. If an airframer launches now, we say plainly that the Open Fan would wait. LOBBY: HOLD. It does nothing without an Open Fan. DUCTED: LAUNCH NOW, AS A DEFENCE UNDER H3. The trigger is the grid's slot-taking columns, S3 (code 2) and S6 (codes 1 and 2), because no rival engine is on the record. It is worth +8.43 to +10.88 against hold wherever an airframer launches. Its loss is bounded at the $4B bill in S1 and is -0.49 in S6. Why now rather than after the 2035 bulletin: launched now it is ready in 2036, ahead of a 2037 entry; launched in 2035 it is ready only in 2041. The board charges R&D undiscounted, so waiting saves money only if no airframer ever launches. EMBRAER AND GEnx: RIDE WITH THE DUCTED under one $2B strain charge, if two tests come back clean: - Ghai's numbers keep the add-on more than $1B ahead of Ducted alone in my weights. - Ali says the supply base carries three projects. Inside ε, the tie-break is safety, quality, delivery and cost. So a supply 'no' from Ali drops Embraer, and GEnx goes too and waits for 2035. FALLBACK: if the Ducted fails a test, GEnx alone, the best plan in S1 and S6. EXPECTED COLUMN, PRELIMINARY: S2. Airbus launches NGSA and keeps today's dual-source A320neo pattern (code 6). I read that from the public pattern, not from a hoped-for selection. S2 sits below S1 for every plan, so it books PV low. Weights: S1 .30, S2 .25, S3 .10, S4 .10, S5 .15, S6 .10. The package is the best plan in S2, so the premium is nil; the RISE allowance stays unspent. SAFRAN GATE: - Ducted: consent assumed. The stated reason is that it keeps both airframers' next aircraft on CFM, and with them the aftermarket the partners split equally. A launch ahead of a committed airframe is not shown in joint practice, hence the stated reason. - Embraer: consent assumed. It is a CFM engine for a third airframer, which fits 'serve every airframer'. - GEnx: no gate; GE alone. - Open Fan and Lobby: held, so no ask. PUBLIC LINE: we serve every airframer; we tell you what we know and what we don't [CX-0436]; RISE remains our next generation; no date we have not tested; no rival named; no price talk. Keep the next narrowbody on CFM and pay only for the risk we can see. It's that simple, ain't that hard.

Larry Culp decides

Orders. Launch ducted engine; Partner with Embraer; GEnx upgrade

Rationale. DECISION. Launch the Ducted, Partner Embraer and the GEnx upgrade (GEnx upgrade). Hold the Open Fan and Lobby. Nothing is cancelled. All five orders follow the frame, and both memos recommend the same five. WHAT GAME, HOW WE WIN [CX-0467]. The game is the installed base on the next narrowbody [CX-0422], not share for its own sake [CX-0493]. Both new narrowbodies, fps and NGSA, are open, and orders are sealed. Hold loses -32.07 to -105.01 in every column where an airframer launches. S3 (NGSA, code 2) and S6 (codes 1 and 2) are the columns where a rival selection takes CFM's slot. "We don't have a birthright on that next order" [CX-0564]. TESTS (1) Additive and paid for the risk [CX-0301]. The package, Ducted + Partner Embraer + GEnx upgrade, is the best grid plan in S2 to S5: S2 -20.69, S3 -71.86, S4 -50.10, S5 -48.96. Its S1 cost is named: -5.22 against hold, or -6.00 against GEnx alone, which is the $4B bill plus the $2B strain and no more. The risk is worth it because the package is worth +10.61 to +13.05 wherever an airframer launches, and the loss is capped at the bill when none does. (2) Low case first [CX-0248, CX-0536]. The expected column is S2: Airbus launches NGSA and keeps today's dual-source A320neo pattern (code 6). That is the record's pattern, not a hoped-for selection. S2 sits below S1 for every plan, so it books low. (3) Hard rule 3. The trigger is the grid's slot-taking columns, because no rival engine is launched, committed or selected on the record. S3 is the column that pays it: the Ducted is worth +10.17 against hold, and the package +13.05 against GEnx alone. S6 names the trigger but does not pay it (-0.49, or -1.38). Ghai accepts the trigger through S3, not S6. (4) My 20% line, rebutted. The 20% line [CX-0217] binds the next-generation product, which is RISE. The ducted engine has "less than half the fuel burn improvements" of an open fan [CX-0183; Ali, CX-0180]. It cannot meet 20%, and it is not offered as the next generation. It is a defence of the installed base under hard rule 3, and it is never called next-generation in public. The durability line [CX-0208] stands: Ali raises no durability or safety flag, and every design gate is cross-functional [CX-0012]. (5) Supply. Two or more projects draw the $2B strain. The grid pays it in S2 to S5. Ali gives no supply 'no', on condition that GEnx is paced behind the Ducted's peak. WHY NOW, NOT AFTER THE 2035 BULLETIN. Launched now, the Ducted is ready in 2036 against a 2037 entry (NGSA or a 7-year fps) and a 2040 entry (10-year fps or the Embraer route). Launched in 2035, it is ready only in 2041. Ghai sizes the cost of waiting at about $4.3B in S2 and S3, $4.5B in S5 and $1.1B in S4. Waiting saves $0.49B in S6, and in S1 it saves up to $4.00B. Net edge for launching now: +$1.06B to +$1.26B on my weights, +$0.64B to +$0.88B on his. Waiting wins only once P(S1) passes about 0.45. Ghai's numbers show deferring Embraer or GEnx to 2035 would still draw the strain while the Ducted is in development, so it saves nothing. THE STACK, AND MY OWN CONDITION MISSED. I said the add-ons had to clear Ducted alone by more than $1B on my weights. They clear it by $0.95B, missing by $0.05B: inside ε. Elsewhere they clear it by +$1.21B in S2, +$1.46B on equal weights and +$0.83B on Ghai's. They lose $1.22B in S1 and $0.11B in S6. So the tie-break decides, "safety, quality, delivery and cost, always in that order" [CX-0658]: - Safety: a tie. No flag on either plan. - Quality: a tie on the evidence. The grid charges the load at $2B, and Ali has no test or field data either way. I don't invent a flag. I take his pacing condition and the supplier watch. - Delivery: the package wins. It puts a CFM engine in front of a third airframer and keeps the 787 on product (H1: "on all the critical platforms" [CX-0587]). It is decided at delivery, with cost (+$0.95B weighted, best plan in S2) confirming it. GEnx never sits beside a lone Ducted (-1.22 to -1.23 in every column). HELD - Open Fan: launched now it is ready in 2045, the same as a 2035 launch. It waits in every launch column, at -$8.00B to -$57.60B against hold (H2) [CX-0205]. RISE stays whole as technology (H5) [CX-0174, CX-0214]. - Lobby: does nothing without an Open Fan. BOARD ITEMS, BY COLUMN, S1 / S2 / S3 / S4 / S5 / S6 - Submitted package: -5.22 / -20.69 / -71.86 / -50.10 / -48.96 / -105.61. Against Do Nothing in S2 that is +11.38; the worst column against Do Nothing is S1, at -5.22. - ducted (package minus GEnx alone, Embraer defaulted with it): -6.00 / +10.61 / +13.05 / +10.17 / +12.85 / -1.38. Weighted +4.96. The worst is S1 at -6.00, equal to its $6B bill. - Embraer partnership (package minus Ducted + GEnx): 0.00 / +2.44 / +4.88 / +3.73 / +3.97 / +1.12. Weighted +2.18. It never goes below zero. - genx (package minus Ducted + Embraer): +0.78 / +0.78 / +0.78 / +0.77 / +0.77 / +0.78. SAFRAN GATE (H7, CFM parity rule) - ducted engine: consent assumed, because it keeps both airframers' next aircraft on CFM and the aftermarket the partners split equally. A launch ahead of a committed airframe is not shown in joint practice, hence the stated reason. - Embraer partnership: consent assumed, as a CFM engine for a third airframer ('serve every airframer'). - Open Fan and emissions lobbying: held, so no ask. - GEnx: GE alone, no gate. No Safran position is asserted [CX-0184]. DOCTRINE, NOT MY RECORD. These calls rest on doctrine: - Embraer: no record; the NMA 'additive' rule [CX-0301] applied by inference. - Lobby: profile §6. - Supply load: Ali's seat doctrine, checked against the strain rule. - The GEnx call: inference [CX-0599, CX-0615]. 2035 REVIEW. If the bulletin shows no airframer launch and no rival engine, I reread the Ducted: a cancel then writes off $3.33B and saves $0.67B, and a reversal is in character. Ghai's numbers favour keeping it if an airframer launches in 2035. The Open Fan product call is made then, on Ali's test gates. ExCo. Culp proposed and decided; Ghai and Ali concur on all five orders. No binding veto is triggered, so there are no overrides.

Weighing the CFO. Weighed heavily: his record is High confidence on terms, capex and profit, and every number checks against the grid; I re-ran them. His binding tests all pass on this plan. - Pays for itself: the package beats hold by +11.38 in S2. - Volumes first: he accepts hard rule 3 through S3 (+13.05), not S6. - Capex: about $1.0B a year against $2.5B of room, with the 70% payout whole. - Premium: $0.00 in S2. - Terms: no price talk. His binding vetoes do not touch this plan: the Open Fan, Lobby alone, GEnx beside a lone Ducted, a Ducted on an S1 expectation without weights, and price talk. I took his non-binding stack flag seriously. It caught my own condition, more than $1B on my weights, missed by $0.05B. I answered it through the tie-break, not by ignoring it. I took his timing math too: launching now is worth +$1.06B to +$1.26B net on my weights, much less than the grid's $10B. That is why I say in private that the edge is thin and that waiting wins once P(S1) passes about 0.45. I adopted his guide-low call and book -21.0. His weights put 0.35 on S1; the package stays the weighted best on them (-36.07).

Weighing the operating head. His record is thin. His own words end in March 2024 and cover engineering, at Medium confidence on durability, the test standard and RISE physics. On supply he states plainly that he has no evidence and follows doctrine [CX-0633]. I weighed his memo that way. - Dates: taken in full. The ready years are the board's development times (Ducted 2036, Embraer counting 2037, GEnx 2042 or the first Re-engine, Open Fan 2045). Every row passes his binding date test. - His candour that 2036 is a board rule, not a turn-on, turn-off result [CX-0009]: taken in full. That is why no Ducted, Embraer or GEnx date and no Open Fan entry year is in the public statement. - Physics: taken in full. A ducted engine has less than half the open fan's gain [CX-0183, CX-0180], which is the basis of my 20% rebuttal. - Durability: he raises no flag, and I record that this is not a clearance; the gates come later, cross-functionally. - Supply: his answer (no 'no', grid pays the strain, pace GEnx) agrees with doctrine. I checked it against the strain rule and adopted his pacing and supplier-watch condition as an operating move. - RISE: his milestones for the 2035 product call are adopted as the gates.

If he says no, Embraer and GEnx drop together. - Timing: the edge for launching now is thin, about $0.6-1.3B net, and it goes once P(S1) passes about 0.45. - Safran: the statement announces two CFM launches with consent assumed, not given. If Safran declines, we withdraw them, plainly. My veto right is an inference from the team rule (binding unless Culp answers it with evidence). No ground is triggered here. Not to the extent of the grid's $10B, but it is progress.

Mohamed Ali (operating head): concurs; veto (not binding): No veto. Every ready year in the orders is at or after launch plus development years. Ducted: 2030 + 6 = 2036. Partner Embraer counts 2030 + 7 = 2037, after the Ducted it needs. GEnx upgrade counts 2030 + 3 = 2033, and widebody shares move only from the first Re-engine's entry (2035 at the earliest) or 2042. Open Fan is held, so there is no ready year to test. The public statement and the public other move give no programme date. Note: my veto right over programme dates is an inference. My words date from 2024, when I was VP of Engineering, and concern believing durability-fix results; the team rule reads them as a binding date test.

Concur. I tested against the brief, not analysis. Dates, recomputed from the rules. Ducted launched 2030 is ready 2036. That is one year ahead of a 2037 entry (NGSA or a 7-year fps) and four years ahead of a 2040 entry (10-year fps or via Embraer). Partner Embraer counts in 2037 and rides on the 2036 Ducted. GEnx upgrade counts in 2033 on the board, but widebody shares move only from the first Re-engine (2035 at the earliest) or 2042. Open Fan held: launched now it would be ready in 2045, 8 years after a 2037 entry, so the hold is right (H2). Every order's value rests on years at or after launch plus development time. Pass. Statement. I read it line by line. It gives no Ducted, Embraer or GEnx year and no Open Fan entry year; 'this year' is the only year in it. 'The open fan won't be ready for' a narrowbody launched now is a negative readiness claim. It is true on the rules (2045 against 2037-2040) and promises nothing. 'We won't give you dates our testing hasn't earned' is my test, in Culp's voice. The Ducted is never called the next generation, and the statement makes no fuel-burn or durability claim for it. RISE stays the next generation: 'less than half' the gain, and the reason is physics [CX-0183, CX-0180]. The public offer of 'a LEAP derivative or the new ducted engine' to every airframer has no date and no price. Pass. The 2036 year stays private, as it should: it is the board's development time. No Ducted engine has been turned on and turned off. Safety and durability. I raise no flag. This is not a clearance. The design and test gates come later, and every gate is a cross-functional call, which Culp has written in as an operating move [CX-0012]. Durability is not traded for schedule [CX-0208]. Any time-on-wing claim later needs test or field data. Supply. Culp has adopted my condition: GEnx paced behind the Ducted peak, and the 9 suppliers at 15 sites watched in the monthly reviews [CX-0613]. One caveat on dates: pacing must not push GEnx readiness past a Re-engine's entry. If the 2035 bulletin shows a 787 or A350 Re-engine, I recheck the GEnx date against that entry year. H3, for the Board. The defensive trigger is anticipatory. It rests on the grid's slot-taking columns (S3, S6), because no rival engine is on the record yet. That trigger is Culp's call on strategy, not my veto ground. With orders sealed, waiting for a launched rival would put the Ducted at 2041, late against a 2037 entry. Reread it in 2035, as Culp commits to. What would change my mind: test or field data only. That means a core or component failure not yet turned off, a slip that puts 2036 at risk, or shortages concentrating again in the same suppliers. RISE gates for the 2035 call are as adopted: flight test done, core durability turned on and off, and more than 20% fuel burn shown in engine test. Promise no RISE date.

The Board's recommendations at review.

  • Safety and quality. We read Ali's 'no flag' as he wrote it: it is not a clearance. - Bring each Ducted design and test gate to the full board as it occurs. Each one is a cross-functional call. - Put turn-on, turn-off evidence behind the 2036 ready year before any Ducted date goes public. Durability is not traded for fuel burn or schedule. - Bring us at once any slip beyond the one year of float to 2037. Ghai puts it at about $1.0-1.2B a year in S2.
  • Quality and supply. - Keep Ali's conditions in the monthly reviews: GEnx paced behind the Ducted's peak, and the watch on the 9 suppliers at 15 sites. - If a supply 'no' or a later cancel drops Embraer, retest GEnx net of the strain it would then add. Beside a lone Ducted it is -1.22 to -1.23 in every column. Bring the two to us together.
  • Delivery, for the 2035 round. - Reread the Ducted on our cancellation test. A cancel passes only if it is worth at least zero in every plausible column. - A cancel of an engine an airframe has selected also needs a stated reason why Safran would agree. - Show the $3.33B write-off beside the cost of keeping the programme. - Bring the RISE product decision to that round on Ali's milestones: flight test done, compact-core durability turned on and off, and more than 20% fuel burn shown in engine test. It becomes a product only on an airframer path. - Keep the one RISE allowance unspent, and declare it separately if it is ever used.
  • CFM parity rule (Safran consent). - The public statement announces two CFM launches with consent assumed, not given. - Record Safran's actual answer from CFM governance in the 2035 notes, together with what Safran funds. If it declines, withdraw plainly, as Ghai says. - From now on, present CFM programmes in public as joint with our partner. - Assert no Safran position until one is on the record.
  • Cost and capital. The case is thinner than the grid's $10B suggests. - The Ducted item stays ahead of GEnx alone only while the chance that no airframer launches (S1) is below about 0.62. - Launching now beats waiting for 2035 only below about 0.45 (Ghai), worth $0.6-1.3B net. - Carry that chance and all six column weights in each round's predictions. - Keep booking low; -21.0 is right. - Keep the 70% payout whole, with the package at about $1.0B a year. - Keep the premium count: $0 of $2.0B this round, $0 of $4.0B for the game, and the RISE allowance $0 of $15B.
  • Objective. Say plainly in the notes that NB share stays below 50% in S3 and S6 even with the package: about 43% in S3 in 2040, on Ghai's arithmetic. We spend no premium on that leg unless the grid pays for it.
  • Public statement. It passes our disclosure checks: - no rival named and no blame; - no price talk; - no Ducted, Embraer or GEnx date and no Open Fan entry year; - the Ducted is not called next-generation. Keep it that way. 'The open fan won't be ready' stays a statement of fact, never a date.

Final

Orders (as adjudicated). Launch ducted engine; Partner with Embraer; GEnx upgrade

Expected scenario. S2: Airbus launches NGSA and selects CFM alongside P&W (code 6), continuing today's dual-source A320neo pattern; Boeing holds this round. Picked from the public record (no launch, no rival engine on it, the A320neo is dual-source today), not from a hoped-for selection, and it sits below S1 for every plan, so it books low. S1 carries the largest single weight (0.30), but the launch columns together carry 0.70 and S2 is the likeliest of them.

Best grid plan in that scenario. Ducted + Partner Embraer + GEnx upgrade, at -20.69 in S2. That is +11.38 against hold (-32.07), +10.61 against GEnx alone (-31.30) and +1.21 against Ducted alone (-21.90). It is the plan chosen, so the premium is nil. It is also the best grid plan in S3, S4 and S5, and the weighted best on my weights (-36.84), on Ghai's (-36.07) and on equal weights (-50.41). Premium paid: +0.00 $B. $0.00. The chosen package is the best grid plan in the expected column, S2 (-20.69), so no PV is given up against it. - Doctrine premium: $0.00. - Objective premium: $0.00. - Running count: this round $0.0 of $2.0B; the game $0.0 of $4.0B. - RISE allowance, stated apart: $0 of $15B, unspent. No Open Fan launch this round. For reference: Ducted alone would have carried $1.21B. On an S1 reading the package gives up $6.00B against GEnx alone, over the cap. I do not book that, because S1 is not my expected column, and on my stated weights the package is the weighted best (-36.84 against GEnx alone at -41.80).

Answers to the Board.

  • Safety first: Ali's readiness and durability review in the package, with test evidence behind 2036; strike or rebut the 20% line; Ducted as a defence, RISE as the next generation; no durability traded for fuel burn. Taken up. Ali's review is in the package. - Every ready year passes his binding date test: Ducted 2036 = 2030 + 6; Embraer counts 2037; GEnx counts 2042 or the first Re-engine; Open Fan 2045. - He states candidly that 2036 is the board's development time, not a turn-on, turn-off result. So 2036 stays inside the company, and no Ducted, Embraer or GEnx date and no Open Fan entry year is in the public statement. - He raises no safety or durability flag. That is recorded as not a clearance: every design and test gate is a cross-functional call [CX-0012]. - The 20% line is rebutted in the rationale. It binds RISE as the next generation; a ducted engine has less than half the open fan's gain [CX-0183, CX-0180], so it stands only as a hard-rule-3 defence of the installed base and is never called next-generation. - Durability is not traded [CX-0208].
  • Delivery and timing: if you expect an airframer to launch this round, launch the Ducted now rather than in 2035, and say why in the rationale. Taken up. Launched now, the Ducted is ready in 2036, against a 2037 NGSA or 7-year fps entry and a 2040 10-year fps; a 2035 launch would be ready only in 2041. - Ghai sizes waiting at about $4.3B in S2 and S3, $4.5B in S5 and $1.1B in S4. Waiting saves $0.49B in S6 and up to $4.00B in S1. - The net edge for now is +$1.06B to +$1.26B on my weights. Waiting wins only once P(S1) passes about 0.45; mine is 0.30. - I record in private that the edge is thinner than the grid's $10B suggests.
  • Put the expected column and weights for all six columns in predictions; show each Board item against Do Nothing in the expected column and the worst column. Taken up. The expected column is S2; the weights are S1 .30, S2 .25, S3 .10, S4 .10, S5 .15, S6 .10. - The package against Do Nothing: +11.38 in S2; worst column S1 at -5.22. - Item rows, S1 to S6: - ducted (with Embraer defaulted): -6.00 / +10.61 / +13.05 / +10.17 / +12.85 / -1.38; weighted +4.96. The worst is S1, equal to its $6B bill. - Embraer partnership: 0.00 / +2.44 / +4.88 / +3.73 / +3.97 / +1.12; weighted +2.18. - GEnx: +0.77 to +0.78 in every column. - On equal weights my reading matches yours: ducted item +6.55.
  • Keep RISE funded as technology and bring the product decision to the 2035 round; if an airframer launches, say plainly the Open Fan would wait; keep the RISE allowance unspent. Taken up. The Open Fan is held and RISE stays funded, with no cancel (H5). - The product call is set for 2035, on Ali's gates: flight test done, core durability turned on and off, and more than 20% shown in engine test. - The public statement says that if an airframer launches a new narrowbody now, the open fan won't be ready for it and we won't ask anyone to wait. It gives no date. - The objective note says 'ready by 2050' would be out of reach on our tests on that path; we don't stretch them. - RISE allowance: $0 of $15B, unspent.
  • Cost and capital: add projects only where the grid pays the $2B strain (Embraer and GEnx with the Ducted, never GEnx beside a lone Ducted); premium in dollars; payout at least 70%; say whether the Ducted comes out of buybacks and what Safran funds. Taken up. - Embraer and GEnx ride together with the Ducted under one strain charge. GEnx beside a lone Ducted is excluded (-1.22 to -1.23 in every column). - Premium: $0.00 against the best plan in S2. Running count: $0.0 of $2.0B this round and $0.0 of $4.0B for the game; the RISE allowance is stated apart and unspent. - New R&D plus strain is about $1.0B a year against about $2.5B of room, and the payout stays at or above 70%. - Analyst context only, per Ghai: unbudgeted spend would come out of buybacks, with payout still well above 70%. - What Safran funds: joint practice on a 50/50 programme would share CFM spend, but the record shows no Safran position, so I assert none. The board charges the full $4B to us.
  • CFM parity rule: name the Safran gate for each narrowbody order, with the reason Safran would agree; do not assert a Safran position. Taken up. - ducted engine: consent assumed. It keeps both airframers' next aircraft on a CFM engine, and with them the aftermarket the partners split equally; that reason is stated because a launch ahead of a committed airframe is not shown in joint practice. - Embraer partnership: consent assumed, as a CFM engine for a third airframer ('serve every airframer'). - Open Fan and emissions lobbying: held, so no ask. - GEnx: GE alone, no gate. No Safran position is asserted, and CFM pricing is not discussed outside the partnership [CX-0184].
  • Public statement: name no rival, blame no one, no CFM price talk without Safran, no Open Fan entry before 2045, no Ducted date that testing does not support. Taken up. The statement: - names no rival engine maker and blames no one; - has no price or terms; - gives no Ducted, Embraer or GEnx date and no Open Fan entry year at all ('it's really not for us to say' [CX-0205]); - makes no fuel-burn or durability claim for the ducted engine and never calls it next-generation; - keeps RISE as our next generation.

Objective. Dominate NB engines (CFM at least 50% in 2040, 2045 and 2050), using Ghai's arithmetic of the share rules (inference): - S1 and S2: met under the package (76% in S1; well above 50% in S2). - S4 and S5 (the code-7 columns): about 43-44% without the Ducted, back above 50% with it. Embraer's +5 pp adds margin, so the package carries the objective there. - S3 and S6: at risk on every non-Open-Fan row. In S3 we keep only the Boeing slot, about 43% in 2040 even with Ducted and Embraer; S6 is far below. No PV is given up for this leg; the package is also the best plan in PV. Introduce the Open Fan (launched and ready by 2050): not met. A 2030 launch is ready in 2045, the same as a 2035 launch, and waits in every launch column at -$8.00B to -$57.60B. The leg stays open only through a 2035 launch, which is ready in 2045. If an airframer launches now with entry in 2037-2040, Ghai sizes the 2035 Open Fan leg at $16.07B to $57.60B against hold on today's grid. That is above the $15B RISE allowance in every launch column, so on that path we would say plainly that 'ready by 2050' is out of reach on our tests, rather than stretch them. Objective premium this round: $0.

Other moves.

  • Offer a CFM engine to every airframer on every new narrowbody (public): This is H1: we refuse no airframer and lock none out [CX-0587, CX-0185]. The offer is a LEAP derivative or the new ducted engine, as each customer chooses. No price or terms are stated in public: CFM narrowbody pricing is a joint decision with Safran [CX-0184].
  • CFM partner consultation on the Ducted and Embraer launches (private): Both CFM orders go through CFM governance with Safran. Consent is assumed, with stated reasons. The Ducted keeps both airframers' next aircraft on a CFM engine, and with them the aftermarket the partners split equally. Embraer puts a CFM engine in front of a third airframer, which fits 'serve every airframer'. The record shows no Safran position, so none is asserted. GEnx is GE alone and needs no gate.
  • Supply-base readiness for a three-project stack (FLIGHT DECK reviews) (private): Ali's condition is taken up. GEnx upgrade work is paced behind the Ducted's development peak; GEnx counts no earlier than 2042 without a Re-engine. Monthly operating reviews cover the 9 suppliers at 15 sites behind 80% of past shortages [CX-0613]. LEAP OE delivery and spares come first, and spares never crowd out OE [CX-0529]. The trigger to drop Embraer and GEnx is a supply 'no' from Ali on field data.
  • Cross-functional design and test gates on the Ducted (private): Every Ducted design and test gate is a cross-functional call, never one person's [CX-0012]. Durability is not traded for fuel burn or schedule [CX-0208]. The 2036 ready year stays inside the company until a turn-on, turn-off test backs it [CX-0009].
  • Keep RISE funded as technology and set the gates for the 2035 product call (private): There is no cancel and no 'program dividend' [CX-0174, CX-0214]. Ali's milestones must be in hand by the 2035 round: (1) the ground and flight test done; (2) compact-core durability turned on and off, with the HPT dust testing closed; (3) more than 20% fuel burn shown in engine test, not analysis; (4) noise below today's LEAP. The product call is made in 2035, on the bulletin and these tests.
  • Fund the package inside the capital allocation framework (private): The package needs about $1.0B a year of new R&D and strain ($0.67B Ducted plus $0.33B strain) against about $2.5B of room. Returns stay at or above 70% of FCF [CX-0645], and the A-range balance sheet is held. Any unbudgeted spend comes out of buybacks, not the dividend or the rating. That is analyst context only, per Ghai.
