Board guidance before the ExCo met

Priorities.

  • Do not miss the cycle. Submit GTF2 Solo: launch if selected. Against hold it is 0 / +50.49 / 0 / +22.16 / +49.76 / 0 / 0 (S1-S7). It is never below Do Nothing, it costs nothing unless an airframer selects P&W, and it is the only order that puts GTF2 on a 2030 NGSA or fps in time. Ready in 2036 against NGSA's EIS of 2037 and fps's of 2037 (7-yr) or 2040 (10-yr/Embraer). A round in which every order is hold leaves -27.76 in S2/S3/S5/S6 and never reaches this Board.
  • Return before commitment. The Board commits capital on a selection on the public record. An unconditional launch must earn its franchise-defence margin on Mitchill's weights: 3.79 x (pS3 + pS6) - 2.00 x (pS1 + pS7) >= +$0.5B over launch if selected. That is about 0.43 odds against a break-even of 0.35. It must also name its 2035 cancel round.
  • Durability first. GTF2 must be ready by the EIS of the airframe it serves (2036 against 2037 leaves one year of margin), with time on wing proven, not fuel burn alone. Parts for the GTF fleet's recovery must not be drawn into a new programme: the fleet beats a new engine.
  • The dividend and the debt path stay whole. GTF2 is about $0.33B a year, roughly 5.6% of the ~$6B self-funded envelope. RTX net debt is below 1x EBITDA by 2030E in both broker models. A new engine competes with buybacks, never the dividend, and no envelope stretch is needed or offered this round.
  • Joint Venture only once Rolls-Royce is on the record. No Joint Venture with RR: commit this round: the grid gives it -2.00 in S7 and 0 elsewhere, no Rolls-Royce commitment is public and no airframe carries code 1, 4, 5 or 7. If one ever forms, it shares risk, never the gear or core technology.

Expects to see. (1) The grid row of the submitted orders and the hold row for each Board item, column by column, S1-S7. (2) Calio's expected scenario, his predictions over S1-S7 and premium, which should be 0 for launch if selected. If the package contains no Joint Venture commit, no premium is needed. (3) Shared-source doctrine relief declared in the rationale, because launch if selected triggers on codes 6 and 7: S2, S4 and S5 are all shared codes. (4) Mitchill's column probabilities, the weighted item value of launch if selected against hold and, if an unconditional launch is proposed, the edge 3.79 x (pS3 + pS6) - 2.00 x (pS1 + pS7) against launch if selected. (5) The cancel round, 2035, with its write-off of $1.67B (2 x 5/6): the cancel saves only $0.33B, so the launch must stand on its edge, not on the option. (6) The envelope check: about $0.33B a year against ~$6B, the dividend covered and debt still on its pre-ASR path. (7) Eddy's ready year (2036 for a 2030 launch) against each live airframe's EIS (NGSA 2037; fps 2037, or 2040 for the 10-yr or Embraer route), plus his parts and AOG result for the GTF fleet. (8) Both veto checks, each stated as cleared or respected: Mitchill's four grounds and Eddy's two. overrides must be empty. (9) A public statement that offers GTF2 to both airframers on standard terms, gives no EIS earlier than launch + 6 and books no selection. Anything missing the Board will compute from the brief and note in a recommendation.

Would approve.

  • GTF2 Solo: launch if selected. Against hold its item value is S1 0, S2 +50.49, S3 0, S4 +22.16, S5 +49.76, S6 0, S7 0: never negative, so it passes Return hurdle and Bounded downside at any weights (+17.49 even with equal weights). Its value in S2/S4/S5 is its own trigger, so it passes Proof before commitment. Ready in 2036, before every possible 2030 EIS. Its $0.33B a year fits the envelope. Needs no premium. Approval is subject to Eddy's durability and parts pass and to no unrespected ExCo veto.
  • GTF2 Solo: launch as franchise defence, only under three conditions. First, Mitchill's weights give 3.79 x (pS3 + pS6) - 2.00 x (pS1 + pS7) >= +$0.5B against launch if selected (L - LIS is -2.00 / 0 / +3.79 / 0 / 0 / +3.79 / -2.00). Second, the 2035 cancel round is named with its $1.67B write-off. Third, Mitchill's 'carrying an unselected engine' ground is cleared in his memo. Its worst column against hold is -2.00 (S1, S7), its own bill, so it passes Bounded downside. Equal weights give +0.51, only just at the bar, so the case must rest on stated weights for S3 and S6.
  • hold on either field is not a Board item and is never vetoed. Joint Venture with RR: hold is what the Board expects this round.

Would veto.

  • Joint Venture with RR: commit in any combination this round, on Joint Venture conditions: no Rolls-Royce commitment is on the public record and no live airframe has code 1, 4, 5 or 7. On the grid it is -2.00 in S7 and 0 elsewhere beside hold or launch if selected, and 0 beside launch, so it never beats hold. No declared premium can carry it, because no live airframe's EIS exists for its engine to serve. Acceptable alternative: hold.
  • GTF2 Solo: launch whose weighted edge over launch if selected is below +$0.5B, or that names no 2035 cancel round, on Committed airframe and Bounded downside. The same order is vetoed on Proof before commitment if its case rests on S2/S4/S5 upside: those columns are identical for launch if selected, so they cannot justify an unconditional launch. A case that books an unrecorded selection is vetoed on the same ground. Acceptable alternatives: launch if selected, hold.
  • Any Board item carrying a Mitchill veto (dividend or debt path, unselected engine, aggressive terms, unproven upside) or an Eddy veto (durability not proven before EIS, parts or capacity short) that the CEO did not respect, or any entry in overrides. Ground: governance.
  • Any engine item that Eddy's memo shows not ready by the EIS of the airframe it serves, or with durability unproven. Ground: Durability first.
  • Any plan that needs the dividend to give, or that pushes debt off its pre-ASR path. Ground: Dividend and envelope.

Recommendations.

  • Miss a cycle. Submit GTF2 Solo: launch if selected this round. It is legal, GTF2 launched in 2030 is ready in 2036 before any 2030 airframe's EIS (2037/2040), and it weakly dominates Do Nothing in every column: +$50.49B if NGSA selects P&W, +$22.16B if fps does, +$49.76B if both do, and nothing spent otherwise. A 2035 trigger would come too late for a 2030 NGSA (ready 2041 against 2037).
  • Declare shared-source doctrine relief in the rationale. launch if selected triggers on codes 6 and 7 as well as 2, and every selection column on this grid (S2, S4, S5) is a shared code. The sole-source doctrine needs that stated explicitly, not assumed.
  • Show the return against Do Nothing and against a buyback. Give each Board item's weighted value against hold, and for any unconditional launch give the S3/S6 weights that carry its +3.79 gain against the -2.00 lost in S1 and S7. The Board asks for an edge of at least +$0.5B over launch if selected. Below that, the $2B is better used to buy back stock.
  • If an unconditional launch is proposed, write the 2035 cancel test into the plan: cancel if no airframe has selected P&W, booking $1.67B. Note in the memo that the cancel saves only $0.33B, so the launch must pass on its weighted edge, not on the option to exit.
  • Durability before entry into service. Eddy's memo should state the ready year (2036) against each EIS and the time-on-wing basis, not efficiency alone. It should also show that GTF2 engineering and castings do not slow the GTF fleet's AOG recovery: the fleet comes first.
  • Joint Venture: hold this round. Revisit in 2035 if Rolls-Royce commits publicly or an airframer selects code 1, 4, 5 or 7. A GTF2 already launched would fold in and speed the Joint Venture engine's readiness. Any commitment shares risk and investment, never the gear or core technology.
  • Public statement. Offer GTF2 to both airframers on standard terms, with entry into service no earlier than launch + 6 (2036 for a 2030 launch). Promise no durability not yet proven, say nothing about either airframer's dates, and do not imply a selection P&W does not hold.
  • Dividend and debt. Mitchill's memo should confirm that the dividend is covered and that debt returns to its pre-ASR path with GTF2 in the plan. At about $0.33B a year (5.6% of the envelope), a new engine competes with buybacks, not with the dividend or the rating.

Chris Calio frames the round

Question. Control what you can control. Nobody has launched anything yet, but 2030 is the round in which a new NGSA or fps would choose its engines. GTF2 launched this round is ready in 2036, so it is the only P&W engine that can meet a 2030 airframe's entry into service (NGSA 2037; fps 2037 on the 7-year route, 2040 on the 10-year or Embraer route). A trigger in 2035 would be ready in 2041, too late for a 2030 NGSA. So the question this round is which order puts GTF2 on any 2030 airframe that selects us without spending $2B on an engine nobody has asked for. The second question: is an unselected NGSA franchise hedge (launch) worth losing $2.00B in S1 and S7 to gain $3.79B in S3 and S6? The fleet comes first throughout. Is the demand visible, do the business model, timing and volume work, and is durability mature at entry into service?

Situation. PUBLIC RECORD (2030 bulletin): - No programme has been launched. Everyone is on today's products (737 MAX, 787, A320neo, A350; LEAP, GTF, GEnx, Trent). - Narrowbody engine share 2026-29: CFM 76%, P&W 24%, RR 0%. Widebody: CFM/GE 42%, RR 58%. - No engine selections are on the record. Rolls-Royce has made no Joint Venture commitment, and no live airframe carries a Rolls-Royce code (1, 4, 5, 7). OUR POSITION: - Status quo ΔPV is +0.00 (yield 100.0%, enterprise value $110B). - Objective: Restore credibility is NOT MET (no new P&W engine on a new airframe). Capitalise on the GTF (ΔPV ≥ 0) is MET at +0.00. THE GRID, in $B: - Do Nothing loses 27.76 in every column where NGSA enters service without us (S2, S3, S5 and S6, since hold cannot answer a selection) and 2.85 in S4. Missing the cycle is large: we lose our half of the A320neo slot. - launch if selected minus hold, S1-S7: 0 / +50.49 / 0 / +22.16 / +49.76 / 0 / 0. - launch minus launch if selected: -2.00 / 0 / +3.79 / 0 / 0 / +3.79 / -2.00. The +3.79 in S3 and S6 is the board's +10 pp for a GTF2 that is ready but not fitted. - A Joint Venture commit adds -2.00 in S7 only. Beside launch it adds 0, because a live GTF2 folds in. TIMING: - GTF2 launched in 2030 is ready in 2036, one year ahead of a 2037 NGSA. - My operating dates have slipped by between one quarter and two years (the GTF Advantage, the H2 2023 inflection, the 2025 AOG decline). Discount my dates; Eddy's readiness check binds. CASH (analyst baseline, real-world context): - GTF2 costs about $0.33B a year, about 5.6% of the ~$6B self-funded envelope. - RTX net debt is below 1x EBITDA by 2030E in both the MS and GS models. 2030E is the strongest balance-sheet year either model shows. THE BOARD'S GUIDANCE: - It approves launch if selected at any weights. - It approves an unconditional launch only if the edge over launch if selected is at least +$0.5B and the 2035 cancel is named. - It vetoes any Joint Venture with RR: commit this round.

Options to test.

  • A. GTF2 Solo: launch if selected, Joint Venture with RR: hold (row 'GTF2 Solo if selected'), S1-S7: 0 / +22.73 / -27.76 / +19.31 / +22.00 / -27.76 / 0. Worst column -27.76 (S3, S6), the same as Do Nothing. Never below hold. My default.
  • B. GTF2 Solo: launch, Joint Venture with RR: hold (row 'GTF2 Solo'), S1-S7: -2.00 / +22.73 / -23.97 / +19.31 / +22.00 / -23.97 / -2.00. This is the NGSA franchise-defence hedge, with a 2035 cancel written in: if no airframe has selected P&W, cancel and book $1.67B. - Edge over A = 3.79 × (pS3 + pS6) − 2.00 × (pS1 + pS7). It breaks even when pS3 + pS6 ≈ 0.53 × (pS1 + pS7); the Board's bar is +0.5. - Its case may not rest on S2, S4 or S5, which are identical to A. - Off-grid, and not to be booked: a 2030 launch is the only way to answer NGSA if it switches to a P&W code in 2035 before a 2037 EIS.
  • C. GTF2 Solo: hold, Joint Venture with RR: hold (Do Nothing), S1-S7: 0 / -27.76 / -27.76 / -2.85 / -27.76 / -27.76 / 0. The baseline for every Board item. It misses the cycle in every column where an airframe selects us.
  • D. launch if selected + Joint Venture with RR: commit: as A but -2.00 in S7. Weakly dominated by A. Tested only to show it fails, and the Board vetoes it.
  • E. launch + Joint Venture with RR: commit: identical to B on the grid (a live GTF2 folds in), but the Joint Venture conditions are unmet, the commitment is public, and the Board vetoes it. For completeness only.
  • F. hold + Joint Venture with RR: commit: 0 everywhere except -2.00 in S7. Dominated. Off.

Red lines.

  • Safety and durability first. No P&W engine goes on an airframe before it is ready. GTF2 (ready 2036 on a 2030 launch) must be ready by the EIS it serves (NGSA 2037; fps 2037, or 2040 on the 10-year or Embraer route), with time on wing and LLP life proven, not fuel burn alone. Eddy's readiness check binds me [PX-0035][PX-0073].
  • The fleet beats a new engine. GTF2 may not draw castings, powder metal or engineering away from the GTF fleet's AOG recovery [PX-0080].
  • No new engine without a committed airframer. launch if selected is the form. An unconditional launch is allowed only as NGSA franchise defence, only where NGSA may launch without P&W, and only if Mitchill's expected edge over launch if selected is ≥ 0 (his ground 2 binds; no premium buys past it), with the 2035 cancel written in. No hedge for fps alone; never a launch for share alone [P-0746][PX-0109][PX-0009].
  • Shared source (codes 6, 7) is accepted as declared doctrine relief against the sole-source rule. 40-50% of a shared platform is acceptable, and we aimed for about 40% of the A320neo [P-1292][PX-0058]. S2, S4 and S5 are all shared codes, and the decide step will state this explicitly.
  • The dividend never funds an engine, and debt stays on its pre-ASR path. A new engine competes with buybacks only. No envelope stretch [PX-0081][P-0669][P-0686].
  • Value, not share. No launch-style discounts, concessions or free upgrades in other moves or the public statement [PX-0055][PX-0100].
  • Joint Venture: no commit before Rolls-Royce is on the public record or a live airframe carries code 1, 4, 5 or 7. If one forms, it shares risk and investment, never the gear or our core technology [P-1233].
  • No widebody engine move [PX-0027].
  • Never speak for an airframer's dates or rates. No EIS earlier than launch + 6. Book no selection that is not on the public record [PX-0062].
  • The Board's would-veto list, carried in: - any Joint Venture with RR: commit this round; - a launch whose weighted edge over launch if selected is below +$0.5B, that names no 2035 cancel, or whose case rests on S2, S4 or S5 or on an unrecorded selection; - any item carrying an unrespected Mitchill or Eddy veto, or anything in overrides; - any engine not ready by the EIS it serves, or with durability unproven; - any plan that needs the dividend to give or pushes debt off its pre-ASR path.
  • Red lines are never traded for PV. Any premium is declared in $B, inside the team's $1B cap. A Board item that trails hold passes only as a declared premium of $0.5B or less that serves the objective.

Initial lean. LEAN: GTF2 Solo: launch if selected, Joint Venture with RR: hold. Premium $0B. Why launch if selected: - It is never below Do Nothing: +50.49 in S2, +22.16 in S4, +49.76 in S5, 0 elsewhere. - It spends nothing unless an airframer selects us. - It makes the commitment coincide with visible demand [PX-0109][PX-0009]. - It is the only form that answers a 2030 selection in time. - It meets both objective tests in exactly the columns where launch does (S2, S4, S5), so the objective needs no premium. - Shared-source relief (codes 6 and 7) will be declared. The unconditional launch (B) is under test, not favoured: - My own rough prior is S1 0.25 / S2 0.25 / S3 0.15 / S4 0.05 / S5 0.10 / S6 0.10 / S7 0.10, which gives an edge of about +$0.25B: positive, but below the Board's +$0.5B. - My incrementalism bias is flagged: I assumed a next single-aisle "mid-next decade" [PX-0093], and a 2030 NGSA with a 2037 EIS is that cycle. - Equal weights give +0.51. - The answer turns on pS3 + pS6 against pS1 + pS7, so Mitchill's weights decide: - edge below 0: B is struck on his ground 2; - edge between 0 and +$0.5B: the Board would veto B, so I keep launch if selected and declare a doctrine premium equal to the edge (within the $1B cap); - edge of +$0.5B or more, with Eddy's readiness and parts pass: I would weigh B as NGSA franchise defence, with the 2035 cancel ($1.67B) written in. Joint Venture: hold. Revisit in 2035 if Rolls-Royce commits publicly or an airframe carries code 1, 4, 5 or 7, with the gear and core technology protected. Other moves (public, no effect on the board): GTF Hot Section durability kit insertion continues across the fleet on standard commercial terms. PROPOSED DISCLOSURE: "We have learned our lesson from the prior iterations of the GTF, and the fleet comes first. Pratt & Whitney will commit its next-generation geared turbofan, GTF2, in any round an airframer selects it, sole or shared source, on standard terms. It will be ready six years from launch, 2036 for a 2030 selection, with time on wing proven before entry into service. We will not speak for any airframer's plans or dates; that is theirs to announce."

The Board's recommendations at review.

  • The cancel test needs one wording fix. The private other move says 'cancel only if no live new narrowbody carries a P&W code'. Read literally, that would cancel a triggered GTF2 where NGSA or fps is live but has dropped P&W. That is the S3/S6-type path, where a ready GTF2 earns its +10 pp, and it is the error Mitchill corrected in my own guidance; the Board accepts his correction. Align the move with his memo: consider a cancel only where no new narrowbody is live at all, and keep GTF2 where an airframe is live without us. Any 2035 cancel will be a Board item, and it must beat hold on the 2035 grid. While a live airframe still carries a P&W code and GTF2 can meet its EIS, it must beat hold in every plausible column (Premature exit). The write-off is $1.67B, which saves only $0.33B.
  • Public statement, adopting Eddy's advice (a). 'Will commit GTF2 in any round an airframer selects it' should read 'where GTF2 can be ready by that airframe's entry into service'. A 2035 selection on a 2030 airframe could not be met (ready 2041 against an EIS of 2037 or 2040), and a promise we cannot keep costs the credibility the 2050 objective is meant to restore.
  • Back the absolute 'no new programme takes parts or engineers away' with the weekly pacing-parts review Eddy names, or soften it to a stated condition. Keep full-life LLPs at EIS and severe-environment validation written as a gate before EIS, not as a durability claim. The Board faces derivative claims over GTF oversight and wants no unproven durability promised.
  • Durability margin. One year between the 2036 ready year and a 2037 EIS is thin, and the Advantage's certification slipped about a year. If GTF2 is triggered, the 2035 package should report severe-environment test status and any slip against the EIS it serves. Eddy's parts pass rests on the board, not on data, so it should also give a GTF fleet AOG and pacing-parts count. The fleet beats a new engine.
  • Premium ledger. Report the Board-item premium (0 here) separately from Calio's doctrine premium of $0.26B against an unconditional launch, so that the company's $1B cap is tracked across rounds without double counting.
  • Next round, Miss a cycle. If no airframe launched in 2030, submit GTF2 Solo: launch if selected again in 2035. Ready in 2041, it would meet a 2035 NGSA or fps 7-year (EIS 2042) and a 10-year or Embraer route (2045). An unconditional 2035 launch is ready in 2041 and can never be cancelled, so it must pass on the grid alone. It must also show an edge over launch if selected of at least +$0.5B on Mitchill's weights.
  • Joint Venture: hold until Rolls-Royce's commitment is on the public record or a live airframe carries code 1, 4, 5 or 7. Then re-test commit on the 2035 grid. A triggered GTF2 folds in and adds no new R&D. Any commitment shares risk and investment, never the gear or core technology.
  • Dividend and debt. If GTF2 fires, Mitchill's 2035 memo should confirm actual spend against the ~$6B envelope, the dividend covered and net debt still on its pre-ASR path. GTF2 competes with buybacks only.

Final

Orders (as adjudicated). Launch GTF2 if selected

Expected scenario. S1, rivals hold (0.28), narrowly ahead of S2, Airbus launches NGSA and selects P&W on code 6 (0.22). Nothing is launched or selected on the record, and Mitchill's first read of any launch date is timing.

Best grid plan in that scenario. In S1, the best plan is GTF2: hold at +0.00, tied with GTF2 Solo if selected at +0.00, which does not fire because there is no selection. Our orders therefore take the best value in the expected column. They also keep +22.73 in S2, +19.31 in S4 and +22.00 in S5, where hold loses 27.76, 2.85 and 27.76. The unconditional launch would give -2.00 in S1. Premium paid: +0.26 $B. This is a doctrine premium, not a Board-item premium. - launch if selected trails the unconditional launch by its expected edge: 3.79 × (pS3 + pS6) − 2.00 × (pS1 + pS7) = +$0.26B at my weights (+$0.34B at Mitchill's). - I keep it for the red line 'no new engine without a committed airframer' [P-0746][PX-0109][PX-0009]. The edge also fails the Board's +$0.5B franchise-defence bar, so the Board would veto launch. - Objective premium: $0. Both orders meet Restore credibility in S2, S4 and S5, and launch if selected meets Capitalise in more columns. - Total: $0.26B, inside the $1B cap. - Against hold, launch if selected is worth +$16.20B at my weights, so no Board premium is needed (the Board's premium for this item is 0).

Answers to the Board.

  • Miss a cycle: submit GTF2 Solo: launch if selected this round. Taken up. GTF2 Solo: launch if selected is submitted. - Against hold: 0 / +50.49 / 0 / +22.16 / +49.76 / 0 / 0. That is +$16.20B at my weights and +$13.69B at Mitchill's, never negative. - Ready in 2036 against NGSA 2037, fps 7-year 2037 and fps 10-year or Embraer 2040, per Eddy's binding check. - A 2035 trigger (ready 2041) would be too late.
  • Declare shared-source doctrine relief in the rationale. Taken up, declared in rationale section 9. - S2 (code 6), S4 (code 7) and S5 (codes 7 and 6) are all shared. - Shared source is accepted against the sole-source rule [P-0746] as doctrine relief. The company accepts 40-50% of a shared platform [P-1292], and we aimed for about 40% of the A320neo [PX-0058]. - On NGSA it is also franchise defence (inference).
  • Show the return against Do Nothing and against a buyback; any unconditional launch needs an edge of at least +$0.5B over launch if selected. Taken up. launch if selected against hold is +$16.20B at my weights and +$13.69B at Mitchill's. - The unconditional launch edge is 3.79 × (pS3 + pS6) − 2.00 × (pS1 + pS7): - my weights (S3 + S6 = 0.27, S1 + S7 = 0.38): +$0.26B; - Mitchill's: +$0.34B; - equal weights: +$0.51B. - At both my weights and Mitchill's it is below the +$0.5B bar. So no unconditional launch is submitted, and the $2B stays uncommitted (buyback capacity) unless an airframer selects us. - The $0.26B is declared as a doctrine premium.
  • If an unconditional launch is proposed, write the 2035 cancel test into the plan; the cancel saves only $0.33B. No unconditional launch is proposed. The cancel test is still written in (private other move) for any GTF2 triggered this round, in Mitchill's corrected form. - In 2035, cancel ($1.67B write-off, saving $0.33B) only if no live new narrowbody carries a P&W code, and only if the 2035 hold row does not beat the cancel row. - The literal 'no selection' test is rejected. The decision stands on the grid, not on the exit option.
  • Durability before entry into service; Eddy's memo to state the ready year against each EIS and show GTF2 does not slow the AOG recovery. Taken up. - Eddy's memo: ready 2036 against 2037, 2037 and 2040. All LLPs at full life at entry into service, validated in severe-environment testing. Field time on wing cannot be proven before entry into service, and I say so. - The durability programme is not compressed: the date moves, not the testing. - GTF2 test hardware and the ramp are ring-fenced from the AOG recovery and from Hot Section kit insertion, with the fleet team protected. This passes on the board; the 2030 data on AOG are thin.
  • Joint Venture: hold this round; revisit in 2035 if Rolls-Royce commits publicly or an airframer selects code 1, 4, 5 or 7. Taken up. Joint Venture with RR: hold. Mitchill's binding ground-4 veto is respected, and Eddy's technical conditions are unmet. - A 2035 review trigger is written in (private other move). - Any future commitment shares risk and investment, never the gear or core technology [P-1233]. A live GTF2 would fold in and count toward our $2B share.

The statement: - offers GTF2 to any airframer, sole or shared source, on standard commercial terms; - says it is ready six years from launch, 2036 for a 2030 commitment and no earlier; - promises full-life LLPs and severe-environment validation, not field time on wing (Eddy's wording); - names no airframer date or rate, and implies no selection [PX-0062].

Then the cost is about $0.33B a year from 2030 to 2035 (5.6% of the ~$6B envelope), and no envelope stretch is needed. - On the analyst baseline (context, not booked): 2030E FCF of $12.1-12.6B against dividends of $5.0-5.6B, and net debt/EBITDA of 0.76-0.94x. That is p = 0.35 at my weights. - launch meets it in the same columns. The off-grid chance of a later code switch is not booked. PV given up: - for the objective: $0; - for doctrine: $0.26B against launch.

Predictions. Column probabilities (sum 1.00): S1 0.28, S2 0.22, S3 0.17, S4 0.05, S5 0.08, S6 0.10, S7 0.10. Expected column: S1, rivals hold. Reading: - Airbus is the likelier mover. An NGSA in 2030 with a 2037 EIS fits my own 'mid-next decade' view of the next single-aisle [PX-0093]. Total p(NGSA launched) = 0.57 across S2, S3, S5 and S6. - If it launches, I expect a shared code with CFM, which is how the A320neo flies today. Pr(P&W on NGSA | NGSA) is about 0.53. - Boeing's fps is less likely this round, at 0.23 across S4, S5 and S6. - Rolls-Royce committing to the Joint Venture in 2030 is 0.10. At these weights: - launch if selected + hold = +0.23; - launch = +0.49; - Do Nothing = -15.97. - Edge of launch over launch if selected: +0.26. If GTF2 is triggered, I expect it ready in 2036 and no earlier. I discount my own dates, so I state no EIS.

Expected ΔPV. +0.23 $B (GM valuation after the round: +3.37 $B)

Other moves.

  • Public conditional GTF2 offer on standard terms (public): Pratt & Whitney will commit GTF2 in any round an airframer selects it, sole or shared source. It is ready six years from launch (2036 for a 2030 commitment, no earlier), with all life-limited parts at full life at entry into service and durability validated in severe-environment testing first. Standard commercial terms: no launch-style discount, concession or free upgrade [PX-0055][PX-0100]. The offer books no selection and names no airframer date.
  • GTF Hot Section durability kit insertion continues across the fleet (public): Continued insertion of the Hot Section kit across the GTF fleet, charged on standard commercial terms and not given away [PX-0088][PX-0106][PX-0100]. It has no effect on the game board. The fleet comes first [PX-0080].
  • Ring-fence the fleet's parts and engineering from GTF2 (private): This is Eddy's condition, adopted. If GTF2 is triggered, its test hardware and later production ramp take no castings, forgings or powder-metal disks from the GTF fleet's AOG recovery or from Hot Section kit insertion. The fleet durability team stays ring-fenced, GTF2 is staffed from the GTF Advantage engineering pool [PX-0351], and the pacing parts are reviewed weekly. If anything gives, the date moves, not the testing.
  • 2035 cancel test written into the plan (Mitchill's corrected form) (private): This applies only if GTF2 is triggered this round. In 2035, cancel it (write-off $2B x 5/6 = $1.67B, saving $0.33B) only if no live new narrowbody carries a P&W code, and only if the 2035 brief's hold row does not beat its cancel row at Mitchill's weights. The test is NOT the literal 'no selection': that would kill a ready GTF2 in exactly the column where it earns its +10 pp. A 2030 GTF2 is ready in 2036 and cannot be cancelled after 2035.
  • Joint Venture review trigger for 2035 (private): Re-test Joint Venture with RR: commit on the 2035 grid if Rolls-Royce's commitment is on the public record or a live airframe carries code 1, 4, 5 or 7. The tests are Mitchill's cash test and Eddy's technical test. The Joint Venture shares risk and investment, never the gear or core technology [P-1233]. A live GTF2 would fold in and count toward our $2B share.

Board guidance before the ExCo met

Priorities.

  • Product safety and maturity before entry into service: no compressed maturity, no entry into service disclosed earlier than launch plus development years (2037 for a 2030 UltraFan NB), and support in place before entry into service. This is our absolute priority. [RG-0027, RG-0025, R-1476, R-0970, RX-0296, RX-0283]
  • Protect the widebody cash cow, as Control has framed it. The board will not have a narrowbody programme and a widebody programme on the record together, which charges a one-off $5B strain whatever the dates. No item may lose more than its own bill. Narrowbody risk should move towards the $4B Joint Venture share wherever a partner route exists. [RG-0019, R-0929, R-1127, RX-0214, R-1574, RG-0068]
  • An airframe first, and profit over share. Narrowbody enters only on a selection, through launch if selected, never on speculation and never with a premium. Narrowbody is an option the company does not need. [R-1005, R-0994, RX-0058, R-1011, R-1561, R-1582]
  • A partner on aligned terms. The Joint Venture with P&W is our preferred way to share narrowbody risk, but we commit only once P&W's commitment is on the public record. [R-1010, RX-0118, R-0318, R-0916, RG-0065]
  • The balance sheet and returns stay intact: strong investment grade, no equity, leverage below about 1.5x, no borrowing for distributions, and payments from sustainable free cash flow. [RX-0242, RG-0041, RG-0059, RG-0060, R-0900]

Expects to see. For each Board item in the package, the board needs the following. (1) The grid row of the submitted orders and the row with each Board item at hold, matched by label. For example, "UltraFan NB if selected" against "UltraFan NB: hold", column by column S1-S9. (2) The CEO's expected scenario and his predictions, with column weights from McCabe or the CEO. With nothing on the record, the ExCo's rule gives 0.1 to a selection column; show the weights. (3) McCabe's co-signature on every launch, launch if selected and commit, with her worst column, the unselected loss and capex a year. A triggered Solo is about $1.14B a year for 7 years (about £0.84bn at 1.36 $/£). Company-funded R&D runs at about £0.6-0.9bn a year in the 2026 analyst baseline (MS IS r129), so set out the funding. (4) Watson's ready year against each live or launching airframe's entry into service, and his support plan before it. A 2030 UltraFan NB is ready in 2037. That is zero margin for an NGSA or fps 7-year launched in 2030 (both enter service in 2037) and 3 years for an fps 10-year or fps via Embraer (2040). (5) Both veto checks (CFO balance-sheet and Civil maturity), with every red-line flag struck or rebutted in the rationale and overrides empty. (6) Any premium in premium, item by item, with its reason. (7) Control's objective metrics for the submitted plan in every column: own narrowbody development money, NB+WB strain, RR widebody and narrowbody share in 2050. Any breach of the $4B bound or the strain line should be stated openly, with the reason. (8) The public statement, checked against the disclosure test.

Would approve.

  • UltraFan NB Solo: launch if selected, with Joint Venture with P&W, UltraFan WB and Trent 1000 upgrade at hold. Compared with the "UltraFan NB: hold" row, the "UltraFan NB if selected" row is worth 0 / +32.60 / 0 / +28.24 / +44.54 / 0 / 0 / 0 / 0 in S1-S9. It is ≥ 0 in every column, so it passes the profit test under any weights. Its worst case is 0, against a bill of -$8B. It passes maturity by construction (it triggers only if ready by entry into service), it is the airframe-first form, and there is no overlap. It needs McCabe's co-signature. We note one trade: in S2, S4 and S5 own narrowbody money is $8.0B, against Control's $4B bound. We would accept that only because the trigger is a selection, the grid pays +$28.24B to +$44.54B there, and this is the only route into an airframe launched in 2030. The ExCo must state the trade in its rationale.
  • Trent 1000 upgrade: launch alone, with UltraFan NB Solo and Joint Venture with P&W at hold. Against hold its value is -0.98 in S1-S7 and -0.29 in S8-S9, so it is negative in every column and the worst case is above its -$2B bill. It passes only with McCabe's co-signature and its weighted shortfall (at most $0.98B, inside the $3B cap) declared in premium with a durability reason. We would approve it on our tests, but we recommend against it this round (see recommendations).
  • A hold on every field. Holds are not Board items and are never vetoed. A plan that holds everything scores 0.00 in every column and meets all of Control's lines, though narrowbody entry stays unmet.

Would veto.

  • UltraFan NB Solo: launch (unconditional). Ground: no airframe on the record. The bulletin shows nothing launched, and the ExCo's own hard rule bars any UltraFan launch without an announcement. Against hold it is worth -8.00 in S1, S7, S8 and S9. Against launch if selected it gains +3.57 only in S3 and S6 and loses 8.00 in S1, S7, S8 and S9. It beats the conditional form only if w(S3)+w(S6) > 2.24 × (w(S1)+w(S7)+w(S8)+w(S9)). It also commits $8B in every column, against Control's $4B. Acceptable alternatives: launch if selected, or hold. [R-1005, R-0994, RX-0058]
  • Joint Venture with P&W: commit. Ground: partner alignment. P&W's commitment is not on the public record, and no live airframe carries a P&W code (2, 4, 6 or 7). Ground: profit. Against hold its value is -4.00 in S7 and 0 elsewhere, so it is weighted below 0 whenever S7 carries any weight. Beside the upgrade it is -9.00 in S7, below its -$4B bill (reasonable worst case). Acceptable alternative: hold. [R-1010, R-0318, R-0916, RG-0033]
  • UltraFan WB: launch. Ground: no airframe on the record, since no 787 or A350 Re-engine is launched or announced. Ground: capped-out premium. It is -4.00 in S1-S7 and -0.90 in S8-S9, so its weighted shortfall far exceeds the $1B limit for an UltraFan WB. Beside launch if selected it is -9.00 in S2, S4 and S5, below its -$4B bill, and it fails the overlap test. Acceptable alternative: hold. [R-1574, RG-0033, RG-0019]
  • Trent 1000 upgrade: launch beside UltraFan NB Solo: launch if selected or launch, or beside Joint Venture with P&W: commit. Ground: one big programme at a time, since no upgrade may run while an UltraFan is in development or could be triggered this round. Ground: reasonable worst case. Against the "UltraFan NB if selected" row it is -5.98 in S2, S4 and S5. Against "hold + commit to JV" it is -5.98 in S7. Both are below its -$2B bill because the $5B strain is stacked on it. Acceptable alternative: hold. [R-0929, R-1127, RX-0214, RG-0033]
  • Any launch, launch if selected or commit without McCabe's co-signature. Any item on which Watson's binding Civil veto still stands against the final orders. Any red-line flag left unresolved, or any non-empty overrides. The ground in each case is governance or safety and maturity. [RX-0213, RG-0044, RX-0296, RX-0283]

Recommendations.

  • An airframe first. Carry narrowbody only as UltraFan NB Solo: launch if selected. Show in the rationale why the conditional form beats an unconditional launch: the launch loses $8B in S1, S7, S8 and S9 for +3.57 in S3 and S6. A 7-year engine launched in 2035 would miss the 2037 entry into service of an airframe launched in 2030, so the conditional order this round is the only route into such an airframe.
  • Control's terms. Put the objective metrics for the submitted plan in the rationale. State plainly that a triggered Solo takes own narrowbody money to $8.0B (S2, S4, S5) against the $4B bound, and that the board accepts this only because the trigger is a selection. Set out now how the ExCo would move towards a shared programme next round. If P&W commits, a 2030 Solo would fold into the Joint Venture, but its spend to date still counts ($5.7B if folded in 2035). Show that grid before proposing it.
  • Keep widebody programmes off the record this round. The Trent 1000 upgrade is negative in every column: -0.98 in S1-S7 and -0.29 in S8-S9, because it counts only from the first Re-engine's entry into service, or 2042. Once it is on the record, it charges the $5B strain on any later narrowbody programme, the Joint Venture included, whatever the dates. That would close the narrowbody route Control's $4B bound points to. The widebody franchise test is not triggered: RR widebody share is 58% in every column and no Re-engine is on the record. Re-test the upgrade or UltraFan WB when a 787 or A350 Re-engine is on the record, or if 2040-2050 widebody share falls below 50%.
  • Public statement: few words, conditional and binding. Say that Rolls-Royce will launch UltraFan for any airframer that selects it, and that our preferred route is a partner, with the Joint Venture open to Pratt & Whitney. Give no entry into service earlier than launch plus seven years (2037 for a 2030 launch), and say nothing about an airframer's dates. A commitment by P&W on the record is our condition for committing next round.
  • Maturity and support. Watson should state the ready year against each airframe that might launch this round. UltraFan NB would be ready in 2037, which is zero margin against an NGSA or fps 7-year entry into service in 2037. A zero-margin pass is acceptable but should be named, with a support and MRO plan in place before entry into service and no compression of test pacing. The board will check his tests against the final orders.
  • Funding and balance sheet. McCabe should give capex a year if the Solo is triggered: about $1.14B, or £0.84bn, a year to 2037. Company-funded R&D is about £0.6-0.9bn a year in the 2026 analyst baseline (MS IS r129). She should confirm that no equity, no leverage above about 1.5x and no borrowing for distributions are needed, and say whether buybacks or other R&D give way first. We cut buybacks first, then the dividend, then new programme spend. The balance-sheet test is not applicable unless she invokes it.

Tufan Erginbilgic frames the round

Question. So, 2030. Nothing is on the record. The question is cash and quality of earnings, not share [RX-0054]. Do we put a narrowbody order on the table that costs nothing unless an airframer picks us: UltraFan NB Solo: launch if selected, worth +28 to +45 $B if we are selected? The price is that a selection takes our own narrowbody money to $8B, against Control's $4B bound. Or do we hold everything, meet every Control line, and give up the only route into an airframe launched in 2030? Second question: does any widebody spend earn its keep this round? Frankly, the grid says no.

Situation. Public record: no programme launched. No fps, no NGSA, no engine selection, no code. No 787 or A350 Re-engine. P&W has no Joint Venture commitment on the record. Observed 2026-29 is flat: NB engines CFM 76 / P&W 24 / RR 0, WB engines CFM/GE 42 / RR 58. Our status quo is +0.00 $B (EV $110B). Objective status: - Narrowbody entry: NOT met (0% in 2045 and 2050). - Widebody dominance: met (58% every year, every column on hold). - Control's terms: own NB money $0 (bound $4B); NB+WB strain $0. Timing: - A 2030 UltraFan NB is ready in 2037. That is zero margin against an NGSA or fps 7-year launched this round (EIS 2037), and 3 years against an fps 10-year or fps via Embraer (EIS 2040). - A 2035 launch is ready in 2042 and misses every airframe launched in 2030. So this round's conditional order is the only way into a 2030 airframe. - A Joint Venture can form no earlier than 2035 on our side, ready 2041, because we commit only after P&W's commitment is public. Board guidance: risk appetite 4 of 5. It would approve launch if selected with everything else at hold. It would veto an unconditional launch, a first Joint Venture commit, UltraFan WB, and the Trent 1000 upgrade beside any narrowbody order. It wants Control's metrics and the $8B trade stated openly. Widebody: 58% in every column on hold, so the 50% franchise test is not triggered. In S8 Airbus's WB airframe share drops to 25.2%, but our engine share on the board holds at 58%.

Options to test.

  • A. "UltraFan NB if selected", all else hold. Expected gain over hold +8.31 at my base weights (below), worst column 0, unselected loss 0. Four-part gate: differentiated (UltraFan about 10% better than today's best), large market (4,000 NB engines a year), viable business model only on a selection (the trigger enforces it), synergy with the UltraFan core. PASSES conditionally. Control: own NB money $8.0B in S2/S4/S5 (BREACH of $4B), $0 elsewhere; strain $0; WB 58% everywhere; NB 2050 share 36.7% / 40.5% / 51.2% in S2 / S4 / S5.
  • B. "UltraFan NB: hold" on all four levers. 0.00 in every column. Meets every Control line; narrowbody entry stays unmet. Gives up +8.31 of expected gain, above the $3B premium cap, so it is only right if McCabe's selection weights fall below about 0.036 per airframer.
  • C. "UltraFan NB Solo", unconditional. Expected +5.20, worst -8.00. FAILS the gate (no airframe, no business model). Board veto; breaks the red line. Tested only to show why the conditional form wins: the unconditional order beats it only if w(S3)+w(S6) > 2.24 x (w(S1)+w(S7)+w(S8)+w(S9)). At my weights it costs 3.11 against A.
  • D. "UltraFan NB if selected + commit to JV". Expected +7.91, worst -4.00 (S7). A first commit with P&W not on the record: Board veto and red line. Costs 0.40 against A.
  • E. "UltraFan NB: hold + T1000 upgrade". Expected -0.91, worst -0.98. Fails the gate on business model, since it pays nothing before 2042 with no Re-engine. Board would approve it but recommends against. It excludes A (red line, Board veto). Our profile default was to fund it in round 1; on this board that default reverses.
  • F. "UltraFan NB if selected + T1000 upgrade". Expected +6.15; -5.98 against A in S2/S4/S5, below the upgrade's own bill; $5B strain breaches Control's line. Board veto. OUT.
  • G. Any UltraFan WB row. Alone: expected -3.69, worst -4.00, far beyond the Board's $1B WB premium cap. Beside A: strain and -9.00 against A in S2/S4/S5. No Re-engine on the record. OUT.

Red lines.

  • Safety and maturity first. No compressed maturity. No disclosed EIS earlier than launch + 7 years for UltraFan NB (2037 for a 2030 launch), + 6 for UltraFan WB or the Joint Venture. Support in place before EIS [RX-0296, RX-0283, R-1476, R-0970].
  • No unconditional UltraFan NB Solo: launch. No airframe and no selection is on the record, so narrowbody goes in only as launch if selected [RX-0058, R-1005, R-0994]. (Board would-veto.)
  • No Joint Venture with P&W: commit until P&W's commitment is on the public record or a live airframe carries a P&W code [R-1010]. (Board would-veto.)
  • No UltraFan WB: launch without an A350 Re-engine on the record, or a 787 Re-engine on which Boeing has named UltraFan. A WB premium is capped at $1B [R-1574]. (Board would-veto.)
  • No Trent 1000 upgrade beside launch if selected, launch or a Joint Venture commit. One big programme at a time; no upgrade while an UltraFan could be triggered [R-0929, R-1127]. (Board would-veto.)
  • Control's terms: never an NB programme and a WB programme on the record together ($5B strain, whatever the dates). Own NB money within $4B, and any breach stated openly with its reason.
  • No item may lose more than its own bill in a plausible column. Size to the reasonable worst case [RG-0033].
  • Every launch, launch if selected or commit needs McCabe's co-signature against mid-to-high-teens hurdles [RX-0213]. Watson's Civil veto binds. overrides stays empty.

Initial lean. Proposal: - UltraFan NB Solo: launch if selected - Joint Venture with P&W: hold - UltraFan WB: hold - Trent 1000 upgrade: hold Why: it is the best grid plan in expectation (+8.31 at base weights) and never worse than hold in any column. Worst column 0, unselected loss 0, no premium. It is airframers first in its purest form: we launch only into a selection [RX-0058], and nothing is spent on options no airframe uses [RX-0051]. In S1, the column I expect most, it ties hold at 0. Control's metrics: - Strain $0 everywhere. - WB share 58% everywhere. - Own NB money $0, except $8.0B in S2/S4/S5. That is a stated breach of the $4B bound. I accept it only because the trigger is a selection, the grid pays +28.24 to +44.54 there, and this is the only route into a 2030 airframe. Next round: if P&W commits, we commit to the Joint Venture for 2035 airframes. A triggered Solo is folded in only if McCabe's grid shows the gain. Widebody: UltraFan WB stays Do Nothing (no Re-engine on the record). The Trent 1000 upgrade is held. That reverses our round-1 default: here it is negative in every column (-0.98 / -0.29) and would put $5B of strain on any narrowbody route. "We won't do anything not profitable." [RX-0058] Draft public statement: "So, plainly: Rolls-Royce launches UltraFan in the round an airframer selects it. Not before. Entry into service no earlier than seven years from launch. Our preference is a partner; the Joint Venture is open to Pratt & Whitney, and we commit once its commitment is on the record. Widebody is our core. We don't commit that easily, and when we commit, we deliver." This stands subject to McCabe's co-signature and Watson's readiness check.

The board approves. Product safety is and always must be our most important priority, and nothing here compresses it. The order launches only if an airframer selects us and we can be ready by its entry into service, 2037 at the earliest, with support in place first. It is never below hold in any column (+8.31 on McCabe's weights). Its worst case is 0 against an $8B bill, and no widebody programme sits beside it. McCabe co-signs; Watson raises no veto. We note openly that a selection takes our own narrowbody money to $8.0B against Control's $4B. We accept that trade only because it comes with an airframe and the grid pays for it. A partner remains our route to share the risk. And we do not want to underestimate the risks: zero margin against 2037 is the one to watch.

The Board's recommendations at review.

  • Maturity, our absolute priority. A 2037 EIS is zero margin. Watson should report the narrowbody gearbox test plan to the Safety, Energy Transition & Tech Committee each round. If maturity testing shows the 7-year path cannot be met without compressing testing, he should say so before any further trigger is offered against a 7-year airframe, and offer it only against a 2040 EIS. The date moves, never the test plan. The support gates (partner MRO agreements by 2034; a shop and an EIS support team by 2036) should be reported against their dates.
  • Control's terms and the shared route. If the order does not trigger and P&W's Joint Venture commitment is on the public record next round, bring Joint Venture with P&W: commit at our $4B share. It needs McCabe's co-signature and a weighted value ≥ 0, and it brings us inside the bound. If the order triggers, own narrowbody money cannot fall below $5.7B. Propose no fold unless that round's fold row is shown against the row that keeps the Solo, column by column, and it pays. Never fold for Control's metric alone.
  • Widebody core. Keep UltraFan WB and the Trent 1000 upgrade off the record while UltraFan NB could be triggered or is in development. Once the order triggers, any widebody programme draws the one-off $5B strain whatever its dates, so responding to a Re-engine costs more. If a 787 or A350 Re-engine is on the record next round, or RR widebody share heads below 50% in 2040-2050, bring the rows for UltraFan WB and the upgrade beside the live narrowbody position. Show each item's worst column against its own bill and any declared premium against our caps ($3B in all, at most $1B for UltraFan WB). The A350 exposure in S8 (Airbus WB airframe share 25.2% in 2050) should be watched, though the board's engine share holds at 58%.
  • Funding discipline if triggered. About £0.84bn a year for 2030-37 is new money above a flat R&D envelope. McCabe should report each quarter how it is met from free cash flow and what it does to the buyback programme. Our order holds: buybacks give way first, then the dividend, then new programme spend. Any need for equity, leverage above about 1.5x or borrowing for distributions comes back to the board before it arises.
  • Public statement. The wording is clean on dates: no EIS earlier than seven years from launch, and no airframer dates. From next round, qualify "we will launch UltraFan for any airframer that selects it" with "where we can be ready by its entry into service" (Watson's note). A 2035 launch is ready in 2042 and cannot serve a 2030 airframe, and we should not promise what the maturity test forbids.
  • Airframe first, still. An unconditional UltraFan NB Solo: launch comes to the board only once an airframer has named UltraFan on the public record, with McCabe's co-signature against the ExCo's bar (+$2B; above 0 in the 2035 round). Until then, narrowbody stays conditional. It is an option the company does not need.

Round 2 · decision year 2035

2035: the Joint Venture forms, and three engine sources become two

  • P&W and Rolls-Royce both committed to the Joint Venture on sealed orders. Both solo programmes folded into it; it inherits GTF2's schedule and is ready in 2036. Rolls-Royce writes off $1.71B, and its own narrowbody money settles at $5.71B.
  • Both new narrowbodies now count two engine sources, CFM and the Joint Venture engine; CFM/GE's narrowbody share from 2040 falls from 31.7% to 27.0%.
  • CFM/GE learned the fps selection from this round's brief and held everything: nothing on its menu could change an engine code.
  • Airbus left poaching out (over its cash line, and its stricter condition); Boeing held the 787 Re-engine on its overlap rule. Both kept code 7.

We haven't built airplanes ahead of a mature design, and we won't. We're working the certification plan with the FAA one step at a time. The data decides our stage gates, not the calendar. I'm not going to give you any new dates today. The heaviest spending years on this airplane are in front of us. That's the pig in the python, and we planned for it. Debt stays first. The balance sheet is where it belongs, and we're going to keep it there through the peak. On engines, CFM, Pratt & Whitney and Rolls-Royce are all on this airplane. CFM certifies first, and the others follow on their durability evidence. Our customers and our production system both need more than one source of supply. Our 737 MAX and 787 customers come first while we do this. Stable production and the KPIs set our rates, and we'll keep growing the 787 out of the capacity we've built in Charleston. We still develop with our suppliers on cost-plus and risk-share terms, not fixed price. I think we're turning it. I don't think it's turned. It is so much more important that we do this right than fast, and we still have a lot of work to do.”

AirbusDo Nothing

Public statement: “Our core principles of safety, quality, integrity, compliance and security will remain at the heart of all we do. Our next-generation single-aisle aircraft is in its final phase of development and remains on track for entry into service in the second half of the 2030s, on the clock we set when we prepared it. We intend to offer a choice of engines. CFM, Pratt & Whitney and Rolls-Royce are all on the programme, and each engine will join the aircraft once its maturity and durability are proven: we will not compromise on certification. Until the new aircraft enters service, the A320neo and A350 families remain our priority, with a disciplined and controlled production ramp-up, delivery performance for our customers through the transition and continued work to secure our own supply chain, engines and critical materials first. We are funding the programme with financial discipline, within our financial flexibility and our existing shareholder return policy. We will continue to work with our industry partners for a tariff-free, zero-for-zero regime for aerospace trade. Preparing the Airbus of the 2030s means one well-prepared programme at a time, for a stronger and more sovereign European aerospace industry.”

CFM/GEDo Nothing

Public statement: “Safety, quality, delivery and cost, always in that order. That doesn't change this year. Let me tell you what we know and what we don't. Both new single-aisle aircraft have launched, and both customers chose to put CFM on them alongside others. We're honored by that. We also know we don't have a birthright on any of it. We keep a place on an airplane the same way we earned it: readiness, durability and support, one customer and one engine at a time. CFM is a 50-50 partnership with our partner, and we do this work together. Our ducted engine is in its last year of development. It goes into service when testing says it's ready, and not a day before. Durability doesn't get traded for schedule. Our work with Embraer continues. There are no new programmes from us this year. We'll fund what we have within our capital allocation framework and keep the balance sheet where it is. RISE remains our next generation. We're all in on the open fan technology, and it stays funded as technology. It's really not for us to say when that architecture enters service. Our customers decide when. The new aircraft come first, and we won't ask anyone to wait. Here's what we don't know: how fast our customers will want to go once they're flying, and how those fleets will split. We won't give you dates or numbers our testing and our customers haven't earned. Commercial matters we work privately, with our customers and with our partner. You'll ask about competition. I won't speak to that. We judge ourselves on our own execution. It's that simple, ain't that hard.”

Pratt & WhitneyCommit to Joint Venture with RR

Public statement: “Bad news first. GTF2 has not yet earned its durability record, and our dates have slipped before. GTF2 is in development for NGSA and fps. It will be ready in 2036 and no earlier, and we are not compressing a single test to hold that date. Before it enters service it has to clear two gates: durability validated in severe-environment testing, and every life-limited part at full life. Those are gates, not claims. If anything has to give, the date moves, not the testing. The fleet still comes first. We keep inserting the Hot Section durability kit across the GTF fleet, and we review the pacing parts every week so that neither the GTF2 ramp nor any Joint Venture work takes parts or engineers from that work. We control what we can control. Airbus has invited us onto its new single-aisle as a risk-sharing partner. We accept on standard commercial terms: we carry our own engine's development, and there is no launch-style discount, no concession and no free upgrade. On fps we follow in sequence once we show maturity and durability. That is the right test, and we will meet it with test data, not with price. Today Pratt & Whitney puts on the record its commitment to a Joint Venture with Rolls-Royce on the next narrowbody engine. It forms only if and when Rolls-Royce also commits, and until then nothing has formed. It shares risk and investment, not technology. The gear, the core and the GTF2 technology stay Pratt & Whitney's, and GTF2's configuration, date and team do not change. We will offer only what can be ready by an airframe's entry into service, and we will not speak for any airframer's plans, dates or rates. Those are theirs to announce. These are responsible bets with responsible paybacks.”

Rolls-RoyceCommit to Joint Venture with P&W

Public statement: “So, plainly. UltraFan narrowbody stays on plan: ready no earlier than seven years from launch, with support in place before entry into service. If testing needs longer, the date moves, not the test plan. Both airframers have selected all three engine makers, Pratt & Whitney included. So if there is to be a partnership, the time to decide it is now. Last time we said we would commit once Pratt & Whitney's commitment was on the record. Frankly, with decisions made at the same time, waiting for that means deciding too late. So our Joint Venture commitment is on the record today, on one condition: it forms only if Pratt & Whitney commits too. If not, nothing is spent, and we will not hold it open. We don't need partnership for capability, but our preference is that. We launch for any airframer that selects us where we can be ready by its entry into service. Widebody is our core: no new widebody programme beside the narrowbody, and Trent time on wing keeps improving. We won't do anything not profitable. When we commit, we deliver.”

How each company decided: Board guidance, ExCo, Board review (private during the game)

In the agents' own words. S1, S2, … are the scenario columns of that company's own payoff grid in its brief (they differ by company); ids in brackets are the agents' evidence citations; order names are shown in plain words.

Boeing: the decision chain (Kelly Ortberg, Jay Malave, Stephanie Pope; Boeing Board)
StepWhat happened
Board guidanceBoeing Board: risk appetite: 4.5 of 5, unchanged. We keep the launched 10-year fps whole and back no second development. Every Board item must stay above -$1B in each column, and S1, S2 and S3 all count as plausible. The plan must stay above -2.78 in the risk case (S3), which is Do …
FrameKelly Ortberg: initial lean: Hold course, and change nothing on the board. - fps: hold. Continue the 10-year ramp to EIS 2040 with its headroom. - fps engine code: 7, resubmitted. I would rather be explicit than rely on None being read as no change. It gives three sources and …
Test (CFO)Jay Malave recommends: Do Nothing. Tests failed: Buffer test (slip leg), plan C: fps cancel + 787 Re-engine hold; Buffer test (slip leg), plan D: fps cancel + 787 Re-engine launch; Cash path of each bill, plan B (CEO asks 2 and 5); Full cost of a cancel (plans C and D). Vetoes on options: fps: cancel, with 787 Re-engine hold (plan C) (binding); fps: cancel, with 787 Re-engine launch (plan D) (binding); 787 Re-engine: launch, with fps hold (plan B) (not binding)
Test (operating head)Stephanie Pope recommends: Do Nothing. Tests failed: Two-front strain, plan B (787 Re-engine launched in 2035) [doctrine B-0341, H4] (CEO ask 3). Vetoes on options: 737 rate: increase (not binding); fps hold + 787 Re-engine: launch (row B), and cancel fps + 787 Re-engine: launch (row D) (not binding); fps: cancel (rows C and D) (not binding); fps engine code changed to give fewer than two sources (1, 2, 3; or 4, which drops CFM) (not binding)
DecideKelly Ortberg: Do Nothing
Veto check (CFO)Jay Malave concurs
Veto check (operating head)Stephanie Pope concurs
Board reviewBoeing Board: not called; no Board item (every launch, commit or cancel order at its default)

Board guidance before the ExCo met

Priorities.

  • Keep the launched fps whole on its 10-year plan, with safety first. EIS stays 2040 with its headroom, and production does not run ahead of certification. Stage gates are KPI-based. If the plan has to move, reset it once and conservatively, and never cancel (H5). Keeping the fps is worth +17.55 to +18.99 against cancelling it in every column.
  • One development at a time. No 787 Re-engine this round. Launched in 2035, it would overlap the fps development (2033-2040) by 5 years, against our 2-year cap, and add $3B of strain before discounting. Against hold it adds only +0.65 in S1 and S3, which is below our $1B tie band (epsilon), and it loses -2.99 in S2. The next round where it would not overlap is 2045, and only if Airbus has not launched the A350 Re-engine by then (H3, second half).
  • Debt stays first. Net debt has been at $0 since 2029 in the base case and since 2030 in the stress case, and the brief's objective cell is 2029 / yes / yes ($0.0B) for every plan that keeps the fps. The fps cash peak is still ahead: $8.4B of programme cash in 2036, which leaves about $2.5B of stress-case free cash flow that year (our computation from the brief). No new equity. The Board reserves any dividend or buyback, and none should come to us before that peak is past and the rating is solidly investment grade.
  • A stable engine supply. Keep engine code 7. That gives CFM + P&W GTF2 (ready 2036) + Rolls-Royce UltraFan NB (ready 2037): three sources on the fps in 2040, 2045 and 2050, and three narrowbody engine makers in the market. The brief shows the enabler met. Do not change the code unless a maker proves not ready by EIS.
  • Hold course in the risk case. S3, covert Delay Tactics, costs the fps 5 percentage points of share for 5 years from EIS. The answer is supplier readiness (engines first) and keeping the workforce. It is never a rushed date or a cancellation.

Would approve.

  • fps: hold, which continues the 10-year fps to its 2040 EIS. A hold is never vetoed, and the Board supports it. Against cancelling, keeping the fps is worth +18.99 / +18.99 / +17.55 (S1 / S2 / S3) with 787 Re-engine at hold, and +17.97 / +17.97 / +16.53 beside a Re-engine. Do Nothing scores +0.66 / -0.80 / -0.78, and S3 sits $2.00B above the -2.78 floor. Objective cell: 2029 / yes / yes ($0.0B) / 3 (3).
  • 787 Re-engine: hold. Never vetoed. In S2 it is the best plan by $2.99B. In S1 and S3 it gives up $0.65B against the Re-engine row, a tie within epsilon that H4 settles; log that $0.65B as premium if the expected column is S1 or S3.
  • fps engine code 7, kept: resubmitted as 7, or None if the GM reads None as no change. It gives CFM + P&W GTF2 + Rolls-Royce UltraFan NB, three sources in 2040, 2045 and 2050 and three narrowbody engine makers. With NGSA's code 7 it forms no disallowed pair, and it does not change Boeing's payoff. We never veto an engine code.

Would veto.

  • fps: cancel, with 787 Re-engine at hold. Its value against keeping the fps is -18.99 / -18.99 / -17.55. - Cancellation test: keeping the fps does not lose $1B in any column; it gains $17.55B to $18.99B in every one (H5). - Downside: below -$1B in every column. - Rating first: S3 is -18.33 against the -2.78 floor, $15.55B below it. Malave's binding buffer veto would also fall on it. - Engine enabler: it collapses from 3 sources to 1. Acceptable alternative: hold.
  • fps: cancel, with 787 Re-engine: launch. Against the same row with the fps kept it scores -17.97 / -17.97 / -16.53. S3 is -16.66, $13.88B below the floor. It fails the same tests as above, plus the Re-engine grounds below. Acceptable alternatives: fps hold and 787 Re-engine hold.
  • 787 Re-engine: launch, with fps at hold. Its value against hold is +0.65 / -2.99 / +0.65. - One development at a time: a 2035 launch (development 2035-2040) overlaps the 10-year fps development (2033-2040) by 5 years, against our 2-year cap, with $3B of strain before discounting (H4). - Downside: S2 is -2.99, below -$1B, and the bulletin has not ruled out an A350 Re-engine. - Business case: +0.65 is below epsilon ($1B) in whatever column the CEO expects. It would pass Rating first (S3 -0.13 against the -2.78 floor), but that does not cure the three failures. Acceptable alternative: hold. Bring it back in 2045, when it would not overlap, and only if Airbus has not launched the A350 Re-engine.

Recommendations.

  • Keep the fps whole and on plan. Hold the 2040 EIS and its headroom. Before the next stage gate, bring the Aerospace Safety Committee four things: written confirmation that MAX 7/10 certification is complete (still open from Round 1), the Chief Engineer's readiness view, the certification plan agreed with the FAA with no production-certification concurrency, and the stage-gate KPIs. If the plan has to move, reset it once and conservatively, never in serial slips. Do not cancel. A cancellation would write off about $30.16B ($60.32B x 5/10) with its debt penalty staying, and the fps is worth $17.55B to $18.99B more kept than cancelled in every column.
  • Hold the 787 Re-engine this round. Against the fps alone, a 2035 launch overlaps the fps development by 5 years (2035-2040) and adds $3B of strain before discounting. Its value is +0.65 in S1 and S3, below our $1B tie band, and -2.99 if Airbus re-engines the A350. Doing less and doing it better is the right call. If you expect S1 or S3, log the $0.65B as a doctrine premium, well inside the $2B cap. Bring the widebody case back in 2045, when it would not overlap the fps, and only if Airbus has not launched the A350 Re-engine by then (H3, second half).
  • Keep engine code 7. On the brief it fits CFM + P&W GTF2 (ready 2036) + Rolls-Royce UltraFan NB (ready 2037) at a 2040 EIS. That gives three sources in 2040, 2045 and 2050 and three narrowbody engine makers, and the enabler is met. CFM certifies first, and the others follow in sequence on durability evidence. Our Aerospace Safety Committee, which includes propulsion expertise, will ask for each maker's life-limited-part and durability status against EIS. Change the code before EIS only if a maker proves not ready, and never to fewer than two sources.
  • Debt stays first, and the cash peak is still ahead. Report the base and stress net-debt path every round. Programme cash runs $7.2B (2035), $8.4B (2036) and $7.8B (2037). By our computation from the brief, stress-case free cash flow falls to about $2.5B in 2036. Seek no new equity and keep the revolvers undrawn. Bring no dividend or buyback proposal before the fps cash peak is past and the rating is solidly investment grade. Those decisions are reserved to the Board, and the tracker's surplus-to-owners rule does not make them for us.
  • Prepare for the risk case without reacting to it. S3, covert Delay Tactics, costs the fps 5 percentage points of share for 5 years from EIS (worth $1.44B on the grid). Keep fragile suppliers funded and hot, engines first, since LEAP-1B remains the 737's sole source until the fps arrives. Report the supplier-shortages KPI at each stage gate and keep the retention and train-before-build measures. Report any supply or talent disruption to the Aerospace Safety Committee as a live problem. The response is a single conservative reset, never a cancellation.
  • Public statement and objectives. Add no new dates and do not answer Airbus's calendar. Reaffirm the plan, the FAA-first certification plan and debt first. Accept plainly that no order this round can lift narrowbody share before 2040: incumbency stays at 38% in 2040 and the 50/50 split is out of reach. Pay no objective premium for either.

Kelly Ortberg frames the round

Question. We are five years into a ten-year fps. NGSA is due in 2037 and our EIS is 2040. Do we keep the plan whole and add nothing? Or does anything on this grid beat that by more than ε ($1B) inside the hard rules? Three parts: (1) Is there any case for touching the fps? Cancel is barred by H5 and loses $17.55-18.99B. A reset needs evidence of a slip, and the brief shows none. (2) Does a 2035 787 Re-engine belong in this round? It would overlap the fps by 5 years against H4's 2-year limit, and it is a bet on an A350 choice we cannot see. (3) Does engine code 7 still give us three sources at a 2040 EIS, and is every maker on track for it? Airbus's calendar does not enter it [B-2313].

Situation. Decision year 2035. Our position. The fps (10-year ramp, Solo) launched in 2030 and is in development, with EIS 2040 on plan. Code 7 is on record, and the brief fits CFM + P&W GTF2 (ready 2036) + RR UltraFan NB (ready 2037): 3 sources in 2040, 2045 and 2050. CFM's ducted engine is ready in 2036, and the CFM-Embraer partnership in 2037. NGSA is in development (EIS 2037), also on code 7, which is not a disallowed pair. The A350 has not been re-engined. The Rate Increase lapsed after 2030. Gates. The brief reports no live quality, FAA, supply-chain or certification problem. So the KPI gate and the FAA-process gate are open, and there is no trigger for a reset. Grid (S1 rivals hold / S2 Airbus launches A350 Re-engine / S3 risk case, covert Delay Tactics): - fps hold + 787 hold (Do Nothing; continues the fps): +0.66 / -0.80 / -0.78 - fps hold + 787 Re-engine: +1.31 / -3.79 / -0.13 - cancel fps + 787 hold: -18.33 / -19.79 / -18.33 - cancel fps + 787 Re-engine: -16.66 / -21.76 / -16.66 Differences: - The Re-engine adds +0.65 / -2.99 / +0.65. - Keeping the fps instead of cancelling is worth +18.99 / +18.99 / +17.55 with the 787 on hold, and +17.97 / +17.97 / +16.53 beside a Re-engine. - Delay Tactics would cost us $1.44B (S1 to S3). An A350 Re-engine costs our 787 $1.46B even if we hold. - Malave's slip leg is S3. The floor is Do Nothing's -0.78 less $2B = -2.78. Debt. Net debt has been $0 since 2029 (base) and 2030 (stress). The fps cash peak, the pig in the python, is still ahead of us. Programme cash is $7.2B (2035), $8.4B (2036), $7.8B (2037), $6.6B (2038) and $5.4B (2039). Base free cash flow is $8.07B, $7.12B and $7.53B in 2035-37. My reading of the tracker puts stress-case free cash flow at about $3.5B, $2.5B and $2.9B; Malave should confirm. The objective cell for both fps-kept rows is 2029 / yes / yes ($0.0B) / 3 (3). The cancel rows fall to 1 (1) engine source. Mission. Debt repair and the engine enabler are met. Incumbency and 50/50 are not met: 38% in 2040 (the worst year), 43% in 2045, 47% in 2050. No order this round can lift narrowbody share. The Re-engine is widebody, the rate is hold only, and the fps cannot be accelerated. A cancel would only make share worse. Board risks (its would-veto list; guidance, not red lines): - any fps cancel, with or without a Re-engine; - 787 Re-engine launch: 5-year overlap, -2.99 in S2, +0.65 is below ε; - any premium above $2B, or any premium not logged. Board items open from Round 1: - written confirmation that MAX 7/10 certification is complete; - the Chief Engineer's readiness view; - the certification plan agreed with the FAA, with no production-certification concurrency; - each engine maker's durability status. The Board's 2040 'in production' question is now answered by the brief: 3 sources counted in 2040.

Options to test.

  • A. Continue: fps hold, code 7, rate hold, 787 Re-engine hold. This is the Do Nothing row: +0.66 / -0.80 / -0.78. It is the baseline for every test. S3 sits $2.00B above the -2.78 floor by construction. Worst column -0.80 (S2). Objective cell 2029 / yes / yes ($0.0B) / 3 (3) in every column. My lean.
  • B. Continue + 787 Re-engine in 2035: +1.31 / -3.79 / -0.13. Against A: +0.65 / -2.99 / +0.65. It passes the slip leg (-0.13, $2.65B above the floor). But H4 strikes it (5-year overlap against a 2-year limit), its gain in S1 and S3 is inside ε, and it loses $2.99B in S2, beyond the Board's -$1B line. Objective cell unchanged at 2029 / yes / yes ($0.0B) / 3 (3). I test it only to put the row and the premium in front of the Board; it is not a live option.
  • C. Cancel fps + 787 hold: -18.33 / -19.79 / -18.33. Struck by H5. It fails the buffer by $15.55B, writes off $30.16B with the penalty staying, and cuts engine sources from 3 to 1. Closed.
  • D. Cancel fps + 787 Re-engine: -16.66 / -21.76 / -16.66. Struck by H5 (and the Re-engine grounds in B). It fails the buffer by $13.88B. Closed.
  • E. Engine code inside plan A: 7 (3 sources) against 6 (CFM + GTF2, 2), 5 (CFM + UltraFan NB, 2) and 3 (CFM, 1). Same payoff in every case. Code 7 keeps at least two sources even if one maker slips past 2040, so it is the resilient choice. I test it only against Pope's readiness and durability results.

Red lines.

  • H1 and H3, first half (Round-1 rules): I ruled on both in 2030, with evidence. H1 was lifted; H3's first half no longer binds. Both are spent; neither is in force in 2035.
  • H2 cannot bind (EIS 2040). H7 has no trigger: the brief reports no crisis and no certification trouble.
  • H3, second half: no 787 Re-engine once Airbus has launched the A350 Re-engine. It has not fired, since the A350 is not re-engined. If it fires, the widebody option closes for the rest of the game.
  • H4: at most 2 years of overlap between a Solo fps and the 787 Re-engine. A 2035 Re-engine overlaps 5 years ($3B strain), so it is struck. The next legal round is 2045 (overlap 0), and only subject to H3.
  • H5: never cancel a launched fps. Both cancel rows are struck. If the plan has to move, one conservative reset, never serial slips [BX-1318, BX-1321].
  • H6: no Rate Increase under a live problem or as a reply to Airbus. Only hold is on offer.
  • H8: ties within ε ($1B) go to doctrine. Doctrine plus objective premium may total at most $2B, and every premium is logged.
  • Team rule: Malave vetoes any plan whose S3 (risk case) is below -2.78. The KPI doctrine vetoes a Rate Increase under a live problem (moot this round).
  • My own: no production-certification concurrency [BX-1263]; no fixed-price development, only cost-plus or risk-share [BX-1262, BX-1304]; never walk away from core customers' programmes [BX-1251]; one major development at a time [BX-1239, B-0341]; no blame on the FAA [BX-1323]; no attribution of a supplier problem to Airbus before exposure (doctrine); no new dates before the data supports them [BX-1268, B-2315].

Initial lean. Hold course, and change nothing on the board. - fps: hold. Continue the 10-year ramp to EIS 2040 with its headroom. - fps engine code: 7, resubmitted. I would rather be explicit than rely on None being read as no change. It gives three sources and three makers. - 737 rate: hold. - 787 Re-engine: hold. Every order is a default, so nothing should go to the Board as a change; the Board never vetoes a code. Expected column: S1. Airbus said it builds 'one well-prepared programme at a time', with the A320neo and A350 as its priority until NGSA enters service in 2037. S2 is close behind, because doctrine still expects an A350 Re-engine attempt. S3 is the risk case. The best grid plan in S1 is fps hold + Re-engine at +1.31, but H4 strikes it. My plan scores +0.66 there, $0.65B behind and inside ε. I log that $0.65B as premium: the known cost of H4 plus doing less and doing it better [BX-1239]. Total premium is $0.65B, inside the $2B cap. In S2 the hold is the best plan and costs nothing. Expected PV: +0.66. Cancel: never (H5). The fps is worth $17.55-18.99B more kept than cancelled in every column. Other moves: - KPI stage gates reported to the Aerospace Safety Committee, with the four open items; - suppliers funded and kept hot, engines first; - retention and train-before-build; - engine durability reviews with each maker; - debt first, with no shareholder returns proposed before the cash peak is past; - 787 growth from Charleston capacity. Public statement. Calm, about execution. No new dates, no reaction to Airbus, no blame on anyone. 'I think that we're turning it. I don't think it's turned.' [BX-1300] What would change my lean: - a failing stage gate or a live problem from Pope, which means one conservative reset, never a cancel; - an engine maker not ready by 2040, which means a code change, to no fewer than two sources; - a stress-path breach from Malave. Nothing Airbus does this round would change it.
