Kelly Ortberg decides

Orders. Do Nothing

Rationale. Decision. We change nothing on the board: fps hold (the 10-year fps continues to EIS 2040), engine code 7 resubmitted, 737 rate hold and 787 Re-engine hold. Every order is a default. Code 7 matches the code on record, and the Board never vetoes a code. So no item goes to the Board as a change. The submitted row and the default row are the same: fps hold + 787 hold, +0.66 / -0.80 / -0.78 (S1 / S2 / S3). My expected column is S1; the risk case is S3. Team rule, applied. (1) Malave's buffer test (slip leg). S3 is the brief's labelled risk case, and the floor is Do Nothing's -0.78 less $2B, or -2.78. - A (hold/hold): -0.78, which passes by $2.00B. - B (hold + Re-engine): -0.13, which passes by $2.65B. - C (cancel + hold): -18.33, which fails by $15.55B. - D (cancel + Re-engine): -16.66, which fails by $13.88B. His veto on C and D binds, and I take it. H5 strikes them anyway. (2) KPI doctrine. The rate is hold only, and the brief reports no live quality, FAA or supply-chain problem. Pope's veto has nothing to bind on. (3) Everything else is mine. The only live choice was A against B. My four questions. - Are the KPIs stable? Yes. The brief reports no live problem, and observed shares have been flat at 40.0% NB and 58.8% WB through 2034. - Are market, technology and balance sheet ready? Yes. Net debt has been $0 since 2029 (base) and 2030 (stress). Malave's stress free cash flow bottoms at $2.52B in 2036, the pig in the python, and net debt holds at $0 through 2040. - What if certification takes longer than we think? On S3, A passes. The grid has no column for our own slip, so I asked for the reset rule in advance: one reset, the bill held, the cash moved right, costed once in full. - Is this doing less, better? Yes. A is Do Nothing. Rulings. - H5: no cancel. Keeping the fps is worth +18.99 / +18.99 / +17.55 against cancelling (787 hold). A cancel would write off $60.32B x 5/10 = $30.16B in 2035 with its debt penalty staying, and it would cut engine sources from 3 to 1. If a gate ever fails, the answer is one conservative reset. - H4: a 2035 787 Re-engine (development 2035-40) overlaps the fps development (2033-40) by 5 years, against a 2-year limit, with $3B of undiscounted strain. B is struck. Even without H4 it would lose: - its gain against A is +0.65 / -2.99 / +0.65, inside ε in S1 and S3; - it lowers the worst column from -0.80 to -3.79; - it roughly halves 2036 stress headroom, from $2.52B to about $1.3B (Malave); - on a probability-weighted view, A beats B whenever S2 carries more than about 18% weight (0.65 / 3.64), and the bulletin has not ruled out an A350 Re-engine. - H3, second half: not fired, since the A350 has not been re-engined. If Airbus launches the A350 Re-engine, the 787 Re-engine option closes for the rest of the game. Otherwise the next H4-legal round is 2045 (overlap 0), and it comes back there as a review. - H1 and H3, first half: ruled on in 2030 and spent. H2 cannot bind. H6 is moot. H7 has no trigger: no certification trouble is reported, so the FAA-process gate is open. Expected column and best grid plan. I expect S1. Airbus said publicly that the A320neo and A350 stay its priority until NGSA enters service, and that it builds 'one well-prepared programme at a time'. S2 is close behind. The best grid plan in S1 is fps hold + 787 Re-engine at +1.31, which H4 strikes. A scores +0.66, $0.65B behind and within ε. Doing less and doing it better [BX-1239], and the higher-confidence plan with the higher worst column [BX-0548], settle the tie. In S2, A is best outright. Premium (H8), logged. - Doctrine premium: $0.65B, for holding the Re-engine (H4, one development at a time). - Objective premium: $0. No order this round moves narrowbody share. - Engine code 7 and keeping the fps: $0 each. - Total: $0.65B, inside the $2B cap. Engine code. Code 7 rests on doctrine, not my record (Low: I have no statement as Boeing CEO on engine selection). Its fitted sources are: - at EIS 2040: CFM + P&W GTF2 (ready 2036) + RR UltraFan NB (ready 2037), three sources; - in 2045 and 2050: the same three, with three narrowbody engine makers in the market. Codes 5 and 6 give 2 sources and codes 1-3 give 1. Only code 7 still leaves two if any one maker slips past 2040. NGSA is also on code 7, which is not a disallowed pair. Where doctrine drove the choice. - the engine code; - the strain arithmetic and the H4 limit; - supplier-ladder detail. Where my record drove it. - debt first [BX-1305]; - doing less [BX-1239]; - one reset and never a cancel [BX-1318, BX-1321, BX-1251]; - no production-certification concurrency [BX-1263]. Cash path (Malave, confirmed). - Programme cash: $7.24B (2035), $8.44B (2036), $7.84B (2037), $6.64B (2038) and $5.43B (2039). - Base free cash flow: 8.07 / 7.12 / 7.53 / 8.43 / 9.32. - Stress free cash flow: 3.47 / 2.52 / 2.94 / 3.83 / 4.72. - Net debt: $0.0B every year, base and stress. A breaks only if 2036 free cash flow falls about 52% below consensus. - The grid already nets the debt penalty (10-year fps $19.1B undiscounted, for scale), so it is not subtracted again. Open Board items. - MAX 7/10 closure: the brief is silent. Our last evidence is 'certification next year' (2025) [BX-1873], and I still treat it as done by inference. Pope's seat tables the written closure at the gate; I won't claim a document the brief doesn't carry. - The Chief Engineer's readiness view and the FAA-agreed plan come in the same package. - Each engine maker's durability status comes through the durability reviews.

Weighing the CFO. Weighted as my independent check [BX-1316]. His record is one call (Low), so I take only his buffer veto as binding and treat the rest as advice. His buffer test binds on C and D (S3 -18.33 and -16.66 against the -2.78 floor), and I take it in full. His rebuild of the cash path matches mine. Stress free cash flow is 3.47 / 2.52 / 2.94 in 2035-37, net debt is $0 in base and stress through 2040, and A breaks only at about 52% below consensus in 2036. I adopted his advice against B: it is inside ε, loses $2.99B in S2, lands a $5B bill beside the $60.32B fps bill at 2040 and halves 2036 stress headroom to about $1.3B. It agrees with my own H4 ruling. His reset rule (bill held, cash moved right, costed once) is now my standing instruction if a gate fails. His point on retaining 2035-39 surplus (a stress cushion of about $17.5B) goes to the Board as a recommendation; the decision is reserved to the Board. I also accepted his premium log: $0.65B, $1.35B inside the cap.

Weighing the operating head. Weighted as a thin seat. Her record is Global Services, and her KPI, strain and supplier results run on the operations doctrine, so I read them as results on the brief's data, not as measured programme documents. Her KPI veto has nothing to bind on: the rate is hold only and there is no live problem. I accept her other results: - Strain: $0 on hold, and $3B over a 5-year overlap for a 2035 Re-engine, which fails H4. - Engine readiness: 4, 4 and 3 years of margin before 2040, with code 7 kept. - Suppliers: kept hot, engines first. - Workforce measures: in place, though not measured. - Headroom: 92% of the fps's value survives the risk case, and none of the headroom has been used. She was right not to invent the design-maturity reading, the FAA plan's sign-off or the Chief Engineer's view. I take her offer to table them, with the MAX 7/10 closure, at the next gate. I note that her conclusion that MAX 7/10 is complete is an inference from a silent record, not a document. Her H4 and H5 flags match my rulings, and I struck nothing that was flagged, since rows B, C and D are not ordered.

Board guidance before the ExCo met

Priorities.

  • Safety and the five pillars first. NGSA's last development years run to entry into service in 2037 with nothing concurrent. The Board accepts no item that the operating head fails on safety, quality, the A320 ramp shield or a supply crunch, and no override of those tests [AG-0038, A-0331, AX-0015, A-0303].

  • Protect liquidity in NGSA's last two spend years, 2035 and 2036. NGSA runs at $5.07B a year against the $5.2B line, leaving $0.13B of headroom, so no new programme cash should be added in those years. Net cash, the A+/A1 rating and the 30-50% payout must stay fundable with no equity raise and no dividend cut [AX-0022, A-0402, AG-0062, AX-0104, AG-0058, AG-0059].
  • Integrity: nothing covert. This is the last round in which Delay Tactics could be ordered, since fps enters service in 2040, before the 2045 round. The Board's position is none [A-0299, AG-0053, A-0474, AG-0022].
  • A stable engine supply. Keep engine code 7. It fits CFM, P&W GTF2 (ready 2036) and Rolls-Royce UltraFan NB (ready 2037), which gives 3 sources and 3 narrowbody makers in 2040, 2045 and 2050 in every hold plan [A-0243, A-0360, A-0218, AX-0054].

Would approve.

  • NGSA: hold, with NGSA engine code 7 unchanged (the default, not a Board item, never vetoed). Plan row with A350 hold and Delay Tactics none: +23.37 (S1) / +22.88 (S2). NGSA stays on its clock to EIS 2037, inside the technology clock (not before 2035).
  • NGSA engine code 7 is the Board's preferred code. It fits CFM, P&W GTF2 and Rolls-Royce UltraFan NB (3 sources), and it meets both enabler metrics in 2040, 2045 and 2050. It is in no barred pair with fps's code. Codes 5 or 6 would still give dual sources. The Board never vetoes a code on its own.
  • A350 Re-engine: hold (the default, not a Board item) is the Board's preferred value this round.
  • Delay Tactics: none (the default, not a Board item) is the Board's preferred value this round. It is the only value the Board expects to approve.

Would veto.

  • NGSA: cancel. Ground: reactive cancellation (Reaction discipline), and the balance sheet. Against cancelling, holding gains $39.65B in both S1 and S2, so continuing does not lose in any column. A cancellation would write off about $25.37B ($35.52B x 5/7) in 2035 and would drop the enabler to 2 sources. Boeing's fps launch is never a ground to cancel. Acceptable alternative: hold.
  • A350 Re-engine: launch (EIS 2040). Ground: balance sheet (Liquidity, and through it Returns kept fundable). - Peak cash in 2035 and 2036 is $5.07B + $1.00B + $0.60B strain = $6.67B, $1.47B over the $5.2B line. - Its item value is +1.54 (S1) / -1.21 (S2). That passes Downside, and the 2-year overlap passes One clean sheet, but under the plan-level rule the added item is vetoed. - An override of the CFO's soft veto cannot clear the Board's Override review on this Qualified Majority item: it trails hold by $1.21B in S2. Liquidity is in any case the Board's own test. - Acceptable alternative: hold, with a return in 2045 once NGSA spend has ended, unless Boeing has launched a 787 Re-engine.
  • Delay Tactics: bottleneck or both. Ground: integrity and abnormal risk. Both moves also fail Liquidity (about $5.41-5.47B in 2035-36), and the second $1B adds -0.47 in both columns. Acceptable alternative: none.
  • Delay Tactics: poaching. Ground: balance sheet (Liquidity, plan-level rule: Delay Tactics is the added item). - One move ordered in 2035 spends $1B before fps EIS 2040, about $0.20B a year. That gives $5.27B in 2035 and 2036 against the $5.2B line, still over the unrounded $5.23B and still over if spread across six years ($5.24B). - Its item value of +1.65 / +1.66 passes Downside, and most integrity conditions now hold: fps is public and not in service, NGSA is in development, and there has been no earlier move. - The Integrity test also requires the CEO to record setting aside the team's stricter condition, which he kept standing in 2030; if he does not set it aside, the item fails Integrity as well. - Acceptable alternative: none.
  • Any plan that combines an A350 Re-engine with Delay Tactics (about $6.87B in 2035-36). Veto the A350 Re-engine first, then Delay Tactics.
  • Any override of the operating head's safety, quality, A320-ramp or supply-crunch tests, or of a five-pillars flag.
  • Never vetoed: a hold or none, an NGSA engine code on its own, or an item for its near-term earnings cost alone.

Recommendations.

  • Hold NGSA on its own clock to entry into service in 2037. Boeing's fps launch (10-yr, EIS 2040) gives NGSA a three-year lead on the public record; the Board reads it as confirmation of the case, not as a trigger. Do not accelerate, delay or cancel. A cancellation needs continuing to lose at least $1B in every plausible column, and here continuing gains $39.65B in both.
  • Engine supply: keep code 7. - All three makers launched in 2030. GTF2 is ready in 2036 (one year of margin) and UltraFan NB in 2037 (no margin); CFM's ducted engine is ready in 2036. - Code 7 meets both enabler metrics in every hold plan (3 sources, 3 makers in 2040, 2045 and 2050). It sits in no barred pair, so no fps code can force a change. - Do not change the code in reaction to Boeing. If P&W and Rolls-Royce form a Joint Venture, code 7 still fits its engine, which counts as one source, so supply stays dual. - The operating head should report to the twice-yearly safety review: the integration and certification load of three engines, with CFM certifying first; and UltraFan NB's zero margin to the 2037 EIS, a real-world risk the board does not price.
  • One programme at a time: keep the A350 Re-engine on hold this round. A 2035 launch runs at $6.67B a year in 2035-2036 against the $5.2B line. Bring it back in 2045, once NGSA spend has ended and it runs at about $1.0B a year, with a fresh grid and peak-cash test. It should come back only if no 787 Re-engine is on the public record. If Boeing launches a 787 Re-engine this round, stay out and compete on price.
  • Delay Tactics: none. This is the last round in which they could be ordered, so the Board states its view plainly: - bottleneck and both are never acceptable; - poaching fails the peak-cash line in 2035-2036 and would be vetoed; - the team's stricter condition should stay standing, as the CEO kept it in 2030; - nothing on Delay Tactics in any public line. The supply-security other_move (in-house work packages, titanium, rare earths) must stay confined to Airbus's own ramp. The Ethics, Compliance and Sustainability Committee should continue to be informed.
  • The CFO's papers, carried over from the 2030 review: - a year-by-year net-cash bridge for 2035-2037 that includes the dividend, on the FY2025 base and on the run-rate; - confirmation of the payout guardrail (lower end of 30-50% if ramp cash falls short); - the effect of the single $35.52B charge at the 2037 EIS on reported earnings and on the payout base, with no dividend cut and no equity raise outside a crisis; - the break-evens, reported if crossed: an NGSA bill above $36.4B, FCF below EUR 4.61bn, or a rate below $1.068 per EUR. Refundable advances, state support and risk-sharing remain upside and are never assumed in the case.
  • Show both columns. Name the expected column and the worst one (S2, a 787 Re-engine, where the hold plan returns +22.88). Read Boeing only from the bulletin: it states debt first and 737 MAX and 787 stability first, and a GEnx upgrade has been ready since 2033. S2 is still not ruled out.
  • Operating head: confirm the following before entry into service: - NGSA production readiness for 2037; - the A320neo ramp shield, with no supply crunch; - engines and critical materials secured for both families through the transition. The Board also asks for his safety and quality results, with any five-pillars flag.
  • Public statement: - give windows, not dates: NGSA on track for entry into service in the second half of the 2030s; - put safety first, with a disciplined and controlled ramp; - nothing timed to Boeing and nothing on Delay Tactics. The Board repeats its 2030 recommendation, which the published statement did not take up: say 'we intend to offer a choice of engines' rather than promise it. Fitting each maker depends on its engine being ready by EIS.
  • The 60/40 objective is not met: the worst year is 2050 at 53%, with 2045 at 57%. A three-year lead sets a long-run split of 53%, and no option this round changes 2045 or 2050. Delay Tactics would act only in 2040-2044, and the A350 is widebody. The Board asks that no PV, cash or integrity be traded for it. Any unpriced other_moves in support, such as delivery performance on the A320neo family or the A220 seat-size gap, are read with the package and are recommendations only.

Guillaume Faury frames the round

Question. 2035 is a consolidation round, with NGSA in its last two development years and on its clock to entry into service in 2037. Do we keep NGSA whole, with engine code 7 confirmed in what is the last round the code can change, the A350 Re-engine on hold and Delay Tactics at none? That plan has no Board items. Or does an A350 Re-engine or a single Delay Tactics move pass the five pillars, Toepfer's cash line, Wagner's production test and the Board's own tests well enough to be worth taking to the Board?

Situation. BOEING AND THE PUBLIC RECORD (bulletin only). - Boeing launched fps with the 10-year ramp in 2030, with entry into service planned for 2040. It selected code 7 with CFM as the baseline engine certifying first, on cost-plus or risk-share terms, with an FAA plan from day one. - Boeing says debt comes first, returns stay off until it is solidly investment grade, and 737 MAX and 787 stability come first, gated by KPIs. It gives no further dates. - No 787 Re-engine and no Rate Increase are on the record. GE's GEnx upgrade for the 787 has been ready since 2033. ENGINE MAKERS. - P&W GTF2 Solo: launched 2030, ready 2036. - Rolls-Royce UltraFan NB Solo: launched 2030, ready 2037, which is zero margin to our EIS. - CFM ducted engine: ready 2036. CFM-Embraer partnership: ready 2037. - P&W made no Joint Venture commitment. Rolls-Royce keeps the Joint Venture door open and would commit once P&W does. PROBLEMS REPORTED. The brief reports no supply crunch, no quality event and no technology or engine maturity slip. Observed shares have been flat since 2026: NB 60/40, WB 41.2%. OUR POSITION. - NGSA has been in development since 2030, with EIS 2037. On code 7 it is fitted with CFM + P&W GTF2 + Rolls-Royce UltraFan NB, 3 sources. - ΔPV if nobody moves is +23.37 (S1) / +22.88 (S2), with yield 115.6%. The components are +39.13 NB operating profit, -15.23 programme investment at EIS and -0.53 debt penalty. - Boeing's fps launch moved us from the S1 to the fps column of last round's grid. The plan is still positive in every column. - Peak cash is $35.52B / 7 = $5.07B a year in 2035 and 2036, against the $5.2B line: $0.13B of headroom, 97% used. The $35.52B charge lands at EIS 2037. OBJECTIVE STATUS (scored by the GM; it never changes the payoff). - Defend 60/40: NOT met. NB share is 62% in 2040, 57% in 2045 and 53% in 2050. A three-year lead (2037 against 2040) sets a 53/47 long-run split. No option this round changes 2045 or 2050: Delay Tactics would act only in 2040-2044, and the A350 is widebody. - Protect the A320 family: met at 60% before EIS. - Enabler, dual or triple sources: met, 3 sources in 2040, 2045 and 2050 on every hold plan. - Enabler, three NB makers in the market: met (CFM, P&W, Rolls-Royce in 2045 and 2050). - Cancelling NGSA would drop the enabler to 2 sources. THE BOARD'S GUIDANCE. - It treats this as a consolidation round, risk-averse at 4 of 5. - It wants NGSA held on its clock, code 7 kept, the A350 Re-engine on hold until 2045, and Delay Tactics at none, with the team's stricter condition left standing. - No new programme cash in 2035-2036. - It would veto an NGSA cancel, an A350 Re-engine launch, any Delay Tactics move and any combination of the two. MY READ OF BOEING. - Expected column: S1, rivals hold. A 787 Re-engine now would open a second front while fps is in development and debt comes first, and the GEnx upgrade already serves the 787. - S2 (787 Re-engine) is not ruled out and is the worst plausible column: +22.88 on the hold plan. - fps does not move NGSA: our own clock.

Options to test.

  • 1. COMPANY DEFAULT AND MY LEAN: NGSA hold (code 7 unchanged) + A350 hold + Delay Tactics none. - Row +23.37 (S1) / +22.88 (S2); worst column S2 at +22.88, positive. - No Board items. - Peak cash $5.07B in 2035 and 2036, nothing in 2037-2039 on programme spend; the $35.52B charge falls at EIS 2037. - Enabler 3 / 3 in 2040, 2045 and 2050.
  • 2. REFERENCE ROW, every Board item at its default: identical to option 1. This round's defaults are hold / 7 / hold / none, so the Board package and the reference row coincide.
  • 3. TEST, then likely REJECT: + A350 Re-engine (A350 Re-engine launch, EIS 2040). - Row +24.91 / +21.67; item +1.54 (S1) / -1.21 (S2). - Rule 6 passes: one launch, overlap exactly 2 years. - Rule 3 does not bind: no 787 Re-engine is on the record. - Peak cash $5.07B + $1.00B + $0.60B = $6.67B in 2035-36, $1.47B over the line. That should fail Toepfer's test and is a stated Board veto on Liquidity. - Break-even probability of S2 is 56%. At my 25-30% the probability-weighted item is only +0.72 to +0.85, under $1B. - An override of Toepfer would clear the team's $1B bar in S1 only. It cannot clear the Board's override review on a Qualified Majority item, since it trails hold by $1.21B in S2, and Liquidity is the Board's own test. - Fallback: return in 2045 with a fresh grid, only if no 787 Re-engine is on the record.
  • 4. TEST, then likely REJECT: + one Delay Tactics move (poaching is the only value the Board could even read). - Row +25.02 / +24.54; item +1.65 / +1.66. It passes the grid's $1B test in both columns. - Rules 4 and 5 now hold: fps is public and not in service, NGSA is in development, and there has been no earlier move. - Blocked on three counts: - the team's stricter condition, read literally: NGSA already enters service first in 2037 and the move shifts share, not EIS. I keep it standing. - the Board's Liquidity veto: $1B over 2035-2039 is $0.20B a year, so $5.27B in 2035-36 against $5.2B (unrounded $5.23B). - the integrity pillar. - It does nothing for the 60/40 metric (it acts only in 2040-2044).
  • 5. REJECT: Delay Tactics 'both'. Row +24.55 / +24.07. The second move adds -0.47 in both columns. It breaks rule 4 (two moves), peak cash is about $5.47B, and the Board vetoes bottleneck and both on integrity.

  • 7. REJECT: any NGSA cancel row (-16.28 / -16.77, or -14.18 / -17.41 with an A350 Re-engine). - The item is -39.65 in both columns, with a $25.37B write-off in 2035. - It breaks rule 7 and the reaction discipline: Boeing's fps is never a ground. It is a stated Board veto.
  • 8. ENGINE CODE, on option 1: keep 7. - Code 7 gives 3 sources and 3 makers in 2040, 2045 and 2050. - Codes 6 or 5 give 2 sources. Code 3 gives CFM alone. Codes 1, 2 and 4 drop CFM as a named source. - Change it only to remove a maker that is off track. Neither P&W (2036) nor Rolls-Royce (2037) is off track on the record. - Never change it in reaction to Boeing. - If P&W and Rolls-Royce form a Joint Venture this round, code 7 still fits its engine, counted as one source, so supply stays dual.

Red lines.

  • Five pillars (safety, quality, integrity, compliance, security). No order or statement that fails them, and nothing that cannot be defended to the Audit Committee or the Ethics, Compliance and Sustainability Committee. Never overridden [AX-0073, AX-0081].
  • Rule 1, NGSA clock: EIS 2037 holds, never before the 2035 technology-ready year. No acceleration or re-timing is on the table [AX-0020, A-0409, A-0225].
  • Rules 2 and 7, our own clock: Boeing's fps (10-yr, EIS 2040) neither moves NGSA nor triggers a cancellation. A cancel needs continuing to lose at least $1B in every plausible column. Here continuing gains $39.65B in both [A-0364].
  • Rule 3: no A350 Re-engine after Boeing has launched a 787 Re-engine. It does not bind this round, since none is on the record. If Boeing launches one now (S2), the A350 Re-engine is off for 2045 and we compete on price.
  • Rule 4: at most one Delay Tactics move per game, only after fps is public and before its 2040 EIS (this is the last round). 'both' counts as two and is barred. Never named in public.
  • Rule 5: poaching only while NGSA is in development (true through 2036).
  • Team's stricter Delay Tactics condition: the move must change who enters service first. On this board it cannot, because NGSA already leads and Delay Tactics shift share, not EIS. It STANDS. I do not set it aside, so Delay Tactics stay off.
  • Rule 6: at most one new launch this round. NGSA / A350 Re-engine overlap of 2 years or less unless the grid shows at least $1B more. A 2035 A350 Re-engine sits exactly at 2 years, so the rule passes, but the peak-cash guardrail is separate [A-0343, A-0401].
  • Peak-cash guardrail (Toepfer's soft veto, and the Board's own Liquidity test): one year's FCF of about $5.2B. NGSA alone runs at $5.07B in 2035 and 2036, so no new programme cash in those years [AX-0104, AX-0022].
  • The Board's would-veto list, carried in full: - NGSA: cancel; - A350 Re-engine: launch ($6.67B in 2035-36); - Delay Tactics bottleneck or both (integrity; about $5.41-5.47B); - Delay Tactics poaching ($5.27B; integrity unless the stricter condition is set aside); - any A350 Re-engine + Delay Tactics combination ($6.87B); - any override of Wagner's safety, quality, A320-ramp or supply-crunch tests, or of a five-pillars flag.
  • Board downside test: each Board item must gain in my expected column (S1) and lose no more than $2B in S1 or S2. Both columns are plausible.
  • Override budget: one per game, unused. Allowed only with at least $1B over the best passing option, recorded as a Board item, never against a pillar or red line, and never against the Board. I have no override against a Board veto. None is planned.
  • Doctrine premium: the $3B allowance covers only staying out of an A350 Re-engine after a 787 Re-engine, or skipping a second Delay Tactics move. No PV is traded for the 60/40 goal or the enabler.
  • Disclosure: windows, not dates. NGSA entry into service is 'in the second half of the 2030s'. 'We intend to offer a choice of engines', not a promise. No internal long-term-plan targets. Nothing timed to Boeing. Nothing on Delay Tactics [AX-0004, AX-0005, AX-0020].

Initial lean. ORDERS. NGSA: hold, which continues NGSA to EIS 2037 on its own clock. NGSA engine code: 7, unchanged and confirmed in its last changeable round. A350 Re-engine: hold. Delay Tactics: none, with the team's stricter condition left standing. No Board items. Row +23.37 (S1) / +22.88 (S2). WHY, IN MY ORDER. - Five pillars first: nothing covert, and safety leads the statement [AX-0081, AX-0073]. - Ramp: no new programme cash or engineering load in NGSA's last two spend years. A disciplined and controlled ramp of the A320neo and A350 until NGSA enters service [AX-0010, AX-0054]. - Preparing the Airbus of the 30s: NGSA whole, EIS in the second half of the decade, three engine sources [AX-0020, A-0409]. - The Board can take it: the package is the Board's own expected package, with nothing to vote and nothing to veto. GRID. - Expected column: S1. Worst plausible: S2 at +22.88, positive. - The best grid plan in S1 is A350 Re-engine + one Delay Tactics move at +26.56, $3.19B over the default. Every route to that gap breaks the cash line, and the Delay Tactics part also fails the stricter condition and integrity. The Board has said it would veto each piece, and I hold no override against the Board. - A350 Re-engine alone (+1.54 / -1.21) fails peak cash at $6.67B. It is worth under $1B probability-weighted and trails hold in S2. It returns in 2045 with a fresh grid if no 787 Re-engine is on the record. - One Delay Tactics move (+1.65 / +1.66) is off. The stricter condition stands, its $5.27B breaks the line, and it does nothing for 2045 or 2050. - The gap is recorded, not paid for. My lean is the best plan that is likely to survive, pending both memos. ENGINE SUPPLY. Code 7 keeps the enabler at 3 / 3 through 2050. It is never changed in reaction to Boeing, and it is locked in once NGSA enters service. 60/40. Not met (2050 at 53%), and no lever this round reaches 2045 or 2050. No PV, cash or integrity is traded for it. PUBLIC LINE (draft register). - Safety and quality first. NGSA on track for entry into service in the second half of the 2030s. 'We intend to offer a choice of engines.' - A disciplined and controlled ramp of the A320neo and A350 families, with our own supply secured first. - Funded within our financial flexibility and existing shareholder return policy. Zero-for-zero trade. - Nothing timed to Boeing, no internal targets, nothing on Delay Tactics. The lean stands unless Thomas or Lars reports a five-pillars flag or a failed test on NGSA itself, or shows an option that passes every test and gains at least $1B.

Board guidance before the ExCo met

Priorities.

  • Safety, quality, delivery and cost, in that order [CG-0009, CX-0658]. The Ducted becomes ready next year (2036), one year before NGSA enters service in 2037. Under Boeing's public engine competition, CFM is the baseline engine and certifies first. We want Ali's turn-on, turn-off evidence behind the 2036 ready year, and every design and test gate decided by a cross-functional team [CX-0009, CX-0012, CG-0018]. Durability is not traded for schedule [CX-0208].
  • Keep what the grid pays for. Hold everything is the best plan in all three columns: S1 -62.61, S2 -89.91, S3 -78.31. Keeping the Ducted is worth +16.86 / +17.37 / +17.65 against cancelling it, and keeping Embraer +4.65 / +6.02 / +5.44 [CG-0017]. No cancel passes our cancellation test. Once the Ducted is ready in 2036 it can no longer be cancelled, so this hold locks it in.
  • Keep RISE whole as technology, and make it a product only on an airframer path [CX-0469, CX-0205, CG-0065]. This is the last round in which a launch could be ready by 2050. But NGSA enters service in 2037 and fps in 2040, both before a 2045 Open Fan, so it waits in every column: -55.79 / -35.38 / -40.09 against hold, or -37.34 / -31.37 / -35.99 with Lobby. Say plainly that 'ready by 2050' is out of reach on our tests rather than stretch them. Keep RISE funded as technology, with no 'program dividend' [CX-0174, CX-0398, CG-0011].
  • Balance sheet: keep the A-range rating and return at least 70% of free cash flow [CG-0022, CX-0645, CG-0063, CG-0064]. Hold commits no new R&D this round. The premium is $0 this round and $0 of $4.0B for the game. The RISE allowance stays at $0 of $15B, unspent.
  • CFM parity rule (Safran consent) [CX-0184, CX-0160, CG-0066]. We expect no new CFM order, so no new gate. Continuing the Ducted and Embraer stays within joint practice, since both airframers have selected CFM. Any cancel or Open Fan launch needs a stated reason why Safran would agree.

Expects to see. (1) The expected_scenario (S1, S2 or S3), with weights for all three columns in predictions. The bulletin rules out none of them, so all three are plausible; without weights we use equal weights. Hold everything is the best plan in every column, so the weights change no ranking, but they do set the booking. (2) The grid's best plan in the expected column and in the worst column, each against Do Nothing (hold everything). For any Board item, the submitted row and the row with that item at its default, column by column. For Lobby, default the Open Fan as well, because Lobby needs it. (4) Ali's report: - the Ducted's 2036 ready year against NGSA's 2037 entry and fps's 2040 entry, either on test evidence or labelled as the board's development time; - Embraer counting from 2037; - any safety or durability flag, from his memo or his veto-check note, with the cross-functional answer to it; - the Open Fan's 2045 ready year, shown as late against both airframes; - the RISE gates set in round 1 (flight test done, compact-core durability turned on and off, more than 20% fuel burn shown in engine test), reported as the state of the technology, not as a product case. For a hold, one line saying that continuing the Ducted and Embraer stays within joint practice. No Safran position asserted. (6) premium in dollars against the best plan in the expected column, with the running counts: $0 of $2.0B this round and $0 of $4.0B for the game. First, no row reaches 50% of NB engines: on hold the share is 31.7% from 2040 in S1, and lower in S2 and S3. Second, 'Open Fan launched and ready by 2050' is out of reach on our tests. No objective premium is spent on either. (8) Every override, with its evidence. We expect none. (9) A board_response to our round-1 recommendations that are still open: rereading the Ducted on our cancellation test (the $3.33B write-off against the $0.67B saved); the RISE product call on Ali's gates; and Safran's consent, now answered by joint practice, since Safran cannot be consulted. (10) A public statement that names no rival and blames no one. It should give no Open Fan entry year, no CFM price or rate talk without Safran, and no Ducted date or certification claim beyond what testing has earned.

Would approve.

  • Hold everything: all five fields at hold. It is not a Board item, and we never veto it. It is the grid's best plan in S1 (-62.61), S2 (-89.91) and S3 (-78.31), so the premium is $0 whichever column is expected. It keeps the Ducted (ready in 2036) and Embraer (counting from 2037) running. Against cancelling them, that is worth +16.86 / +17.37 / +17.65 for the Ducted and +4.65 / +6.02 / +5.44 for Embraer. No new R&D is committed, so the 70% payout and the rating are untouched. CFM parity rule: a hold needs no gate, and continuing both programmes stays within joint practice, since both airframers selected CFM (code 7).
  • GEnx: hold, the only option this round. The upgrade has been ready since 2033 and counts from 2042, or from the first Re-engine's entry. It is GE alone, so there is no Safran gate.
  • Nothing else on this grid passes our tests. No Open Fan, Lobby or cancel row reaches zero against hold in any column, so no choice of expected column or weights can change this. We approve a hold on every field.

Would veto.

  • Open Fan: launch, alone or in any combination. Against hold it is -55.79 / -35.38 / -40.09 on an $8B bill, so it loses $27.38B to $47.79B more than its bill in every column. Grounds: - Bounded downside fails. - Airframer path fails: under (a), NGSA enters service in 2037 and fps in 2040, both before a 2045 Open Fan, so it waits in every plausible column. Under (b), the cheapest Open Fan row (Open Fan + Lobby) costs $31.37B to $37.34B against the best non-RISE plan, over the $15B RISE allowance. - Our horizon of 3 does not let the allowance carry an Open Fan the grid shows waiting. - CFM parity rule (Safran consent): a RISE product launch with no airframer path is not joint practice. Without a stated reason it fails on that ground as well. Acceptable alternative: hold.
  • emissions lobbying: launch. With the Open Fan, the pair is -37.34 / -31.37 / -35.99 against hold on a $9B bill, so its downside is unbounded. On its own, Lobby costs $1B and does nothing on the board, so it fails 'paid for the risk' and our rule that Lobby goes only with an Open Fan launched or live. If the Open Fan is vetoed, we veto Lobby with it at review. Acceptable alternative: hold.
  • ducted engine: cancel, alone or as a swap for the Open Fan. On its own it is -16.86 / -17.37 / -17.65 against hold; as a swap (Ducted cancel + Open Fan) it is -58.46 / -35.73 / -42.76. It fails our cancellation test, which needs at least zero in every plausible column: the cancel writes off $3.33B to save $0.67B and gives up the +10 pp. CFM parity rule (Safran consent): both new narrowbodies have selected CFM, and Safran has never been seen to cancel the engine it offers them. Without a stated reason the item fails, and hard rule 5 bars cancelling what a live airframe would fly. Acceptable alternative: hold.
  • Embraer partnership: cancel: -4.65 / -6.02 / -5.44 against hold. It fails the cancellation test, and no stated Safran reason exists for withdrawing a CFM engine from a third airframer. Acceptable alternative: hold.
  • Any Board item with a premium. Hold is the best plan in every column, so any item this round gives up at least its loss against hold. The smallest such loss is $4.65B (the Embraer cancel in S1), over the $2.0B cap. The only exception would be the RISE allowance, which fails the airframer-path test above.

Recommendations.

  • Safety and quality. The Ducted is due to be ready in 2036, one year before NGSA enters service in 2037. - Bring Ali's readiness and durability review to the full board before that entry into service, on turn-on, turn-off evidence and not analysis. - Make every design and test gate a cross-functional call. - Bring us any durability flag or schedule slip at once; Ghai put a slip past 2037 at about $1.0-1.2B a year. - Durability is not traded for schedule. Ali's 'no flag' in round 1 was not a clearance.
  • Delivery, framed for the customer. Two of the three columns are code switches that would take a CFM slot (S2 and S3), and nothing on the grid can defend against them. Boeing's public terms give the answer: CFM is the baseline engine, it certifies first, and other engines follow only once they show maturity and durability. Keep both airframers on CFM through readiness, durability evidence and service, not through price. Boeing asks that CFM support both airframers' rates. Rate commitments are made by GE and Safran together, so give any capacity commitment only jointly, on Ali's supply data (the 9 suppliers at 15 sites), with no number in public without Safran.
  • RISE. Keep it funded as technology inside the R&D we protect first; holding the product is no 'program dividend'. It becomes a product only on an airframer path. In the objective_note, say plainly that 'Open Fan launched and ready by 2050' is out of reach on our tests. The last launch that meets it, this round's, is ready in 2045, after NGSA (2037) and fps (2040), and costs $31.37B to $37.34B against hold. Do not stretch the test. Keep the one RISE allowance unspent, and report Ali's RISE gates as the state of the technology.
  • Cost and capital. - Hold commits no new R&D. The Ducted is in its last development year, and the 70% payout and the A-range rating are untouched. - Do not redeploy any room this frees into a product the grid shows waiting. - State the premium in dollars: $0 this round, $0 of $4.0B for the game, and the RISE allowance $0 of $15B, shown separately. - Book low: at or below hold in the expected column, with S2 (-89.91) as the low case.
  • Objective, NB share of at least 50%. Say plainly that no row on this grid reaches it: on hold the share is 31.7% from 2040 in S1, and lower in S2 and S3. Spend no premium on it. Any commercial campaign to keep both airframers on CFM stays on standard terms, priced jointly with Safran and kept out of the public statement. We are not going for share at any price, and launch-era pricing is behind us.
  • CFM parity rule (Safran consent). On a hold, state in the rationale that continuing the Ducted and Embraer stays within joint practice, because both airframers selected CFM and the partners split the aftermarket equally. In round 1 we asked you to record Safran's actual answer. The answer is joint practice: Safran cannot be consulted in this game, so assert no Safran position. Any cancel or Open Fan launch needs a stated reason why Safran would agree.
  • Public statement. - Name no rival and blame no one, even with code switches in play. - Give no Open Fan entry year; 'RISE remains our next generation, and our customers decide when' is enough. - No CFM price or rate talk without Safran. - The 2036 ready year is on the public record as the game's ready date. Add no certification or entry-into-service claim for the Ducted that testing has not earned, and never call it next-generation.

Larry Culp frames the round

Question. What game are we playing, and how do we win? [CX-0467] The selections are made. Both new narrowbodies launched in 2030, and both chose all three engine makers (code 7). NGSA enters service in 2037 and fps in 2040. Two rival new narrowbody engines have launched and been selected on both aircraft. So the game is no longer whether we get on the next aircraft. It is the installed base on two aircraft we now share three ways ("Our major economics happen in and around the first and second" [CX-0422]), and keeping both slots through entry into service. "We don't have a birthright on that next order" [CX-0564]. Three doors close this round: - It is the last round either airframer can change its engine code. Both enter service before the 2045 round. - It is the last round we can cancel the Ducted (ready in 2036) or Embraer (counting from 2037). - It is the last round an Open Fan launch could be ready by 2050 (2035 + 10 = 2045). We win this round on execution, not on launches: - get the Ducted ready with its durability earned by testing; - keep both airframers on CFM through readiness, durability and support, not price ("we are not the low bid" [CX-0250]); - keep RISE whole as technology until an airframer wants it as a product [CX-0469, CX-0205]. So the question for this room has two parts. Does anything on this grid pay us to move, or do we hold everything and put the work into delivery? And do we say plainly that the Open Fan leg of our objective is out of reach on our tests?

Situation. PUBLIC RECORD, 2035 (round 1 adjudicated) - Airframes. NGSA (Airbus) launched in 2030 and enters service in 2037. fps (Boeing) launched in 2030 on the 10-year ramp and enters service in 2040. Both chose code 7 (RR, P&W, CFM), and both will be fitted CFM + P&W + RR if nothing changes. Either can still change its code this round. Both enter service before the 2045 round, so after this round the codes lock. - Rival narrowbody engines on the record. P&W GTF2 Solo launched in 2030 and is ready in 2036. RR UltraFan NB Solo launched in 2030 and is ready in 2037. Both are selected on both aircraft. There is no Joint Venture commitment: RR's door is open, and P&W made none. H3's trigger now sits on the public record, not just on the grid. - Airframers' terms. Boeing: CFM is the baseline launch engine and certifies first; the others follow once they show maturity and durability. CFM must support both airframers' rates. Development is cost-plus or risk-share, never fixed price, and Boeing wants more than one source. Airbus: a choice of engines on the successor, as on the A320 family, and all three makers invited in as risk-sharing partners. - Our programmes. The Ducted is in its last development year and is ready in 2036. Embraer counts from 2037. The GEnx upgrade has been ready since 2033 and counts from 2042, since no Re-engine is on the record. - Observed market, 2026-34: flat. NB engines: CFM 76%, P&W 24%, RR 0%. WB engines: GEnx 42%, Trent 58%. OUR POSITION (hold everything, S1) - ΔPV is -62.61: engine value -56.61, R&D -4.00, strain -2.00. Yield 60.87%. - NB share: - 76% through 2036; - 56.5% in 2037, 55.9% in 2038 and 55.2% in 2039, as NGSA splits the Airbus slot three ways; - 31.7% from 2040, as fps splits the 737 slot. - WB share: 42%, then 44.8% from 2042. - Objective, NB at least 50% in 2040, 2045 and 2050: NOT MET. The share is 31.7% in S1 and lower in S2 and S3. No row on the grid reaches 50%. - Objective, Open Fan launched and ready by 2050: NOT MET. This is the last round in which it can still be met. GRID READING - Hold everything is the best plan in all three columns: S1 -62.61, S2 -89.91, S3 -78.31. - What the code switches cost us on hold: S2 (Airbus moves NGSA to P&W only) -27.30 against S1; S3 (Boeing moves fps to RR only) -15.70. No lever on this grid defends against either. Only delivery, durability and support can, and the board does not price them. - Every alternative loses in every column: - Embraer cancel: -4.65 to -6.02; - Ducted cancel: -16.86 to -17.65; - any Open Fan row: -31.37 to -59.98. - Weighted hold: -73.36 on my preliminary weights (S1 .50, S2 .25, S3 .25); -76.94 on equal weights. BOARD GUIDANCE (non-binding, labelled as such) - Would approve: all five fields at hold, including GEnx: hold. - Would VETO: - Open Fan: launch, alone or in any combination. It waits in every column. The cheapest row, Open Fan + Lobby, is -31.37 to -37.34 against hold, over the $15B RISE allowance. There is no airframer path, and with no stated reason it is not joint practice with Safran. - emissions lobbying: launch, which does nothing without a live Open Fan. - ducted engine: cancel, alone or as a swap for the Open Fan. It fails the cancellation test: $3.33B written off to save $0.67B, while both airframers have selected CFM. - Embraer partnership: cancel. - Any Board item carrying a premium. The smallest loss is $4.65B, over the $2.0B cap. - It expects to see: - the expected column, with weights for all three columns; - the best plan against Do Nothing, in the expected column and in the worst column; - Ghai's tests, in numbers; - Ali's readiness and durability report, with any flag and its cross-functional answer, the Open Fan's 2045 shown as late, and the RISE gates reported as the state of the technology; - one Safran-gate line for a hold; - the premium counts; - an objective note saying plainly that both legs are missed and the Open Fan leg is out of reach on our tests; - no overrides; - a board_response to its open round-1 recommendations: the Ducted reread on the cancellation test, the RISE product call on Ali's gates, and Safran consent answered by joint practice; - a public statement with no rival named, no blame, no Open Fan entry year, no price or rate talk without Safran, no Ducted certification or entry claim beyond what testing has earned, and never 'next-generation' for the Ducted.

Options to test.

  • Row A, hold everything (the reference row; no new lever moves). S1 / S2 / S3: -62.61 / -89.91 / -78.31. - Best plan in every column, so the premium is $0 whichever column is expected. - Weighted: -73.36 on my preliminary weights, -76.94 on equal weights. - The Ducted and Embraer continue; no new R&D is committed.
  • Row B, Ducted cancel. Embraer falls with it, so this is the same row as Ducted cancel + Embraer cancel. - S1 / S2 / S3: -79.47 / -107.28 / -95.96, which is -16.86 / -17.37 / -17.65 against hold. - This is the reread I committed to in round 1. Both airframers selected CFM, and two rival engines are now selected on both aircraft (profile §6, cancel).
  • Row C, Embraer cancel. S1 / S2 / S3: -67.26 / -95.93 / -83.75, which is -4.65 / -6.02 / -5.44 against hold. It fails the cancellation test.

  • Row F, the swap: Ducted cancel + Open Fan. S1 / S2 / S3: -58.46 / -35.73 / -42.76 against hold; with Lobby, -50.84 / -34.04 / -38.75. It fails twice: it cancels the defence the record now calls for, and it still waits.

All of them lose in every column and break H2, H3 or the cancellation test.
  • Other moves to test (the board does not price them; Ghai and Ali to check): (1) Bring a Ducted readiness and durability review to the full Board before NGSA's 2037 entry, on turn-on, turn-off evidence. Every design and test gate is a cross-functional call [CX-0012]. (2) A joint CFM capacity plan with Safran to support both airframers' rates, built on Ali's supply data. Haircut any growth promise by a quarter to a half, and put no number in public. (3) Answer Boeing's engine competition (CFM as baseline, certifying first; cost-plus or risk-share development) and Airbus's risk-sharing invitation through CFM governance. Standard terms, priced jointly with Safran, no launch-era pricing, private. (4) Keep RISE funded as technology, and report Ali's gates as the state of the technology, with no product date.

Red lines.

  • Safety, quality, delivery and cost, always in that order [CX-0658]. No launch, and no programme carried into service, while a safety or durability flag from Ali stands without a cross-functional answer on evidence [CX-0012]. Ramp or schedule never trades against safety [CX-0603].
  • My line: durability is not traded for fuel burn or for schedule [CX-0208]. That applies to the Ducted's 2036 readiness above all.
  • My line: a next engine needs at least a 20% fuel-burn improvement [CX-0217]. It binds RISE as the next generation. The Ducted gets 'less than half' the open fan's gain [CX-0183, CX-0180] and stands only as an H3 defence, so it is never called next-generation.
  • H1: never refuse an airframer and never lock one out [CX-0587, CX-0185]. The CFM offer stands on both aircraft, and on Embraer.
  • H2: never press an airframer into the Open Fan wait [CX-0205]. NGSA (2037) and fps (2040) both enter service before a 2045 Open Fan, so there is no launch. The one exception is the declared RISE allowance (up to $15B), and the cheapest row is over it.
  • H3: a Ducted only as a defence. The trigger is now on the public record: two rival NB engines are launched and selected on both aircraft.
  • H5: never cancel RISE for cost while an airframer may want it [CX-0174, CX-0398]. No 'program dividend'.
  • H6, applied through Ali's test: no date without test evidence [CX-0009]. No Ducted certification or entry claim beyond what testing has earned, and no Open Fan entry year.
  • H7: the Safran gate on every CFM narrowbody order (Ducted, Open Fan, Embraer, Lobby) [CX-0184, CX-0166]. A cancel or an Open Fan launch needs a stated reason why Safran would agree. Rate and price commitments are made only jointly. GEnx is GE alone.
  • H8: no public blame and no comment on rivals [CX-0625, CX-0580], even with code switches in play.
  • H9: the doctrine plus objective premium is at most $2.0B this round and $4.0B for the game. Running count: $0 of $2.0B, $0 of $4.0B. The one RISE allowance (up to $15B) is declared in full against the best non-RISE plan and is unspent so far.

Initial lean. This is a lean, not a decision; your memos decide it. I lean to HOLD EVERYTHING: all five fields at hold. EMBRAER: HOLD (continue). A cancel loses 4.65 to 6.02. OPEN FAN: HOLD. - The RISE product call I set for this round is made, and it is 'not now'. The cap holds, and I won't stretch our tests. - RISE stays funded as technology: no cancel (H5) and no 'program dividend' [CX-0174, CX-0214]. LOBBY: HOLD. GEnx: HOLD (the only option). EXPECTED COLUMN AND BOOKING (preliminary). - Expected column S1; weights S1 .50, S2 .25, S3 .25. - Book about -75, below the weighted -73.36. - Premium: $0 of $2.0B this round and $0 of $4.0B for the game. GEnx is GE alone. OTHER MOVES. - Readiness and durability review to the full Board before 2037. - A joint capacity plan for both airframers' rates, with no number in public. - Standard terms on both airframers' invitations, priced jointly with Safran. - RISE gates reported as the state of the technology. PUBLIC LINE. - Safety first, and what we know and what we don't [CX-0436]. - We're honored to be on both new aircraft [CX-0452], and we earn that on readiness, durability and support. - RISE remains our next generation, and our customers decide when. - No dates our testing hasn't earned. No price or rate talk without our partner. No rival named. It's that simple, ain't that hard.

Larry, it's a hold round, and there's nothing to hide in the numbers. Hold is the best row in every column: -62.61, -89.91, -78.31. Every alternative loses $4.65B to $59.98B against it in every column, so the premium is nil whichever column you expect. Count: $0 of $2.0B, $0 of $4.0B, RISE allowance $0 of $15B. The Ducted reread holds. A cancel gives up about $19.5-20.3B of engine value. On the board it saves $2.67B, not $0.67B, because the strain goes with it, and the row still loses $16.86-17.65B. An Embraer cancel saves nothing at all. Keep both. Open Fan: the cheapest row is $31.37B below hold, twice the allowance. Say plainly the leg is out of reach. Capex: no new R&D. The Ducted's last $0.67B and the strain we already carry come to about $1.0B a year against $2.5B of room. The 70% payout and the rating are whole. What the case leaves out: a code switch costs $15.70-27.30B, and no lever here stops it. A Ducted slip past 2037 costs about $1.2B for the first year, $1.5-1.6B if Embraer waits with it. And the grid's volume falls, from 3,040 CFM engines a year to 1,270 from 2040, so we don't build for a ramp it doesn't show. Rates get planned privately with Safran, with no number until each airframer's volumes are worked. Booking: -77, not -75, and raise when 2045 locks the codes. We've been proven wrong before.

Larry Culp decides

Orders. Do Nothing

Rationale. DECISION: HOLD EVERYTHING. All five fields are at hold. That is the default, so no order is a Board item. WHAT GAME, HOW WE WIN [CX-0467] The selections are made. NGSA (2037) and fps (2040) both chose code 7, and two rival NB engines are selected on both. The game now is the installed base on two aircraft we share three ways [CX-0422]. This is the last round either airframer can change its code. Nothing on this grid defends against a switch, and S2 and S3 cost $27.30B and $15.70B against S1. So we win on execution, not launches: - the Ducted ready on test, with durability earned; - both customers kept on readiness, durability and support, not price [CX-0250]; - RISE kept whole as technology. We have no birthright [CX-0564]. GRID AGAINST DO NOTHING (hold = Do Nothing = default) Hold is the best plan in every column: S1 -62.61, S2 -89.91, S3 -78.31. - Expected column (S1): best plan hold, 0.00 against Do Nothing. - Worst column (S2): best plan hold, 0.00. Every alternative loses in every column (S1 / S2 / S3 against hold): - Embraer cancel: -4.65 / -6.02 / -5.44. - Ducted cancel, with Embraer falling with it: -16.86 / -17.37 / -17.65. - Open Fan: -55.79 / -35.38 / -40.09. - Open Fan + Lobby: -37.34 / -31.37 / -35.99. - Ducted cancel + Open Fan: -58.46 / -35.73 / -42.76. Weighted on my weights (.50 / .25 / .25), hold is -73.36: - Ducted cancel -17.19; - Embraer cancel -5.19; - Open Fan -46.76; - Open Fan + Lobby -35.51. No weighting changes the ranking. Ghai's weights (.60 / .20 / .20) and equal weights give the same answer. TESTS - Additive and paid for the risk: no move off hold beats hold in any column. - Low case first: S1 is the record, and I book well below it. - H2, the airframer sets the date: a 2035 Open Fan is ready in 2045. That is eight years after NGSA's entry and five after fps's, so it waits in every column. - H3, the Ducted only as a defence: the trigger is now on the public record. Two rival NB engines are launched and selected on both aircraft, so keeping the Ducted is the defence the rule calls for. - Cancel doctrine: the trigger is not met. Both airframes would fly the engine, and the threat is present. - My 20% line binds RISE, not the Ducted. The Ducted gets 'less than half' the gain [CX-0183] and stands only under H3. The public line never calls it the next generation. - Durability line [CX-0208]: no order trades durability for schedule. The readiness review is how I enforce that. - Tie-break: not needed. No alternative is within $1B of hold, and the smallest gap is $4.65B. DUCTED REREAD (round-1 commitment) A cancel writes off $4B x 5/6 = $3.33B and saves $0.67B of R&D. Ghai's correction: on the board, the saving is $2.67B including the $2B strain released. The row still loses $16.86-17.65B, because it gives up about $19.6-20.3B of engine value. In S1 the NB share in 2037 would fall from 56.5% to 44.3%. Keep it. Once it is ready in 2036 it can no longer be cancelled, so this hold locks it in. If a test gate fails, we fix the part, not cancel the engine [CX-0005]. OPEN FAN AND THE RISE ALLOWANCE My installed-base lens pulls hardest here [CX-0555], because this is the last round 'ready by 2050' can be met. But the cheapest row, Open Fan + Lobby, is $31.37B to $37.34B below hold ($35.51B weighted), more than twice the $15B allowance. Ali reports none of the three Board RISE gates closed on the record. So I keep RISE as technology, with no cancel (H5) and no program dividend [CX-0174]. Lobby does nothing without a live Open Fan. SAFRAN GATE (H7) No new CFM narrowbody order. Continuing the Ducted and Embraer stays within joint practice: both airframers selected CFM, and the partners split the aftermarket equally [CX-0219]. No Safran position is asserted. GEnx is GE alone. EXCO Ghai's binding tests pass on hold, and he and Ali both recommend all-hold, so there are no overrides. - I adopt Ghai's booking of -77 over my -75. - I keep my more conservative weights; he agrees they err on the right side. - Ali's date test passes. 2036 is labelled the board's development time, not a test result. - Ali gives no flag, and I don't read that as a clearance. The readiness review goes to the full Board before 2037. DOCTRINE, NOT MY RECORD, DROVE: - the Embraer hold (profile §6; my record is silent on Embraer); - the Lobby rule; - the supply-load read, which uses the strain rule because Ali has no supply field data. CAPITAL No new R&D. The Ducted's last $0.67B in 2035 and the strain already carried come to about $1.0B a year against about $2.5B of room. The 70% payout and the A-range rating are whole [CX-0645].

Weighing the CFO. I weighted Ghai fully. His record is strong on money, and his profit calls land [CX-0910]. He passes every binding test on hold: - pays for itself, with no new R&D; - volumes first: S1 is the record, and the Ducted beats a cancel in all three columns without assuming any selection; - no overcapitalisation: about $1.0B a year against about $2.5B of room; - premium $0; - terms: no price talk, and standard joint terms on both invitations. I took three things from him: (1) His correction that a Ducted cancel saves $2.67B on the board, not $0.67B, because the strain goes with it. The row still loses $16.86-17.65B. (2) His booking of -77 (the equal-weight value, rounded down) in place of my -75. It's the 'guide low, then raise' discipline [CX-0270, CX-0654]. We raise to S1 when the 2045 bulletin shows the codes locked. (3) His terms conditions on the airframers' invitations and his warning that the grid's CFM volume falls to 1,270 a year from 2040, so no facility build. He would put S1 at .60; I keep .50, which he calls the right side to err on. His slip costing ($1.18B for the first year, $3.34B to 2040) goes to the Board with Ali's review.

Weighing the operating head. Ali's record is thin. His own words end in March 2024 and cover engineering only, and on supply his record is my own description of his job [CX-0633]. So I took his dates and his test standard at full weight and checked his supply read against doctrine. - Dates: every order passes. Ducted 2036 (launch + 6), Embraer 2037, GEnx ready since 2033 and counting from 2042, and an Open Fan at 2045 if launched now, 2055 if not. He rightly labels 2036 the board's development time: no Ducted turn-on, turn-off result exists. - Flag: he raises none, and states it is not a clearance. I hold him to that. I applied doctrine (the strain rule; hold adds no project) and my own haircut to any ramp promise. - Public line: he pre-noticed the claims to avoid (Ducted certification or entry year, Ducted on NGSA or fps, RISE year, ramp date, Ducted fuel-burn or durability claim). Note: my veto right over programme dates is an inference. That is one year of float to NGSA's 2037 entry and four years to fps in 2040. Embraer counts 2037, after the engine it needs. Would veto.

  • GTF2 Solo: cancel, in any combination. Against hold it is -32.79 / -11.47 / -20.98 / -32.79 (S1-S4), or -32.79 / -11.47 / -20.98 / -1.67 beside a commit: -24.51 and -16.73 at equal weights, negative at any weights. It fails Return hurdle. It also fails Premature exit: live airframes not yet in service carry code 7, GTF2 is ready in 2036 before both EIS dates, and cancel trails hold in every plausible column. It writes off $1.67B. Acceptable alternative: hold.
  • Joint Venture with RR: commit whose terms put P&W's gear, core or GTF2 technology into the Joint Venture rather than sharing risk and investment, or that carries a core-technology red-line flag Calio neither strikes nor rebuts. Grounds: Joint Venture conditions and governance [P-1233, PG-0047]. Acceptable alternative: hold.
  • Joint Venture with RR: commit that Eddy fails on durability or parts, unless his veto check shows the failure resolved. That covers a fold or integration that moves GTF2's 2036 date past NGSA's 2037 EIS, or that draws GTF fleet parts or engineers. Ground: Durability first. Acceptable alternative: hold.
  • Any Board item carrying a Mitchill veto (dividend or debt path, unselected engine, aggressive terms, unproven upside) or an Eddy veto (durability, parts or capacity) that the CEO did not respect, or any entry in overrides. Ground: governance.
  • Any plan that needs the dividend to give or pushes debt off its pre-ASR path. None is expected, since no new R&D is on this grid. Ground: Dividend and envelope.

Recommendations.

  • Hold GTF2. It is selected on both new narrowbodies (code 7) and is ready in 2036 against EIS dates of 2037 and 2040. Hold beats cancel by 11.47 to 32.79 in every column, and a cancel writes off $1.67B for nothing. The round-1 cancel test is now moot: a live airframe carries a P&W code. Show the whole-programme value against hold, as the board once reviewed GTF NPV every year.
  • Durability report, which carries over from round 1. Eddy's memo should give the GTF2 severe-environment validation status, full-life LLPs at EIS and any slip against NGSA's 2037 EIS (one year of margin). It should also give a GTF fleet AOG and pacing-parts count. Boeing says P&W follows CFM on fps 'once it shows maturity and durability', and losing fps (S3) costs 11.81 and losing NGSA (S2) 21.32 against S1. Validated durability, not price, is the lever that keeps code 7. The date moves, not the testing.
  • Joint Venture: put Joint Venture with RR: commit to the test this round. Our round-1 trigger is met (code 7 on both live airframes), it is never below hold (0 / 0 / 0 / +5.51) and it adds no R&D with GTF2 live. The Board would approve it on conditions. It shares risk and investment, never the gear or core technology, which stay P&W modules inside the geared architecture. A Joint Venture holds only while both partners are on the same new engine, so confirm that the folded GTF2 and UltraFan NB become one engine and that the fold write-off is $0. Staff integration outside the fleet and GTF2 validation teams.
  • If commit goes in, write the 2045 test into the plan now. Rolls-Royce says it commits once ours is on the record, so formation is likelier in 2045 than in 2035, and that effect is not on this grid. Keep the commitment standing only if the 2045 grid shows hold at or above withdraw at Mitchill's weights. Book no off-grid value either way: the 'equal NB shares' rule could raise P&W where an airframer keeps RR and drops us, or lower P&W where RR is dropped.
  • Show the return against Do Nothing and against a buyback. Give each Board item's weighted value against hold at Mitchill's and Calio's weights (commit = 5.51 x pS4; cancel at least -11.47 in every column). Report premium of 0 for Board items and the round-1 doctrine premium of $0.26B separately, so that the $1B cap is tracked without double counting.
  • Dividend and debt. Mitchill should confirm that no new R&D is committed this round, that GTF2's $2B ($0.33B a year, 2030-35) came in within the ~$6B envelope, that the dividend is covered and that debt is on its pre-ASR path. The Board's one-round stretch stays unused.
  • Public statement. Report GTF2 as in development for NGSA and fps, ready in 2036 and no earlier, with severe-environment validation and full-life LLPs as gates before EIS, not claims. Name no airframer date. If committing, say the Joint Venture forms only when Rolls-Royce also commits, and that it shares risk and investment, not technology. Answer Airbus's risk-sharing invitation on standard commercial terms: no launch discount or concession. Keep the round-1 fix: offer only what can be ready by an airframe's EIS.
  • Fleet first. Keep the ring-fence and back the public 'no new programme takes parts or engineers away' with the weekly pacing-parts review. Through 2036 GTF2 validation and any Joint Venture work must not compete with AOG recovery or Hot Section kit insertion.

Chris Calio frames the round

Question. Control what you can control. Both new narrowbodies now carry code 7. NGSA and fps have each selected CFM, Pratt & Whitney and Rolls-Royce, and our 2030 launch if selected fired. GTF2 is live and will be ready in 2036, ahead of both entries into service on the record. This is the last round in which GTF2 can be cancelled: it is ready in 2036, and after that its bill is sunk. On the rules it is also the last round in which either airframer can change its code before entry into service, since the next round is 2045 (inference). So I put three questions to the ExCo. (1) Do we keep GTF2 whole? On the grid, cancel loses in every column, and it would throw away two selections our customers put on the record. (2) Both live airframes now carry a Rolls-Royce code, so do we put a standing, public Joint Venture commitment on the record, and on what terms? Risk and investment are shared. The gear, the core and the GTF2 technology stay ours. (3) What protects the code 7 selections? They are worth more than any order on this grid: losing NGSA (S1 to S2) swings 21.32, and losing fps (S1 to S3) swings 11.81. The lever is durability validated before entry into service, not price, and the fleet still comes first. My usual questions apply. Is the demand visible? It is on the record. Do the business model, timing and volume work? Is durability mature at entry into service? Is this a responsible bet with a responsible payback? Is the dividend safe?

Situation. PUBLIC RECORD (2035 bulletin) - Launched in 2030: - NGSA (Airbus), EIS 2037; - fps (Boeing), 10-year ramp-up, EIS 2040. - Both selected code 7 (RR, P&W and CFM). 'Fitted if nothing changes': CFM + PW + RR on both. - Engines on the record: - P&W GTF2 (solo), triggered in 2030, ready 2036; - RR UltraFan NB (solo), ready 2037; - CFM ducted, ready 2036; - CFM-Embraer partnership, ready 2037; - GEnx upgrade (widebody), ready since 2033. - Joint Venture stance: - Rolls-Royce: 'we commit once [P&W's] commitment is on the record.' It has made no commitment. - We said in 2030 that we were making no Joint Venture commitment that round. - No Joint Venture commitment from either side is on the record. - Airframers: - Airbus invites all three engine makers to NGSA as risk-sharing partners (unpriced) and keeps 'a choice of engines' as on the A320 family. - Boeing: CFM is the baseline and certifies first. A P&W or RR engine follows 'once it shows maturity and durability'. Boeing wants two or three sources, and development is cost-plus or risk-share, never fixed price. - Observed market, 2026-34: unchanged. NB engines CFM 76% / P&W 24% / RR 0%. OUR POSITION (private brief) - If nobody moves: ΔPV +3.37 $B (engine value +5.37, R&D -2.00), yield 103.06%. - Our NB share: - dips to 19.4-20.0% in 2037-39, while NGSA enters service with three makers and the 737 flies CFM; - then 31.7% from 2040, once fps is in service. - Objective: - Restore credibility: MET, with GTF2 on NGSA and fps. That holds only while we keep code 7 and GTF2 is ready by EIS. - Capitalise (ΔPV ≥ 0): MET at +3.37. - Under hold, credibility is still met in every column (fps in S2, NGSA in S3). Capitalise fails in S2 and S3 in every row. THE GRID ($B, S1-S4) - Columns: - S1: rivals hold; - S2: Airbus moves NGSA to code 5 (RR + CFM); - S3: Boeing moves fps to code 3 (CFM); - S4: RR commits to the Joint Venture. - Rows: - hold: +3.37 / -17.95 / -8.44 / +3.37; - hold + commit: +3.37 / -17.95 / -8.44 / +8.88; - cancel: -29.42 in every column; - cancel + commit: -29.42 / -29.42 / -29.42 / +7.21. - Board items against hold: - commit: 0 / 0 / 0 / +5.51, never negative; - cancel: -32.79 / -11.47 / -20.98 / -32.79. - At my prior (S1 0.65 / S2 0.10 / S3 0.10 / S4 0.15): - hold: +0.06; - hold + commit: +0.88 (commit item +0.83); - cancel: -29.42; - cancel + commit: -23.93. - At equal weights: commit item +1.38, cancel item -24.51. - Bad news first: at hold our expected value is close to zero. S2 and S3 drag it down, and no order on this grid moves those columns. Only the airframers' confidence in our durability does. THE BOARD'S GUIDANCE - Approves: - Joint Venture with RR: commit beside GTF2 Solo: hold, on conditions. The gear, core and GTF2 technology are not shared; Eddy passes it on durability and parts; no ExCo veto is left unrespected; a 2045 hold-or-withdraw re-test is written in. - hold/hold, which is not a Board item. - Vetoes: - any cancel; - any commit that puts our technology into the Joint Venture or fails Eddy's checks. - Expects: - premium of 0, with the round-1 doctrine premium of $0.26B reported separately; - no new R&D and no envelope stretch.

Options to test.

  • A. GTF2 Solo: hold, Joint Venture with RR: commit (row 'GTF2: hold + commit to JV'). - S1-S4: +3.37 / -17.95 / -8.44 / +8.88. Worst column -17.95 (S2), the same as hold. - Board item against hold: 0 / 0 / 0 / +5.51. It is weakly dominant and never below hold: +0.83 at my prior, +1.38 at equal weights. - It adds no new R&D while GTF2 is live (the fold). - Off-grid, and not to be booked either way: - Rolls-Royce says it commits once ours is on the record, so a 2045 formation is likelier than a 2035 one. - In 2045 both airframes are in service and codes are fixed. The 'equal NB shares' rule could then lift us where RR is fitted and we are not (an S2-type world) or trim us where RR is dropped. - Hence the 2045 re-test. - This is my lean.
  • B. GTF2 Solo: hold, Joint Venture with RR: hold (row 'GTF2: hold'), the default. - S1-S4: +3.37 / -17.95 / -8.44 / +3.37. +0.06 at my prior. - It is not a Board item. It keeps GTF2 on both selections. - It is the fallback if the Joint Venture terms cannot keep our technology, or if Eddy fails the integration on durability or parts. The PV given up would then be 5.51 × pS4, declared as the cost of a red line, not traded.
  • C. GTF2 Solo: cancel, Joint Venture with RR: hold (row 'cancel GTF2'). - -29.42 in every column. Against hold: -32.79 / -11.47 / -20.98 / -32.79. - It writes off $1.67B to throw away two selections on the record. - Tested only to show it fails. It breaks my no-harvesting line while airframers have chosen us, fails the return test at any weights, and the Board vetoes it.
  • D. GTF2 Solo: cancel, Joint Venture with RR: commit (row 'cancel GTF2 + commit to JV'). - -29.42 / -29.42 / -29.42 / +7.21. - Against A: -32.79 / -11.47 / -20.98 / -1.67. - It would make us a junior partner on Rolls-Royce's engine instead of our own. That cuts against 'joining RR's engine shares RR's, not yours' and against the geared architecture [P-0772][PX-0014]. - Struck, and the Board vetoes it.

Red lines.

  • Safety and durability first; Eddy's readiness check binds me [PX-0035][PX-0073]. - GTF2 must be ready by the EIS it serves: 2036 against NGSA 2037 (one year of margin) and fps 2040 (four years). - If the Joint Venture forms in 2035, its engine is ready 2036 only through the GTF2 fold. Nothing in a Joint Venture integration may move GTF2's 2036 or compress its testing. - Full-life LLPs at EIS and severe-environment validation are gates, not claims. If anything gives, the date moves, not the testing.
  • The fleet beats a new engine [PX-0080]. Eddy flagged in 2030 that the real draw comes with the GTF2 production ramp around 2035-36, which is now. - Neither GTF2's ramp nor any Joint Venture work may take castings, forgings, powder-metal disks or engineers from the GTF fleet's AOG recovery or from Hot Section kit insertion. - The ring-fence is backed by the weekly pacing-parts review.
  • No cancel of a selected GTF2. I do not harvest a programme while airframers have chosen it (inference from [PX-0064][P-1342], read the other way: we reset what has stopped working, and this has not). The round-1 cancel test is moot: both live airframes carry a P&W code.
  • Joint Venture: share risk and investment, never our core technology [P-1233]. - The gear, the core and the GTF2 technology stay Pratt & Whitney modules inside the geared architecture, not transferred IP. - The folded GTF2 and UltraFan NB become one engine, not two competing ones [P-1875]. The team is integrated [P-1240] and staffed outside the fleet and GTF2 validation teams. - The commitment is public at once. We never present Rolls-Royce's commitment, or the Joint Venture's formation, as done. - If these terms cannot be met, the order is hold, and I declare the cost.
  • The dividend never funds an engine, and debt stays on its pre-ASR path [PX-0081][P-0669][P-0686]. This round commits no new R&D (the commit folds into GTF2's spent $2B). No envelope stretch: the Board's one stretch stays unused.
  • Value, not share [PX-0055][PX-0100]. - Airbus's risk-sharing invitation is answered on standard commercial terms: no launch-style discount, concession or free upgrade, to Airbus or to Boeing. - A rival's discount never moves the answer.
  • Never speak for an airframer's dates or rates [PX-0062]. No ready year earlier than 2036. Offer only what can be ready by an airframe's EIS (the Board's round-1 fix).
  • No widebody engine move [PX-0027].
  • The Board's would-veto list, carried in: - GTF2 Solo: cancel in any combination; - a Joint Venture with RR: commit whose terms put P&W's gear, core or GTF2 technology into the Joint Venture, or that carries an unrebutted core-technology flag; - a commit that Eddy fails on durability or parts: a fold that moves GTF2 past 2037, or that draws GTF fleet parts or engineers; - any Board item carrying an unrespected Mitchill or Eddy veto, or any entry in overrides; - any plan that needs the dividend to give or pushes debt off its pre-ASR path.
  • Red lines are never traded for PV. - Premiums are declared in $B inside the team's $1B cap. A Board item that trails hold passes only as a declared premium of $0.5B or less that serves the objective. - Ledger: round-1 doctrine premium $0.26B; this round's Board premium is expected at 0.

Initial lean. LEAN: GTF2 Solo: hold, Joint Venture with RR: commit (row A). Premium: $0 this round. GTF2: hold. Two airframers have put us on the record, so the demand is visible [PX-0109]. GTF2 is ready before both entries into service, and cancel trails hold by 11.47 to 32.79 in every column. Cancelling now would also throw away the credibility objective. Joint Venture: commit. My round-1 trigger is met: both live airframes carry code 7, which includes Rolls-Royce. - The grid makes it weakly dominant: 0 / 0 / 0 / +5.51 against hold, +0.83 at my prior. It costs no new R&D while GTF2 is live. - I have no record of my own on a Rolls-Royce Joint Venture (Low). This is doctrine plus Neil's cash test and Shane's technical test. The company has run Joint Ventures to spread risk and investment [P-1233][P-1676], and I call our GTF partnerships 'critical' [PX-0038]. - The lean holds only on four conditions: - the gear, core and GTF2 technology stay P&W modules; - Shane passes it on durability and parts, so GTF2's 2036 date and team are untouched and nothing is drawn from the fleet; - Neil confirms a $0 fold write-off and raises no veto; - a 2045 hold-or-withdraw re-test is written in. - If any condition fails, I fall back to hold/hold (B), the Board's own alternative. I would declare the PV given up (5.51 × pS4) as the cost of a red line, and I have no override. Bias check: - Architecture loyalty would keep me on GTF2 alone. The grid says the commit never costs the GTF2 anything, so loyalty does not get to cost PV. - Optimism on dates: I state no EIS for any airframer and no ready year before 2036. One year of margin on NGSA is thin, and my own dates have slipped by between a quarter and two years. Expected column: S1, rivals hold. Airbus has said 'a choice of engines', Boeing wants two or three sources, and Rolls-Royce waits for our commitment. Premium ledger: Board item 0 (the commit never trails hold); doctrine 0; objective 0. The round-1 doctrine premium of $0.26B is carried separately. PROPOSED DISCLOSURE (public): "Bad news first. GTF2 will be ready in 2036 and no earlier, and our dates have slipped before. So we are not compressing a single test to hold that date. Before GTF2 enters service on NGSA or fps it has to clear two gates: durability validated in severe-environment testing, and every life-limited part at full life. If anything has to give, the date moves, not the testing. The fleet still comes first. We keep inserting the Hot Section durability kit across the GTF fleet, and we review the pacing parts every week so that no new programme takes parts or engineers from that work. We control what we can control. Airbus has invited us to join its new single-aisle as a risk-sharing partner, and we accept on standard commercial terms: no launch-style discount, no concession, no free upgrade. Today Pratt & Whitney puts on the record its commitment to a Joint Venture with Rolls-Royce on the next narrowbody engine. It forms only when Rolls-Royce also commits, and until then nothing has formed. It shares risk and investment; it does not share technology. The gear and the core stay Pratt & Whitney's, and GTF2's date and team do not change. We will offer only what can be ready by an airframe's entry into service, and we will not speak for any airframer's plans, dates or rates. These are responsible bets with responsible paybacks." If Shane or Neil strikes the commit, the Joint Venture paragraph comes out and the rest stands.

GTF2: hold. - The demand is visible: code 7 on both live airframes, on the record [PX-0109]. - Cancel trails hold in every column: -32.79 / -11.47 / -20.98 / -32.79. That is -29.26 at my weights and -29.05 at Mitchill's. It would write off $1.67B to save $0.33B and throw away two selections. - I do not harvest a programme its customers chose. Joint Venture: commit. - My round-1 trigger is met: code 7 on both live airframes includes Rolls-Royce. - The item against hold is 0 / 0 / 0 / +5.51, never negative. That is +0.55 at my weights, +0.44 at Mitchill's and +1.38 at equal weights. - It needs $0 of new cash: GTF2's $2B equals our share, so the fold write-off is $0 (Mitchill). IN MY VOICE: I won't tell you there's no surprise coming. I said that in June 2023, and the recall came five weeks later. What I'll tell you is that the orders keep GTF2 ready for both airframes on the board, the gates stand, and the fleet's parts are ring-fenced. If anything gives, the date moves, not the testing. That's on us, and we've got this. WHERE MY RECORD IS THIN: it is one investor day, 19 June 2023, before the recall. My Joint Venture and cancel views are seat and company doctrine, not my record.
