The Board's recommendations at review.

  • Durability and parts reporting before NGSA's EIS, not with the next package. The decision says the first AOG and pacing-parts count 'comes to the Board with the next package', but the next round is 2045, after both EIS dates (2037 and 2040). Eddy himself advised against waiting. Through GTF2's entry into service, the Board's Governance and Public Policy Committee (product safety and quality) should receive on a standing cadence: the GTF fleet AOG and pacing-parts count, Hot Section kit progress, severe-environment validation status and full-life LLP certification. Eddy reads the real margin as thinner than the board's, about 2037.5-2038 at the derivative prior, and losing NGSA costs 21.32. If testing threatens 2037, disclose fast and let the date move, not the testing. The Board accepts that red-line cost.
  • Align the 2045 hold-or-withdraw rule with the Board's Premature exit test. A 2045 withdraw is a Board item and passes only if its weighted item value on the 2045 grid, at Mitchill's weights, is at least 0. Clauses (1) and (2) of the written rule fit that test. Clause (3), withdraw on any lapsed condition, could produce a withdraw that trails hold. Bring any such withdraw with its 2045 grid numbers and the lapsed condition named, and the Board will test it. Because orders are simultaneous, a standing commitment held in 2045 forms if Rolls-Royce commits that round, so the decision must be in the sealed 2045 orders. Carry Mitchill's $2B contingency, for the case where a ready GTF2 no longer counts toward our share, into that test, not into today's value.
  • Any P&W cash beyond GTF2's $2B is a new capital appropriation. That covers a contribution under Airbus's risk-sharing invitation beyond our own engine's development, a Joint Venture top-up or buy-in, a fresh share in 2045, and a post-EIS merged derivative carrying UltraFan NB content. Each comes through Mitchill's gate and the Finance Committee to the Board, with its own return case against hold and a buyback and, for a derivative, its own durability programme. The commit is worth +0.44 at Mitchill's weights only because it is free.
  • Public statement: it passes Disclosure. It says ready in 2036 and no earlier, gives validation and full-life LLPs as gates, names no airframer date, and says the Joint Venture forms only when Rolls-Royce commits. One tightening: write 'the Joint Venture does not change GTF2's configuration, date or team' rather than 'GTF2's configuration, date and team do not change'. Otherwise the line can be read as a promise of 2036, which Eddy's margin does not support and which sits against 'the date moves, not the testing'. Keep the credibility objective out of public claims, as Mitchill advises.
  • GTF2: the cancel option lapses with this round, and from 2036 GTF2's $2B is sunk, as the Board guided. Its whole-programme value against cancel is +32.79 / +11.47 / +20.98 / +32.79 (+29.05 at Mitchill's weights). In 2045, report GTF2's in-service value against this plan, together with the selections actually fitted on NGSA and fps. The Board once reviewed the GTF's NPV every year.
  • Dividend, debt and ledger: confirmed as reported. There is no new R&D this round, GTF2 cost about $0.33B a year (5.6% of the ~$6B envelope), the dividend is covered, debt is on its pre-ASR path and the Board's one-round stretch is unused. The premium ledger stands at $0.26B of $1B. Because the analyst models stop at 2030E, the 2045 memo should show GTF2's actual 2030-35 spend and any Joint Venture cash against the envelope and the debt path.

She should also give the cash cost of the narrowbody ramp after 2037, which is not in the grid, and in S4 the effect of a fold (own narrowbody money stops at $5.7B, with $1.71B written off). (4) Watson's ready year against each live airframe: UltraFan NB 2037 against NGSA 2037 (zero margin) and fps 2040 (3 years). He should report the status of last round's support gates: partner MRO agreements were due by 2034, and the first partner shop and an EIS support team by 2036. For any Joint Venture commit, he should give the ready year if it forms in 2035, folding our Solo (ready 2037) and GTF2 (ready 2036), against each EIS. (5) Both veto checks, with every red-line flag struck or rebutted in rationale and overrides empty. A Joint Venture commit must explicitly rebut the ExCo's own rule and last round's public word ('we commit once its commitment is on the record'). (6) Any premium in premium, item by item, with its reason. (7) Control's metrics for the submitted plan in every column: own narrowbody money, NB+WB strain, RR widebody share in 2050 and RR narrowbody share in 2050. The package should state plainly that no order this round brings own narrowbody money within $4B: hold leaves $8.0B, a cancel $5.7B, and a fold in S4 $5.7B. (8) A forward plan for any standing Joint Venture commitment. If P&W commits in 2045, formation would come after both airframes are in service, and a ready Solo might fold with spend beyond $4B written off. The package should give the trigger for withdraw in the 2045 round. (9) The public statement, checked against the disclosure test.

Would approve.

  • Joint Venture with P&W: commit, with UltraFan NB Solo, UltraFan WB and Trent 1000 upgrade at hold. "UltraFan NB: hold + commit to JV" against "UltraFan NB: hold" is 0 / 0 / 0 / +2.28 / 0 / 0 (+0.23 at illustrative weights). It passes each test. - Partner alignment: fps and NGSA both carry code 7 on the public record, which includes P&W, and the weighted value is ≥ 0 under any weights. - Profit: ≥ 0 with no premium. - Reasonable worst case: 0, against a $4B bill. - Maturity: if P&W commits this round, the Joint Venture forms in 2035 and folds our Solo (ready 2037) and GTF2 (2036). It is then ready by NGSA's 2037 EIS (zero margin) and fps's 2040. If P&W does not commit, nothing forms and nothing is spent. - Overlap: no widebody programme sits beside it. Recommendations.

  • Maturity and support first. Watson should report to the Safety, Energy Transition & Tech Committee against last round's gates. Were the partner MRO agreements, due by 2034, signed? Is the first partner shop with an EIS support team on track for 2036? He should also give the narrowbody gearbox test status and name the zero margin against NGSA's 2037 EIS. If 2037 cannot be met without compressing testing, he says so now; the date moves, never the test plan. Our largest exposures are an airframer dropping us, S2 (-21.32 against S1) and S3 (-11.81). No order cures them. Delivered maturity, durability and support are the only defence we have.
  • The Joint Venture: now or not at all. A commitment that forms in 2045 would come after both airframes are in service (NGSA 2037, fps 2040), so this round is its last useful window. We would approve Joint Venture with P&W: commit: it is never below hold, +2.28 in S4, and it cuts our own narrowbody money to $5.7B there. The call is the CEO's. He must square it with last round's word ('we commit once its commitment is on the record') and the ExCo's own rule, and we would not ask him to break a public word for +$0.23B expected. If he brings it, the package should show what the standing commitment does if P&W commits only in 2045. In that case a ready Solo might fold and write off spend beyond $4B, so the package should commit to withdraw in the 2045 round unless that grid shows it pays.
  • Control's terms, stated plainly. No order this round brings our own narrowbody money within $4B: hold leaves $8.0B, a cancel $5.7B, and a fold in S4 $5.7B. Never cancel or fold for the metric alone. The line still in our hands is strain, and it should stay at $0. From now on any widebody programme carries a one-off $5B, and once the Solo is ready in 2037 it can no longer be removed by a cancel. Every future widebody item will be judged with that $5B stacked on its own bill.
  • The widebody core. Defend Trent through time on wing and fleet support inside the existing budget, as an unpriced other move, rather than through a new programme this round. Our widebody share is 58% to 2041 and 55.2% from 2042, when the GEnx upgrade counts, so it stays above our 50% line. If a 787 or A350 Re-engine goes on the record (S5, S6), bring the upgrade and UltraFan WB rows next round with the strain shown, and apply the widebody franchise test. In S5 the A350 airframe share falls to 30.2% by 2050. We power the A350 alone, so that is the sole-source exposure to watch, even though the board's engine share does not move with it.
  • Funding discipline. McCabe should report each quarter how the remaining Solo spend is met from free cash flow: about $2.29B, or about £1.7bn, over 2035-37. She should also set out the cash cost of the narrowbody ramp and support build after 2037. That cost is not in the grid, and neither analyst model has a narrowbody line. Our order holds: buybacks give way first, then the dividend, then new programme spend. Any need for equity, leverage above about 1.5x or borrowing for distributions comes back to the board before it arises.
  • Public statement and other moves. Restate that UltraFan NB is ready no earlier than seven years from launch, with support in place before entry into service. Give no new date and nothing on any airframer's dates. Qualify 'we launch for any airframer that selects us' with 'where we can be ready by its entry into service', since a 2035 launch is ready only in 2042. Answer Airbus's risk-sharing invitation and Boeing's code-7 competition on standard commercial terms, with no launch-style concessions to hold a selection: profit over share. If the Joint Venture commit is brought, say in the statement why we move before P&W.

Tufan Erginbilgic frames the round

Question. So, 2035. We launched UltraFan NB in 2030 because both airframers selected us. Both still carry code 7, and the engine is ready in 2037. The question is about cash and quality of earnings, not share [RX-0054]. It has three parts. (1) Do we deliver what we launched? Frankly, yes. Cancel is -36.35 against hold in four columns, and it is not an orphan. (2) Do we put our Joint Venture commitment on the record now? This is the last round it can serve these airframes. It costs nothing unless P&W commits in the same round. If P&W does commit, it stops our remaining Solo spend: +2.28 in S4, 0 in every other column. (3) Does any widebody spend earn its keep beside the narrowbody? No. Every widebody row carries $5B of strain and is negative in every column. The real exposure is an airframer dropping us: S2 is -21.32 against S1 and S3 is -11.81. No order cures that. Only delivered maturity and support do.

Situation. PUBLIC RECORD (bulletin, round 2) - NGSA (Airbus) and fps (Boeing, 10-year ramp-up) were both launched in 2030. EIS is 2037 for NGSA and 2040 for fps. Both selected code 7: RR, P&W and CFM. - Engine programmes: our UltraFan NB Solo (2030, ready 2037); P&W GTF2 Solo (2030, ready 2036); CFM ducted (ready 2036); CFM-Embraer partnership (ready 2037); GEnx upgrade (ready since 2033). - No 787 or A350 Re-engine is on the record. - P&W said "We are making no Joint Venture commitment this round" (2030). It commits GTF2 for any airframer that selects it. - Boeing: CFM is the baseline and certifies first. A P&W or RR engine follows in sequence once it shows maturity and durability. - Airbus invites all three engine makers as risk-sharing partners. - Our 2030 public word: "the Joint Venture is open to Pratt & Whitney, and we commit once its commitment is on the record." OUR POSITION (brief) - Hold is worth +30.07 (yield 127.3%). - $5.71B is spent on the Solo; about $2.29B is still to come over 2035-37. - NB engine share: 24.1% from 2037, 36.5% from 2040. - WB engine share: 58% to 2041, 55.2% from 2042, when the GEnx upgrade counts. OBJECTIVE STATUS ON HOLD - NB entry: met. 36.5% in 2045 and 2050 (19.7% in S2, 21.6% in S3). - WB dominance: met. 55.2% worst year, every column. - Control, bounded NB risk: NOT met. $8.0B, sunk since the 2030 trigger and already stated. No order this round brings it within $4B: hold leaves $8.0B, a cancel $5.7B, and a fold in S4 $5.7B. - Control, strain: met at $0. TIMING - UltraFan NB ready 2037 gives zero margin against NGSA 2037 and 3 years against fps 2040. - A Joint Venture formed in 2035 folds our Solo (2037) and GTF2 (2036): ready by 2037 at the latest, the Board's reading. Watson to confirm. - A Joint Venture formed in 2045 comes after both EIS and would fold a ready Solo. BOARD GUIDANCE (risk aversion 4 of 5) - Would approve: all fields at hold, or Joint Venture with P&W: commit with everything else at hold. - Would veto: a cancel; the Trent 1000 upgrade; UltraFan WB; any commit without McCabe's co-signature; any standing Civil veto; any unresolved red-line flag or non-empty overrides. - On the Joint Venture: "now or not at all". The call is mine, but I must square it with last round's word.

Options to test.

  • A. All four levers at hold. - Expected PV +27.34 at my weights (+26.74 at the Board's illustration). It is the baseline for every gain below. - Control: $8.0B / $0 / 55.2% / 36.5% in S1, S4-S6; 19.7% in S2; 21.6% in S3. - Gate: the Solo was gated in 2030 and is selected. Delivers what we committed. PASS.
  • B. "UltraFan NB: hold + commit to JV", everything else at hold. - Gain over hold: +0.23 at my weights and +0.23 at the Board's. Worst column 0, against a $4B bill. At least 0 under any weights. - Four-part gate: - differentiated: UltraFan core plus P&W's gearbox; - large market: 4,000 NB engines a year; - viable business model: both live airframes carry code 7, which includes P&W, and it forms only if P&W commits, so nothing is spent otherwise; - synergy: it answers our gearbox-sizing constraint and our missing NB MRO scale. PASSES. - It meets the condition I set last round: a fold only if the fold row beats keeping the Solo. It does in S4 and ties elsewhere. - Control in S4: $5.7B / $0 / 55.2% / 36.5%. Elsewhere as A.
  • C. "cancel UltraFan NB". - Gain over hold: -33.63 at my weights (-33.04 at the Board's). Worst -36.35, far below its own $5.71B write-off. - FAILS the gate: not an orphan. Company red line and Board veto. - Control: $5.7B, still a breach. - Tested only to close it.
  • D. "cancel UltraFan NB + commit to JV". - Gain over hold: -30.16. Worst -36.35. In S4 it is -1.72 against hold and -4.00 against B. - Control in S4: $9.7B, worse than A. - Red line and Board veto. OUT.
  • E. "hold + T1000 upgrade", with or without the Joint Venture. - Gain over hold: -6.01 (-5.78 with the Joint Venture, against hold). Worst -6.03, three times the $2B bill, because the $5B strain is stacked on it. - Red line: no upgrade while an UltraFan is in development. Board veto. Control's strain line breached. The premium would be above the $3B cap. - The widebody franchise test is not triggered (55.2% or more everywhere). OUT.
  • F. "hold + UltraFan WB", with or without the Joint Venture. - Gain over hold: -8.80 (-8.57 with the Joint Venture). Worst -9.00, against a $4B bill. - No Re-engine on the record. Overlap with a Solo that is not 'both selected'. Above the Board's $1B UltraFan WB sub-cap. Strain breached. - FAILS the gate on business model. OUT.

Red lines.

  • Safety and maturity first [RX-0296, RX-0284, RG-0027]. - No compressed testing. If narrowbody testing needs longer, the date moves, never the test plan. - No disclosed date earlier than launch + 7 for UltraFan NB (2037). No Joint Venture ready date disclosed at all. - Partner-shop support in place before EIS [RX-0283].
  • cancel only a programme no live airframe flies [R-1573]. UltraFan NB is selected on NGSA and fps (code 7) and ready by both EIS. NO CANCEL. Board would-veto.
  • Joint Venture with P&W: commit only once P&W's commitment is on the public record, or a live airframe's engine code includes P&W [R-1010; Board rule]. The second limb is met: code 7 on both. Conditions on a commit: - McCabe's co-signature; - an explicit rebuttal of last round's public word and of the ExCo's 'P&W first' default; - a public statement saying why we move now; - a 2045 withdraw trigger. The commitment is public at once.
  • No options management [RX-0051]. A standing Joint Venture commitment that no airframe can use is withdrawn: in the 2045 round, if P&W has not committed by then, unless that round's grid shows the commit row at or above hold.
  • No Trent 1000 upgrade while an UltraFan is in development (to 2037) [R-0929, R-1127]. The $5B strain now attaches to any widebody programme for good. Board would-veto.
  • No UltraFan WB without an A350 Re-engine on the record, or a 787 Re-engine on which Boeing has named UltraFan. Never beside the Solo unless both are selected. UltraFan WB premium capped at $1B [R-1574]. Board would-veto.
  • Control's terms: - strain stays at $0; - the $8.0B own-NB-money breach is stated plainly with its cause; - never cancel or fold for the metric alone.
  • No item may lose more than its own bill in a plausible column [RG-0033].
  • Any premium is declared item by item, within $3B a round.
  • Governance [RX-0213]: - every commit needs McCabe's co-signature against mid-to-high-teens hurdles; - Watson's Civil veto binds; - overrides stays empty.
  • No equity, leverage below about 1.5x, no borrowing for distributions. Buybacks give way first [RG-0041].
  • Pricing: answer Airbus's risk-sharing invitation and Boeing's code-7 competition on standard commercial terms. No launch-style concessions to hold a selection [R-1582].

Initial lean. PROPOSAL - UltraFan NB Solo: hold: the Solo continues as launched. - Joint Venture with P&W: commit - UltraFan WB: hold - Trent 1000 upgrade: hold WHY THE SOLO STAYS We deliver what we committed. Both airframers fly it, and a cancel is -36.35 in four columns. "When we commit, we deliver" [RX-0124]. WHY THE JOINT VENTURE NOW - On the grid it is never below hold: +2.28 in S4, 0 elsewhere. That is +0.23 expected at my weights and at the Board's. - Worst column 0, against a $4B bill. Partnership is our stated preference [RX-0118, R-1009]. REBUTTING LAST ROUND'S WORD, "we commit once its commitment is on the record" Orders are sealed and simultaneous. Waiting for P&W's commitment to appear on the record means committing in 2045 at the earliest. By then both airframes are in service, and a fold would write off about $4B of a ready engine. That is the opposite of what the word was for. The word existed so that there is no Joint Venture without a partner and an airframe. This commit keeps that: - it forms only if P&W commits in the same round; - both live airframes already carry code 7, which includes P&W (the Board's partner limb); - the fold-row condition I set last round is met. If P&W does not commit, nothing forms and nothing is spent. We withdraw in the 2045 round unless that grid shows the commit pays. This is a choice with a trigger, not options management [RX-0051]. It is the same logic as last round's launch if selected. The IAE lesson holds too: partners need alignment, and here both are on the new engine [R-0318]. CONDITIONS - McCabe's co-signature. - Watson confirms that a 2035 fold is ready by 2037 without compressed testing. - If either fails, the Joint Venture goes to hold, with a declared premium of $0.23B, within the cap. WIDEBODY Do Nothing. Every widebody row carries $5B of strain and is negative in every column. No Re-engine is on the record, and the share is 55.2% or more. Trent time on wing continues inside the budget. EXPECTED VALUE AND CONTROL - Expected PV +27.57 at my weights (hold +27.34). Premium $0. - Control: $8.0B, or $5.7B in S4. A stated breach that no order cures. Strain $0. WB 55.2%. NB 36.5% in 2050. DRAFT STATEMENT "So, plainly. UltraFan narrowbody stays on plan: ready no earlier than seven years from launch, with support in place before entry into service. If testing needs longer, the date moves, not the test plan. Both airframers have selected all three engine makers, so this is the round a partnership can still serve them. Our Joint Venture commitment to Pratt & Whitney is on the record. It forms only if Pratt & Whitney commits too; if not, nothing is spent and we will not hold it open. We launch for any airframer that selects us where we can be ready by its entry into service. Widebody is our core: no new widebody programme beside the narrowbody. We won't do anything not profitable. When we commit, we deliver."

We want their status reported with evidence: partner MRO agreements (2034), and the first partner shop with an EIS support team (2036). If the Joint Venture forms, the joint support agreement must be in the formation documents before 2037. The folded engine flies on its own frozen test plan, with no reconfiguration before EIS. An UltraFan-core, P&W-gearbox engine comes to the board as a new programme with its own full test plan. Before fps in 2040, show Boeing's sequence the full test plan complete, life-limited parts at full life and NGSA in-service durability data.
  • The Joint Venture forward plan. The commitment stands until withdrawn. In the 2045 round, bring the withdraw row against the keep row, column by column. The default is withdraw, unless keeping it is at or above withdraw in every column, with the worst column at or above 0, no premium, and support of the in-service UltraFan NB fleet undisturbed. Confirm from the 2045 brief how a same-round withdraw is adjudicated against a P&W commit. A fold of a ready engine would write off about $4B, gain nothing on Control's metric, and could disturb fleet support. If the Joint Venture forms this round, report the $1.71B fold write-off as non-cash, on spend already made. Any request for RR money beyond our $4B share comes back to the board before it arises.
  • Funding order: reconcile McCabe's correction before the board pack goes out. Buybacks give way first, as in 2015. The 30-40% dividend ranks after the balance sheet in our capital frame. The remaining Solo spend (about $2.29B, about £0.84bn a year in 2035-36, 9-12% of analyst free cash flow) belongs to a selected programme in delivery, not new programme spend. It is not to be re-phased in any way that moves the date or compresses testing. Any step beyond buybacks, on the dividend or on programme phasing, comes to the board before it arises. McCabe should report quarterly, including the narrowbody ramp after 2037. That ramp is not in the grid: $2-5B is her base case, planned at the top, and about $10B her reasonable worst case.
  • The widebody core and Control's strain line. Strain stays at $0. From 2037 the Solo can no longer be cancelled, so every future widebody item will carry the $5B strain on top of its own bill, and we will judge it that way. If a 787 or A350 Re-engine goes on the record (S5, S6), or RR widebody share heads toward 50%, bring the upgrade and UltraFan WB rows next round with the strain shown and the premium caps applied ($3B in all, at most $1B for UltraFan WB). Trent time on wing inside the existing budget is the right defence now. Watch the A350 sole-source exposure: Airbus widebody airframe share falls to 30.2% in S5, even though the board's engine share holds at 55.2%.
  • Control's terms and the public word. Keep stating plainly that our own narrowbody money is $8.0B ($5.7B only if P&W commits) against $4B. The cause is the 2030 double selection, and we never cancel or fold for the metric alone. The statement is clean on disclosure: no early date, no Joint Venture date, nothing on airframer dates. Next round, say plainly where the Joint Venture stands once P&W's 2035 orders are published, and do not describe a Joint Venture engine as able to serve either airframe before the bulletin shows a ready date. Answer Airbus's risk-sharing invitation and Boeing's code-7 competition on standard commercial terms, with no launch-style concessions to hold a selection.

  • Joint Venture commitment to Pratt & Whitney: public, standing, conditional by rule (public): Rolls-Royce puts its Joint Venture commitment on the record this round. It forms only in a round in which Pratt & Whitney is also committed. Until then nothing is spent. Our technology comes into it: 'we are actually bringing a technology' [RX-0072]. No terms, no ready date and no airframer date are disclosed.
  • Joint narrowbody support plan before first EIS (Watson) (private): Last round's gates are re-committed. Watson reports them on plan; the board does not track them, so no signature is claimed beyond the record. (1) Singapore-model partner MRO agreements, gate 2034. (2) First partner shop inducting engines and an EIS support team (field service, spares pool, repair technology) by 2036, ahead of a first EIS no earlier than 2037. (3) Narrowbody work only with high-performing suppliers. If the Joint Venture forms, a joint support agreement goes into the formation documents in 2035-36, before the first EIS: our partner shops plus the partner's in-service narrowbody shops. A folded programme carries on its own frozen test plan. An UltraFan-core, P&W-gearbox configuration would be a later engine with its own full programme, not a 2037 engine. Internal gates; inference; not disclosed.
  • Funding plan for the remaining Solo spend and the narrowbody ramp (McCabe) (private): About $2.29B (about £1.7bn, roughly £0.84bn a year in 2035-36) remains on the Solo, about 9-12% of analyst free cash flow. In S4 it is £0 from the 2035 fold, with $1.71B written off (non-cash, about £1.26bn, shown outside underlying profit; inference). Ramp after 2037, not in the grid: base $2-5B (£1.5-3.7bn) over 2037-43, planned at the top of that range; reasonable worst case about $10B over a decade if durability bites. Order: buybacks give way first, then the dividend, then programme spend. No equity, leverage well below about 1.5x, no borrowing for distributions. McCabe reports to the Board each quarter. Any need beyond buybacks comes back to the Board before it arises.
  • 2045 withdraw trigger for the standing Joint Venture commitment (private): If P&W has not committed by the 2045 round, the default order is Joint Venture with P&W: withdraw. We keep the commitment only if that round's grid shows it at or above withdraw in every column, with the worst column at or above 0, no premium needed, and no disruption to support of the in-service UltraFan NB fleet (about 10,000 engines by end-2044 in S1). The test is run on the 2045 grid before P&W's move is known. No options management [RX-0051].
  • Trent time on wing and fleet support inside the existing budget (Watson) (public): Longer-life HP turbine blades on the Trent 1000 and Trent 7000, life extension for life-limited parts, UltraFan technology inserted into the Trent fleet, and Trent XWB shop-visit cost down. Funded inside the existing fleet budget. It is not the Trent 1000 upgrade order and not a new programme, and it carries no strain. No dates disclosed.
  • Commercial terms with Airbus and Boeing (public): We answer Airbus's invitation on NGSA and Boeing's code-7 engine competition on fps on standard commercial terms: value remunerated, win-win, with no launch-style concessions to hold a selection. Every new contract goes through the Investment Committee [RX-0081, RX-0097, R-1582]. We will show the maturity and durability Boeing's sequence asks for, and we do not speak for any airframer's dates.

Round 3 · decision year 2045

2045: everyone holds; neither airframer re-engines its widebody

  • Both new narrowbodies are in service. The live levers were the Re-engines, the Open Fan and Rolls-Royce's widebody engines, and every company held.
  • Airbus: the A350 Re-engine was worth +$0.89B if Boeing held, under its $1B bar, and no widebody engine would be ready for it.
  • Boeing: its Board would have vetoed the 787 Re-engine on its business case: +$0.30B if Airbus held, −$1.26B if Airbus re-engined too. The enabler is met at two sources, "not the three we planned".
  • Rolls-Royce: both widebody programmes carried the $5B strain beside the Joint Venture.

What each player ordered

PlayerOrders (as adjudicated) and public statement
BoeingDo Nothing

Public statement: “Our new single-aisle airplane has been in service for five years now, so let me tell you plainly where it stands. It's in production, it's flying, and our customers have two engine sources on it: CFM, and the engine from Pratt & Whitney and Rolls-Royce. Every step up in production is gated on our KPIs: rework, escapes, traveled work, supplier shortages and training. The data sets the pace, not the calendar. I'd much rather be a month late than go a month early. Safety and quality come first, ahead of rate. We review how both engines are doing in service, every time our Board's safety committee meets, and we keep our suppliers healthy, engines first. On the 787, we're not starting a new development this year. We'll keep growing that airplane out of the capacity we built in Charleston, at the pace our KPIs allow. We'd rather do less and do it better. When there's a business case for the next step on the widebody, we'll bring it, and not before. The balance sheet is where it belongs, and it stayed there through the heaviest spending years. Debt stays first. How and when we return cash to our shareholders is a decision for our Board, and you'll hear about it when the Board has made it. We still develop with our suppliers on cost-plus and risk-share terms, not fixed price. I'm not going to give you any new dates today. We have more share to earn back, and we'll earn it one airplane and one customer at a time. The financials will follow our production performance. We've come a long way. We still have work to do.”

AirbusDo Nothing

Our priority is the fleet in service, with a disciplined and controlled production ramp of the new single-aisle and the A320neo family and delivery performance for our customers. We continue to secure our own supply chain, engines and critical materials first. The A350 family, passenger and freighter, remains the backbone of our widebody offer, and we will keep developing it and offering it on value to our customers. We will take a further step on the A350 only when the technology, the engine and the business case are all ready. We manage the company with financial discipline, within our financial flexibility and our existing shareholder return policy. We will continue to work with our industry partners for a tariff-free, zero-for-zero regime for aerospace trade. We prepare the next generation of Airbus aircraft on technology gates, one well-prepared programme at a time, for a stronger and more sovereign European aerospace industry.”

CFM/GEDo Nothing

Public statement: “Safety, quality, delivery and cost, always in that order. That doesn't change this year. Let me tell you what we know and what we don't. Both new single-aisle aircraft are flying, and CFM is on both of them alongside others. We're honored by that. We also know we don't have a birthright on the next order. We keep our place the same way we earned it: readiness, durability and support, one customer and one engine at a time. CFM is a 50-50 partnership with our partner, and we do this work together. Board guidance before the ExCo met

Priorities.

  • Safety and quality on the fps in service. The 10-year fps has been in service since 2040. On the brief its narrowbody share climbs 1 pp a year, from 38% in 2040 to 43% in 2045 and 47% from 2049. That ramp runs on stable production and KPI gates, not on the calendar. In-service reliability and the durability of both engine sources (CFM and the P&W-Rolls-Royce Joint Venture engine) report to the Aerospace Safety Committee.
  • No second development without a business case. The 787 Re-engine is the only live order this round, and it fails two of our tests. Its item value is +0.30 in S1, inside our $1B tie band (epsilon), and -1.26 in S2, below our -$1B downside limit. The bulletin does not rule out an A350 Re-engine. One development at a time no longer bars it (overlap 0), but the business case does. Hold, and bring the case back in 2050 as a review only if the A350 has not been re-engined.
  • Keep the balance sheet repaired. Net debt has been at the historical level since 2029 in the base case and 2030 in the stress case, and it is held at every checkpoint in both plans. The 2036 cash peak passed without strain. By our computation from the brief, stress-case free cash flow is about $15-17B a year from 2040. Capital returns are reserved to this Board. Any proposal comes to us sized on the stress case. No new equity.
  • Keep the engine supply stable. The fps code has been fixed since EIS. It flies two sources, CFM and the P&W-Rolls-Royce Joint Venture engine, in 2045 and 2050, and three narrowbody engine makers stay in the market. The enabler is met at two sources, not the three we planned in 2035: the Joint Venture folded both solo engines into one source. Protect both sources, and watch CFM capacity across LEAP, the fps, NGSA and the aftermarket.
  • Long-cycle discipline in public. Give no new dates and do not react to Airbus. Accept that no order this round moves narrowbody share: 2040 incumbency (38%) is history and the 50/50 split stays out of reach (47% in 2050). Pay no objective premium for either.

Expects to see. 1. The submitted row and, for each Board item, the same row with that item at its default. Do Nothing (fps: hold + 787: hold) scores +0.66 / +0.34 and fps: hold + 787 Re-engine scores +0.96 / -0.92 (S1 / S2). Give the 787 Re-engine's item value, +0.30 / -1.26. Name the CEO's expected column, and say whether the ExCo treats S2 as its risk case (the brief labels none). 2. Malave's buffer test with numbers. If S2 is the risk case, the floor is +0.34 - 2.00 = -1.66, and the Re-engine row (-0.92) passes by $0.74B. If not, say 'not applicable'. Also his base and stress net-debt path with and without a 2045 Re-engine: about $5B of programme cash over 2045-49, against stress free cash flow of about $16B a year (our computation). His 'Fundable when the 777X turns' test is not applicable, since there is no fps launch. 3. Pope's results: - fps production KPIs and the ramp; - a statement that no live quality, FAA or certification problem exists, since the brief reports none; - strain: $0, because the fps development (2033-40) and a 2045 Re-engine (2045-50) do not overlap; - suppliers, engines first: CFM capacity, the Joint Venture engine's in-service durability, and LEAP-1B while the 737 MAX stays in production; - for any Re-engine case, which engine maker would supply it and whether its engine would be ready by a 2050 EIS. 4. The CEO's rulings: - H3, second half: not fired, since there is no A350 Re-engine on the public record; - H4: overlap 0; - H5: nothing to cancel; - H8: the premium. Also the best grid plan in his expected column. 5. The premium, logged: $0.30B if he expects S1 and holds the Re-engine; $0 if he expects S2. 6. The objective cell for the chosen plan: 2029 / yes / yes ($0.0B) / 2 (2) in both columns. Also a plain statement that the enabler is met at two sources, and that no order moves narrowbody share. 7. Capital allocation: management's view on returns now that the cash peak is past, as a proposal for our reserved decision. Bring it with the stress-case path and the rating view; it is not a game order. 8. A public statement with no new dates and no reaction to Airbus.

Would approve.

  • fps: hold, the only value offered. The 10-year fps has been in service since 2040, and a hold is never vetoed.
  • 787 Re-engine: hold. It is the Do Nothing row: +0.66 / +0.34 (S1 / S2). It is best in S2 by $1.26B and holds the higher worst column (+0.34 against -0.92). In S1 it gives up $0.30B, inside epsilon; log that as doctrine premium (H8) if S1 is expected. Objective cell: 2029 / yes / yes ($0.0B) / 2 (2) in both columns. We never veto a hold.
  • 737 rate: hold (the only value), and fps engine code none. The code has been fixed since EIS, and the fps flies CFM plus the P&W-Rolls-Royce Joint Venture engine, two sources in 2045 and 2050.
  • Unpriced other_moves we would welcome, as recommendations only: - a KPI-gated fps production ramp; - in-service engine durability reviews to the Aerospace Safety Committee; - supplier health, engines first; - 787 growth from Charleston capacity, KPI-gated; - a capital-return proposal brought to this Board as a reserved matter, sized on the stress case.

Would veto.

  • 787 Re-engine: launch. Its item value against hold is +0.30 (S1) / -1.26 (S2). (1) Business case fails: +0.30 is below epsilon ($1B) in S1, and S2 is negative, so it fails in whichever column the CEO expects [BG-0022, BG-0066]. (2) Downside fails: S2 at -1.26 is below our -$1B limit. S2 is plausible: the bulletin does not rule out an A350 Re-engine, and Airbus's priority line held only until NGSA's EIS, which came in 2037 [BG-0029, BG-0062]. Tests it passes: - One development at a time: overlap 0 years, fps development 2033-40 against Re-engine development 2045-50. - Rating first: S2 at -0.92 against a -1.66 floor if S2 is the risk case; otherwise not applicable. - Safety: the brief reports no live problem, subject to Pope's results. - H3, second half: not fired. Doctrine's preference for a Re-engine once there is no overlap does not override a failed Board test. Hold also keeps the option: if Airbus re-engines now, hold is best by $1.26B; if it does not, the case can return in 2050. Acceptable alternative: hold.
  • Any total of doctrine plus objective premium above $2B, or any premium not logged (H8). We would veto the item whose return to its default cures the excess. The most at stake on this grid is $0.30B.

Recommendations.

  • Hold the 787 Re-engine this round. Against hold it is worth +0.30 in S1, inside our $1B tie band, and -1.26 in S2, below our -$1B limit. Hold beats it on expectation whenever S2 carries more than about 19% weight (0.30 / 1.56). One development at a time no longer stands in the way, since the overlap is 0 years. The business case does. If you expect S1, log the $0.30B as doctrine premium. If Airbus re-engines the A350 now, H3 closes the option and hold is the better row by $1.26B. If it does not, bring the widebody case back in 2050 as a review, with: - the grid then; - the engine maker and its readiness by EIS; - Pope's KPI, strain and supplier results.
  • The fps is in its production ramp. Safety and quality come before rate. Gate each production step on the KPIs (rework, escapes, traveled work, supplier shortages, training), never on the calendar. Bring in-service reliability and the durability of both engine sources (CFM and the Joint Venture engine) to the Aerospace Safety Committee at each meeting. That committee brings propulsion expertise to that review. Report any quality, FAA or supply problem to us as a live problem.
  • Engine supply. The enabler is met at two sources, CFM and the P&W-Rolls-Royce Joint Venture engine, not the three planned in 2035, because the Joint Venture folded both solo engines into one source. Keep both sources supplied and hot. Watch CFM capacity across LEAP-1B, the fps, NGSA and the aftermarket. Report the supplier-shortages KPI, engines first. Keep development and support terms on risk-share or cost-plus, never fixed price.
  • Capital allocation, answering the CEO's 2035 recommendation: - The 2036 cash peak is past. Net debt has stayed at the historical level since 2029 in the base case and 2030 in the stress case. By our computation from the brief, stress-case free cash flow runs about $15.2B (2040), $16.4B (2045) and $17.2B (2050). - Any dividend or buyback is reserved to this Board, and the tracker's surplus-to-owners rule does not decide it for us. We are open to a proposal. - Bring it with the rating view and the stress-case net-debt path. Size it so net debt stays at or below the historical level in the stress case, with a liquidity cushion kept through the fps ramp and any 2050 widebody decision. - Keep returns well short of the pre-2019 practice of returning about all free cash flow. - No new equity.
  • Public statement and objectives: - Give no new dates, and do not answer Airbus's calendar. - Reaffirm safety, quality, KPI-gated production, two engine sources and debt first. - Accept plainly that no order this round moves narrowbody share: incumbency was missed in 2040 (38%), and the 50/50 split stays out of reach (47% in 2050). Pay no objective premium for either. - Debt repair and the engine enabler are met in both plans.

Kelly Ortberg frames the round

Question. The fps has been in service since 2040, and its ramp runs on the KPIs. This round has one live order: the 787 Re-engine, launched now for EIS 2050. Does it beat Do Nothing by more than ε ($1B) in the column I expect, inside the hard rules, and without a downside our Board will not carry? H4 no longer stands in the way (overlap 0), and H3's second half has not fired. So the business case decides it: +0.30 in S1 and -1.26 in S2. Two questions sit beside the grid: (1) Is the fps production ramp stable, and are both engine sources holding up in service? (2) The cash peak is past, and net debt has sat at the historical level since 2029. What do we bring the Board on capital returns, sized on the stress case? Airbus's calendar does not enter any of it [B-2313].

Situation. Decision year 2045. Our position. The 10-year fps (Solo, launched 2030) has been in service since 2040, and its engine code has been fixed since EIS. It flies CFM and the P&W-Rolls-Royce Joint Venture engine, which counts as one source. That gives two sources in 2045 and 2050, with three narrowbody engine makers in the market. - Narrowbody share bottomed at 37% in 2039 and has climbed 1 pp a year since EIS, to 42% in 2044. On the brief it is 43% in 2045 and 47% from 2049. - NGSA has been in service since 2037. - The A350 has not been re-engined, and our widebody share is flat at 58.8%. - The 2045 row: 860 narrowbody and 100 widebody deliveries, and $15.7B of operating profit against $6.7B in the status quo. Gates. The brief reports no live quality, FAA, supply-chain or certification problem, so the KPI gate and the FAA-process gate are open. The 777X and MAX 7/10 count as done (inference). The three work streams are not the question this round, since no new airplane is on offer. Grid (S1: rivals hold; S2: Airbus launches the A350 Re-engine; the brief labels no risk case): - A. fps hold + 787 hold (Do Nothing): +0.66 / +0.34. - B. fps hold + 787 Re-engine: +0.96 / -0.92. - The Re-engine's item value is +0.30 / -1.26. On expectation, hold beats it once S2 carries more than about 19% weight (0.30 / 1.56). - An A350 Re-engine costs us $0.32B even if we hold (+0.66 down to +0.34). - If we re-engine too, both airplanes enter service in 2050, so neither gains share, and the 787's margin falls from 20% to 15.77%. - Do Nothing's +0.66 is narrowbody profit +20.30, less programme investment of 14.91 and a debt penalty of 4.73. The grid already nets every penalty, so none is subtracted again. Debt. Net debt has been $0 since 2029 (base case) and 2030 (stress case), and it is held at every checkpoint in both plans. The 2036 cash peak passed without strain. - Base free cash flow: $19.8B (2040), $20.9B (2045), $21.8B (2050). - Stress case, my reading: about $15.2B, $16.4B and $17.2B. Malave should confirm. - A 2045 Re-engine would spend $5B over 2045-49, about $1B a year, against that. Mission. The objective cell is 2029 / yes / yes ($0.0B) / 2 (2) for both plans in both columns. - Debt repair: met, and held. - Engine enabler: met at two sources, not the three we planned in 2035, because the Joint Venture folded both solo engines into one source. - Incumbency and the 50/50 split: not met. Share was 38% in 2040 (the worst year), and is 43% in 2045 and 47% in 2050. No order this round moves narrowbody share. Board risks (its would-veto list; guidance, not red lines): - a 787 Re-engine launch: +0.30 is below its $1B launch test, and -1.26 in S2 breaches its -$1B downside limit; - any premium above $2B, or any premium not logged. It never vetoes a hold. It wants a capital-return proposal for its reserved decision, sized on the stress case and brought with the rating view.

Options to test.

  • A. Do Nothing: fps hold, engine code null, 737 rate hold, 787 Re-engine hold. It scores +0.66 / +0.34 (S1 / S2), is best in S2 by $1.26B and has the higher worst column (+0.34). Objective cell: 2029 / yes / yes ($0.0B) / 2 (2) in both columns. No Board item. This is my lean.
  • B. Do Nothing plus a 787 Re-engine in 2045 (EIS 2050): +0.96 / -0.92, which is +0.30 / -1.26 against A. - It is legal: H4 overlap is 0, and H3's second half has not fired. - It fails doing less, better: +0.30 is inside ε. - It fails doctrine's own Re-engine rule, which needs a gain above ε. - It loses $1.26B in S2, past the Board's -$1B limit, so the Board would veto it. - Malave's buffer test is not applicable without a risk-case column. If S2 were treated as the risk case, B would pass at -0.92 against a -1.66 floor, by $0.74B. - The objective cell is unchanged. I test it to put the row and its item value in front of the Board. It is not my lean.
  • C. A against B, weighted by probability. Hold wins once S2 carries more than about 19.2% weight (0.30 / 1.56). At 30% weight, A is ahead by $0.17B; at 50%, by $0.48B. Malave gives his own weight on S2.
  • D. Beside A, unpriced: a capital-return proposal for the Board's reserved decision, on the same grid row as A. Sized on the stress case: - net debt at or below $0 at every checkpoint; - a liquidity cushion kept through the fps ramp and any 2050 widebody decision; - no new equity; - returns well short of all free cash flow.
  • E. Not an order: a widebody review in 2050, held only if the A350 has not been re-engined (H3, second half). It would bring the grid as it stands then, the engine maker's readiness by EIS, and Pope's KPI, strain and supplier results. Holding now keeps this option open.

Red lines.

  • H1 and H3 first half: I ruled on both in 2030, with evidence. Both are spent and not in force.
  • H2 cannot bind. H7 has no trigger: the brief reports no crisis and no certification trouble, so the FAA-process gate is open.
  • H3 second half: no 787 Re-engine once Airbus has launched the A350 Re-engine. It has not fired, since no A350 Re-engine is on the public record. If Airbus launches one this round, the widebody option closes for the rest of the game. A 787 Re-engine launched in the same sealed round would be kept (H5).
  • H4: a Solo fps and the 787 Re-engine may overlap by at most 2 years. A 2045 Re-engine overlaps the fps development (2033-40) by 0 years, so H4 does not strike it.
  • H5: never cancel a launched fps or 787 Re-engine. Nothing is up for cancellation this round.
  • H6: no Rate Increase under a live problem or as a reply to Airbus. Only hold is on offer.
  • H8: ties within ε ($1B) go to doctrine. Doctrine plus objective premium may total at most $2B, and every premium is logged. The most at stake on this grid is $0.30B.
  • Team rule: Malave's buffer test binds where the brief has a risk-case column. This brief labels none, so by my ruling there is no slip leg this round, and each plan's worst column is advice. Malave may contest that. The KPI doctrine's veto on a Rate Increase under a live problem is moot, since the rate is hold only.
  • My own red lines: - no production-certification concurrency on any development [BX-1263]; - no fixed-price development, only cost-plus or risk-share [BX-1262, BX-1304]; - never walk away from core customers' programmes [BX-1251]; - no blame on the FAA [BX-1323]; - no attribution of a supplier problem to Airbus before exposure (doctrine); - no new dates before the data supports them [BX-1268, B-2315].

Initial lean. Hold everything, and change nothing on the board: - fps: hold. It is in service and on its ramp. - fps engine code: null. The code has been fixed since EIS. - 737 rate: hold. - 787 Re-engine: hold. Every order is a default, so nothing goes to the Board as a change. Why hold. This is the Do Nothing row: +0.66 / +0.34. - The Re-engine is +0.30 in S1, inside ε. So doing less and doing it better wins [BX-1239], and so does doctrine's own rule, which allows a Re-engine only if the gain exceeds ε. - In S2 the Re-engine loses $1.26B, and hold has the higher worst column (+0.34 against -0.92). It is the higher-confidence plan [BX-0548]. - Hold also keeps the option. If Airbus re-engines the A350 now, H3 closes the widebody and hold was right by $1.26B. If it does not, the case comes back in 2050 as a review, with the grid as it stands then and Pope's readiness results. Expected column: S2, provisionally and narrowly. - Why S2: Airbus tied its A350 priority to 'until the new aircraft enters service', and NGSA has been in service since 2037. Its one-programme-at-a-time rule no longer holds it back. - Why S1 is close behind: Rolls-Royce, the A350's engine maker, says it will run no new widebody programme beside the narrowbody. - Malave gives me his independent read. - Premium: the best grid plan in S2 is A, so the premium is $0. If I land on S1, the best plan there is B at +0.96, and I log $0.30B as doctrine premium. Either way it is inside the $2B cap. - Hold is right on expectation once S2 carries more than about 19% weight, and I put it well above that. This is not an answer to Airbus. The business case decides. Off the board: - a KPI-gated fps ramp; - durability reviews of both engine sources for the Aerospace Safety Committee; - supplier health, engines first; - 787 growth from Charleston; - a measured capital-return proposal for the Board's reserved decision, sized on the stress case. Public statement. No new dates, no word on Airbus and no blame on anyone. 'the financials will follow our production performance' [BX-1287]. What would change my lean: - a grid gain above ε in my expected column with no breach of the Board's -$1B limit (there is none on this brief); - a live KPI or supply problem from Pope, which would make me hold harder and add nothing; - a stress-path breach from Malave, which would shrink or defer the return proposal.

Board guidance before the ExCo met

Priorities.

  • Safety and the five pillars come first. NGSA has been in service since 2037, and the A320neo GTF fleet still flies. The full Board's twice-yearly safety review should see three things: NGSA fleet results, the durability of the P&W-Rolls-Royce Joint Venture engine, and CFM capacity across both new narrowbodies. The Board will accept no item that the operating head fails on safety, quality, the ramp or a supply crunch, and no override of those tests [AG-0038, A-0331, AX-0015, A-0303, AG-0067, AG-0068].
  • The A350 Re-engine gets the fresh test the Board asked for in 2035. NGSA spending ended in 2036, so a 2045 launch (in service 2050) costs $1.0B a year with no overlap and no strain, and no 787 Re-engine is on the public record. On the brief the item is worth +0.89 if rivals hold (S1) and -0.50 if Boeing launches a 787 Re-engine (S2). It passes the Board's cash, one-programme-at-a-time and downside tests. It falls short of the company's own $1B gain test. The Board would accept a launch that properly clears the ExCo's tests, or a hold. It would not accept an override [A-0343, A-0401, AG-0049, A-0302, AX-0019].
  • Liquidity, the rating and returns. Programme cash in 2045-2049 is $0 on hold, or $1.0B a year with the A350 Re-engine: 19% of the $5.2B line (one year's free cash flow). Net cash, the A+/A1 rating and the 30-50% payout remain fundable. There is to be no equity raise and no dividend cut, and any new buyback is a reserved matter [AX-0022, AX-0104, A-0402, AG-0062, AG-0058, AG-0059, AG-0035].
  • A stable engine supply. NGSA flies CFM plus the P&W-Rolls-Royce Joint Venture engine, which gives 2 sources. Three narrowbody engine makers stay in the market in 2045 and 2050 under either plan. The NGSA engine code can no longer change, so the Board's attention moves to keeping both sources healthy, and to the engine behind any A350 Re-engine: Rolls-Royce is today the A350's only engine source [A-0243, A-0360, A-0218, AX-0054, A-0253].
  • Integrity and the 60/40 objective. Delay Tactics are closed for the rest of the game, since fps has been in service since 2040, and none was ordered in any round. The 60/40 objective is not met (57% in 2045, 53% in 2050), and no option this round reaches it. The Board asks that no PV, cash or integrity be traded for it [A-0299, AG-0053, A-0474, AG-0022, AX-0025].

Expects to see. The Board expects one agreed ExCo package. (1) The submitted row and the default row, with the item value in each column. - Hold: +23.37 (S1) / +23.26 (S2). - A350 Re-engine: +24.26 (S1) / +22.76 (S2). - The Re-engine item is therefore +0.89 (S1) / -0.50 (S2). - It breaks even at a 64% chance of S2. Weighted at 25-30% S2, it is worth +0.47 to +0.54. (2) The CEO's expected column, named, and the worst plausible column. - S2 is not ruled out. Boeing's own statement put its fps cash peak in 2036-37, and that peak is past. - The worst plausible column is S2 in both plans: +23.26 on hold, +22.76 with the Re-engine. (3) The CFO's cash figures for 2045-2050. - Programme cash: $0 on hold. With the Re-engine, $5B / 5 = $1.00B a year in 2045-2049, against the $5.2B line (EUR 4,753m at $1.10). No overlap with NGSA and $0 strain. - The net-cash bridge with the dividend. - Returns inside 30-50%. Any new buyback comes to the Board as a reserved matter. No equity raise and no dividend cut. - His added-move robustness test on the A350 Re-engine, with its result and how it was resolved. (4) The operating head's results. - Safety and quality, with any five-pillars flag. - The A320neo and NGSA ramp, and any supply crunch. - For a Re-engine: engineering capacity and A350 production readiness for a 2050 entry into service, and a committed engine source. The board does not price the engine, but in practice the A350 Re-engine depends on Rolls-Royce or a second maker committing. (5) The engine enabler. - The NGSA code is unchanged and cannot change after entry into service. - 2 sources (CFM + P&W-RR Joint Venture) and 3 makers in 2045 and 2050, in both plans. - A status report on the Joint Venture engine's durability and on CFM capacity. (6) The rule 3 check on the record: no 787 Re-engine is on the public record. (7) Any soft veto and how it was resolved. No override has been used this game. No override can carry the A350 Re-engine: +0.89 is under the $1B bar, and the item trails hold by $0.50B in S2. (8) A public statement that: - puts safety first; - gives windows, not dates (for a Re-engine, entry into service 'at the end of the decade'); - times nothing to Boeing and says nothing on Delay Tactics. If a piece is missing, the Board will compute it from the brief and say so.

Would approve.

  • A350 Re-engine: launch (entry into service 2050), if it reaches the Board with the ExCo's own tests resolved and S1 named as the expected column. - Cash: passes. $1.0B a year in 2045-2049 is 19% of the $5.2B line, with 0 years of overlap with NGSA and $0 strain. - One programme at a time: passes. It is the only launch this round, and NGSA has been in service since 2037. - Downside: passes. +0.89 in S1 and -0.50 in S2, within the $2B limit. - Returns stay fundable. - Rule 3 is met: no 787 Re-engine is on the record. - Row: +24.26 / +22.76, against hold at +23.37 / +23.26. - It needs a Qualified Majority: $5B is about EUR 4.55bn at $1.10, above EUR 800m.
  • A350 Re-engine: hold. This is the default, not a Board item, and is never vetoed. The Board finds it equally acceptable: the company's own test asks for at least $1B over Do Nothing, and the item reaches +0.89 at best. Row: +23.37 / +23.26.
  • NGSA: hold, with the engine code unchanged. It is the only NGSA value open now that NGSA is in service, and it is not a Board item. It keeps 2 sources (CFM + P&W-RR Joint Venture) and 3 makers in 2045 and 2050.
  • Delay Tactics: none. It is the only value open, since fps has been in service since 2040, and it is not a Board item.

Would veto.

  • A350 Re-engine: launch submitted over a standing soft veto. This applies if the CFO's added-move test fails the item (+0.89 is under $1B, and -0.50 is negative in S2) and the CEO neither respects that test nor validly overrides it. Ground: governance (an unresolved objection). Acceptable alternative: hold.
  • A350 Re-engine: launch carried by an override. Ground: governance (override review). - Its margin over the best passing option (hold) is +0.89 in S1, under the $1B bar. - On this Qualified Majority item it also trails hold by $0.50B in the worst plausible column (S2). - No override of this item can pass. Acceptable alternative: hold.
  • A350 Re-engine: launch if the operating head fails it on safety, quality, the A320neo or NGSA ramp, or a supply crunch. Ground: safety and ramp, with no override accepted. A soft veto on engineering capacity or production readiness would go through override review, which this item cannot pass. Acceptable alternative: hold.
  • A350 Re-engine: launch if the CEO names S2 (787 Re-engine) as the expected column, since the item would then lose $0.50B in the column where it should gain. Ground: downside. Acceptable alternative: hold.
  • The Board never vetoes a hold or none, the engine code on its own, an item for its near-term earnings cost alone, or the A350 Re-engine merely because hold scores higher in S2.

Recommendations.

  • Put the A350 Re-engine to its fresh test, as the Board asked in 2035, and decide by the ExCo's own rule. - The Board's tests pass: $1.0B a year, no overlap, and +0.89 / -0.50 within the $2B limit. - The company's $1B gain test does not. On the team rule, that points to hold. - The Board will approve either a launch that properly clears the ExCo's tests or a hold. - It does not ask the ExCo to set its $1B test aside for this item. It would veto any override: +0.89 cannot reach $1B, and the item trails hold by $0.50B in S2.
  • If the A350 Re-engine is launched: - Name and secure its engine before the vote. The A350 flies Rolls-Royce Trent XWB today, and Rolls-Royce has said it plans no new widebody programme beside the narrowbody. The board does not price the engine, but supply does. - Make no reactive cancellation in 2050. If Boeing re-engines the 787 in the same round, both enter service in 2050 and Boeing's does not enter service first, so the Board's rule against reactive cancellation holds. - Keep to one launch this round: the A220-500 stays a study.
  • If the A350 Re-engine is held: compete on A350 price and product, as Airbus did when it sold the A330neo on price. Bring the Re-engine back in 2050 only on a fresh grid that shows at least $1B over Do Nothing, and only if no 787 Re-engine is on the record (rule 3).
  • Engine supply (the enabler). Dual sourcing on NGSA (CFM + P&W-RR Joint Venture) and three narrowbody makers in 2045 and 2050 are met in both plans. The Joint Venture engine counts as one source. The operating head should report three things to the twice-yearly safety review: - the Joint Venture engine's durability and deliveries; - CFM capacity across NGSA, the A320neo and the aftermarket (Boeing has flagged it as a watch item); - the GTF fleet's Hot Section kit insertion on the A320neo. Keep the risk-sharing invitation on standard terms.
  • The CFO's papers for 2045-2050: - the net-cash bridge with the dividend; - programme cash at $0, or $1.0B a year with the Re-engine; - confirmation that returns stay inside the 30-50% policy; - any new buyback brought to the Board as a reserved matter, within the AGM authority, with the bridge attached. There is to be no equity raise and no dividend cut. Refundable advances and state support remain upside and are never assumed in the case.
  • Show both columns. Name the expected column and give its probability. Show the worst plausible column (S2) for each plan and the 64% break-even for the Re-engine. Read Boeing only from the bulletin: by its own statement its fps cash peak (2036-37) is past, so S2 is not ruled out.
  • Integrity and the 60/40 objective. - Delay Tactics are closed for the game, and none was ordered in any round. - The supply-security move stays confined to Airbus's own ramp, with the Ethics, Compliance and Sustainability Committee kept informed. - The 60/40 objective is not met, and no PV, cash or integrity should be traded for it. - Unpriced moves in support, such as delivery performance and the A220-500 study, are read with the package as recommendations only.
  • Public statement: - open with the five pillars; - give windows, not dates; - say 'we intend to offer a choice of engines'; - time nothing to Boeing and say nothing on Delay Tactics. If the A350 Re-engine is launched, give its entry into service as a window.

Guillaume Faury frames the round

Question. 2045 is the A350 Re-engine's fresh test, which the Board asked for in 2035. NGSA has been in service since 2037 and its spending ended in 2036. Should we launch the A350 Re-engine now? It would enter service at the end of the decade (2050) at $1.0B a year, with no overlap and no strain. On the grid the item is +0.89 if rivals hold (S1) and -0.50 if Boeing launches a 787 Re-engine (S2), so it falls short of the company's own $1B gain test. Or do we hold everything at the default, with no Board items, and compete on A350 price and product?

Situation. BOEING AND THE PUBLIC RECORD (bulletin only) - fps was launched in 2030 on the 10-year ramp and has been in service since 2040. It flies code 7, with CFM certifying first. Boeing says it develops on cost-plus and risk-share terms, never fixed price. - Boeing's last statement put debt first through its fps cash peak in 2036-37. That peak is now past. - It puts 737 MAX and 787 customers first and will "keep growing the 787 out of the capacity we've built in Charleston". That reads as rate on today's 787, not a new engine. - No 787 Re-engine and no Rate Increase are on the record. The GEnx upgrade has served the 787 since 2033, and CFM/GE's widebody engine share moved from 42.0% to 44.8% in 2042. ENGINE MAKERS - P&W and Rolls-Royce both committed in 2035, so the Joint Venture formed. GTF2 Solo and UltraFan NB Solo folded into it, and the Joint Venture engine has been ready since 2036. - CFM: the ducted engine has been ready since 2036 and the Embraer partnership since 2037. RISE stays funded as technology, with no date. - Rolls-Royce: "Widebody is our core: no new widebody programme beside the narrowbody." It is improving Trent time on wing inside its existing budget. Today it is the A350's only engine source [A-0253]. PROBLEMS REPORTED The brief reports no supply crunch, no quality event and no technology or engine slip. Our narrowbody deliveries are falling from 1,260 (2039) to 1,140 (2045). That is the board's share mechanics after fps entered service, not a supply event. OUR POSITION - NGSA has been in service since 2037. On code 7 it is fitted with CFM + the P&W-RR Joint Venture engine (2 sources). The code can no longer change. - If nobody moves, ΔPV is +23.37 (yield 115.58%): narrowbody operating profit +39.13, programme investment -15.23 (booked at the 2037 EIS), debt penalty -0.53. - Grid: - Hold: +23.37 (S1) / +23.26 (S2). A 787 Re-engine costs the hold plan only $0.11B. - A350 Re-engine: +24.26 (S1) / +22.76 (S2). - The item is +0.89 / -0.50 and breaks even at a 64% chance of S2. - No programme cash runs in 2045-2049 on hold. The A350 Re-engine would add $5B / 5 = $1.0B a year, 19% of the $5.2B line. OBJECTIVE STATUS (scored by the GM; it never changes the payoff) - Defend 60/40: NOT met. Narrowbody share is 62% in 2040, 57% in 2045 and 53% in 2050. No option this round reaches it, because the A350 is widebody. - Protect the A320 family: met at 60% before NGSA's EIS. - Enabler: met in both plans. NGSA has 2 sources (CFM + the Joint Venture engine) in 2040, 2045 and 2050, and 3 narrowbody makers (CFM, P&W, RR) are in the market in 2045 and 2050. THE BOARD'S GUIDANCE (risk-averse, 4 of 5) - It will approve either a hold or an A350 Re-engine launch that properly clears the ExCo's own tests, with S1 named as the expected column. - It will veto a launch that goes through over a standing soft veto, a launch carried by an override, a launch Wagner fails on safety, quality, the ramp or a supply crunch, and a launch where S2 is named as the expected column. MY READ OF BOEING - Expected column: S1 (rivals hold), at about 70%. Boeing's stated priority is current 787 and 737 MAX stability, the GEnx upgrade already serves the 787, and Rolls-Royce says it plans no new widebody programme. - S2 is more plausible than in 2035 because fps spending is past. I put it at about 30% (range 25-35%). It is the worst plausible column. - Boeing's moves do not set our clock.

Options to test.

  • 1. COMPANY DEFAULT AND MY LEAN: NGSA hold (code unchanged) + A350 hold + Delay Tactics none. - Row: +23.37 (S1) / +23.26 (S2). The worst plausible column is S2 at +23.26, which is positive and the higher of the two rows' worst columns. - Weighted at 25-35% S2: about +23.33 to +23.34. - No Board items and $0 programme cash in 2045-2049. - Enabler: 2 sources and 3 makers in 2045 and 2050. - This is also the reference row: every order is at its default.
  • 2. TEST, likely to fail the company's $1B test: + A350 Re-engine (A350 Re-engine: launch, entry into service 2050). Row and item - Row: +24.26 (S1) / +22.76 (S2). Item against hold: +0.89 / -0.50. - It breaks even at a 64% chance of S2. Weighted, it is worth +0.54 at 25% S2, +0.47 at 30% and +0.40 at 35%. What it passes - Cash: $1.0B a year, 19% of the $5.2B line, with 0 years of overlap and $0 strain. - Rule 6 (one launch, no overlap) and rule 3 (no 787 Re-engine on the record). - The Board's downside test: it gains in S1 and loses less than $2B in S2. What it fails - The company's launch test (profile §6): at least $1B over Do Nothing, by $0.11B. - The doctrine default: hold is within $1B of the best S1 plan. - Probably Toepfer's added-move robustness test (under $1B, and negative in S2). Override and engine - No override can carry it: +0.89 is under the $1B bar, and it trails hold by $0.50B in S2. - Unpriced dependency: the engine. Rolls-Royce is the A350's only source and has said it plans no new widebody programme beside the narrowbody.
  • 3. ON RECORD, NOT A CHOICE: - Delay Tactics: closed (fps in service since 2040). - NGSA engine code: locked. - NGSA cancel: not an option, and rule 7 bars it in any case. None of these changes the grid this round.
  • 4. IF THE A350 RE-ENGINE IS HELD (unpriced): - Compete on A350 and A350F price and product, as we sold the A330neo on price [A-0090, A-0091]. - Bring the Re-engine back in 2050 only on a fresh grid showing at least $1B over Do Nothing, and only if no 787 Re-engine is on the record (rule 3). - My inference: a 2055 entry into service leaves fewer years in the board's table (which runs to 2060), so I do not count on that option.
  • 5. IF THE A350 RE-ENGINE WERE LAUNCHED: - Name and secure its engine before the vote. - Keep to one launch: the A220-500 stays a study. - No reactive cancellation in 2050. If Boeing launches a 787 Re-engine in the same round, both enter service in 2050 and Boeing's does not enter service first.

Red lines.

  • Five pillars (safety, quality, integrity, compliance, security). No order or statement that fails them, and nothing we could not defend to the Audit Committee or the Ethics, Compliance and Sustainability Committee. Never overridden [AX-0073, AX-0081].
  • Rule 3: no A350 Re-engine after Boeing has launched a 787 Re-engine. It does not bind this round, since none is on the record. A launch in the same round is not 'after'. If Boeing launches one now, any 2050 return is off and we compete on price.
  • A350 Re-engine cancel rule: cancel only if Boeing's 787 Re-engine enters service first and its remaining spend loses at least $1B. A same-year entry into service (2050) is not first, so there is no reactive cancellation.
  • Rule 6: at most one new launch this round. Overlap with NGSA is 0, since NGSA has been in service since 2037. The A220-500 stays a study.
  • Rule 7 (never cancel NGSA) and our own clock: Boeing's moves never re-time or cancel our programmes.
  • Rules 4 and 5, Delay Tactics: closed for the game, since fps has been in service since 2040. Only 'none' is open, and Delay Tactics are never named in public.
  • Company launch test for the A350 Re-engine (profile §6): at least $1B over Do Nothing including strain, no 787 Re-engine, overlap of 2 years or less. The item reaches +0.89 at best, so it fails on the $1B leg. 'Do Nothing is a legitimate choice wherever the red lines or the $1B test bind' [A-0440].
  • Doctrine default: take the company default when it is within $1B of the best grid plan in the expected column. The S1 gap is $0.89B. The $3B premium allowance is not engaged.
  • Override budget: one per game, still unused. It needs at least $1B over the best passing option, must be recorded as a Board item, and can never go against a pillar, a red line or the Board. It cannot carry the A350 Re-engine (+0.89 is under $1B, and the item trails hold by $0.50B in S2).
  • Peak-cash line: about $5.2B, one year's free cash flow (EUR 4,753m at $1.10) [AX-0104, AX-0022]. Hold uses $0 and the Re-engine $1.0B a year.
  • The Board's would-veto list, carried in full: - a launch submitted over a standing soft veto; - a launch carried by an override; - a launch Wagner fails on safety, quality, the A320neo or NGSA ramp, or a supply crunch; - a launch with S2 named as the expected column. The Board never vetoes a hold, 'none' or the engine code on its own.
  • Board downside test: each Board item must gain in the expected column (S1) and lose less than $2B in any plausible column. Both columns are plausible.
  • Balance sheet: no equity raise and no dividend cut. Returns stay inside 30-50%, and any new buyback is a reserved Board matter [AX-0022, AX-0001].
  • Disclosure: windows, not dates. No internal long-term-plan targets. Nothing timed to Boeing and nothing on Delay Tactics [AX-0004, AX-0005, AX-0020].
  • 60/40 and the enabler are scored, not paid for. No PV, cash or integrity is traded for either.

Initial lean. ORDERS - NGSA: hold - NGSA engine code: none (unchanged and locked) - A350 Re-engine: hold - Delay Tactics: none No Board items. Row: +23.37 (S1) / +23.26 (S2). WHY, IN MY ORDER - Five pillars: nothing covert. Safety leads, and the engine-supply report goes to the Board's safety review [AX-0081, AX-0073, AX-0015]. - The ramp: no new programme load while the NGSA fleet matures. CFM capacity and the durability of the Joint Venture engine are the watch items [AX-0010, AX-0054]. - Preparing the Airbus of the 2030s: NGSA is in service, with 2 engine sources and 3 makers. We prepare the next step on technology gates, not on Boeing's calendar [AX-0020]. - The Board: hold is a default it finds equally acceptable, and it vetoes nothing in it. THE GRID - Expected column: S1, about 70%. Worst plausible column: S2, about 30%. - The A350 Re-engine is my derivative instinct, and this is the round the Board set for its fresh test [AX-0019, A-0302]. It fails the company's own $1B gain test by $0.11B and loses $0.50B in S2. It is worth only +0.40 to +0.54 weighted. - Hold is within $1B of the best S1 plan. It is also the best plan in S2 and the more robust row: its worst column is +23.26, against +22.76. - So the doctrine default carries. The $0.89B gap in S1 is the doctrine premium, recorded and not hidden. The $3B allowance is not engaged. WHAT WOULD CHANGE MY LEAN Only a corrected grid, or a five-pillars flag on the hold plan. Even if both your tests passed the Re-engine, the $1B default rule keeps hold. No override is available. IF HELD - We compete on A350 and A350F price and product, as with the A330neo [A-0090, A-0091]. - The Re-engine returns in 2050 only on a fresh grid showing at least $1B over Do Nothing, and only with no 787 Re-engine on the record. 60/40 Not met (57% in 2045, 53% in 2050), and no lever reaches it. Nothing is traded for it. PUBLIC LINE (draft) - Open with the five pillars. - Say NGSA is in service, and 'we intend to offer a choice of engines'. - A disciplined and controlled ramp; the A350 family developed and offered on value. - Funded within our financial flexibility and existing return policy. - Zero-for-zero trade, and a more sovereign European industry. - Windows, not dates. Nothing timed to Boeing, nothing on Delay Tactics.

Orders. Do Nothing

Rationale. DECISION: hold on every lever. The orders are ngsa hold, NGSA engine code null (locked at entry into service), A350 Re-engine hold and Delay Tactics none. There are no Board items and no override. THE TEAM RULE, STEP BY STEP (1) Delete red-line and five-pillars breaches. Neither row breaks a pillar. - Rule 3 holds: no 787 Re-engine is on the record. - Rule 6 holds: one launch, 0 years of overlap. - Rule 7 holds: no NGSA cancel. - Rules 4 and 5: Delay Tactics are closed, because fps has been in service since 2040. - The A350 Re-engine does fail the company's own launch test (profile §6: at least $1B over Do Nothing). It reaches +0.89 at best, short by $0.11B. 'Do Nothing is a legitimate choice wherever the red lines or the $1B test bind' [A-0440]. (2) Survivors: options that pass both colleagues' tests. - Hold passes every test in both memos. - The Re-engine carries two binding soft vetoes: - Toepfer: the added-move robustness test fails (+0.89 in S1, -0.50 in S2, under $1B in every column); - Wagner: engine production readiness fails. Rolls-Royce is the A350's only source and said 'no new widebody programme beside the narrowbody'. An UltraFan widebody launched in 2045 is ready only in 2051 under rules.md, a year after a 2050 entry into service. No second maker is on the record. - Neither veto rests on safety, quality, the ramp or a supply crunch. (3) Highest-grid survivor in the expected column (S1): hold, at +23.37 (S1) and +23.26 (S2). Hold is also the company default, within $1B of the best S1 plan (gap $0.89B). It is the best plan in S2 and the more robust row: its worst column is +23.26, against +22.76. (4) Override: none is possible. - The margin over the best passing option (hold) is +0.89 in S1, under the $1B bar, and -0.50 in S2. Weighted, it is +0.54 / +0.47 / +0.40 at 25 / 30 / 35% S2. - The Board said it would veto any launch carried by an override. - The override budget stays unused. (5) Tie-breaks within $1B all favour hold: - later capex start: none, against $1.0B a year from 2045; - strain: equal at $0; - Board items: 0 against 1 (Qualified Majority, $5B, about EUR 4.55bn). WHY, IN MY ORDER - Five pillars: nothing covert. Safety leads, and the engine-supply report goes to the safety review [AX-0081, AX-0073]. - The ramp: no new load while the NGSA fleet matures. Joint Venture engine durability and CFM capacity are the watch items [AX-0010, AX-0054]. - Preparing the Airbus of the next decades: the A350 Re-engine is my derivative instinct [AX-0019, AX-0082]. A derivative without a committed engine is not prepared, and the grid does not clear the company's own bar. - The Board: it named hold as equally acceptable, and it vetoes nothing in it. WHAT WE GIVE UP, PLAINLY - +0.89 in S1, about +0.47 weighted at 30% S2. - A 2050 return (entry into service 2055) is bounded below about $0.61B on today's mechanics (Toepfer's inference), so in practice we are forgoing the A350 Re-engine for this game. - I accept that as the doctrine premium. It is within the $1B default; the $3B allowance is not engaged. - Wagner's own note stands as a lesson: the engine gap existed in 2035 too, so any return now needs a committed engine on the record before the vote. PACKAGE LINE FOR THE BOARD (no items to vote) - Five pillars: pass, no flag. - Toepfer: hold passes all tests. Nil programme cash in 2045-2049 against $5.2B. Worst column S2 at +23.26. Net cash rises about $2.45B a year after the dividend on the FY2025 floor. Returns stay inside 30-50%, with no buyback proposed. - Wagner: pass. No quality event, no supply crunch, ramp shield intact. The engine code is locked: 2 sources and 3 makers. - Grid: +23.37 (S1) / +23.26 (S2). - Re-engine held: +0.89 / -0.50, two soft vetoes respected, no override. - Rule 3 check: no 787 Re-engine on the record. Boeing's moves set none of this. The order is the same in both columns.
