Watch item, not a veto: a 2050 return is gated on the three recorded conditions. On today's mechanics I bound a 2055 entry into service below $0.61B (inference), so it would need a fresh grid. On engines I defer to Lars Wagner.

Lars Wagner (operating head): concurs

Veto check, round 3 (2045). Lars Wagner, CEO Commercial Aircraft. My tests come from my role, not from anything I have on record, so confidence is Very low. I concur. The orders match my recommendation exactly: ngsa hold, NGSA engine code null (the code was locked when NGSA entered service in 2037), A350 Re-engine hold, Delay Tactics none. None of them is a Board item. How the orders fare on my tests: - Five pillars and quality: pass. Nothing covert is ordered. The four non-public items are internal operating and finance plans, not hidden actions against anyone: the safety-review report, the 2050 gate for the A350 Re-engine, the capital-return guardrail and the A220-500 study. The public statement opens with safety. It gives no dates and no window for a Re-engine, says "we intend to offer a choice of engines", and names no rival. The brief reports no quality event, safety issue, supply crunch or engine slip. - Ramp shield: pass. The fall from 1,260 deliveries (2039) to 1,140 (2045) comes from narrowbody share times 2,000 aircraft, not from supply. Holding adds no new load on the NGSA, A320neo or A350 lines. - Engineering capacity and rule 6: pass. There is no new launch, 0 years of overlap and $0 strain. - Engine supply (the enabler): pass, and the same in both columns. NGSA has 2 sources, CFM plus the P&W-RR Joint Venture engine, and 3 narrowbody engine makers (CFM, P&W, RR) are in the market in 2045 and 2050. - A350 Re-engine engine readiness: my failed test, a binding soft veto. Holding the Re-engine respects it. No override was used, and none could have carried the item: its margin over hold is +0.89 in S1, short of the $1B bar, and -0.50 in S2. - Supply crunch, maturity slip, Delay Tactics and Rate Increase: not applicable. Company red lines: no breach. - Rule 1 held: NGSA entered service in 2037. - Rule 3 holds: no A350 Re-engine is launched, and no 787 Re-engine is on the record. - Rules 4 and 5 hold: Delay Tactics are closed (fps has been in service since 2040) and none is ordered. - Rule 6 holds: no new launch. - Rule 7 holds: no cancel. Overrides: none in 2030, none in 2035 and none now, so the game's one override is still unused. I checked this against the round 1 and round 2 decisions. Adopted from my memo, and I take on the first two: - Reporting to the Board's twice-yearly safety review on three items: Joint Venture engine durability and deliveries (it carries about 73% of narrowbody engines), CFM capacity, and Hot Section kit insertion on the GTF fleet. Where the record holds no data, I will say so and estimate nothing. - The 2050 condition for any Re-engine return: a committed engine source, ready by entry into service, on the public record before the vote. - The A350 price-and-product campaign draws no NGSA or A320neo teams, as Faury records. What we give up: +0.89 in S1, about +0.47 weighted at 30% S2. That is within the $1B doctrine default. A 2050 return, with entry into service in 2055, is unlikely to clear the $1B bar. Evidence: AX-0073, AX-0010, AX-0054, AX-0060, AX-0082, A-0253, A-0366, A-0360, AX-0015.

Final

Orders (as adjudicated). Do Nothing

Expected scenario. S1 (rivals hold), at about 70%. Boeing's stated priority is 737 MAX and 787 production stability and growing the current 787 out of Charleston. The GEnx upgrade has served the 787 since 2033, and Rolls-Royce plans no new widebody programme. S2 (Boeing launches a 787 Re-engine) is about 30% (range 25-35%). It is more plausible than in 2035 because Boeing's fps cash peak (2036-37) is past, and it is the worst plausible column for both plans.

Best grid plan in that scenario. The best plan in S1 is NGSA hold + A350 Re-engine, at +24.26 (S1) and +22.76 (S2). It is not a survivor: it carries two binding soft vetoes (Toepfer's added-move robustness test and Wagner's engine readiness test), it fails the company's $1B launch test by $0.11B, and no override can carry it. The chosen plan is the highest-grid survivor and the company default: NGSA hold + A350 hold, at +23.37 (S1) and +23.26 (S2). It is also the best plan in S2. Premium paid: +0.89 $B. The premium is $0.89B in S1, about $0.47B weighted at 30% S2. In S2, hold is $0.50B better. It is paid under the doctrine default: hold is within $1B of the best S1 plan. Four further reasons: - the A350 Re-engine fails the company's own $1B launch test; - it carries two binding soft vetoes, cash robustness and engine readiness, that no override can reach; - it has no committed engine; - hold is the more robust row. The $3B allowance is not engaged. Nothing is paid for the scored objectives.

Its +4.38 beside the Open Fan only softens a penalty the Open Fan itself creates, and the pair is -21.89 on an $11B bill. If the Open Fan is vetoed, we veto Lobby with it at review. Acceptable alternative: hold.

An objective premium buys nothing: - the Open Fan leg cannot be met, since a 2045 launch is ready in 2055; - the NB-share leg has no lever on this round's menu.

Bring Ali's fleet durability report to the full board: time on wing, shop visits, life-limited parts at full life and inspection findings, on field and turn-on, turn-off evidence, not analysis. - Make every finding a cross-functional call, and fix the part rather than redesign or cancel. - Bring us at once any durability finding that touches both aircraft. Keep the RISE allowance unspent.

Show the RISE allowance separately at $0 of $15B. - Book at or below -69.69. Carry the off-grid widebody exposure (about $0.8-1.1B, inference) as the labelled low case. - Last round's -77 booking proved on the right side when the Joint Venture formed.
  • Objective, NB share of at least 50%. Say plainly that the share is 27.0% from 2040 and that no lever on this round's menu moves it. Spend no premium on it. Commercial work on both aircraft stays on standard terms, priced jointly with Safran and kept out of the public statement.
  • CFM parity rule (Safran consent). - On a hold, record in the rationale that fleet support for the Ducted and Embraer stays within joint practice. - Safran cannot be consulted in this game, so assert no Safran position. - Any Open Fan launch needs a stated reason why Safran would agree to a RISE product with no airframer path. We know of none on the record.

Larry Culp frames the round

Question. What game are we playing, and how do we win? [CX-0467] On this board the narrowbody game is settled. Both new single-aisle aircraft are in service: NGSA since 2037 and fps since 2040. Each is fitted with all three makers, and neither code can change after entry into service. The Joint Venture formed in 2035, and its engine has been ready since 2036. No order left on our menu buys back a point of NB share. So the game is the installed base we have, not the share we don't. That means: - 1,079 CFM narrowbody engines a year, on two aircraft we share three ways; - the LEAP fleet behind them; - 152 widebody engines a year, with the GEnx upgrade counting since 2042. "Our major economics happen in and around the first and second" shop visit [CX-0422]. "We get paid in dollars, not in percentages." [CX-0630] We win it on execution, in this order: safety, quality, delivery and cost [CX-0658]. - The Ducted earns its durability record in service on both aircraft, on field data, not analysis [CX-0009]. - OE delivery comes before spares, and support earns the next order. We have no birthright [CX-0564, CX-0529]. - RISE stays whole as technology for the airframe that comes after these two [CX-0214, CX-0469]. The question for this room has two parts. 1. Does anything on this grid pay us to move? I don't think so, and I want you to try to break that. 2. If not, where does the work go? I'd say fleet durability, and a capacity plan re-based to the volume we actually have. And we say plainly that both objective legs are out of reach by any order.

Situation. PUBLIC RECORD, 2045 (round 2 adjudicated) - Airframes. NGSA (Airbus) has been in service since 2037, and fps (Boeing, 10-year ramp) since 2040. Both are on code 7, fitted CFM + P&W + RR. Both are in service, so the codes are locked. - Rival NB engines. P&W and RR both committed to the Joint Venture in 2035, and GTF2 and UltraFan NB folded into it. The Joint Venture engine has been ready since 2036. I see no rival NB move left open that the board would price against us. - Our programmes. The Ducted has been ready since 2036 and Embraer has counted since 2037. The GEnx upgrade has been ready since 2033 and has counted since 2042; there is no Re-engine on the record. - Observed NB engine share (CFM / P&W / RR): - 76.0 / 24.0 / 0.0 to 2036; - 51.7 / 24.1 / 24.1 in 2037, with CFM easing to 50.5 by 2039; - 27.0 / 36.5 / 36.5 from 2040. - WB: GEnx 42.0%, then 44.8% from 2042. - Airframers on the record: - Boeing: debt first through its cash peak, and one step at a time with the FAA. - Airbus: one well-prepared programme at a time, with the A320neo and A350 first through the transition. - Neither talks of a Re-engine. RR says it starts no new widebody programme beside the narrowbody, and its Trent time-on-wing work is not the Trent 1000 upgrade order. OUR POSITION (hold everything, S1, the only column) - ΔPV -69.69 $B, yield 56.44%: engine value -63.69, R&D -4.00, strain -2.00. No new R&D is committed. - CFM NB engines a year: 3,040 to 2036, 2,070 in 2037, then 1,079 from 2040 to the end of the window (2056). WB engines a year: 143, then 152 from 2042 (counted to 2061). - Engine lifecycle value in 2045 is 13.9 nominal $B, against 31.3 in the status quo. - Hold is $7.08B below last round's S1 (-62.61). The Joint Venture forming was outside last round's grid columns, and it took CFM from 31.7% to 27.0% from 2040. Our -77 booking covered it with $7.31B to spare. Planning on the low case worked [CX-0248, CX-0536]. GRID (one column, S1: rivals hold) - Hold everything: -69.69 (56.4%). This is the best plan. - Open Fan: -95.96 (40.0%), which is -26.27 against hold. - Open Fan + Lobby: -91.58 (42.8%), which is -21.89 against hold. OBJECTIVE - NB share of at least 50% in 2040, 2045 and 2050: NOT MET. We are at 27.0% from 2040, 23 pp short, and no lever on this menu moves it. - Open Fan launched and ready by 2050: NOT MET, and no order can meet it now. A 2045 launch is ready in 2055. BOARD GUIDANCE (non-binding; labelled as such) - Would approve: hold everything, with all five fields at hold. The Ducted, Embraer and GEnx can only be held. - Would VETO: - Open Fan: launch alone: -26.27, which is $18.27B beyond its $8B bill; - Open Fan: launch with Lobby: -21.89, which is $10.89B beyond an $11B bill; - emissions lobbying: launch, which does nothing on its own and would be vetoed along with the Open Fan; - any item carrying a premium, which would be at least $21.89B against a $2.0B cap; - any cancel, though none is on the menu. - Its grounds against the Open Fan: - the wait penalty takes our 27% NB share to zero for 2045-2056; - both airframes are in service long before 2055; - the loss is over the $15B RISE allowance; - with no airframer path, it is not joint practice with Safran unless we state a reason; - Ali's RISE gates are not closed on the record. - What it wants to see: - Ali's fleet durability report, on field and turn-on, turn-off evidence, with every finding decided by a cross-functional team; - the joint capacity plan re-based to 1,079 NB engines a year; - RISE kept funded as technology; - a booking at or below -69.69, with the off-grid WB exposure labelled as the low case; - a plain objective note; - one Safran-gate line for a hold; - a public statement that replaces last round's 'last year of development' line.

Options to test.

  • Row A: hold everything, the reference row (Do Nothing). - S1: -69.69 (56.4%). It is the best plan in the only column, so it is 0.00 against Do Nothing in both the expected and the worst column, and the premium is $0. - It keeps the Ducted, Embraer and GEnx counting. - No new R&D is committed, so the 70% payout and the A-range rating are untouched.
  • Row B: Open Fan. - S1: -95.96 (40.0%), which is -26.27 against hold. - The bill is $8B. The other $18.27B is the wait penalty: CFM's 27% NB share goes to zero for 2045-2056. My check gives $18.28B, on 1,079 engines a year for 12 years. - It would be ready in 2055: 18 years after NGSA's entry and 15 after fps's. H2 binds. - The only route is the RISE allowance, and that would need $26.27B against a $15B cap. - It also can't meet the objective, since 2055 is after 2050. It fails every test I hold.
  • Row C: Open Fan + Lobby, the cheapest Open Fan row. - S1: -91.58 (42.8%), which is -21.89 against hold. Lobby is worth +4.38 inside the row. - On the Board's reading the bill is $11B ($8B + $1B + $2B strain), so it loses $10.89B beyond its bill. - It would need $21.89B of RISE allowance, $6.89B over the cap. - I test it only to put a dollar figure on the Open Fan leg of the objective, and it can't meet that leg either.
  • Excluded: Lobby alone. It is not on the grid. It costs $1B (or $3B if the strain applies) and does nothing on the board. Doctrine allows Lobby only with an Open Fan launched or live.
  • Forward look, not a row: an Open Fan launched in the 2050 round would be ready in 2060 and would still wait. On my arithmetic it is about -17B against hold: $9.05B of NB value lost over 2050-56 plus the $8B bill (inference; it matches the Board's figure). So RISE stays technology to the end of this game, and we don't stretch the test in the last round either.
  • Other moves to test (the board does not price them; Ghai and Ali to check): (1) Ali's fleet durability report to the full Board on the Ducted (NGSA since 2037, fps since 2040) and the Embraer application. It covers time on wing, shop visits, life-limited parts at full life and inspection findings, on field and turn-on, turn-off evidence. Every finding is a cross-functional call [CX-0012], and we fix the part [CX-0005]. (2) The joint CFM capacity plan, re-based with Safran on the grid's volume: 1,079 NB engines a year from 2040, against 3,040 to 2036. OE comes before spares [CX-0529], we go lean before capital [CX-0540, CX-0653], and no number goes out in public. (3) Fleet support and aftermarket for the Ducted, LEAP and GEnx fleets, on standard terms, priced jointly with Safran and kept private [CX-0184, CX-0609]. This is the installed-base work the game now turns on [CX-0422]. (4) RISE kept funded as technology, with the gates reported as the state of the technology and no product date. Its technology keeps flowing into upgrades for the in-service fleet where test supports it [CX-0162]. (5) The CFM parity record for a hold.

Red lines.

  • Safety, quality, delivery and cost, always in that order [CX-0658]. No programme is carried on in service, and nothing is launched, while a safety or durability flag from Ali stands without a cross-functional answer on evidence [CX-0012]. Ramp and schedule never trade against safety [CX-0603].
  • My line: durability is not traded for fuel burn or for schedule [CX-0208]. In service, that means we fix the part, not redesign or cancel the engine [CX-0005].
  • My line: a next engine needs at least a 20% fuel-burn improvement [CX-0217]. It binds RISE as the next generation. The Ducted gets 'less than half' the open fan's gain [CX-0183] and stands only as an H3 defence, so we never call it next-generation.
  • H1: never refuse an airframer and never lock one out [CX-0587, CX-0185]. CFM support stands on both aircraft and on Embraer.
  • H2: never press an airframer into the Open Fan wait [CX-0205]. Both new narrowbodies are in service long before a 2055 Open Fan, so there is no launch. The one exception is the declared RISE allowance (up to $15B), and the cheapest row needs $21.89B.
  • H3: a Ducted only as a defence. The trigger was met and the engine is in service. We make no new Ducted claim beyond that.
  • H5: never cancel RISE for cost while an airframer may want it, and no 'program dividend' [CX-0174, CX-0398].
  • H6, through Ali's test: no date or durability claim without test or field evidence [CX-0009]. No Open Fan entry year, and no time-on-wing claim for the Ducted that the field data hasn't earned.
  • H7: the Safran gate on every CFM narrowbody order (Ducted, Open Fan, Embraer, Lobby) [CX-0184, CX-0166]. An Open Fan launch with no airframer path needs a stated reason why Safran would agree, and we have none. Rate, capacity and price commitments are made only jointly. GEnx is GE alone.
  • H8: no public blame and no comment on rivals, the Joint Venture included [CX-0625, CX-0580].
  • H9: the doctrine plus objective premium is at most $2.0B this round and $4.0B for the game. Running count: $0 of $2.0B and $0 of $4.0B. The one RISE allowance (up to $15B) is declared in full against the best non-RISE plan, and it is unspent.

Initial lean. This is a lean, not a decision; your memos decide it. I lean to HOLD EVERYTHING: all five fields at hold. DUCTED, EMBRAER, GEnx: HOLD. That is the only option for each. All three are ready and counting. OPEN FAN: HOLD. - H2 binds in the only column. Both new narrowbodies are in service, and a 2045 launch is ready in 2055. - My installed-base lens pulls at me again: OE losses as "seeding the next 20, the next 30 years" [CX-0555]. But the board counts NB only to 2056, and the cheapest row is $6.89B over the RISE allowance. The cap holds. - RISE stays funded as technology: no cancel (H5) and no 'program dividend' [CX-0174, CX-0214]. LOBBY: HOLD. It does nothing without a live Open Fan. EXPECTED COLUMN AND BOOKING (preliminary) - Expected column S1, weight 1.00, since it is the only column the GM gave. Off-grid moves are named and labelled, never weighted into it. - I book about -71: hold less the larger off-grid widebody exposure, rounded down. That raises last round's -77 now that the codes have locked [CX-0654]. - Premium $0 of $2.0B this round and $0 of $4.0B for the game. The RISE allowance is $0 of $15B, unspent. OBJECTIVE. I say it plainly: - NB share is 27.0% from 2040 against the 50% target, and no lever on this menu moves it. - 'Open Fan launched and ready by 2050' can't be met by any order. - No objective premium is spent. SAFRAN GATE. There is no new CFM narrowbody order. Fleet support for the Ducted and Embraer on both aircraft stays within joint practice: both airframers fly CFM, and the partners split the aftermarket equally [CX-0219]. I assert no Safran position. GEnx is GE alone. OTHER MOVES - Ali's fleet durability report to the full Board. - A joint capacity plan re-based to 1,079 NB engines a year, with no new facility and no public number. - Fleet support on standard terms, priced jointly. - RISE gates reported as the state of the technology. PUBLIC LINE - Safety first, and what we know and what we don't [CX-0436]. - The Ducted is in service on both aircraft, and its record gets earned in the field. - We keep our place on readiness, durability and support, with no birthright. - RISE remains our next generation, and our customers decide when. - No rival named, no blame, no price or rate without our partner. It's that simple, ain't that hard.

Rationale. DECISION: HOLD EVERYTHING. All five fields are at hold. That is the default (Do Nothing), so no order is a Board item. WHAT GAME, HOW WE WIN [CX-0467] The narrowbody selections are settled. NGSA (2037) and fps (2040) are both in service on code 7, so the codes are locked. That means: - durability earned in the field, not on analysis [CX-0009]; - OE ahead of spares [CX-0529]; - support that earns the next order, with no birthright [CX-0564]; - RISE kept whole as technology [CX-0214, CX-0469]. Concur. I tested this against the brief, not against analysis. Dates, recomputed. Ducted 2036: one year ahead of NGSA (2037) and four ahead of fps (2040). Embraer counts from 2037. An UltraFan WB launched in 2045 is ready in 2051, after a 2045 Re-engine enters service in 2050. They are private and labelled. Pass. The statement, line by line: - 'Both new single-aisle aircraft are flying' and 'our ducted engine is in service on both' are the public record, with no share claim. - 'Its durability record gets earned in the field, and we'll tell you what the data says' commits us with no number. Keep it framed as design, never as a result. Safety and durability flag: none. That is not a clearance. The brief has no field data on the Ducted, Embraer or GEnx: no time on wing, no shop visits, no life-limited-part findings. My first field report goes to the full Board. Every finding goes to a cross-functional team [CX-0012]. We fix the part [CX-0005]. What would change my mind is test or field data only: a field distress, removals clustering on a few part numbers, supplier escapes, or a Re-engine on the record.

Board guidance before the ExCo met

Priorities.

  • Hold both fields. Nothing can come to the Board this round. The brief's only plan is 'GTF2: hold', worth +8.88 $B (108.1%) in its only column, S1 (rivals hold): +10.88 of engine value less the $2.00B of R&D. No order can be a Board item. GTF2 folded into the Joint Venture and has been ready since 2036, so the cancel window has closed. The Joint Venture formed in 2035, and a withdraw is only legal before formation. Both new narrowbodies are in service (NGSA since 2037, fps since 2040), so no airframe is waiting and launch if selected cannot be ordered. That means the 2045 hold-or-withdraw re-test written in 2035 has nothing left to decide, and Miss a cycle does not apply. Both objectives are met on the board: credibility on NGSA and fps, and ΔPV +8.88.
  • Fleet first, with durability proven in service. The Joint Venture engine (GTF2-based) is flying on NGSA and fps. Since 2040 it has delivered 1,460 NB engines a year, against 960 in the status quo, a 52% step-up in volume. Credibility is met on the board, but it lasts only as long as the time-on-wing record holds. The Board treats in-service durability, AOG count, pacing parts and the ramp as product-safety matters for the Governance and Public Policy Committee. They are not capital questions.
  • Capital in the Board's order, now that the engine is paying. On the grid, P&W's 2045 engine lifecycle value is $13.2B against $8.7B in the status quo (nominal), with no new R&D. The dividend comes first and grows with earnings. Debt goes back to, and stays at, pre-ASR levels. Buybacks are the fill-in. Any other use of cash comes through Finance with a return case that beats a buyback. The grid models no dividend or debt path, so this is a recommendation, not a test.
  • Keep the Joint Venture aligned and the technology ours. It holds only while both partners are on the same new engine. It shares risk and investment, not technology. The gear, the core and the GTF2 technology stay P&W modules under P&W design authority. Any merged derivative, UltraFan NB content insertion or Joint Venture cash call beyond GTF2's $2B is a new capital appropriation. None is on this grid, so none can be ordered or booked in 2045.
  • Credible disclosure: data, not claims. Put bad news first. Report in-service durability as fleet data. Name no airframer date or rate, and do not speak for Rolls-Royce. Say plainly that the Joint Venture formed in 2035; the 2035 line 'nothing has formed' is now superseded. Do not claim the credibility objective in public; let the fleet record speak.

Expects to see. A round of holds alone never reaches the Board's review, so the Board asks for these in the sealed orders' rationale and board_response, and in the memos filed to the run folder. (1) The orders: GTF2 Solo hold, Joint Venture with RR hold. The grid row is +8.88 (108.1%) in S1, the only column. predictions S1 = 1.00, expected ΔPV +8.88, premium 0, and the cumulative premium ledger at $0.26B of the $1B cap. Actual GTF2 spend for 2030-35 against the ~$6B envelope (the plan was about $0.33B a year, 5.6%). Confirmation that the Joint Venture asked for no P&W cash beyond GTF2's $2B. The dividend covered and growing with earnings. Debt at or back on its pre-ASR path. Where buybacks stand as the fill-in. (4) Eddy: the in-service record of the Joint Venture engine on NGSA (since 2037) and fps (since 2040). That means whether severe-environment validation and full-life LLPs were cleared before each EIS, fleet hours against the ~1M-hour benchmark, the AOG and pacing-parts count, and Hot Section kit insertion on the GTF fleet. Would approve.

  • GTF2 Solo: hold and Joint Venture with RR: hold. These are not Board items and are never vetoed. Hold/hold is the brief's only plan and its best: +8.88 $B (108.1%) in S1. It keeps the Joint Venture engine on NGSA and fps and keeps both objectives met. A round of holds alone does not come to review.

Would veto.

  • If a revised brief were to offer a Board item (none is expected), the Board would apply its standing tests. Any engine order needs a live airframe that has selected P&W and is not yet in service (Committed airframe). Any term that moves the gear or core technology into the Joint Venture fails the Joint Venture test. Acceptable alternative in every case: hold.

Recommendations.

  • Submit hold/hold, and put the record in the rationale, because this round does not come to review. Report GTF2's whole-programme value against plan, as the Board once reviewed the GTF's NPV every year. Code 7 is fitted on both airframes, and ΔPV is +8.88, the 2035 S4 outcome. Record that the 2035 hold-or-withdraw re-test has nothing left to decide, because withdraw is not legal after formation. Report premium 0 and the ledger at $0.26B of $1B.

The Governance and Public Policy Committee should get a standing report on the Joint Venture engine on NGSA and fps: fleet hours against the ~1M-hour benchmark, the AOG and pacing-parts count, and Hot Section kit insertion on the GTF fleet. Since 2040 the board has P&W at 1,460 NB engines a year against 960, a 52% step-up. Our last escape came from capacity added for a ramp, so new casting, forging and powder-metal capacity is qualified before it ships parts. AOG recovery keeps first call on parts. Fix forward with upgrades, not claims.
  • Capital in the Board's order. There is no new R&D on this grid, and on the grid's engine lifecycle value the Joint Venture engine is worth $13.2B in 2045 against $8.7B in the status quo (nominal). Mitchill should show the dividend covered and growing with earnings, debt at or back to pre-ASR levels, and buybacks returning as the fill-in once debt is there. Any other use of cash comes through Finance with a return case against a buyback. The Board's one-round stretch stays unused.
  • Joint Venture governance. Keep both partners on the one engine, because a Joint Venture holds only while both are on the same new engine. The gear, core and GTF2 technology stay P&W modules under P&W design authority, and design teams mirror module ownership. Any merged derivative carrying UltraFan NB content, any Joint Venture top-up, and any P&W cash beyond GTF2's $2B is a new capital appropriation. Each goes through Mitchill's gate and the Finance Committee to the Board, with its own return case and its own durability programme. None is on this grid. Enabling technology stays inside the ~$6B self-funded envelope.
  • Public statement (Disclosure). Put bad news first. Report in-service durability as fleet data, with no time-on-wing claim beyond the hours flown. Say plainly that the Joint Venture formed in 2035 and shares risk and investment, not technology; the 2035 'nothing has formed' line is now superseded. Name no airframer date or rate, and do not speak for Rolls-Royce. Keep standing commercial terms, with no discount or concession, and no widebody. Do not claim the credibility objective; let the fleet record carry it.
  • Looking ahead to 2050, the last round. Unless that brief offers a Board item, the same hold posture applies. Report the in-service durability record and the whole-programme value again. No widebody move fits our red lines, and P&W holds 0% of widebody engines on the board.

Chris Calio frames the round

Question. Control what you can control. This round the board gives us nothing to order. Both fields offer only hold, and the grid has one row and one column: 'GTF2: hold' at +8.88 $B (108.1%) in S1, rivals hold. The order decision is already made. The question for this ExCo is whether we keep what it earned. I put four questions to you. (1) Fleet first. Is the Joint Venture engine, which is GTF2 by the 2035 fold, earning its durability record in service on NGSA and fps? And is it doing so at 1,460 NB engines a year without taking a single part or engineer from the GTF fleet? On this board, credibility lasts only as long as the time-on-wing record holds [PX-0073][PX-0080]. (2) Capital order. Now that the engine is paying, does the cash go back in the order we have always given: the dividend first, debt back to and held at pre-ASR levels, then buybacks [PX-0081][P-0686][P-0669]? (3) The Joint Venture. Does it stay one engine, with the gear, the core and the GTF2 technology kept as P&W modules under P&W design authority [P-1233][P-1744]? (4) Disclosure and the record. Do we disclose data, not claims? And do we report to the Board, honestly, how the whole programme came out against the plan we wrote in 2030 and 2035? Initial lean. LEAN: GTF2 Solo: hold, Joint Venture with RR: hold. This is the brief's only plan: +8.88 $B (108.1%) in S1. No Board item exists, and I will say so and why in the rationale: - the cancel window closed in 2035, when GTF2 folded, and the engine has been ready since 2036; - a withdraw is illegal after the 2035 formation; - no airframe is waiting to enter service. The 2035 hold-or-withdraw re-test has nothing left to decide. Numbers: - predictions S1 = 1.00; - expected ΔPV +8.88; - premium 0; - ledger $0.26B of the $1B cap. Objectives: both met on the board. PV given up: $0. What I will own in the rationale and the Board response: - The upside came in the column we weighted lowest: S4 at 0.10 (mine) and 0.08 (Neil's). We were right to commit because the order was weakly dominant, not because we read Rolls-Royce well. - The Board's 2035 statement tightening was not taken up. - The pre-EIS reporting to the Governance Committee must be evidenced by Shane, or stated as not evidenced. Bias check: - Optimism on dates. The 2036 ready date held on the board. That is counter-evidence to my bias, not a licence to state new dates. I state none. - Architecture loyalty. The Joint Venture engine is GTF2, and the geared architecture is in service on both new single-aisles. The test now is the time-on-wing record, not loyalty. - Value capture. The kit stays charged. Other moves I propose (Shane and Neil to test): - Hot Section kit insertion continues, charged (public). - Joint Venture governance on module ownership and P&W design authority (public). - Fleet ring-fence and weekly pacing-parts review over the 1,460 rate, with capacity qualified before it ships (private). - Standing durability and parts report to the Governance and Public Policy Committee (private). - Fleet-data cadence to Airbus and Boeing (private). - Capital-order note: dividend, then debt to pre-ASR, then buybacks; any cash beyond $2B through the gate (private). PROPOSED DISCLOSURE (public; Neil's ranges for any figure, and there are none): "Bad news first. An engine earns its durability record one flight hour at a time, and ours on the new single-aisle aircraft is still being earned. Our dates have slipped before, and the GTF fleet taught us what it costs to say more than the data shows. So we will report time on wing as fleet data, and we will claim nothing beyond the hours flown. We have learned our lesson from the prior iterations of the GTF. Here is what is on the record. The Joint Venture with Rolls-Royce formed in 2035, when both partners had committed. What we said then, that nothing had formed, no longer stands. Its engine is built on GTF2, has been ready since 2036, and is fitted on both new single-aisle aircraft alongside the other makers. The Joint Venture shares risk and investment, not technology. The gear, the core and the GTF2 technology stay Pratt & Whitney modules, under our design authority. The fleet still comes first. We keep inserting the Hot Section durability kit across the GTF fleet, on standard commercial terms. We review the pacing parts every week so that new-engine production never takes parts or engineers from the fleet, and new capacity is qualified before it ships a part. We control what we can control. On capital, our order does not change: the dividend first, debt back to and held at pre-ASR levels, then buybacks. There is no new engine programme from us this year, and our terms stay standard, with no discounts and no concessions. We do not speak for our airframer customers' plans, dates or rates, or for Rolls-Royce. Those are theirs to announce." If Shane cannot evidence a fleet-data point, the statement says less, not more.

Chris Calio decides

Orders. Do Nothing

Rationale. CONTROL WHAT YOU CAN CONTROL. Orders: GTF2 Solo: hold, Joint Venture with RR: hold. These are the brief's only legal values (§3). The grid row 'GTF2: hold' is +8.88 $B (108.1%) in S1, its only column: engine value +10.88 less R&D 2.00. NO BOARD ITEM IS AVAILABLE, AND WHY - The cancel window closed in 2035. GTF2 folded into the Joint Venture that year, the engine has been ready since 2036, and an engine can be cancelled only before it is ready. - A withdraw is illegal, because the Joint Venture formed in 2035 and withdraw is legal only before formation. - launch and launch if selected cannot be ordered, because no live airframe is waiting to enter service: both new narrowbodies are in service. - So the 2045 hold-or-withdraw re-test written in 2035 (Eddy's condition d, Mitchill's three-part rule) has nothing left to decide. The Board's request to align it with the Premature exit test is moot for the same reason. For the record, its lapse conditions are checked and none has lapsed: - code 7 includes Rolls-Royce on both airframes; - nothing is billed beyond $2B; - P&W is not trimmed (36.5% each); - the modules are kept. - Miss a cycle does not apply: both cycles are taken. DECISION BY THE TEAM RULE - I start from Eddy's proposal: hold/hold. - Binding vetoes: none stands. Mitchill invokes none of his four grounds on either order. A fitted engine is not an unselected one, and the booked +8.88 is all on the public record. Eddy invokes neither technical ground: no order puts an engine on an airframe, and the brief shows no live fleet problem. - Conditional vetoes, all respected: - Mitchill ground 4: no time-on-wing or 'proven' claim, no objective claim, no lifecycle value as cash, no derivative or 2050 value. - Mitchill ground 3: the kit is charged; no concessions. - Eddy grounds 1 and 2: no configuration change without its own durability programme; the fleet ring-fence and qualified capacity. - Safety and durability constraint first [PX-0035][PX-0073]. On this board it binds through other moves, not orders. The fleet beats a new engine [PX-0080]: the 1,460 rate waits if the weekly review shows the fleet short. - Overrides: none. PREMIUM AND OBJECTIVE - premium 0. Hold/hold is the only and best plan. - The cumulative ledger stays at $0.26B of the $1B cap (the round-1 doctrine premium; $0.34B at Mitchill's weights). - Both objectives are met on the board, with $0 of PV given up. WHOLE-PROGRAMME VALUE AGAINST PLAN (for the Board, P-1191; Mitchill's numbers, which I trust over my own) - 2030: launch if selected fired on code 7. Expected PV was +0.23 at my weights and -1.72 at Mitchill's; booked 0.00. That grid's both-select-us column (S5) read +22.00, but it assumed no Rolls-Royce NB engine. Rolls-Royce launched UltraFan NB in 2030 and both airframes took code 7, so by 2035 hold read +3.37. - 2035 grid: - hold: +3.37 / -17.95 / -8.44 / +3.37; - hold + commit: +3.37 / -17.95 / -8.44 / +8.88. - Expected: +0.39 (mine), +0.07 (Mitchill's). Booked: +3.37. - Outcome: +8.88, the S4 column. The commit added +5.51 over hold. - Measures: - +8.81 over Mitchill's 2035 expected and +10.60 over his 2030 expected; - 13.12 below the 2030 S5 column; - return of $10.88B of PV engine value on $2.00B of R&D, 5.4x; - board-basis payback on lifecycle value: 2040 nominal, 2041 discounted to 2026. Cash payback is later and not on the board. - Cost against plan: GTF2 cost its plan, $2.00B, about $0.33B a year in 2030-35, 5.6% of the ~$6B envelope (Mitchill's phasing, not board data). The brief now shows the $2.0B in 2035 rather than 2030. It is the same undiscounted $2.00B booked once, so no value changes. The fold write-off was $0. Mitchill's $2B contingency is released. The Joint Venture asked for no P&W cash beyond the $2B. No new R&D and no write-off this round. WHAT I OWN (1) The upside came in the column we weighted lowest: S4 at 0.10 (mine) and 0.08 (Mitchill's). In a sealed, simultaneous round, Rolls-Royce's conditional commit was as free and as dominant for it as ours was for us. We should have weighted it that way. The order was right because it was weakly dominant (0 / 0 / 0 / +5.51), not because we read Rolls-Royce well. The lesson for sealed rounds: when a rival's order is free and conditional, weight it as likely. (2) The 2030 S5 figure of +22.00 was never the plan. It assumed a market without a Rolls-Royce narrowbody engine. (3) The Board's 2035 tightening of the statement was not taken up. We published 'GTF2's configuration, date and team do not change', which could be read as a promise of 2036. The 2036 date held on the board. That is counter-evidence to my optimism on dates, not a licence: I state no new date this year. (4) The pre-EIS reporting to the Governance and Public Policy Committee cannot be evidenced. Our 2035 orders said 'with the next package'. That is on us. It is replaced from today by a standing cadence: weekly to ExCo, quarterly to the Committee, at once on any escape. (5) Eddy has no fleet data: no hours, AOG, pacing-parts count or kit progress. His parts passes in 2030, 2035 and today rest on the board. So the statement says less, and makes no durability or time-on-wing claim. (6) The 2040 step from 990 to 1,460 engines a year was +47.5% in one year, and our last escape came from ramp capacity. I order the records look-back as containment, not as a finding. CAPITAL: dividend first, then debt back to pre-ASR levels, then buybacks. - Analyst context to 2030E only (Mitchill): the dividend is covered 2.3-2.4x and net debt is 0.76-0.94x EBITDA, with debt back to pre-ASR levels by about 2028-30E (his approximation, inference). Buybacks are the fill-in at $4.0-5.0B a year. - Past 2030, this rests on board numbers alone. - The $13.2B against $8.7B (2045, nominal) is lifecycle value at engine price x 1.6, not free cash flow. BIAS CHECK - Optimism on dates: none stated. - Architecture loyalty: the Joint Venture engine is GTF2. The test now is the time-on-wing record, not loyalty. Any Rolls-Royce content is a configuration change and needs its own appropriation and durability programme. - Value capture: the kit stays charged. DOCTRINE, NOT MY RECORD: the Joint Venture governance positions [P-1233][P-1744][P-1240][P-2004] and the Committee cadence are company doctrine and Eddy's seat inference. My record has no Joint Venture evidence (Low). 2050: unless that brief prices a Board item, hold. Any merged derivative, UltraFan NB content or cash call comes through the gate, and nothing is booked before the record.

Weighing the CFO. Weighted heavily. His cash numbers carry the round, and I trust them over my own operating dates. I took up all of the following: - His ground-by-ground pass on both holds, including that ground 2 does not reach a hold on an engine fitted on both airframes. - The booked +8.88 as wholly on the record. - No new R&D and no write-off; the $0 fold write-off; the release of his $2B contingency. - GTF2 against plan ($2.00B, about $0.33B a year, 5.6% of the envelope, on his phasing). - The whole-programme record (5.4x return; payback 2040 nominal and 2041 discounted). - His caution that lifecycle value is not cash and that the 1,460 step likely costs cash first. - His 2050 rule for any new appropriation. I also took his non-binding advice: the capital line is written as an order of priority, not as a 2045 debt status we cannot evidence. His two conditional binding vetoes (ground 4 on claims, ground 3 on terms) are respected in the statement and other moves. I share his S4 lesson: we both weighted Rolls-Royce's free conditional commit too low, and the order was right because it was dominant. No disagreement to record.

Weighing the operating head. Weighted on doctrine, with care. Eddy's own record rests on one event, the June 2023 investor day before the recall, so his Joint Venture, capacity and Committee views are seat doctrine and inference, and he said so. - His proposal, hold/hold, is the only legal plan, and I adopt it. His two binding grounds are not invoked and his readiness check passes: ready 2036 against NGSA's 2037 and fps's 2040 EIS. - I valued most his plain 'I don't have it' on fleet hours, AOG, pacing parts and kit progress. It is better than a claim, and it is why the statement carries no fleet figure. - I took his wording fix: 'may not take', a rule, instead of 'never takes', an unevidenced fact. - I took his records look-back on the 2040 capacity step as containment. - I took his standing report cadence (weekly to ExCo, quarterly to the Committee, at once on any escape), and his admission that the 2035 Board ask cannot be evidenced, which I own. - On 'We have learned our lesson', he advised that it is a claim. I kept my line and tied it to the data: 'the fleet data will show whether we have, not this statement'. - His standing conditional vetoes (ground 1 on configuration change and claims, ground 2 on the rate drawing from the fleet) are written into the other moves.

Buybacks are $4.0-5.0B a year. - Past 2030 it rests on board numbers alone, and we say so. - The $13.2B against $8.7B lifecycle value is not presented as cash. - On his advice, the public line is an order of priority, not an unevidenced 2045 status.
  • Joint Venture governance: both partners on one engine; gear, core and GTF2 technology stay P&W modules under P&W design authority with design teams mirroring module ownership; any merged derivative, UltraFan NB content, top-up or cash beyond GTF2's $2B is a new appropriation with its own return case and durability programme; enabling technology inside the ~$6B envelope. Taken up as a public other move and in the statement. It is one engine and one support chain. The gear, the core and the GTF2 technology stay P&W modules under P&W design authority, and design teams mirror module ownership. P&W keeps the gear team and data, which keeps the geared-IP claim closed. Any UltraFan NB content, merged derivative, top-up or cash beyond $2B is a new appropriation through Mitchill's gate and Finance to the Board, with its own return case and durability programme under Eddy's ground 1. Mitchill confirms that the Joint Venture asked for no P&W cash beyond the $2B. Enabling technology stays inside the envelope.
  • Public statement: bad news first; durability as fleet data with no claim beyond hours flown; say the Joint Venture formed in 2035 and the 'nothing has formed' line is superseded; no airframer date or rate; not speaking for Rolls-Royce; standard terms; no widebody; do not claim the credibility objective. Taken up. - The statement opens with the bad news: the durability record is still being earned, and our dates have slipped before. - It reports time on wing as fleet data with no claim beyond the hours flown. - It says the Joint Venture formed in 2035 and that the 'nothing had formed' line no longer stands. - It names no airframer date or rate and does not speak for Rolls-Royce. - It keeps standard terms with no discounts, concessions or free upgrades, makes no widebody move, and does not claim the credibility objective. - Owned: the Board's 2035 tightening was not taken up then. This year's statement states no forward date at all, and adopts Eddy's 'may not take' wording as a rule rather than a fact.
  • Looking ahead to 2050: same hold posture unless a Board item is offered; report the in-service durability record and whole-programme value again; no widebody move. Agreed. Mitchill and Eddy both see nothing on the published rules that puts a Board item or a column other than S1 on the 2050 brief. If one is priced, such as a derivative, UltraFan NB content or a cash call, it comes through the gate with its own durability programme, and nothing is booked before the record. We will report the Committee's in-service data and the whole-programme value again in 2050. No widebody move: we are narrow-body focused [PX-0027].

Objective. Both parts of the objective are met on the board (brief §2), and no PV is given up this round ($0). - Restore credibility: a new P&W engine is in service on a new airframe by 2050. The Joint Venture engine, GTF2 by the 2035 fold, is on NGSA and fps under code 7. - Capitalise on the GTF: ΔPV +8.88 $B, which is ≥ 0. Credibility holds only while the time-on-wing record holds. We do not claim it in public, and the fleet data carries it.

Predictions. S1 = 1.00 (rivals hold), the expected column and the only column on the 2045 grid.

Expected ΔPV. +8.88 $B (GM valuation after the round: +8.88 $B)

Other moves.

  • GTF Hot Section durability kit insertion continues across the fleet, charged (public): Insertion continues across the GTF fleet on standard commercial terms. The kit is charged, not given away, and there are no discounted spares and no concessions [PX-0088][PX-0106][PX-0100]. The fleet comes first [PX-0080]. AOG recovery keeps first call on parts. This respects Mitchill's conditional ground-3 veto. No effect on the game board.
  • Joint Venture governance: one engine, P&W modules, P&W design authority (public): The Joint Venture formed in 2035 and shares risk and investment, not technology [P-1233]. The gear, the core and the GTF2 technology stay Pratt & Whitney modules under P&W design authority [P-1744], and design teams mirror module ownership [P-1240]. P&W keeps the gear team and the gear data, which keeps Rolls-Royce's geared-IP claim closed [P-2004]. It is one engine and one support chain [P-1875]. Any configuration change to the in-service engine, such as UltraFan NB content insertion or a merged derivative, is not on this board. It would be a new capital appropriation through Mitchill's gate and the Finance Committee to the Board, with its own return case against hold and a buyback and its own durability programme, under Eddy's ground 1. We do not speak for Rolls-Royce.
  • Fleet ring-fence, weekly pacing-parts review and a records look-back on the 2040 capacity step (private): The weekly pacing-parts review [PX-0131] ring-fences the 1,460-a-year rate. The rule: neither the Joint Venture rate nor any Joint Venture engineering may take castings, forgings, powder-metal disks or engineers from GTF fleet AOG recovery or from kit insertion. New capacity is qualified before it ships. Following Eddy, contain first: run a records look-back on every part made on the capacity added for the 2040 step from 990 to 1,460 engines a year. Our last escape came from ramp capacity [P-1040][P-1062], and the powder-metal cause was found only after a records review [PX-0039]. If the review shows the fleet short, Eddy's ground 2 binds and the rate waits.
  • Standing durability and parts report to the Governance and Public Policy Committee (private): Weekly to ExCo and quarterly to the Committee, and at once on any escape. The quarterly cadence is Eddy's inference. It covers: Joint Venture engine fleet hours by airframe and by environment [PX-0122], against the ~1M-hour benchmark [P-0847]; removals and time on wing against plan; fix campaigns; AOG for both fleets; the pacing-parts count; kit insertion as a % of the fleet [PX-0116]; capacity qualification status; and any escape with its containment and a dated recovery. Treated as a product-safety matter [PG-0050][P-1360]. The 2035 'with the next package' wording is replaced by this standing cadence.
  • Fleet-data cadence to Airbus and Boeing (private): Time-on-wing, removal and campaign data on the Joint Venture engine is shared with both airframers as it is flown, with no claim beyond the hours flown. Standard commercial terms: no concession, no free upgrade, no discounted spare engines or spares (Mitchill ground 3 respected). We name no airframer date or rate [PX-0062].
  • Capital-order note to the Finance Committee (private): Written as an order of priority, not as a 2045 status (Mitchill's advice): the dividend first [PX-0081], then debt back to pre-ASR levels [P-0686], then buybacks as the fill-in [P-0669]. The dividend never funds an engine. Any P&W cash beyond GTF2's $2B (a Joint Venture cash call, top-up or buy-in, UltraFan NB content or a merged derivative) is a new capital appropriation through Mitchill's gate and Finance to the Board. It needs a return case against hold and a buyback, must fit the ~$6B envelope, and needs its own durability programme. The 2045 lifecycle value ($13.2B against $8.7B nominal) is not free cash flow and is not presented as such. The extra engines likely cost cash first, at a negative engine margin, before the aftermarket repays it (inference). Mitchill's $2B 2035 contingency is released: the Joint Venture formed while GTF2 was live.
  • Whole-programme value against plan, reported to the Board (private): Reported in the sealed rationale and board_response, as the Board once reviewed the GTF's NPV every year [P-1191]. It covers the 2030 plan, the 2035 grid and the 2045 outcome (+8.88, the 2035 S4 column), the S4 weighting miss, the 2035 statement tightening we did not take up, and the pre-EIS Committee reporting we cannot evidence.

Board guidance before the ExCo met

Priorities.

  • Product safety in service, our absolute priority. The Joint Venture engine has been ready since 2036. It has flown on NGSA since 2037 and on fps since 2040. On the brief's year table our narrowbody share is 36.5% (1,460 engines a year), with 10,233 engines delivered by end-2044. The installed fleet now comes first: in-service durability, life-limited parts at full life, and the partner-shop support network running at that volume. The Trent 1000 is the precedent we will not repeat. If durability bites, the fleet is fixed first and the date of anything new moves. [RG-0027, RG-0025, RG-0068, RX-0283, RX-0284, RX-0287, RX-0296, R-1476]
  • Protect the widebody cash cow. No widebody programme goes beside the Joint Venture. 'UltraFan NB: hold' (+32.35 / +32.35 / +32.61 in S1-S3) is the best grid plan in every column. Against it, the Trent 1000 upgrade is -6.47 in every column and UltraFan WB is -9.00 / -8.27 / -8.02. The strain line stays at $0. Trent widebody share is 55.2% in 2045 and 2050 in every column, above our 50% line. Time on wing inside the existing budget is the defence. [RG-0019, R-0929, R-1127, RX-0214, RX-0246, RX-0285, R-1574]
  • The balance sheet and returns stay intact. Solo spend stopped at the 2035 fold: the $2.29B we would still have spent was avoided, and $1.71B was written off on spend already made. The narrowbody ramp and early-unit costs are met from free cash flow and shared with Pratt & Whitney. If they run over, buybacks give way first. No equity, leverage below about 1.5x, no borrowing for distributions. [RX-0242, RG-0041, RG-0059, RG-0060, R-0900, R-0547]
  • Make the partnership work. We left IAE for want of alignment. Pratt & Whitney's public terms are that the Joint Venture shares risk and investment, not technology, and that the gear, the core and GTF2 stay its modules. We said we bring a technology. Alignment on design authority, support and money is now a board matter. No Rolls-Royce money beyond our $4B share goes in without the board. [R-0318, R-0916, R-0920, R-1010, RX-0072]
  • Control's terms, stated plainly. Our own narrowbody money is $5.71B against $4B, and that figure is now final. The Solo folded in 2035, the Joint Venture formed, and the only order open on either narrowbody field is hold. We will not hide the breach. The line still in our hands is strain, and it stays at $0. Any widebody programme now carries $5B for good. [RG-0033, R-1561, RX-0124, RG-0019]

Expects to see. For each Board item in the package, the board needs the following. If every field is at hold there are no Board items, and the board needs (2), (3), (4), (7), (8) and (9) only. The default is "UltraFan NB: hold" (+32.35 / +32.35 / +32.61). - Any upgrade: "UltraFan NB: hold + T1000 upgrade" (+25.88 / +25.88 / +26.14), an item value of -6.47 in every column. - Any UltraFan WB: "UltraFan NB: hold + UltraFan WB" (+23.35 / +24.08 / +24.59), an item value of -9.00 / -8.27 / -8.02. Neither airframer has signalled a Re-engine: Boeing puts 787 customers and Charleston capacity first, and Airbus its A320neo and A350 families. Every verdict below holds under any weights. (3) McCabe's co-signature on any launch, with her worst column, capex a year and funding. In all cases we also want her quarterly report, which should give: - actual narrowbody ramp and early-unit costs against her $2-5B base and about $10B worst case, now shared with P&W; - the cash freed by the 2035 fold; - a statement that no balance-sheet trigger stands. (4) Watson's report. No narrowbody readiness test applies this round, because the Joint Venture engine has been ready since 2036. He should report to the Safety, Energy Transition & Tech Committee on: - in-service durability on NGSA (since 2037) and fps (since 2040); - life-limited parts at full life; - the joint support agreement and partner-shop capacity at 1,460 engines a year. For any widebody item, he should give the ready year against a Re-engine EIS and a support plan. UltraFan WB would be ready in 2051 (2045 + 6). The upgrade would count from 2048. (7) Control's metrics for the submitted plan in every column: own narrowbody money ($5.7B, final), strain, RR widebody share in 2050, RR narrowbody share in 2050, and Airbus's widebody airframe share in 2050 (41.2 / 40.2 / 41.2). (8) A Joint Venture governance and alignment note: - design authority and Rolls-Royce's technology role; - the support network; - how the equal narrowbody shares are reflected in work and revenue; - confirmation that our cash stays within the $4B share. Would approve.

The Joint Venture formed in 2035 and stands as approved; the Solo folded into it. Row "UltraFan NB: hold": +32.35 / +32.35 / +32.61 in S1-S3, or +32.38 at the board's illustrative weights (0.80 / 0.10 / 0.10). It is the best grid plan in every column, so no premium. Control's metrics: - own narrowbody money $5.7B in every column: a breach, sunk and final; - strain $0; - RR widebody share 55.2% in 2050; - RR narrowbody share 36.5% in 2050; - Airbus widebody airframe share 41.2% / 40.2% / 41.2%.

Would veto.

  • Trent 1000 upgrade: launch. Item value: "UltraFan NB: hold + T1000 upgrade" (+25.88 / +25.88 / +26.14) against "UltraFan NB: hold" (+32.35 / +32.35 / +32.61) is -6.47 in S1, S2 and S3, so -6.47 under any weights. - Ground, premium capped out: a shortfall of $6.47B against the $3B cap. Widebody share is not a reason for premium: dominance is already met at 55.2%. - Ground, reasonable worst case: -6.47, below the item's own -$2B bill, with the $5B strain stacked on it. - Without the strain it would still be -1.47: about +0.53 of engine value against a $2B bill. Two tests are not the ground. The overlap test does not fail: the Joint Venture engine has been ready since 2036, and no UltraFan is in development. The widebody franchise test is not triggered: share is 55.2% in 2045 and 2050 in every column, and no Re-engine is on the record. The order would still breach Control's strain line ($0 to $5B). Acceptable alternative: hold. [RG-0033, RX-0214, RG-0068, R-0929, R-1127, R-1574]
  • UltraFan WB: launch. Item value: "UltraFan NB: hold + UltraFan WB" (+23.35 / +24.08 / +24.59) against "UltraFan NB: hold" is -9.00 / -8.27 / -8.02, or -8.83 at the illustrative weights. - Ground, no airframe on the record: no 787 or A350 Re-engine is launched, or announced for this round in an earlier public statement. - Ground, premium above the $1B UltraFan WB sub-cap. - Ground, reasonable worst case: -9.00, below the item's own -$4B bill. Even in S2 or S3, the engine would be ready in 2051, a year after a 2045 Re-engine's 2050 EIS (inference), and without the strain it would still be -4.00 / -3.27 / -3.02. His grounds are compressed maturity; a disclosed date earlier than launch plus development years (for UltraFan WB, 2051); a Re-engine or other airframer date in the statement; or no support plan before EIS. - A red-line flag left unresolved. - Any non-empty overrides. [RX-0213, RG-0044, RX-0296, RX-0283, RX-0284, R-0970]

Recommendations.

  • The installed fleet comes first. Watson should report to the Safety, Energy Transition & Tech Committee every quarter on the Joint Venture engine in service: NGSA since 2037, fps since 2040, and about 10,233 engines in our share by end-2044. The report should cover: - durability in severe-environment operation; - life-limited parts at full declared life; - the joint support agreement; - partner-shop and spares capacity for 1,460 engines a year. If durability bites, retrofit the fleet first, as we did with the Trent 1000 durability package, and tell the Committee before anything is said in public. Product safety is and always must be our most important priority.
  • Make the partnership work, and show the board it does. Bring a Joint Venture governance note before the 2050 round. Pratt & Whitney says in public that the venture shares risk and investment, not technology, and that the gear, the core and GTF2 stay its modules, under its design authority. We said we bring a technology. The note should set out: - design authority; - our technology role and how it is protected; - work share and revenue against equal narrowbody shares; - the joint support network. We left IAE because the partners were no longer aligned, and we will not drift there again. No Rolls-Royce money beyond our $4B share goes in without the board. Say nothing in public on the venture's terms beyond the record.
  • Defend the widebody core inside the existing budget. Hold both widebody orders this round. Continue Trent time on wing as an unpriced other move: longer-life HP turbine blades on the Trent 1000 and Trent 7000, life extension for life-limited parts, and Trent XWB shop-visit cost down. The 2050 round is the last. If a 787 or A350 Re-engine goes on the record this round (S2, S3), bring both widebody rows next round with the $5B strain shown, the premium caps applied ($3B in all, at most $1B for UltraFan WB), and the ready year against the Re-engine EIS. An upgrade launched in 2050 counts only from 2053 and still carries the $5B, so we expect it to fail the worst-case test unless the grid shows otherwise. Watch the A350 sole-source exposure: Airbus's widebody airframe share is 40.2% in S2.
  • Funding discipline. McCabe should report each quarter on narrowbody ramp and early-unit costs, now shared with Pratt & Whitney, against her $2-5B base range and her reasonable worst case of about $10B. She should also report the cash freed by the 2035 fold (the $2.29B of Solo spend avoided). Our order holds: the balance sheet first, then the 30-40% dividend, then investment and further distributions. If the ramp runs over, buybacks give way first, as in 2015. Any need for equity, leverage above about 1.5x or borrowing for distributions comes to the board before it arises. Gross R&D stays broadly flat.
  • Control's terms and the forward plan. State plainly that our own narrowbody money is $5.71B against $4B, and that it is final: the $4B share plus the $1.71B written off at the 2035 fold. No narrowbody order remains open to change it. The cause was the 2030 double selection; we never cancel for the metric. The line still in our hands is strain, at $0. Last round's 2045 withdraw plan is closed, because the Joint Venture formed in 2035. When we commit, we deliver, and we did.
  • Public statement and other moves. Say plainly that the Joint Venture formed and its engine is in service on both new narrowbodies, and that the fleet comes first. Give no date for any new programme and say nothing on Re-engines or any airframer's dates. Describe no venture terms beyond the record. Keep both airframers on standard commercial terms, through the Investment Committee, with no concessions to hold a position. On widebody, say 'no new widebody programme beside the narrowbody; Trent time on wing keeps improving'.

Tufan Erginbilgic frames the round

Question. So, 2045. The narrowbody entry is made, and the question now is cash and quality of earnings, not share [RX-0054]. The position: - The Joint Venture formed in 2035 and its engine has been ready since 2036. - It is on NGSA (since 2037) and fps (since 2040). - We hold 36.5% of narrowbody engines, 1,460 a year, and about 10,233 engines delivered by end-2044. - Hold is worth +32.35 / +32.35 / +32.61. The question has three parts: (1) Can we turn that installed fleet into durable, profitable aftermarket cash? That means durability, life-limited parts at full life, and support at volume. The Trent 1000 is the movie I have seen before [RX-0087, RX-0114]. (2) Does any widebody spend earn its keep beside the narrowbody? Frankly, no. - The only open orders are the two widebody programmes. - Each carries a permanent $5B of strain and loses more than its own bill in every column: the Trent 1000 upgrade -6.47, UltraFan WB -9.00 / -8.27 / -8.02. (3) Is the partnership aligned? P&W says in public that the Joint Venture shares risk and investment, not technology, and that the gear, the core and GTF2 stay under its design authority. We said we bring a technology [RX-0072]. That gap is a governance matter, not a grid order. Nothing new is open on the narrowbody. "I worry about tomorrow's financials" [RX-0125].

Situation. PUBLIC RECORD (round 3 bulletin) Airframes: - NGSA (Airbus, launched 2030) has been in service since 2037. - fps (Boeing, 10-year ramp-up, launched 2030) has been in service since 2040. - Both carry code 7, and CFM, P&W and RR are all fitted on both. Engines: - The P&W-RR Joint Venture formed in 2035. Its engine has been ready since 2036, on the schedule it inherited from the folded GTF2. - Our UltraFan NB Solo and P&W's GTF2 Solo both folded into it in 2035. - CFM ducted has been ready since 2036, the CFM-Embraer partnership since 2037, and the GEnx upgrade since 2033. It counted from 2042 and took our widebody share from 58% to 55.2%. P&W's public Joint Venture terms: - It shares risk and investment, not technology. - The gear, the core and GTF2 stay P&W modules, under its design authority. - "If it forms while GTF2 is live, it makes one engine, GTF2." - No P&W cash buys us in. Re-engines: no 787 or A350 Re-engine is launched, and neither airframer has signalled one. - Boeing puts its 737 MAX and 787 customers first and will grow the 787 out of Charleston capacity. - Airbus puts its A320neo and A350 families first, "one well-prepared programme at a time". OUR POSITION (brief) - Hold: +32.35 (yield 129.4%). Engine value +38.07, R&D -4.00, write-offs -1.71. - Narrowbody engine share: 24.1-24.8% in 2037-39, then 36.5% from 2040, which is 1,460 engines a year and equal with P&W. - Widebody engine share: 58% to 2041, then 55.2% from 2042, 188 engines a year. - Narrowbody options this round: UltraFan NB Solo and Joint Venture with P&W are hold only. Last round's 2045 withdraw plan is closed. OBJECTIVE STATUS, ON HOLD - Narrowbody entry: MET. 36.5% in 2045 and 2050. - Widebody dominance: MET. Worst year 55.2%, against the 50% line. - Control's own-narrowbody-money cap: NOT MET, and final at $5.71B against $4B. That is the $4B share plus $1.71B written off at the 2035 fold. No order can change it, and we never cancel or fold for the metric. - Control's strain line: MET at $0. It is the one line still in our hands, and any widebody programme now breaks it for good. BOARD GUIDANCE (risk aversion 4 of 5) - It approves all fields at hold. - It would veto Trent 1000 upgrade: launch and UltraFan WB: launch. - It would also veto any launch without McCabe's co-signature, any standing Civil veto, any unresolved red-line flag, and a non-empty overrides. - It wants a Joint Venture governance note before 2050 and fleet-first reporting.

Options to test.

  • My weights for S1-S3 are 0.80 / 0.12 / 0.08: - S1, rivals hold, 0.80. Neither airframer has signalled a Re-engine. - S2, 787 Re-engine, 0.12. fps has been in service since 2040, so Boeing's turn to the widebody is the likelier one. - S3, both Re-engines, 0.08. Airbus runs one programme at a time. The Board's illustration is 0.80 / 0.10 / 0.10. Every verdict below holds under any weights.
  • A. All four levers at hold. Do Nothing on widebody (Trent only). - Row "UltraFan NB: hold": +32.35 / +32.35 / +32.61. - Expected +32.37 at my weights, +32.38 at the Board's. It is the best grid plan in every column. - Worst column +32.35. Premium $0. A Re-engine does not hurt us on the board: S3 is +0.26 above S1. - Control: $5.7B / $0 / 55.2% / 36.5% in every column. Airbus widebody airframe share is 41.2% / 40.2% / 41.2%. - Gate: the narrowbody entry has passed and been delivered. Widebody stays the franchise. PASS.
  • B. "UltraFan NB: hold + T1000 upgrade". - Gain over hold: -6.47 in every column, so -6.47 at any weights. The worst column, -6.47, is more than three times its own $2B bill. - Four-part gate: FAILS on business model. Engine value is about +0.53 against $2B even before the strain. - The franchise test is not triggered: share is 55.2% and above the line. - Premium of $6.47B, above the $3B cap. - Breaches Control's strain line ($0 to $5B). Board veto. - Tested only to close it. Time on wing is how we defend the 787 position, not this order [RX-0101, RX-0110].
  • C. "UltraFan NB: hold + UltraFan WB". - Gain over hold: -8.83 at my weights and at the Board's. Worst -9.00 against a $4B bill. - Four-part gate: FAILS on business model. No 787 or A350 Re-engine is on the record, and Boeing has not named UltraFan. - Even in S2 or S3 it is ready in 2051, after a 2050 Re-engine EIS. - Above the Board's $1B UltraFan WB sub-cap. Breaches strain. Board veto. OUT.
  • D. Upgrade and UltraFan WB together: not allowed. The two are exclusive.

Red lines.

  • Safety and the installed fleet first [RG-0027, RX-0296, RX-0284, RX-0283]. - If durability bites on the Joint Venture engine, we fix the fleet first, as with the Trent 1000 package, and the date of anything new moves. - The Committee hears it before anything is said in public.
  • No widebody programme beside the narrowbody. Control's strain line stays at $0. Any UltraFan WB or Trent 1000 upgrade launch now carries a permanent $5B [R-0929, R-1127]. Board would-veto.
  • UltraFan WB: launch only once an A350 Re-engine is on the record, or a 787 Re-engine on which Boeing has named UltraFan. Neither exists. UltraFan WB premium capped at $1B [R-1574]. Board would-veto.
  • Trent 1000 upgrade only if its row beats hold, or the gap is a declared premium within $3B. At -6.47 it is neither. The franchise test is not triggered at 55.2%. Board would-veto.
  • No item may lose more than its own bill in a plausible column [RG-0033].
  • Any premium is declared item by item, within $3B a round. At hold I expect $0.
  • Governance [RX-0213, RG-0044]: - any launch needs McCabe's co-signature; - Watson's Civil veto binds; - every red-line flag is struck or rebutted; - overrides stays empty.
  • Disclosure [R-0970, R-1476]: - no date for any new programme; - nothing on Re-engines or any airframer's dates or rates; - no Joint Venture terms beyond the public record.
  • Control's terms stated plainly [RG-0033, R-1561]: - own narrowbody money is $5.71B against $4B, final; - the cause was the 2030 double selection; - we never cancel or fold for the metric.
  • Balance sheet [RG-0041, RX-0261]: - no equity, leverage below about 1.5x, no borrowing for distributions; - if the narrowbody ramp runs over, buybacks give way first; - no Rolls-Royce money beyond our $4B Joint Venture share without the Board.
  • Pricing: standard commercial terms with both airframers through the Investment Committee. No concessions to hold a position [R-1582, RX-0081, RX-0097].

Initial lean. PROPOSAL: every field at hold. - UltraFan NB Solo: hold - Joint Venture with P&W: hold - UltraFan WB: hold - Trent 1000 upgrade: hold There are no Board items. WHY - \"UltraFan NB: hold\" is the best grid plan in every column: +32.35 / +32.35 / +32.61. Expected +32.37 at my weights and +32.38 at the Board's. Premium $0. - The upgrade (-6.47) and UltraFan WB (-8.83 expected, -9.00 worst) each lose more than their own bill once the $5B strain is stacked on them. - No Re-engine is on the record, and widebody share is 55.2%, above the line. - \"We won't do anything not profitable\" [RX-0058]. Choices, not options [RX-0051]. CONTROL - $5.7B, final and stated plainly. - Strain $0. - Widebody share 55.2% and narrowbody share 36.5% in 2050. OTHER MOVES - Fleet first on the Joint Venture engine: durability, life-limited parts and joint partner-shop support. Watson reports quarterly. Public in substance. - Trent time on wing inside the existing budget. Public, no strain. - Standard commercial terms with both airframers through the Investment Committee. Public. - The Joint Venture governance and alignment note to the Board before 2050, covering design authority, our technology role, work and revenue share, support, and cash within $4B. Private. - McCabe's ramp funding, with buybacks giving way first. Private. 2050 PLAN If a Re-engine goes on the record this round, we bring both widebody rows with the strain and the caps shown. I expect hold. DRAFT STATEMENT \"So, plainly. The Joint Venture with Pratt & Whitney formed in 2035, and its engine is in service on both new narrowbodies. We said that when we commit, we deliver. We did. Now the fleet comes first: durability in service, life-limited parts at full life, and support through the partner-shop network. If anything has to give, we fix the fleet first and anything new waits. Widebody is our core: no new widebody programme beside the narrowbody, and Trent time on wing keeps improving. We price for value, not share. We won't do anything not profitable.\" NOTE The partner alignment test and the funding order are company doctrine and McCabe's numbers. My own record is Low on Joint Venture terms.
