Each quarter Watson reports: - durability in severe-environment operation; - life-limited parts at full declared life; - the joint support agreement; - partner-shop induction slots ahead of the first shop-visit wave from the 2037-40 cohorts; - life-limited-part and hot-section spares; - spare engines for severe-environment operators. Retrofit rule if durability bites, on the Trent 1000 model: (1) the Committee hears first, before anything is said in public; (2) protect the fleet with inspection intervals and a spare-engine pool; (3) the design authority issues the kit, inserted at shop visit through the joint partner shops; (4) the date of anything new moves; (5) McCabe sets the cost split. Watson claims no data, signature or shop count the record cannot show.
  • Joint Venture governance and alignment note to the Board before the 2050 round (private): Owners: Watson and McCabe. It covers: (1) Design authority. Plainly: on the record P&W keeps the gear, the core and the GTF2 technology as its modules under its design authority. In this engine we bring risk, investment and the support network. (2) Our technology role. UltraFan technology stays ours and feeds the Trent fleet. 'We are actually bringing a technology' [RX-0072] applies to any later engine under our own design authority, which would come to the Board as a new programme with its own full test plan. (3) Data. We ask for access to hot-section and life-limited-part data through the joint support agreement, since we carry an equal share of the risk. (4) Retrofit liability. Cost follows design authority, or we get a joint say in the fix. Until that is settled we plan on half of a Trent 1000-type bill, about £1.1bn; the worst case is about £2.2bn. (5) Work share and revenue. Both should be reflected at 36.5% each, matching the equal narrowbody shares. If our content per engine is below half, the board's engine value overstates our cash, and McCabe re-prices it. (6) The joint support network. (7) Cash stays within our $4B share. Nothing more goes in without the Board. The IAE lesson is not to drift out of alignment [R-0318]. Doctrine and McCabe's and Watson's inference: my own record is Low on Joint Venture terms.
  • Funding discipline and quarterly report to the Board (McCabe) (private): Narrowbody ramp and early-unit costs for our part, now shared with P&W, measured against: - her corrected base of about $1.9-4.3B (£1.4-3.1bn) over 2037-44, held at the top of the range; - a reasonable worst case of about $7.5B (£5.5bn), or about $9B (£6.7bn) if we carry a retrofit alone, against the ~$10B solo case. The board carries no ramp line, so she reports the range until actuals exist. She also reports: - the cash freed by the 2035 fold: $2.29B of Solo spend avoided, about £1.7bn; - the $1.71B write-off, non-cash, about £1.26bn; - the net LTSA balance movement, shop visits and time on wing, and any onerous-contract provision on early units. Funding order: the balance sheet first, then the 30-40% dividend, then investment and further distributions. If the ramp runs over, buybacks give way first, and a fleet fix is never re-phased. No equity, leverage below about 1.5x, no borrowing for distributions. Any step beyond buybacks comes to the Board before it arises. Gross R&D stays broadly flat.
  • Trent time on wing and fleet support inside the existing budget (Watson) (public): Longer-life HP turbine blades on the Trent 1000 and Trent 7000, life extension for life-limited parts, UltraFan technology fed into the Trent fleet, and Trent XWB shop-visit cost down. Funded inside the existing fleet budget. This is not the Trent 1000 upgrade order and not a new programme, and it carries no strain. No dates disclosed.
  • Commercial terms with Airbus and Boeing (public): Standard commercial terms with both airframers on NGSA, fps and the widebody fleets: value remunerated, win-win. No launch-style concession, discount or free upgrade to hold a position. Every new contract goes through the Investment Committee [RX-0081, RX-0097, R-1582]. We do not speak for any airframer's dates or rates.
  • The 2050 test, set in advance (private): This is the last round. Both widebody rows come to the ExCo only if a 787 or A350 Re-engine goes on the record this round, or if RR widebody share heads toward 50%. Both carry the permanent $5B of strain. - Upgrade launched in 2050: it counts from 2053. To pass the worst-case test it must be no more than $2.00B below hold in every plausible column, which needs about +$5B of engine value against about +0.53 today. Within the $3B cap it needs about +$4B. - UltraFan WB launched in 2050: it is ready in 2056. It qualifies only against an A350 Re-engine, or a 787 Re-engine naming UltraFan, on the record. It must be within $1.00B of hold, which needs about +$8B of engine value against +0.73 to +0.98 today. I expect hold. The narrowbody fields stay at hold.

Round 4 · decision year 2050

2050: everyone holds again, and the final state is the 2035 state

Every company held, and no value has changed since 2035. A Re-engine ordered in 2050 would enter service only in 2055. Airbus's A350 Re-engine was worth +$0.57B if Boeing held and −$0.41B if not; Boeing's 787 Re-engine +$0.05B or −$1.00B. Boeing's Board turned to capital returns sized on the stress case.

What each player ordered

PlayerOrders (as adjudicated) and public statement
BoeingDo Nothing

Public statement: “Our new single-aisle airplane has been in service for ten years now. It's in production, it's flying, and our customers have two engine sources on it: CFM, and the engine from Pratt & Whitney and Rolls-Royce. We're holding the line where the data tells us to hold it. Every step in production has been gated on our KPIs: rework, escapes, traveled work, supplier shortages and training. That doesn't change. The data sets the pace, not the calendar. I'd much rather be a month late than go a month early. Safety and quality come first, ahead of rate. Both engines are reviewed for how they're doing in service every time our Board's safety committee meets, and we keep our suppliers healthy, engines first. Our development and support work with suppliers stays on cost-plus and risk-share terms, not fixed price. On the 787, we're not starting a new development. We'll keep growing that airplane out of the capacity we built in Charleston, at the pace our KPIs and our customers' orders allow. We'd rather do less and do it better. The balance sheet is where it belongs, and debt stays first. How and when we return cash to our shareholders is a decision for our Board, and you'll hear about it when the Board has made it. I'm not going to give you any new dates today. We have more share to earn back, and we'll earn it one airplane and one customer at a time. The financials will follow our production performance. We've come a long way. We still have work to do.”

AirbusDo Nothing

Public statement: “Our core principles of safety, quality, integrity, compliance and security will remain at the heart of all we do. Our new single-aisle aircraft is in service, and we intend to offer a choice of engines. Every engine joins the aircraft, and stays on it, on proven maturity and durability, never on the calendar. We review the fleet and our engine partners' durability and capacity with our Board as a matter of routine, and we keep working with our partners to keep every source healthy. Our priority is the fleet in service, with a disciplined and controlled production ramp of the new single-aisle and the A320neo family and delivery performance for our customers. We continue to secure our own supply chain, engines and critical materials first. The A350 family, passenger and freighter, remains the backbone of our widebody offer. We will keep developing it and offering it on value to our customers. We have looked again at a further step on the A350. Today the engine and the business case are not both there, so we are not taking that step. As we have said, we will take it only when the technology, the engine and the business case are all ready. We manage the company with financial discipline, within our financial flexibility and our existing shareholder return policy. We will continue to work with our industry partners for a tariff-free, zero-for-zero regime for aerospace trade. We prepare the next generation of Airbus aircraft on technology gates, one well-prepared programme at a time, for a stronger and more sovereign European aerospace industry.”

CFM/GEDo Nothing

Public statement: “Safety, quality, delivery and cost, always in that order. That doesn't change this year. Let me tell you what we know and what we don't. Both new single-aisle aircraft are in service, and CFM is on both of them alongside others. We're honored by that. We don't have a birthright on any order. We keep our place the same way we earned it: readiness, durability and support, one customer and one engine at a time. CFM is a 50-50 partnership with our partner, and we do this work together. Our ducted engine is in service on both new single-aisle aircraft. Its durability record is earned in the field, and we'll tell you what the data says as it comes in. If the data shows us something, we'll fix it, together with our customers. Durability doesn't get traded for anything. Our work with Embraer continues, and so does our work on the GEnx. There are no new programmes from us this year. The job is the fleet we've put in the air. New engines for our customers' deliveries come first, then the shop work behind the fleet. We'll fund that within our capital allocation framework and keep the balance sheet where it is. RISE remains our next generation. We're all in on the open fan technology, and it stays funded as technology. It's really not for us to say when that architecture enters service. Our customers decide when, and we won't ask anyone to wait. Here's what we don't know: how these fleets will mature in service, and what our customers will want next. We won't give you dates or numbers that our testing and our customers haven't earned. Commercial matters we work privately, with our customers and with our partner. You'll ask about competition. I won't speak to that. We judge ourselves on our own execution. It's that simple, ain't that hard.”

Pratt & WhitneyDo Nothing

Public statement: “Bad news first. All of our new single-aisle business now rides on one engine, and that engine's durability record on the new single-aisle aircraft is still being earned, one flight hour at a time. Our dates have slipped before, and the GTF fleet taught us what it costs to say more than the data shows. We have said we learned our lesson from the prior iterations of the GTF. Take that as a commitment, not a finding, and measure us on the fleet data, not on this statement. Our customers have said plainly where the bar is. An engine joins an aircraft, and stays on it, on proven durability, and any durability finding is a live problem. That is fair, and we accept it. We answer it with the engine and with the data, not with price. Our rule is that time on wing, removals and fix campaigns go to both airframers as the fleet flies, and we claim nothing beyond the hours flown. Our terms stay standard: no discounts, no concessions, no free upgrades. Which engines go on an aircraft, and how many sources it carries, is our customers' decision and theirs to announce. What is on the record: the Joint Venture with Rolls-Royce formed in 2035. Its engine has been ready since 2036 and is on both new single-aisle aircraft alongside the other engine makers. The gear, the core and the GTF2 technology stay Pratt & Whitney modules, under our design authority. It is one engine, and any change to its configuration would have to earn its own durability record first. The fleet still comes first. Insertion of the Hot Section durability kit continues across the GTF fleet, charged, on standard commercial terms. Our rules: we review the pacing parts every week, new-engine production may not take parts or engineers from fleet recovery, and new capacity is qualified before it ships a part. If we find a problem, you will hear it from us, with containment and a dated recovery. We control what we can control. On capital, our order of priority does not change: the dividend first, then debt back to and held at pre-ASR levels, then buybacks. There is no new engine programme from us this year. Any further investment would come to our Board on its own return case. We do not speak for our airframer customers' plans, dates, rates or sourcing, or for Rolls-Royce.”

Rolls-RoyceDo Nothing

Public statement: “So, plainly. The Joint Venture with Pratt & Whitney formed in 2035, and its engine is in service on both new narrowbodies. Now it has to earn its keep in the fleet. The fleet comes first: durability in service, life-limited parts at full life, and support through the joint partner-shop network. We will report what the fleet shows, and claim nothing more. If anything has to give, we fix the fleet first and anything new waits. Widebody is our core: no new widebody programme beside the narrowbody, and Trent time on wing keeps improving. We price for value, not share, on standard commercial terms with both airframers. Frankly, there is nothing to launch this year. We won't do anything not profitable. I will say that categorically.”

Board guidance before the ExCo met

Priorities.

  • Safety and quality on the fps in service. The 10-year fps has been in service since 2040, and its production ramp is the business now. On the brief, narrowbody share holds at 47% (940 deliveries a year) from 2049. Every production step stays gated on the KPIs, not the calendar. In-service reliability and the durability of both engine sources (CFM and the P&W-Rolls-Royce Joint Venture engine) go to the Aerospace Safety Committee at each meeting.
  • No second development without a business case. This is the last decision year of the game. The 787 Re-engine is the only live order, and against hold its item value is +0.05 (S1) / -1.00 (S2). That fails our $1B launch test in both columns. Hold wins whenever S2 carries more than 4.8% weight. Our recommendation: close the widebody question for this game, and keep 787 growth from Charleston capacity as the widebody answer.
  • Keep the balance sheet repaired, then settle capital returns. Net debt reached the historical level in 2029 (2030 in the stress case). It is held at every checkpoint in both rows and both columns. Stress free cash flow is about $17.2B in 2050 (our computation from the brief). The Round 3 capital-return proposal is a matter reserved to this Board: bring it back updated, with the agencies' rating view, for our decision. No new equity.
  • Keep the engine supply stable. The fps engine code has been locked since EIS. The fps flies two sources, CFM and the Joint Venture engine, in 2045 and 2050, and three narrowbody engine makers stay in the market. The enabler is met. Protect both sources: the Joint Venture engine is the single point of fragility.
  • Long-cycle discipline in public, and an honest record for the game. Give no new dates and do not react to Airbus. Accept that no order this round moves narrowbody share: incumbency was missed in 2040 (38%) and the 50/50 split is missed in 2050 (47%). Pay no objective premium for either.

Would approve.

Would veto.

Recommendations.

  • Hold the 787 Re-engine and close the widebody question for this game. - Against hold it is worth +0.05 in S1 and -1.00 in S2. Neither clears our $1B launch test. - Hold wins at any S2 weight above 4.8% (0.05 / 1.05). At even odds it leads by $0.48B (+0.62 against +0.14). - 2050 is the last decision year, so this is not a deferral to a later review. - The 787 stays on two engine sources. A 2055 Re-engine could draw only on GE's GEnx upgrade. - Keep growing the 787 from Charleston capacity, KPI-gated, as the widebody answer: doing less and doing it better. - Log $0.05B as doctrine premium if S1 is your expected column, or $0 if S2.
  • Safety and quality before rate on the fps. - Keep each production step gated on the FAA-agreed KPIs: rework, escapes, traveled work, supplier shortages, training and ticketing. - Table the KPI values and in-service reliability at every Aerospace Safety Committee meeting. - Bring the durability and life-limited-part status of both engine sources to that committee, where it gets propulsion expertise. - Report any quality, FAA or supply problem to us as a live problem the day you see it.
  • Engine supply. - The enabler is met at two sources and three makers. The code is locked, so no order can add a third source. - Keep CFM and the Joint Venture engine supplied and hot, and LEAP-1B for the 737 MAX and its aftermarket. - Report the supplier-shortages KPI engines first. - If the Joint Venture engine shows a durability finding, treat it as a live problem and bring us a third-source case outside the board. - Keep all terms risk-share or cost-plus, never fixed price.
  • Capital allocation, our reserved matter (inference: our record holds no reinstatement). Net debt has been at the historical level since 2029 (2030 under stress), and stress free cash flow is about $17.2B in 2050. We are minded to take up the Round 3 proposal in this form: - reinstate a common dividend of about $3B a year first; - add a buyback of $0-5B a year, authorised by this Board each year on Finance Committee review and paced on actual free cash flow; - cap the two together at $8B a year, about 46% of 2050 stress free cash flow and 37% of base, well short of the pre-2019 practice of returning about all free cash flow. Conditions: - net debt at or below zero in the stress case; - revolvers undrawn and no new equity; - supplier funding first; - the buyback goes to zero first on any live problem; - the agencies' confirmation that the rating is solidly investment grade, not management's inference. Nothing is announced before we decide.
  • Public statement and the record for the game. - Give no new dates, and do not answer Airbus's calendar. - Reaffirm safety, quality, KPI-gated production, two engine sources and debt first. - Say nothing on returns until this Board decides. - Debt repair and the engine enabler are met in every row and column. - Incumbency (38% in 2040) and the 50/50 split (47% in 2050) are missed. No order this round moves narrowbody share, and no objective premium is paid for them.

Kelly Ortberg frames the round

Question. This is the last decision year of the game, and there is one live order: the 787 Re-engine. Launched now, it enters service in 2055 and is worth +0.05 in S1 and -1.00 in S2 against hold. Does it beat Do Nothing by more than ε ($1B) in the column I expect, inside the hard rules and without a downside our Board will not carry? H4 does not stand in the way (overlap 0), and H3's second half has not fired. So the business case decides it, and there is no later round in which an option to wait pays back. Two questions sit beside the grid: (1) Is fps production stable at about 78 a month, and are both engine sources holding up in service? (2) What do we bring the Board on capital returns, updated to 2050, for its reserved decision? Airbus's calendar does not enter any of it [B-2313].

Situation. Decision year 2050, the final round. Our position. The 10-year fps (Solo, launched 2030) has been in service since 2040. Its engine code has been fixed since EIS. It flies CFM and the P&W-Rolls-Royce Joint Venture engine, which counts as one source. That gives two sources in 2045 and 2050, with three narrowbody engine makers in the market. - Narrowbody share bottomed at 37% (2039), was 38% in 2040 and 43% in 2045, and holds at 47% from 2049. That is the long-run split from NGSA's 3-year lead (2037 against 2040). - The 2050 row: 940 narrowbody and 100 widebody deliveries, $69.7B revenue, and $16.9B operating profit against $6.7B in the status quo. - Airbus held the A350 Re-engine in 2045 and said so in public. Our widebody share is flat at 58.8%. My four questions: 1. *Are the KPIs stable?* The brief reports no live quality, FAA, supply-chain or certification problem [BX-1271]. Pope confirms. 2. *Are market, technology and our balance sheet ready?* The balance sheet is: net debt has been at the historical level since 2029, and since 2030 under stress. No new airplane is on offer. For the 787 Re-engine, the market case does not clear, and on the record only GE's GEnx upgrade is ready, which would put the 787 on one engine source. 3. *What if certification takes longer?* The brief has no risk-case column. A 5-year Re-engine clock has no headroom against our slip prior. 4. *Is this doing less, better?* +0.05 is well inside ε [BX-1239]. Grid (S1: rivals hold; S2: Airbus launches the A350 Re-engine; the brief labels no risk case): - A. fps hold + 787 hold (Do Nothing): +0.66 / +0.57. - B. fps hold + 787 Re-engine: +0.71 / -0.43. - The Re-engine's item value is +0.05 / -1.00. Hold wins on expectation at any S2 weight above 4.8% (0.05 / 1.05). - If we hold, an A350 Re-engine now costs us only $0.09B (+0.66 down to +0.57). - Do Nothing's +0.66 is narrowbody profit +20.30, less programme investment of 14.91 and a debt penalty of 4.73. The grid already nets every penalty, so none is subtracted again. Debt. Net debt is $0.0B at end-2035, 2040, 2045 and 2050 in both rows and both columns, base and stress. - Base free cash flow in 2050 is $21.83B. My stress reading is about $17.23B (9.19 + 0.79 × 10.18). Malave confirms. - A 2050 Re-engine would spend $5B over 2050-54. Mission. The objective cell is 2029 / yes / yes ($0.0B) / 2 (2) for both plans in both columns. - Debt repair: met and held. - Engine enabler: met at two sources and three makers. No code can change it, because no airframe is still short of service. - Incumbency (38% in 2040) and the 50/50 split (47% in 2050): missed. No order this round moves narrowbody share. Board risks (its would-veto list; guidance, not red lines): - 787 Re-engine launch: +0.05 / -1.00 fails its $1B launch test in either column, and S2 sits at its -$1B downside limit; - any premium above $2B, or any premium not logged. It never vetoes a hold. It wants the capital-return proposal updated to 2050, with the agencies' rating view confirmed rather than inferred, for its reserved decision.

Options to test.

  • A. Do Nothing: fps hold, engine code null, 737 rate hold, 787 Re-engine hold. - Scores +0.66 / +0.57 (S1 / S2). - Best in S2 by $1.00B; $0.05B behind B in S1, well inside ε. - Higher worst column: +0.57 against -0.43. - Objective cell: 2029 / yes / yes ($0.0B) / 2 (2) in both columns. - No Board item. This is my lean.
  • B. Do Nothing plus a 787 Re-engine in 2050 (EIS 2055): +0.71 / -0.43, which is +0.05 / -1.00 against A. - Legal: H4 overlap is 0, and H3's second half has not fired. - Fails doing less, better: +0.05 is inside ε. - Fails doctrine's Re-engine rule, which needs a gain above ε. - Fails the Board's $1B launch test in either column, so the Board would veto it. - If S2 were treated as the risk case, it would pass Malave's buffer as advice: -0.43 against a -1.43 floor, by $1.00B. - On Pope's Round 3 finding, only GE's GEnx upgrade could make a 2055 EIS, which would put the 787 on one engine source where it flies two today. I test it to put the row and its item value in front of the Board. It is not my lean.
  • C. A against B, weighted by probability. - Hold wins once S2 carries more than 4.8% weight. - At even odds, A leads by about $0.48B (+0.62 against +0.14). - Even at 0% weight on S2, B's +0.05 sits inside ε. No plausible weight on this grid changes the answer. Malave gives his own read on S2.
  • D. Beside A, unpriced: the capital-return proposal for the Board's reserved decision, updated to 2050. - A common dividend of about $3B a year, plus a buyback of $0-5B authorised each year. - The two capped at $8B: about 46% of 2050 stress free cash flow ($17.23B) and 37% of base ($21.83B). - Net debt at or below $0 under stress, revolvers undrawn, no new equity, supplier funding first. - The buyback goes to zero first on any live problem. - The rating confirmed by the agencies, not inferred by us. Nothing is announced before the Board decides.
  • E. Not an order: close the widebody question for this game. - 787 growth from Charleston capacity, KPI-gated, is the widebody answer [BX-1317, B-2336]. - There is no later review: 2050 is the last decision year. - The record says plainly that the Re-engine never cleared ε in any round we tested (+0.30 / -1.26 in 2045, +0.05 / -1.00 now).

Red lines.

  • H1 and H3 first half: ruled on in 2030 with evidence (777X, MAX 7/10 and the debt repair). Both are spent and not in force.
  • H2 cannot bind. H7 has no trigger: the brief reports no crisis and no certification trouble, so the FAA-process gate is open.
  • H3 second half: no 787 Re-engine once Airbus has launched the A350 Re-engine. It has not fired: Airbus held the A350 Re-engine in 2045, and none is on the public record. A 787 Re-engine launched in the same sealed round as an A350 Re-engine would be kept (H5).
  • H4: a Solo fps and the 787 Re-engine may overlap by at most 2 years. A 2050 Re-engine (development 2050-55) overlaps the fps development (2033-40) by 0 years, so H4 does not strike it.
  • H5: never cancel a launched fps or 787 Re-engine. Nothing is up for cancellation.
  • H6: no Rate Increase under a live problem or as a reply to Airbus. Only hold is on offer.
  • H8: ties within ε ($1B) go to doctrine. Doctrine plus objective premium may total at most $2B, and every premium is logged. The most at stake on this grid is $0.05B. The running log is $0.46B (Round 1), $0.65B (Round 2) and $0 logged in Round 3, which was $0.30B after the fact since Airbus held. This round adds $0.05B if S1, for at most $1.46B.
  • Team rule: Malave's buffer test binds where the brief has a risk-case column. This brief labels none, so by my ruling there is no slip leg this round and each plan's worst column is advice. The KPI doctrine's veto on a Rate Increase under a live problem is moot, since the rate is hold only.
  • My own red lines: - no production-certification concurrency on any development [BX-1263]; - no fixed-price development, only cost-plus or risk-share [BX-1262, BX-1304]; - never walk away from core customers' programmes [BX-1251]; - no blame on the FAA [BX-1323]; - no attribution of a supplier problem to Airbus before exposure (doctrine); - no new dates before the data supports them [BX-1268, B-2315].

Initial lean. Hold everything, and change nothing on the board: - fps: hold; - fps engine code: null; - 737 rate: hold; - 787 Re-engine: hold. Every order is a default, so nothing goes to the Board as a change. Why hold. This is the Do Nothing row: +0.66 / +0.57. - The Re-engine adds +0.05 in S1, well inside ε. Doing less and doing it better wins [BX-1239], and so does doctrine's rule that a Re-engine needs a gain above ε. - In S2 it loses $1.00B, and hold has the higher worst column (+0.57 against -0.43). It is the higher-confidence plan [BX-0548]. - It would put the 787 on one engine source. - This is the last decision year, so there is no option value in waiting. I close the widebody question for the game and grow the 787 out of Charleston. Expected column: S1, provisionally. Airbus held the A350 Re-engine in 2045 and said so publicly. It gates any further A350 step on technology, engine and business case, and Rolls-Royce says it has nothing to launch. My Round 3 read of S2 was wrong, and I'll own that [BX-1319]. My evidence on Airbus is Low, and Malave gives me his read. - In S1, holding costs $0.05B, logged as doctrine premium under H8. That brings the running total to at most $1.46B, inside the cap. - If S2, the premium is $0. - The order is the same in either column. This is not an answer to Airbus; the business case decides. Off the board: - a KPI-gated fps ramp; - durability reviews of both engine sources for the Aerospace Safety Committee; - supplier health, engines first; - Charleston growth; - the capital-return proposal brought back for the Board's reserved decision, sized on the stress case, with the rating confirmation left to the agencies. Public statement. No new dates, no word on Airbus, nothing on returns before the Board decides, and no blame on anyone. 'I think that we're turning it. I don't think it's turned.' [BX-1300] 'the financials will follow our production performance' [BX-1287]. What would change my lean: - a grid gain above ε with no column below -$1B (there is none on this brief); - a live problem from Pope, which would make me hold harder and pull the buyback first; - a stress-path breach from Malave, which would shrink the return proposal, not the orders.

  • Public statement and the record for the game: no new dates, no answer to Airbus's calendar; reaffirm safety, quality, KPI-gated production, two engine sources and debt first; nothing on returns until the Board decides; debt repair and the enabler met; incumbency and the 50/50 split missed, with no objective premium paid. Taken up. The statement gives no dates and does not mention Airbus. It reaffirms safety and quality ahead of rate, KPI-gated production, two engine sources, supplier health, Charleston growth, no fixed price and debt first. It says returns are the Board's decision. For the record: - debt repair is met (2029 base, 2030 stress, $0 at every checkpoint); - the enabler is met at two sources and three makers; - incumbency was missed at 38% in 2040, and the 50/50 split at 47% in 2050; - no order this round moves share, and the objective premium is $0. In public I say only that we have share to earn back.

Objective. Debt repair: met and held. - Net debt reached the historical level in 2029 (base) and 2030 (stress). - It is $0.0B at end-2035, 2040, 2045 and 2050 in both plans and both columns. - The capital-return proposal is sized so that net debt stays at or below $0 in the stress case, building about $44B of net cash by end-2054. Engine enabler: met at two sources and three makers. - The fps flies CFM and the P&W-Rolls-Royce Joint Venture engine, which counts as one source, so two sources in 2040, 2045 and 2050. - CFM, P&W and Rolls-Royce stay in the narrowbody market in 2045 and 2050. - The code is locked since EIS, so no order this round can change it. The Joint Venture engine is the fragility, managed by durability reviews and the keep-hot list. - Holding the 787 Re-engine also keeps the 787 on two engine sources instead of GE alone. Incumbency and the 50/50 split: not met. - Share was 38% in 2040 (the worst year), 43% in 2045 and 47% in 2050. - No order this round moves narrowbody share, and I pay no objective premium for either goal. Cell for the chosen plan: 2029 / yes / yes ($0.0B) / 2 (2) in both columns.

Predictions. Airbus. I put the A350 Re-engine at about 20-30%: - it held in 2045 and gates any step on technology, engine and business case; - Rolls-Royce's widebody caution holds it back. No new narrowbody move from Airbus is likely; NGSA's production ramp is its priority. Engine makers. - CFM holds, with RISE kept as technology and no launch. - The P&W-Rolls-Royce Joint Venture holds on the narrowbody. - Rolls-Royce launches no widebody engine unless Airbus re-engines the A350. - P&W holds. Boeing on the board. - Narrowbody share flat at 47% (940 a year). - Widebody share flat at 58.8% (100 a year). - Operating profit of $16.9B a year from 2049. Balance sheet. 2050 free cash flow is $21.83B base and $17.23B stress, with net debt $0 throughout. Problems. No live quality, FAA or supply problem is expected. The Joint Venture engine's durability is the watch item. ΔPV. - +0.66 in S1 (expected); - +0.57 if Airbus re-engines the A350; - about +0.63 at a 30% S2 weight.

Expected ΔPV. +0.66 $B (GM valuation after the round: +0.66 $B)

Other moves.

  • KPI-gated fps production, with every step reported to the Aerospace Safety Committee (public): fps production holds at about 78 a month (940 a year from 2049 on the brief). Narrowbody share is flat at 47%, so visible demand calls for no further step. Any step stays in increments of 5 a month, at least 6 months apart, and is gated on the six FAA-agreed KPIs: rework, escapes, traveled work, supplier shortages, training and ticketing. The data decides, not the calendar [BX-1259, BX-1291, B-2283]. Pope tables the KPI values and in-service reliability at every Committee meeting. The brief gives none of them as numbers, so we invent none. Any quality, FAA or supply problem goes to the Board as a live problem the day we see it. No production runs ahead of a mature design [BX-1263].
  • In-service durability reviews of both fps engine sources (public): CFM, and the P&W-Rolls-Royce Joint Venture engine, report reliability, durability and life-limited-part status to the Aerospace Safety Committee at each meeting, where the Committee brings its propulsion expertise to bear [BX-1298]. We sit at exactly two sources, and the Joint Venture engine is the single point of fragility. If it stumbles, CFM would need up to 1,880 fps engines a year, about 62% of what it built before 2037. That is feasible, but it leaves the fps on one source. CFM capacity across LEAP-1B, the fps, NGSA and the aftermarket stays a watch item [BX-1264, BX-1325].
  • Supplier health, engines first: keep fragile suppliers funded and hot (private): We keep these funded and hot: - CFM on the fps; - the Joint Venture engine; - LEAP-1B, the sole source for any 737 MAX still built and for the aftermarket of at least 22,160 installed engines [B-1449]; - any supplier flagged on the supplier-shortages KPI, which is reported engines first. The ladder is embed, buffer, keep above rate, requalify, fund, acquire [BX-1243, B-2330, B-2043]. Terms stay risk-share or cost-plus, never fixed price [BX-1262, BX-1304]. This cash, then KPI-gated Charleston capex, comes ahead of any buyback.
  • Third-source contingency for the fps, outside the board, held ready but not triggered (private): This is triggered only by an Aerospace Safety Committee durability or life-limited-part finding on the Joint Venture engine, and it would be treated as a live problem. The case would need: - CFM as the bridge; - a maker funding a separate engine on its own return case; - risk-share or cost-plus terms; - that engine's own durability record before it joins the airplane; - about 6-7 years of lead time (Pope, inference); - a Board decision. None of these is triggered today.
  • Widebody question closed for this game: 787 growth from Charleston capacity, KPI-gated (public): We are not starting a 787 Re-engine. We grow the 787 from the capacity built in Charleston where customer orders are visible, gated on the same KPIs [BX-1317, B-2336]. That loads the factory, not engineering (strain $0), and it is our widebody answer in place of a second development: doing less and doing it better [BX-1239]. The board does not price it. 2050 is the last decision year, so this is a close, not a deferral to a later review.
  • Capital-return proposal for the Board's reserved decision, updated to 2050 and sized on the stress case (private): This is Malave's sizing, in the form the Board says it is minded to take, and I endorse it. It is inference: neither of us has a record on returns. The proposal: - reinstate a common dividend of about $3B a year, covered 5.7x by 2050 stress free cash flow ($17.23B) and 7.3x by base ($21.83B); - add a buyback of $0-5B a year, authorised by the Board each year on Finance Committee review and paced on actual free cash flow; - cap the two together at $8B a year, 46% of stress free cash flow and 37% of base, well short of the pre-2019 practice of returning about all free cash flow [B-1164]. Stress-case net debt (2026 $B, year end, full $8B paid every year): -9.24 / -18.27 / -27.11 / -35.77 / -44.23 for 2050-54. That retains about $9.2B a year and builds about $44B of net cash by end-2054. The $10B of revolvers stays undrawn and no new equity is needed. Breakpoints: - the buyback goes to zero first on any live quality, FAA or supply problem (a Joint Venture engine durability finding included), or if free cash flow runs below the $8B cap (54% below stress); - the dividend holds unless free cash flow falls about 83% below stress, and below that only while net debt stays at or below $0. Condition: the package takes effect only on the rating agencies' written confirmation. Our files carry no rating and no rating thresholds. Last round's 'solidly investment grade' was our inference, and Malave withdraws it. If the agencies confirm investment grade but not a solid one, we recommend the dividend only. Nothing is announced before the Board decides.
  • No fixed-price development; no new dates; no blame (public): All development and support with suppliers stays on cost-plus or risk-share terms [BX-1262, BX-1304]. We give no programme date before the data supports it [BX-1268, B-2315]. We blame no one, the FAA included [BX-1323], and we attribute no supplier problem to anyone else before exposure.

Board guidance before the ExCo met

Priorities.

  • Safety and the five pillars come first. NGSA has been in service since 2037, and the A320neo GTF fleet still flies. The full Board's twice-yearly safety review should see three things: NGSA fleet results, the durability of the P&W-Rolls-Royce Joint Venture engine, and CFM capacity. The Board will accept no item that the operating head fails on safety, quality, the ramp or a supply crunch, and no override of those tests [AG-0038, A-0331, AX-0015, A-0303, AG-0067, AG-0068].
  • The A350 Re-engine gets its last test of the game, under the gate the ExCo itself set in 2045. A 2050 launch would enter service in 2055 and cost $1.0B a year, with no overlap with NGSA and no strain. It is worth +0.57 if rivals hold (S1) and -0.41 if Boeing launches a 787 Re-engine (S2). It passes the Board's cash, one-programme-at-a-time and downside tests. It fails the company's $1B launch test, and two of the ExCo's three gate conditions: it is short of $1B, and no committed engine is on the record. The Board would accept a hold, or a launch that properly clears the ExCo's tests. It would not accept an override [A-0343, A-0401, AG-0049, A-0302, AX-0019, AX-0008].
  • Liquidity, the rating and returns. Programme cash in 2050-2054 is $0 on hold, or $1.0B a year with the A350 Re-engine, which is 19% of the $5.2B line (one year's free cash flow). Net cash, the A+/A1 rating and the 30-50% payout remain fundable. There is to be no equity raise and no dividend cut, and any new buyback comes to the Board as a reserved matter [AX-0022, AX-0104, A-0402, AG-0062, AG-0058, AG-0059, AG-0035].
  • A stable engine supply. NGSA has 2 sources: CFM and the Joint Venture engine, which counts as one. Three narrowbody makers remain in the market in 2050, in every plan and column. The NGSA engine code is locked, so nothing this round can trigger a conditional engine launch. The Board's attention is on keeping both sources healthy, and on the engine behind any A350 Re-engine, where Rolls-Royce is today the only source [A-0243, A-0360, A-0218, AX-0054, A-0253].
  • Integrity, the 60/40 objective and the long view. Delay Tactics have been closed since fps entered service in 2040, and none was ordered in any round. The 60/40 objective is not met: share is 53% from 2049, the board's long-run split after a 3-year lead. No option this round reaches it, and the Board asks that no PV, cash or integrity be traded for it. In this last round the Board supplies the long view: the next generation should keep being prepared on technology gates [A-0299, AG-0053, A-0474, AG-0022, AX-0025, AG-0039, AG-0028].

Expects to see. The Board expects one agreed ExCo package containing the following. (1) The submitted row and the default row, with the item value in each column: - Hold: +23.37 (S1) / +23.33 (S2). - A350 Re-engine: +23.94 (S1) / +22.92 (S2). - The item is therefore +0.57 (S1) / -0.41 (S2). - It breaks even at a 58% chance of S2. Weighted at 20 / 25 / 30 / 35% S2, it is worth +0.37 / +0.33 / +0.28 / +0.23. (2) The CEO's expected column, named with its probability, and the worst plausible column. S2 is not ruled out. Boeing's 2045 statement and its 787 growth from Charleston 'in place of a second development' lower its likelihood but do not exclude it. The worst plausible column is S2 in both plans: +23.33 on hold and +22.92 with the Re-engine. (3) The CFO's cash figures for 2050-2055: - Programme cash: $0 on hold. With the Re-engine, $5B / 5 = $1.00B a year in 2050-2054, against the $5.2B line (EUR 4,753m at $1.10 = $5.23B). No overlap with NGSA and $0 strain. - The net-cash bridge with the dividend, and returns inside 30-50%. - Any new buyback brought to the Board as a reserved matter. - Confirmation of no equity raise and no dividend cut. - His added-move robustness test on the Re-engine, with its result and how it was resolved. (4) The operating head's results: - safety and quality, with any five-pillars flag; - the A320neo and NGSA ramp, and any supply crunch; - for a Re-engine: engineering capacity, A350 production readiness for a 2055 entry into service, and condition 3 of the ExCo's own gate (a committed engine source on the public record, ready by entry into service). Rolls-Royce has said it plans 'no new widebody programme beside the narrowbody', and under rules.md an UltraFan widebody launched in 2050 is ready only in 2056. (5) The engine enabler: - the NGSA code locked; - 2 sources (CFM plus the P&W-RR Joint Venture engine) and 3 makers in 2050, in every cell; - a status line on Joint Venture engine durability, CFM capacity and GTF Hot Section kit insertion. (6) The rule 3 check: no 787 Re-engine is on the public record. (7) Each soft veto and how it was resolved. No override has been used this game. No override can carry the Re-engine: +0.57 is under the $1B bar, and the item trails hold by $0.41B in S2. (8) The public statement: safety first, windows not dates, nothing timed to Boeing and nothing on Delay Tactics. If a piece is missing, the Board will compute it from the brief and say so.

Would approve.

  • A350 Re-engine: hold. This is the default, not a Board item, and is never vetoed. The Board expects it: the ExCo's own 2050 gate fails on the $1B condition (+0.57) and on the committed-engine condition. Row: +23.37 (S1) / +23.33 (S2), the better row in S2 and the more robust of the two.
  • A350 Re-engine: launch (entry into service 2055), but only if it reaches the Board with the ExCo's own tests properly resolved (no standing soft veto) and S1 named as the expected column. - Cash: passes. $1.0B a year in 2050-2054 is 19% of the $5.2B line, with 0 years of overlap and $0 strain. - One programme at a time: passes. It would be the only launch. - Downside: passes. +0.57 in S1 and -0.41 in S2, within the $2B limit. - Returns stay fundable, and rule 3 is met. - Row: +23.94 / +22.92. - It needs a Qualified Majority: $5B is about EUR 4.55bn at $1.10.
  • NGSA: hold, with the engine code unchanged (locked since entry into service). It is the only value open and is not a Board item. It keeps 2 sources and 3 makers in 2050.
  • Delay Tactics: none. It is the only value open, since fps has been in service since 2040, and it is not a Board item.

Would veto.

  • A350 Re-engine: launch submitted over a standing soft veto that the CEO neither respects nor validly overrides. This covers the CFO's added-move robustness test (+0.57 is under $1B, and the item is negative in S2) and the operating head's engine-readiness test (no committed engine ready by 2055). It also covers a launch that sets aside the ExCo's own recorded three-condition gate without resolving it. Ground: governance (an unresolved objection). Acceptable alternative: hold.
  • A350 Re-engine: launch carried by an override. Ground: governance (override review). - Its margin over the best passing option (hold) is +0.57 in S1, under the $1B bar. - On this Qualified Majority item it also trails hold by $0.41B in the worst plausible column (S2). - No override of this item can pass. Acceptable alternative: hold.
  • A350 Re-engine: launch if the operating head fails it on safety, quality, the A320neo or NGSA ramp, or a supply crunch. Ground: safety and ramp, and the Board accepts no override of these tests. A readiness or capacity soft veto would instead go through override review, which this item cannot pass. Acceptable alternative: hold.
  • A350 Re-engine: launch if the CEO names S2 (787 Re-engine) as the expected column. The item would then lose $0.41B in the column where it must gain. Ground: downside. Acceptable alternative: hold.
  • The Board never vetoes a hold or none, the engine code on its own, an item for its near-term earnings cost alone, or the A350 Re-engine merely because hold scores higher in S2.

Recommendations.

  • Put the A350 Re-engine to its last test of the game under the ExCo's own 2050 gate, and decide by the team rule. - The Board's tests pass: $1.0B a year, no overlap, and +0.57 / -0.41 within the $2B limit. - The company's $1B launch test fails by $0.43B. Gate condition 1 (at least $1B over Do Nothing) fails. Condition 3 (a committed engine on the record before the vote) is not met on the bulletin. - On the team rule this points to hold. The Board will approve a hold, or a launch that properly clears the ExCo's tests. - It does not ask the ExCo to set its tests aside, and it would veto any override.
  • If the A350 Re-engine is held, compete on A350 and A350F price and product, as Airbus did with the A330neo. Record the hold as a business-case decision (short of $1B, no committed engine), not as a reaction to Boeing. This closes the Re-engine for the game.
  • If the A350 Re-engine is launched: - Name and secure its engine before the vote. Rolls-Royce is the A350's only source and has said it plans no new widebody programme beside the narrowbody. Under rules.md, an UltraFan widebody launched in 2050 is ready only in 2056, a year after a 2055 entry into service. - Give entry into service in public as a window ('in the middle of the next decade'), not a date. - Keep to one launch: the A220-500 stays a study.
  • Engine supply (the enabler). Dual sourcing on NGSA and three narrowbody makers in 2050 are met in every plan and column. The Joint Venture engine counts as one source, so a Joint Venture durability finding would leave NGSA on CFM alone. - The operating head should keep reporting to the twice-yearly safety review on Joint Venture engine durability and deliveries, CFM capacity, and GTF Hot Section kit insertion. - He should bring an unpriced contingency view, with no money committed, for keeping two sources healthy. - Keep the risk-sharing invitation on standard terms: no concession, no refundable advance assumed.
  • The CFO's papers for 2050-2055: - the net-cash bridge with the dividend; - programme cash at $0, or $1.0B a year with the Re-engine; - returns inside the 30-50% policy; - any new buyback brought to the Board as a reserved matter, within the 18-month AGM authority, with the bridge attached. There is to be no equity raise and no dividend cut. State support and refundable advances are upside and are never assumed in the case.
  • Show both columns. - Name the expected column and give its probability. - Show the worst plausible column (S2) for each plan, and the 58% break-even for the Re-engine. - Read Boeing only from the bulletin. Its 2045 statement and the Charleston 787 growth lower the chance of S2, but they do not rule it out for 2050.
  • Integrity, the 60/40 objective and the long view. - Delay Tactics stay closed, and none was ordered all game. - Supply security stays confined to Airbus's own ramp, with the Ethics, Compliance and Sustainability Committee informed. - The 60/40 objective is not met (53%, the board's long-run split), and no PV, cash or integrity should be traded for it. - Pay rewards nothing beyond about four years, so the Board asks that the next generation keep being prepared on technology gates, as an unpriced move with no programme cash.
  • Public statement: - open with the five pillars; - give windows, not dates; - say 'we intend to offer a choice of engines'; - time nothing to Boeing and say nothing on Delay Tactics.

Guillaume Faury frames the round

Question. 2050 is the last round, and the A350 Re-engine faces the last test of the game, under the three-condition gate this ExCo set in 2045. Launched now, it would enter service in the middle of the next decade (2055) at $1.0B a year, with no overlap and no strain. On the grid the item is +0.57 if rivals hold (S1) and -0.41 if Boeing launches a 787 Re-engine (S2). It fails gate condition 1 (at least $1B over Do Nothing), and condition 3 (a committed engine on the record) is not met. So do we launch, or hold every lever at the default with no Board items, compete on A350 price and product, and close the Re-engine for the game as a business-case decision?

Situation. BOEING AND THE PUBLIC RECORD (bulletin only) - fps was launched in 2030 on the 10-year ramp and has been in service since 2040. It flies CFM plus the P&W-RR Joint Venture engine (two sources). Boeing ramps it in KPI-gated steps of 5 a month: deliveries went from 760 (2040) to 860 (2045) and 940 (2049). - On the 787, Boeing said in 2045 that it was "not starting a new development this year". It grows the 787 out of its Charleston capacity, "in place of a second development". That statement covered 2045 only, so a 787 Re-engine in 2050 is not ruled out. No 787 Re-engine and no Rate Increase are on the record. - Boeing will give "no new dates". It develops on cost-plus and risk-share terms and flags CFM capacity as a watch item, which it says has eased. ENGINE MAKERS - P&W says the Joint Venture engine's durability record "is still being earned". It claims nothing beyond the hours flown, and Hot Section kit insertion continues across the GTF fleet on standard terms. - CFM's ducted engine is in service on both new narrowbodies. CFM launches no new programme, and RISE stays funded as technology with no date. On the record: no flight test, no compact-core durability result, and the fuel-burn figure not yet shown in engine test. - Rolls-Royce: "no new widebody programme beside the narrowbody". It is improving Trent time on wing inside its own budget, and it is the A350's only engine source [A-0253]. - No maker launches anything this year. PROBLEMS REPORTED The brief reports no supply crunch, no quality or safety event and no engine slip. Our narrowbody deliveries fall to 1,060 a year from 2049. That is 53% of 2,000, the board's share mechanics after fps entered service, not supply. OUR POSITION - NGSA has been in service since 2037. Its code is locked: CFM plus the Joint Venture engine, 2 sources. - If nobody moves: +23.37 (yield 115.58%). That is narrowbody operating profit +39.13, programme investment -15.23 and debt penalty -0.53. - The grid: - hold: +23.37 (S1) / +23.33 (S2), so a 787 Re-engine costs the hold row only $0.04B; - A350 Re-engine: +23.94 / +22.92. - The item is therefore +0.57 / -0.41. It breaks even at 58% S2. Weighted at 20/25/30/35% S2, it is worth +0.37 / +0.33 / +0.28 / +0.23. - Programme cash is $0 on hold, or $1.0B a year in 2050-2054 with the Re-engine: 19% of the $5.23B line (EUR 4,753m at $1.10). OBJECTIVES (the GM scores these; they never change the payoff) - 60/40: not met. Share is 53% from 2049, the board's long-run split after a 3-year lead, and no lever this round reaches it. - A320 family: protected, at 60% before NGSA's entry into service. - Engine enabler: met in every plan and column. NGSA has 2 sources and 3 narrowbody makers are in the market in 2050. With the code locked, nothing can trigger a conditional engine launch. THE BOARD (risk-averse, 4 of 5) - It would approve a hold, or a launch that properly clears the ExCo's tests with S1 named as the expected column. - It would veto a launch that goes over a standing soft veto or sets the gate aside, one carried by an override, one Wagner fails on safety, quality, the ramp or a supply crunch, and one with S2 named as the expected column. MY READ OF BOEING - Expected column: S1, about 75% (range 65-80%). - Worst plausible column: S2, about 25% (range 20-35%). That is lower than my 30% in 2045 because of Boeing's 2045 statement and its Charleston growth, but not zero. - Boeing's moves set none of our clock.

Options to test.

  • 1. COMPANY DEFAULT AND MY LEAN: NGSA hold (code unchanged) + A350 hold + Delay Tactics none. - Row: +23.37 (S1) / +23.33 (S2). The worst plausible column is S2 at +23.33, positive, and the higher of the two rows' worst columns. - At 75/25 it is worth about +23.36. - No Board items and $0 programme cash in 2050-2055. - Enabler: 2 sources and 3 makers in 2050. - It is the reference row, with every order at its default.
  • 2. TEST, expected to fail our own gate: + A350 Re-engine (A350 Re-engine: launch, entry into service 2055). Row and item - Row: +23.94 (S1) / +22.92 (S2). Item against hold: +0.57 / -0.41. - It breaks even at 58% S2. Weighted at 20/25/30/35% S2, it is worth +0.37 / +0.33 / +0.28 / +0.23. What it passes - Board cash: 19% of the line, 0 overlap, $0 strain. - Rule 6 (one launch) and rule 3 (no 787 Re-engine on the record). - The Board's downside test: it gains in S1 and loses under $2B in S2. What it fails - The company launch test (profile §6, at least $1B over Do Nothing): it falls short by $0.43B. - Gate condition 1: same ground. - Gate condition 3: no committed engine source on the record. Rolls-Royce plans no new widebody programme, and under rules.md an UltraFan widebody launched in 2050 is ready only in 2056, a year after a 2055 entry into service. - The doctrine default: hold is within $1B of the best S1 plan, with a gap of $0.57B. - Probably Toepfer's added-move robustness test. Override None can carry it: the margin is +0.57, under $1B, and it trails hold by $0.41B in S2.
  • 3. ON RECORD, NOT A CHOICE: Delay Tactics closed, the NGSA engine code locked, and no NGSA cancel (barred by rule 7 in any case). None of these changes the grid.
  • 4. IF HELD (unpriced): compete on A350 and A350F price and product on the existing A350 teams [A-0090, A-0091]. Record the hold as a business-case decision (short of $1B, no committed engine), not as a reaction to Boeing. This closes the Re-engine for the game. 'Do Nothing is a legitimate choice wherever the red lines or the $1B test bind' [A-0440].
  • 5. IF LAUNCHED (only if both memos cleared it, which I do not expect): - name and secure its engine before the vote; - give a public window, not a date ('in the middle of the next decade'); - keep to one launch, with the A220-500 a study; - no reactive cancellation. A 787 Re-engine launched this round would enter service in the same year, 2055, which on the board leaves widebody shares unchanged and is not 'first'.

Red lines.

  • Five pillars (safety, quality, integrity, compliance, security). No order or statement that fails them, and nothing we could not defend to the Audit Committee or the Ethics, Compliance and Sustainability Committee. They are never overridden [AX-0073, AX-0081].
  • Rule 3: no A350 Re-engine after Boeing has launched a 787 Re-engine. It does not bind, since none is on the record, and a launch in the same round is not 'after'.
  • A350 Re-engine cancel rule: cancel only if a 787 Re-engine enters service first and the remaining spend loses at least $1B. This is the last round, and no reactive cancellation is planned.
  • Rule 6: at most one new launch, with NGSA overlap at 0. The A220-500 stays a study.
  • Rules 2 and 7: our own clock, and never cancel NGSA. Boeing's moves re-time and cancel none of our programmes.

  • Company launch test (profile §6) and the ExCo's own 2050 gate, recorded in 2045: (1) at least $1B over Do Nothing; (2) no 787 Re-engine on the record; (3) a committed engine source, ready by entry into service, on the public record before the vote.   • Doctrine default: take the default when it is within $1B of the best plan in the expected column (the gap is $0.57B). The $3B allowance is not engaged.
  • Override budget: one per game, unused all game. It needs at least $1B over the best passing option and a Board item, and never goes against a pillar, a red line or the Board. It cannot carry the Re-engine: +0.57 is under $1B, and the item trails hold by $0.41B in S2.
  • The Board's would-veto list, carried in full: - a launch over a standing soft veto, or one that sets the ExCo's three-condition gate aside unresolved; - a launch carried by an override; - a launch Wagner fails on safety, quality, the A320neo or NGSA ramp, or a supply crunch; - a launch with S2 named as the expected column. The Board never vetoes a hold, 'none' or the engine code on its own.
  • Board downside test: each item must gain in the expected column (S1) and lose less than $2B in any plausible column. Both columns are plausible.
  • Peak-cash line: about $5.2B, one year's FCF (EUR 4,753m at $1.10 = $5.23B) [AX-0104, AX-0022].
  • Balance sheet: no equity raise and no dividend cut. Returns stay inside 30-50%, and any new buyback is a reserved Board matter [AX-0022, AX-0001].
  • Disclosure: windows, not dates; no internal long-term-plan targets; nothing timed to Boeing; nothing on Delay Tactics [AX-0004, AX-0005, AX-0020].
  • 60/40 and the engine enabler are scored, not paid for. No PV, cash or integrity is traded for either.

Board guidance before the ExCo met

Priorities.

  • Safety, quality, delivery and cost, in that order [CG-0009, CX-0658]. This is the last round. The Ducted has flown on NGSA since 2037 and on fps since 2040, and Embraer has counted since 2037. Boeing now reviews both fps engine sources at every meeting of its safety committee. Our first job is still the fleet, not a new programme. We want Ali's durability report to the full board, built on field and turn-on, turn-off evidence. Every finding should be a cross-functional call, and the fix should be to the part [CX-0009, CX-0012, CX-0005, CG-0018]. Durability is never traded [CX-0208]. Ali's 'no flag' last round meant nothing was in front of him. It was not a clearance.
  • Keep what the grid pays for. There is one column, S1 (rivals hold), and hold everything is its best plan at -69.69 (yield 56.4%). Against hold, Open Fan is -86.74, an item value of -17.05. Open Fan + Lobby is -85.08, or -15.39. The Ducted, Embraer and GEnx can only be held. The only possible Board items are Open Fan: launch and emissions lobbying: launch, and both fail our tests [CG-0017, CX-0493, CX-0609].
  • RISE stays whole as technology. It becomes a product only on an airframer path, and that path does not exist in this game [CX-0469, CX-0205, CX-0147, CX-0214]. A 2050 launch would be ready in 2060. That is 23 years after NGSA's entry into service and 20 after fps's, and four years after the board stops counting the NB market (2056). The grid shows the wait penalty: CFM's 27% NB share goes to zero for 2050-2056, about $9.06B PV on our reconstruction (inference). Keep RISE funded inside the R&D we protect first: no cancel for cost and no 'program dividend' [CX-0174, CX-0398, CG-0011, CG-0065]. Being the last round is not a reason to stretch the test.
  • Balance sheet: keep the A-range rating and return at least 70% of free cash flow [CG-0022, CX-0645, CG-0063, CG-0064, CG-0012]. A hold commits no new R&D. Premium: $0 this round and $0 of $4.0B for the game. The RISE allowance stays at $0 of $15B, unspent, and ends the game unspent.
  • CFM parity rule (Safran consent) [CX-0184, CX-0160, CX-0219, CG-0065, CG-0066]. On a hold no gate is needed, and fleet support for the Ducted and Embraer on both airframers stays within joint practice. A RISE product launch with no airframer path is not joint practice. It would need a stated reason why Safran would agree, and the record has none.

Expects to see. (1) expected_scenario S1 (rivals hold), the only column the GM gave, weighted S1 1.00 in predictions. Name any rival move outside the grid and label it off-grid; never weight it into a column the GM did not give. The record argues against such moves this round: P&W and RR say there is nothing to launch, RR rules out a new widebody programme beside the narrowbody, Airbus holds the A350 Re-engine, and Boeing starts no new 787 development. (2) Each row against Do Nothing (hold everything): - hold: -69.69; - Open Fan: -86.74 (-17.05); - Open Fan + Lobby: -85.08 (-15.39); Lobby is +1.66 inside the row, and only against a penalty the Open Fan itself creates. For any Board item, show the submitted row and the row with that item at its default. For Lobby, default the Open Fan as well. Lobby alone is not on the grid: -1.00 for no board effect, on Ghai's round 3 reading. (3) Ghai's tests, with numbers: - pays for itself; - the payout floor: $0 a year on a hold; an Open Fan would be $0.8B a year, or $0.9B with Lobby, against about $2.5B of room; - the premium; - the booking: at or below -69.69. Label the off-grid widebody exposure as the low case. If ordered in 2050, Ghai's round 3 figures were about $0.41B for a Trent 1000 upgrade and about $0.50B for UltraFan WB (inference) [CX-0965, CX-0654]. The RISE allowance stated apart in premium_reason: $0 of $15B, unspent at the end of the game. (8) Every override, with its evidence. We expect none. (9) A board_response to each recommendation below.
