Would approve.

  • Hold everything, with all five fields at hold. It is not a Board item, and we never veto it. It is the grid's best plan in S1, the only column, at -69.69 (yield 56.4%), so the premium is $0. It keeps the Ducted, Embraer and GEnx in service and counting. It commits no new R&D, so the 70% payout and the A-range rating are untouched. CFM parity rule: no gate is needed, and fleet support for programmes both airframers fly stays within joint practice.
  • ducted engine: hold, Embraer partnership: hold and GEnx: hold, the only options this round. All three are ready: the Ducted since 2036, Embraer since 2037 and the GEnx upgrade since 2033, counting from 2042. None can be cancelled.
  • Nothing else on this grid passes. Neither off-default row reaches zero against hold in S1. S1 is the only column, so no choice of weights changes this.

Would veto.

  • Open Fan: launch, alone: -17.05 against hold on an $8B bill, $9.05B beyond it. Grounds: - Bounded downside fails. The loss beyond the bill is the wait penalty: CFM's 27% NB share goes to zero for 2050-2056, about $9.06B PV on our reconstruction. - Airframer path fails on (a): NGSA (2037) and fps (2040) entered service long before a 2060 ready year, so it waits in the only column. - Airframer path fails on (b): $17.05B is over the $15B allowance. - CFM parity rule (Safran consent): a RISE product with no airframer path is not joint practice, and no reason Safran would agree is on the record. - Safety and readiness: Ali's RISE gates are not closed. There is no compact-core turn-off result, and 20% is not shown in engine test. Any flag he raises on it, if unresolved, fails it too. The payout floor passes at $0.8B a year, but that does not rescue the item. Acceptable alternative: hold.
  • Open Fan: launch with emissions lobbying: launch: -15.39 against hold on a $9B bill ($8B + $1B; Ghai found no second strain), $6.39B beyond it. That is $0.39B over the RISE allowance. Putting the $0.39B into premium would not save it. At a horizon of 3 the allowance cannot carry an Open Fan the grid shows waiting, and it waits in the only column (airframer path, test (a)). It is also late for the objective, ready in 2060 against 'ready by 2050', so an objective premium buys nothing. The same CFM parity rule and safety and readiness grounds apply as for the Open Fan alone. We would veto both items together. Acceptable alternative: hold for both.
  • emissions lobbying: launch alone. It is -1.00 for no board effect, so it fails 'paid for the risk'. It also fails our rule that Lobby goes only with an Open Fan launched this round or already live, and no Open Fan is live. Acceptable alternative: hold.
  • Any Board item that carries a premium. Hold is the only passing plan, so any item this round carries at least $15.39B against a $2.0B cap. An objective premium buys nothing: the Open Fan leg cannot be met, and the NB-share leg has no lever on this menu.
  • Any cancel, should one be put forward. None is on the menu, because all three programmes are ready. A cancel of an engine that live airframes fly would fail hard rule 5, the cancellation test and the CFM parity rule.

Recommendations.

  • Safety and quality, in service. - Bring Ali's fleet durability report on the Ducted (NGSA and fps), Embraer and GEnx to the full board. It should cover time on wing, removals by part number, life-limited parts at full life and inspection findings, on field and turn-on, turn-off evidence, with the CFM56 in the same environment as the yardstick. - Boeing reviews both fps engine sources at every meeting of its safety committee. Give our customers the data they ask for through CFM governance, jointly with Safran. - Make every finding a cross-functional call, fix the part, and bring to us at once any finding that touches both aircraft. - If the brief still has no field data, say so. 'No flag' is not a clearance.
  • Delivery, framed for the customer. - Keep CFM's place through readiness, durability and support, not price. We are not going for share, and there is no birthright. - The public record suggests a customer may want more engine sources on the fps. That is not ours to chase with terms. - Keep the joint capacity plan with Safran on 1,079 NB engines a year, with no new facility. The risk is stranded capacity. - OE comes before spares, after safety-critical parts. - Capex stays within 2-3% of revenue, aimed at MRO turnaround. - No capacity or rate number goes out until each airframer's volumes are agreed.
  • RISE in the last round. - Keep it funded as technology inside the R&D we protect first, with no cancel for cost and no 'program dividend'. - State in the rationale that a 2050 launch is ready in 2060, after the 2056 NB window, and waits in the only column. Do not stretch the airframer-path test because the game ends. - Report Ali's gates as the state of the technology, and keep the allowance at $0. - RISE content goes into in-service engines only where turn-on, turn-off testing supports it.
  • Cost and capital. - Commit no new R&D, keep the 70% payout and the A-range rating whole, and do not redeploy the room into a product the grid shows waiting. - State the premium in dollars: $0 this round and $0 of $4.0B for the game. Show the RISE allowance separately at $0 of $15B. - Book at or below -69.69, with the off-grid widebody exposure (about $0.4-0.5B if ordered in 2050; Ghai, inference) as the labelled low case, and guide cautiously.
  • Objectives. State plainly that NB share is 27.0% from 2040, against 50%, and that 'Open Fan launched and ready by 2050' cannot be met by any order. Spend no premium on either. Claim no NB share for the Ducted, as Ali's reconciliation showed. Commercial work stays on standard terms, priced jointly with Safran and kept out of the statement.
  • CFM parity rule (Safran consent). On a hold, record that fleet support for the Ducted and Embraer on both aircraft stays within joint practice, with the aftermarket split equally. Assert no Safran position. Any Open Fan launch needs a stated reason why Safran would agree to a RISE product with no airframer path, and we know of none.
  • Public statement. - Name no rival, the Joint Venture included, and blame no one. - Give no Open Fan or RISE year, and use no fuel-burn number as a result. - Give no CFM price, rate or capacity number without Safran. - Claim the Ducted's record only as far as field data has earned it. - Take up Ali's round 3 caution: 'New engines for our customers' deliveries come first', not 'on time'. - Do not answer, in public, any airframer remark on engine sources.

Larry Culp frames the round

Question. What game are we playing, and how do we win? [CX-0467] This is the last decision year. The narrowbody game was settled when fps entered service in 2040. NGSA (2037) and fps (2040) are both flying with all three makers fitted, and the codes are locked. The board counts the narrowbody market to 2056 and the widebody to 2061. No order on this menu buys back a point of NB share. So the game is the fleet we've put in the air, not the share we don't have: - 1,079 CFM narrowbody engines a year on two aircraft we share three ways; - the LEAP fleet behind them; - 152 GEnx a year, with the upgrade counting since 2042. "Our major economics happen in and around the first and second" shop visit [CX-0422]. "We get paid in dollars, not in percentages." [CX-0630] We win it on execution: safety, quality, delivery and cost, always in that order [CX-0658]. - Durability earned in the field and shown to customers. Both airframers now say an engine stays on their aircraft on proven durability. One of them reviews both engine sources at every meeting of its safety committee. That is the scoreboard now, and field data is the only thing that moves it [CX-0009]. We have no birthright [CX-0564]. - Delivery and support that promise nothing we would have to walk back. - RISE kept whole as technology for the airframe after these two. That airframe is off this board [CX-0214, CX-0469]. - The balance sheet and the 70% payout kept whole [CX-0645]. The question for this room is whether the last round changes the answer. - The temptation is the end-game. The board stops counting in 2056, so a 2050 Open Fan can be dressed up as "seeding the next 20, the next 30 years" [CX-0555]. It would also tick the 'launched' half of an objective we can't meet. - I want Rahul and Mohamed to test that hard, and I expect it to fail. - If it does, the work goes to the fleet durability report, to customer data through CFM governance with our partner, to a capacity plan that doesn't strand capital, and to a public statement that says only what the data has earned.

Situation. PUBLIC RECORD, 2050 (round 3 adjudicated; no public events) - Airframes. NGSA (Airbus) has been in service since 2037 and fps (Boeing, 10-year ramp) since 2040. Both are fitted CFM + P&W + RR, and both codes are locked. - No new airframe is on the record. Boeing starts no new 787 development and grows the 787 out of Charleston capacity. Airbus holds the A350 Re-engine. - Airbus says it prepares its next generation "on technology gates, one well-prepared programme at a time", with no date and no programme. If that is RISE's airframer path, it lies past this board. - Rival NB engines. The Joint Venture engine has been ready since 2036 and is on both aircraft. Both rival makers say there is no new engine programme this year. One rules out a new widebody programme beside the narrowbody, and its Trent time-on-wing work is not the Trent 1000 upgrade order. I see no rival move left that the board would price against us. - Customers on the record: - Boeing reviews reliability, durability and life-limited-part status for both fps engine sources at every safety committee meeting. - Boeing counts the Joint Venture engine as one source, which leaves it at exactly two. It says CFM capacity "stays a watch item". It would want a third source if a durability finding hit the other engine. - Airbus says every engine joins the aircraft and stays on it "on proven maturity and durability, never on the calendar". - Neither airframer has given us a rate. - On the board, fps deliveries are 860 in 2045 and 940 in 2049, which is about 1,720 and 1,880 engines. - Our programmes: - Ducted: ready since 2036. By 2050 it has 13 years in service on NGSA and 10 on fps. - Embraer: counting since 2037. - GEnx upgrade: ready since 2033 and counting since 2042. - None can be cancelled. - Observed engine shares: - NB (CFM / P&W / RR): 76.0 / 24.0 / 0.0 to 2036; about 51-52 / 24 / 24 in 2037-39; 27.0 / 36.5 / 36.5 since 2040. - WB (GEnx): 44.8% since 2042. - Ali's round 3 reconciliation: 27.0% fits only without the Ducted's +10 pp. We claim no NB share for the Ducted. OUR POSITION (hold everything, S1, the only column) - ΔPV -69.69 $B, yield 56.44%. That is engine value -63.69, R&D -4.00 and strain -2.00. No new R&D is committed. - Engine lifecycle value in 2050 is 15.5 nominal $B, against 34.9 in the status quo. - Hold is unchanged from last round's S1. We booked -71 and came in at -69.69, $1.31B better. We guided low and delivered [CX-0654]. GRID (S1: rivals hold) - Hold everything: -69.69 (56.4%). This is the best plan. - Open Fan: -86.74 (45.8%), which is -17.05 against hold. - Open Fan + Lobby: -85.08 (46.8%), which is -15.39 against hold. - My check reconciles to the cent: - CFM's NB value over 2050-2056 at 1,079 engines a year is $9.05B PV. - Open Fan = the $8B bill + $9.05B lost. - Open Fan + Lobby = a $9B bill + $6.39B lost. CFM keeps 7.9% NB rather than 0%, and the grid charges no second strain. - A 2050 launch is ready in 2060. That is 23 years after NGSA's entry, 20 after fps's, and 4 years after the board stops counting NB. OBJECTIVE - NB share of at least 50% in 2040, 2045 and 2050: NOT MET. We are at 27.0%, 23 pp short, and no lever on this menu moves it. - Open Fan launched and ready by 2050: NOT MET, and no order can meet it. A 2050 launch is ready in 2060. BOARD GUIDANCE (non-binding; labelled as such; its veto comes after my decision) - Would approve: hold everything, all five fields at hold. This is not a Board item. - Would VETO: - Open Fan: launch alone: -17.05, which is $9.05B beyond its $8B bill and over the $15B allowance. It waits in the only column. It is not joint practice with Safran with no airframer path. Ali's RISE gates are not closed. - Open Fan + emissions lobbying: -15.39, which is $0.39B over the allowance. Putting $0.39B into premium won't save it. - Lobby alone: -1.00, with no Open Fan live. - Any item carrying a premium. - Any cancel. - Wants: - Ali's fleet durability report to the full Board, on field and turn-on, turn-off evidence, with the CFM56 as the yardstick. 'No flag' is not a clearance. - The data customers ask for, given through CFM governance jointly with Safran. - Capacity held at 1,079 NB engines a year with no new facility. - RISE kept as technology. - A booking at or below -69.69, with the off-grid WB exposure as the labelled low case. - A plain objective note. - A public statement that takes up Ali's caution on 'on time'.

Options to test.

  • Row A: hold everything, the reference row (Do Nothing). - S1: -69.69 (56.4%). It is the best plan in the only column, so it is 0.00 against Do Nothing in both the expected and the worst column, and the premium is $0. - It keeps the Ducted, Embraer and GEnx in service. - No new R&D, so the 70% payout and the A-range rating are untouched. - CFM parity: no gate is needed.
  • Row B: Open Fan, the end-game test. - S1: -86.74 (45.8%), which is -17.05 against hold: the $8B bill plus $9.05B of NB value lost for 2050-2056 (my check: $9.05B). - It would be ready in 2060, after both airframes and after the 2056 NB window, so it gains nothing on the board in any year. - H2 binds. The allowance would need $17.05B against a $15B cap. - It ticks 'launched' but not 'ready by 2050', so an objective premium buys nothing. - The case for it is entirely off the board: 'seeding' the airframe after these two. That is my installed-base bias talking [CX-0555], and I name it so we can test it rather than act on it.
  • Row C: Open Fan + Lobby, the cheapest Open Fan row. - S1: -85.08 (46.8%), which is -15.39 against hold: a $9B bill plus $6.39B lost (CFM keeps 7.9% NB). Lobby is worth +1.66 inside the row. - It needs $15.39B of RISE allowance, $0.39B over the cap. - Even if the gap were covered, it still waits in the only column, so it fails H2 and the Board's no-wait test. - I test it only to put the last dollar figure on RISE as a product in this game.
  • Excluded: Lobby alone. It is not on the grid: -1.00 for no board effect. Doctrine allows Lobby only with an Open Fan launched or live, and none is.
  • Other moves to test (unpriced; Ghai and Ali to check): (1) Fleet durability report to the full Board on the Ducted (NGSA since 2037, fps since 2040), the Embraer application and the GEnx upgrade. It covers time on wing, removals by part number, life-limited parts at full life and inspection findings, on field and turn-on, turn-off evidence, with the CFM56 in the same environment as the yardstick [CX-0006, CX-0009]. Every finding is a cross-functional call [CX-0012], and we fix the part [CX-0005]. (2) Customer data. Give both airframers the reliability, durability and life-limited-part data their safety reviews ask for, through CFM governance, jointly with Safran. Keep it private. No public answer to any airframer remark on engine sources [CX-0580]. (3) The joint capacity plan, held privately with Safran on 1,079 NB engines a year: - no new facility, because the risk is stranded capacity; - lean flex only if an airframer's agreed volume moves [CX-0540, CX-0944]; - safety-critical parts first, then OE before spares [CX-0529]; - no number out. (4) Fleet support and aftermarket for the Ducted, LEAP, Embraer and GEnx fleets, on standard terms, priced jointly with Safran and kept private. No price used to buy share [CX-0493, CX-0609]. (5) RISE funded as technology, with Ali's gates reported as the state of the technology. Its content goes into in-service engines only where turn-on, turn-off testing supports it [CX-0162]. (6) The CFM parity record for a hold.

Red lines.

  • Safety, quality, delivery and cost, always in that order [CX-0658]. Nothing is launched, and no in-service programme is carried on, while a safety or durability flag from Ali stands without a cross-functional answer on evidence [CX-0012]. Ramp and schedule never trade against safety [CX-0603].
  • My line: durability is not traded for fuel burn or for schedule [CX-0208]. In service, we fix the part rather than redesign or cancel the engine [CX-0005].
  • My line: a next engine needs at least a 20% fuel-burn improvement [CX-0217]. It binds RISE as the next generation, and no RISE gate shows 20% in engine test yet. The Ducted is never called the next generation [CX-0183].
  • H1: never refuse an airframer and never lock one out [CX-0587, CX-0185]. CFM support stands on both aircraft and on Embraer, including any data a customer's safety review asks for.
  • H2: never press an airframer into the Open Fan wait [CX-0205]. Both new narrowbodies have been in service for years before a 2060 Open Fan, so there is no launch. The one exception is the declared RISE allowance, and the cheapest row needs $15.39B against $15B, and waits.
  • H3: a Ducted only as a defence. It is in service. We make no new claim for it, and no NB share claim.
  • H5: never cancel RISE for cost while an airframer may want it, and no 'program dividend' [CX-0174, CX-0398]. The last round is not a reason to harvest it.
  • H6, through Ali's test: no date or durability claim without test or field evidence [CX-0009]. No Open Fan or RISE year, no fuel-burn result, and no time-on-wing claim for the Ducted that the field data hasn't earned.
  • H7: the Safran gate on every CFM narrowbody order (Ducted, Open Fan, Embraer, Lobby) [CX-0184, CX-0166]. An Open Fan with no airframer path needs a stated reason why Safran would agree, and I have none. Rate, capacity and price only jointly. GEnx is GE alone.
  • H8: no public blame and no comment on rivals, the Joint Venture included [CX-0625, CX-0580]. That covers any airframer remark about engine sources.
  • H9: the doctrine plus objective premium is at most $2.0B this round and $4.0B for the game. Running count: $0 of $2.0B and $0 of $4.0B. The one RISE allowance (up to $15B) is declared in full against the best non-RISE plan, and it is unspent.

Initial lean. This is a lean, not a decision. Your memos decide it. I lean to HOLD EVERYTHING: all five fields at hold. DUCTED, EMBRAER, GEnx: HOLD. That is the only option for each. All three are ready and in service. OPEN FAN: HOLD. - A 2050 launch is ready in 2060. That is after both airframes and after the board's NB window, so it gains nothing in any year and costs $17.05B. H2 binds. - I'll be straight about the pull. In the last round, the installed-base lens says launch for the next 30 years [CX-0555]. But no airframer has asked, the record gives Safran no reason to agree, and none of the RISE gates is closed in test. - The end of the game is not a reason to stretch the test. RISE stays whole as technology: no cancel, no program dividend [CX-0174, CX-0214]. It's really not for us to say when [CX-0205]. LOBBY: HOLD. It does nothing without a live Open Fan. EXPECTED COLUMN AND BOOKING (preliminary) - S1, weight 1.00, the only column. Off-grid moves are named and labelled, never weighted. - Book -71: hold less the larger 2050-ordered WB exposure (about $0.50B), rounded down. PREMIUM - $0 of $2.0B this round and $0 of $4.0B for the game. - The RISE allowance is $0 of $15B and ends the game unspent. OBJECTIVE. I say it plainly: - NB share is 27.0% from 2040 against 50%, and no lever moves it. - 'Open Fan launched and ready by 2050' can't be met by any order. - No objective premium is spent. SAFRAN GATE. There is no new CFM narrowbody order. Fleet support and customer data for the Ducted and Embraer on both aircraft stay within joint practice, with the aftermarket split equally [CX-0219]. No Safran position is asserted. GEnx is GE alone. OTHER MOVES - Ali's durability report to the full Board. - Customer data through CFM governance with Safran. - Capacity held at 1,079, with no new facility. - Fleet support on standard terms, priced jointly. - RISE gates reported as the state of the technology. PUBLIC LINE - Safety first, and what we know and what we don't [CX-0436]. - The Ducted's record is claimed only as far as the field data has earned it. - 'New engines for our customers' deliveries come first.' - No rival named, no remark on engine sources, and no blame. - No RISE year, and no price, rate or capacity number without our partner. It's that simple, ain't that hard.

We win it on safety, quality, delivery and cost, in that order [CX-0658]. Both airframers now judge engines on proven durability, and only field data moves that [CX-0009, CX-0564]. OFF-GRID LOW CASE (labelled, not weighted; Ghai's arithmetic, inference) - Trent 1000 upgrade ordered in 2050, counting from 2053: GEnx goes from 44.8% to about 40.0% WB, about $0.41B. - UltraFan WB after a 2050 Re-engine, counting from 2056: GEnx goes to about 35.2%, about $0.50B. - These two are exclusive. - A lone Re-engine: unsized, about $0.063B per WB point over 2055-61. - A 10% delivery shortfall: about $0.91B NB and $0.57B WB. - A Ducted durability finding across both aircraft: about $0.336B per NB point over 2050-56. A reserve is booked in the quarter we find the need. PRIVATE READING FOR THE CLOSE OF THE GAME - The rivals and both airframers hold. - CFM stays at 27.0% NB through 2056, 1,079 engines a year. - GEnx stays at 44.8% WB through 2061, unless a Trent 1000 upgrade or a Re-engine is ordered in 2050, which the record argues against. - The likeliest off-grid move is still a widebody step by the rival WB engine maker, and the booking covers it. - Upside, not booked: the Ducted's +10 pp, and any shift to a third source on fps. TO WATCH - Ali's first field data on the Ducted on both aircraft. - Any airframer finding on any engine source. - Any agreed airframer volume. - The RISE gates.

Expected ΔPV. −71.00 $B (GM valuation after the round: −69.69 $B)

Other moves.

  • Fleet durability report to the full Board: the Ducted on NGSA and fps, the Embraer application and the GEnx upgrade (private): Ali brings it on field data and turn-on, turn-off evidence, not analysis [CX-0009]. We say plainly that the brief still carries no field data: no time on wing, removals, life-limited-part status or inspection findings for any of the three. What he measures: (1) fleet-leader and fleet-average cycles to first shop visit, by aircraft (NGSA, fps, Embraer) and by environment, with hot and harsh kept separate [CX-0161]; (2) the yardstick: the CFM56 in the same environment [CX-0006], with the LEAP-1A's return to CFM56 parity as the floor (inference) [CX-0209]; (3) unscheduled removals and their causes, by part number; (4) life-limited parts at full life against certified life; (5) enhanced-inspection findings on safety-critical parts, in new-make shops and in MRO [CX-0010]; (6) every distress turned on in test and turned off by the fix, with root cause, and the fix accepted by the airframer and the regulator [CX-0003]. Embraer is measured on its own airframe. GEnx is measured against the baseline GEnx fleet [CX-0169]. Every finding is a cross-functional call, never one person's [CX-0012]. The Ducted flies both aircraft, so every Ducted finding touches both and comes to the Board at once. We fix the part; we don't redesign or cancel the engine [CX-0005]. Fleet support comes before any new spend, and Ghai books any reserve in the quarter we find the need. Ali raises no flag. The record shows that as 'nothing in front of him', not as a clearance.
  • Customer durability data given through CFM governance, jointly with Safran (private): Both airframers get the same data on the same engine: items (1) to (5) of the fleet report, plus the status of every open finding (root cause, turned on or not, turned off or not, the fix and its acceptance). It goes privately, through CFM governance, jointly with our partner. We hold back claims, never findings. There is no projected time-on-wing gain, kit date or fix benefit until it has been turned on and turned off in test. A finding is never held back from a customer's safety review. No commercial term goes with the data (Ghai's terms test): no time-on-wing guarantee, warranty extension, free kit or price offered to keep or win a source position. That includes the remark on a third source. We give no public answer to any airframer remark on engine sources [CX-0580].
  • Joint CFM capacity plan held with Safran at the board's volume, no new facility (private): Private planning basis: 1,079 NB engines a year (about 572 on NGSA and 507 on fps) and 152 GEnx. This is a planning basis, not a promise. It was built jointly with Safran through CFM governance. - No new facility. The stranded-capacity line (Ghai, inference) is any new facility or OE-line capital sized above 1,079 without an agreed airframer volume. 1,079 is 35.5% of the 3,040 a year we built for to 2036. Even the customer's own worst case, fps back on CFM alone, is about 2,452 with NGSA and fits that footprint. Whether today's supply base carries it is unproven: Ali has no supplier field data, so there is no 'yes' on test. - Lean flex only, and only once an airframer's volume is agreed [CX-0540, CX-0944]. Any ramp promise takes a quarter to a half off [CX-0590, CX-0592]. - Order of call: parts for safety-critical findings first, then OE before spares [CX-0529]. The ramp never trades against safety [CX-0603]. - Capex stays within 2-3% of revenue, aimed at MRO turnaround for the shop load. That load is LEAP, the Ducted's first and second shop visits on two aircraft, GE9X and the durability kits, behind the 9 suppliers at 15 sites [CX-0613]. - No capacity or rate number goes to an airframer or the public before that airframer's volume is agreed, and never without Safran [CX-0184].
  • Fleet support and aftermarket for the Ducted, LEAP, Embraer and GEnx fleets, on standard terms (private): On standard terms. Narrowbody prices are set jointly with Safran and kept private [CX-0184]. CFM-performed shop visits are split equally with our partner [CX-0219]. GEnx is GE alone. No price is used to buy share or a source slot [CX-0493, CX-0609]. Durability fixes go through reserves and existing service agreements as contracted. Service contracts are modelled conservatively. This passes Ghai's price/cost test on those conditions.
  • Keep RISE funded as technology, and report its gates as the state of the technology (public): RISE stays funded inside the R&D we protect first. There is no cancel for cost (H5) and no 'program dividend' [CX-0174, CX-0398]. Ali's report to the Board, unchanged since last round: - flight test: not shown on the record; - compact-core durability: dust testing has started, but no turn-off result is shown; - the fuel-burn gain: a design and physics case, not yet shown in engine test; - noise below today's LEAP: shown as a capability. RISE technology goes into in-service engines only where turn-on, turn-off testing supports it [CX-0162]. In public: no RISE date, no flight-test year, no fuel-burn number and no Open Fan entry year.
  • CFM parity record for a hold (private): There is no new CFM narrowbody order this round: Ducted, Open Fan, Embraer and Lobby are all at hold, so no Safran gate is triggered. Fleet support, customer data and the capacity plan for the Ducted and Embraer on both aircraft stay within joint practice, with the aftermarket split equally [CX-0219, CX-0184]. No Safran position is asserted. An Open Fan launch would have needed a stated reason why Safran would agree to a RISE product with no airframer path, and we have none. GEnx is GE alone.

Board guidance before the ExCo met

Priorities.

  • Hold both fields. As in 2045, nothing can come to the Board this round. The brief offers only GTF2 Solo: hold and Joint Venture with RR: hold. Its one plan, 'GTF2: hold', is worth +8.88 $B (108.1%) in S1, the only column. That is +10.88 of engine value less the $2.00B of R&D. - The cancel window has closed: GTF2 folded into the Joint Venture in 2035 and has been ready since 2036. - A withdraw is not legal: the Joint Venture formed in 2035, and a commitment can only be withdrawn before formation. - No airframe is waiting: NGSA has been in service since 2037 and fps since 2040, so launch if selected cannot be ordered and Miss a cycle does not apply. Both objectives are met on the board: credibility on NGSA and fps, and ΔPV +8.88 ≥ 0.
  • Close out the programme record. 2050 is the last round, so the Board wants a final whole-programme account against plan, as the GTF's NPV was once reviewed every year. - GTF2 and the Joint Venture deliver $10.88B of PV engine value on $2.00B of R&D, about 5.4x. - Since 2040 P&W ships 1,460 NB engines a year against 960 in the status quo, 52% more. - In 2050 lifecycle value is $14.7B against $9.7B (nominal), +$5.0B. - The board counts the NB market to 2056. The Board's 2035 approval of the standing commit realised +5.51 over hold.
  • Fleet first, with durability proven in service. This is the one live risk to the value above, and it is a product-safety matter for the Governance and Public Policy Committee, not a capital question. On the public record, Boeing counts the Joint Venture engine as one source. It says that if that engine stumbles, the fps is back on CFM alone and it would want a third source. Airbus says every engine joins the aircraft and stays on it only on proven maturity and durability. On the board the codes are locked at entry into service. In practice, P&W's 36.5% share lasts only as long as its time on wing does (inference).
  • Capital in the Board's order, now that the engine pays. The dividend comes first and grows with earnings. Debt goes back to, and stays at, pre-ASR levels. Buybacks are the fill-in. There is no new R&D, no write-off and no envelope stretch, and the stretch has never been used. Lifecycle value is not free cash flow and must not be presented as such.
  • Keep the Joint Venture aligned and the technology ours, and keep disclosure to the data. The gear, the core and the GTF2 technology stay P&W modules under P&W design authority. Any derivative, UltraFan NB content or cash call is a new appropriation, and none is on this grid. Put bad news first. Make no time-on-wing claim beyond the hours flown, give no airframer dates, and do not speak for Rolls-Royce.

Expects to see. A round of holds alone never reaches the Board's review. The Board therefore asks for the following in the sealed orders' rationale, in board_response and in the memos filed to the run folder. (1) The orders: GTF2 Solo hold and Joint Venture with RR hold. - The grid row: +8.88 (108.1%) in S1. - predictions S1 = 1.00, expected ΔPV +8.88 and premium 0, with the cumulative premium ledger at $0.26B of $1B. (2) From Calio: - a plain statement that no Board item is legal, and why: the cancel window closed in 2035, a withdraw is not legal after formation, and no airframe is waiting to enter service; - a final whole-programme account against plan for 2030, 2035, 2045 and 2050: expected values against the booked outcome, the 5.4x return, and payback in 2040 nominal and 2041 discounted on lifecycle value; - his answer to Boeing's public 'one source, back on CFM alone' line, and confirmation that no concession or free upgrade is offered in reply. (3) From Mitchill: - no new R&D, no write-off, envelope not applicable, and no Joint Venture cash call beyond GTF2's $2B; - the dividend covered and growing, debt at or on its pre-ASR path, and buybacks as the fill-in; - the analyst baseline he relies on runs only to 2030E (net debt 0.76-0.94x EBITDA, dividends $5.0-5.6B and buybacks $4.0-5.0B in 2030E), so he should say where his numbers rest on the board alone; - confirmation that lifecycle value ($14.7B against $9.7B in 2050, nominal) is not presented as cash. (4) From Eddy: - readiness: ready in 2036, against NGSA's 2037 EIS and fps's 2040 EIS, which passes; - the in-service record of the Joint Venture engine: fleet hours by airframe and environment against the ~1M-hour benchmark, removals and time on wing, fix campaigns, AOG counts and the pacing-parts count; - Hot Section kit insertion progress on the GTF fleet; - the result of the records look-back on parts made on the capacity added for the 2040 step from 990 to 1,460 engines a year, ordered in 2045; - what the quarterly Committee reports since 2045 have shown; - if he has no fleet data, a plain 'I don't have it', not a claim. (5) Other moves, read against the red lines: standard commercial terms, no widebody, no core or gear technology to the Joint Venture, and no airframer dates or rates. Anything missing the Board will compute from the brief and note.

Would approve.

  • GTF2 Solo: hold and Joint Venture with RR: hold. These are not Board items and are never vetoed. Hold/hold is the brief's only plan and therefore its best: +8.88 $B (108.1%) in S1. It keeps the Joint Venture engine fitted on fps and NGSA (code 7, 36.5% NB share, 1,460 engines a year) and keeps both objectives met with $0 of PV given up.
  • Other moves, which the Board recommends on rather than votes: - Hot Section kit insertion, charged and on standard commercial terms. - The weekly pacing-parts review, ring-fencing the 1,460-a-year rate from GTF fleet AOG recovery. - The records look-back on the 2040 capacity step, with new capacity qualified before it ships. - The standing durability report: weekly to ExCo, quarterly to the Governance and Public Policy Committee, and at once on any escape. - Fleet data shared with Airbus and Boeing, with no claim beyond the hours flown. - Joint Venture governance that keeps the gear, core and GTF2 technology as P&W modules under P&W design authority. - The capital-order note to Finance (dividend, debt, buybacks).

Would veto.

  • Nothing this round. Both fields offer only hold. The Board never vetoes a hold, and other moves and the public statement are recommended on, not voted.
  • If a revised brief priced a Board item (none is expected), the Board's standing tests would apply. Acceptable alternative in every case: hold. - Premature exit: a cancel or withdraw must beat hold's +8.88 at the weights and must trail hold in no plausible column. - Committed airframe: any launch or launch if selected needs a live airframe that is not yet in service and has selected P&W. None exists. - Dividend and envelope, and governance: any P&W cash beyond GTF2's $2B (a Joint Venture cash call, UltraFan NB content or a merged derivative) needs Mitchill's gate, Finance review, its own return case against hold and a buyback, and the dividend kept whole. - Joint Venture: any term that moves gear or core technology into the Joint Venture fails the test. - Durability first: any configuration change to the in-service engine without its own durability programme fails Eddy's ground 1.

Recommendations.

  • Submit hold/hold and put the final record in the rationale, because this round does not come to review. Give the whole-programme account against plan, as the GTF's NPV was once reviewed every year: - The 2030 launch if selected was expected at +0.23 (Calio) and -1.72 (Mitchill), and booked 0.00. - The 2035 commit added +5.51 over hold's +3.37, in the column both weighted lowest. - The 2045 and 2050 outcome is +8.88: $10.88B of PV engine value on $2.00B of R&D, about 5.4x, well above a buyback at the 10% grid rate. Also report premium 0 and the ledger at $0.26B of $1B. Record the lesson for the file: the order was right because it was weakly dominant, not because Rolls-Royce was read well.
  • Fleet first, and durability proven in service. Boeing says in public that the Joint Venture engine is one source, that the fps falls back to CFM alone if it stumbles, and that any durability finding is a live problem. The Governance and Public Policy Committee should therefore receive, and the ExCo should state in the rationale: - fleet hours by airframe and environment against the ~1M-hour benchmark; - removals and time on wing against plan, and fix campaigns; - AOG counts on both fleets, and the pacing-parts count; - Hot Section kit insertion progress; - the outcome of the records look-back on the 2040 capacity step. Our last escape came from capacity added for a ramp, and the powder-metal cause was found only after a records review. AOG recovery keeps first call on parts. Fix forward with upgrades, not claims. If Eddy has no data, he should say so.
  • Capital in the Board's order. With no new R&D on this grid, Mitchill should show four things: - the dividend covered and growing with earnings; - debt at, or back to, pre-ASR levels; - buybacks as the fill-in; - any other use of cash coming through Finance with a return case against a buyback. The analyst baseline stops at 2030E, so he should say where his numbers rest on the board alone. Lifecycle value ($14.7B against $9.7B nominal in 2050) is engine price x 1.6, not free cash flow; present it that way. The Board's one-round stretch stays unused.
  • Joint Venture governance. Keep both partners on the one engine; a Joint Venture holds only while both are on the same new engine. - The gear, core and GTF2 technology stay P&W modules under P&W design authority, and design teams mirror module ownership. - Any merged derivative, any UltraFan NB content, any Joint Venture top-up and any P&W cash beyond GTF2's $2B is a new capital appropriation. It goes through Mitchill's gate and the Finance Committee to the Board, with its own return case and its own durability programme. None is on this grid. - Do not answer Boeing's 'third source' remark with a concession, discount or free upgrade. Terms stay standard.
  • Public statement (Disclosure). Keep the 2045 structure: bad news first, durability reported as fleet data, and no time-on-wing claim beyond the hours flown. - The Board suggests restating 'We have learned our lesson from the prior iterations of the GTF' as a commitment to be measured by the fleet data, not a finding. Eddy flagged it as a claim in 2045. This is a recommendation, not a veto ground. - Name no airframer date or rate, and do not speak for Rolls-Royce. - Keep standard terms and make no widebody move: P&W holds 0% of widebody engines on the board. - Do not claim the credibility objective; let the fleet record carry it.
  • Report to the Audit Committee. Carry the Joint Venture engine's in-service durability, the capacity added for the 1,460-a-year rate and the concentration of P&W's NB share on one engine into the annual top enterprise risks reported to the Audit Committee and the full Board. That is where the remaining value at stake, to 2056 on the board, now sits.

Chris Calio frames the round

Question. Control what you can control. This is the last round, and once again the board gives us nothing to order. Both fields offer only hold. The grid has one row and one column: 'GTF2: hold' at +8.88 $B (108.1%) in S1, rivals hold. The order is already decided. What we still control is whether we keep what it earned, and whether we close the book honestly. I put five questions to you. (1) Fleet first. Is the Joint Venture engine (GTF2, by the 2035 fold) earning its durability record on NGSA and fps? Is it doing so at 1,460 engines a year without taking a part or an engineer from GTF fleet recovery [PX-0080][PX-0073]? - Boeing has said in public that it counts our engine as one source. If that engine stumbles, the fps is back on CFM alone and Boeing would want a third source. - On the board the codes are locked at entry into service. In practice our 36.5% lasts only as long as our time on wing does (inference). - How do we answer that line with the product and the data, not with price [PX-0055][P-0768]? (2) Close-out. How did the whole programme come out against the plans we wrote in 2030, 2035 and 2045, and today? I want expected against booked, the return, the payback and what we got wrong, as the Board once reviewed the GTF's NPV every year [P-1191]. (3) Capital order. Does the cash the engine earns go back in our order: the dividend first, then debt back to and held at pre-ASR levels, then buybacks as the fill-in [PX-0081][P-0686][P-0669]? Do we keep lifecycle value from being read as cash? (4) The Joint Venture. Does it stay one engine, with the gear, the core and the GTF2 technology kept as P&W modules under P&W design authority [P-1233]? (5) Disclosure and risk. Do we disclose data, not claims? Does the remaining risk sit where the Board can see it? That risk is one engine carrying all of our new narrowbody share, and the place is the Governance and Public Policy Committee and the Audit Committee's top enterprise risks [PG-0050][PG-0034]. My usual questions, read backwards one last time: - The demand was visible, and two airframers put us on the record [PX-0109]. - Was durability mature at entry into service [PX-0073]? - Was it a responsible bet with a responsible payback [PX-0010]? - Is the dividend safe [PX-0081]?

Situation. BAD NEWS FIRST - We still have no fleet data on this board. The bulletin and the brief carry none of the following, for either the Joint Venture engine or the GTF fleet: - fleet hours, removals or time on wing; - fix campaigns; - AOG counts or the pacing-parts count; - Hot Section kit insertion progress. In 2045 Shane said plainly "I don't have it". His parts passes in 2030, 2035 and 2045 rested on the board, not on data. Until we have numbers, 'durability proven in service' is a claim. - In 2045 we ordered a records look-back on the capacity added for the 2040 step (990 to 1,460 engines a year, +47.5% in one year). Its result is not on the board. Our last escape came from capacity added for a ramp [P-1040][P-1062], and the powder-metal cause was found only after a records review [PX-0039]. - In 2045 we ordered a standing durability report (weekly to ExCo, quarterly to the Governance and Public Policy Committee) as a private other move. What it has shown is not on the board. - Both customers have put our engine on durability probation in public: - Boeing counts the Joint Venture engine as one source. If it stumbles, the fps is back on CFM alone, any durability finding is a live problem, and Boeing would then want a third source. - Airbus says every engine joins the aircraft and stays on it only on proven maturity and durability. - Our 2045 statement kept "We have learned our lesson from the prior iterations of the GTF". Shane flagged it as a claim. The Board now asks us to restate it as a commitment measured by fleet data. - Concentration. All of P&W's new narrowbody share (36.5%) rides on one engine, and P&W holds 0% of the widebody. PUBLIC RECORD (2050 bulletin) - Round 3 (2045) was adjudicated with no public events. No player launched anything new. - NGSA (Airbus) has been in service since 2037 and fps (Boeing, 10-year ramp-up) since 2040. Both carry code 7 and are fitted CFM + PW + RR. - The Joint Venture formed in 2035. GTF2 and UltraFan NB (solo) both folded in, and the engine has been ready since 2036. - CFM: - ducted engine ready since 2036; Embraer partnership counts from 2037; GEnx upgrade since 2033; - no new programmes; - RISE funded as technology, with no date. - Rolls-Royce: fleet first on the Joint Venture engine, nothing to launch, standard terms. - Boeing runs in-service durability reviews of both fps engine sources at its safety committee. - Observed NB engine shares (CFM / P&W / RR): - 76 / 24 / 0 through 2036; - about 51 / 24 / 24 in 2037-39; - 27.0 / 36.5 / 36.5 since 2040. P&W's widebody share is 0%. OUR POSITION (private brief) - ΔPV +8.88 $B: engine value +10.88 less R&D 2.00 (undiscounted, shown in 2035). Yield 108.07% on an enterprise value of $110B. - Since 2040 we ship 1,460 NB engines a year against 960 in the status quo (+500, +52%). - 2050 lifecycle value is $14.7B against $9.7B nominal (+$5.0B). The board counts the NB market to 2056. - My arithmetic on the brief's rounded year table, for Neil to confirm (scratch in /tmp/wargame-pratt_whitney/dash-2050-obj/work/r4_check.py): - discounted deltas for 2037-56 sum to about +10.82 (the brief says +10.88); - about +8.4 of that is in deliveries through 2050 and about +2.4 in 2051-56; - payback on lifecycle value: 2040 nominal (cumulative +4.4); 2041 discounted (+2.15 against 2.00); - return about 5.4x. - No R&D or write-off since 2035. The fold write-off was $0. LEGAL ORDERS AND WHY (rules.md) - GTF2 Solo: hold only. - The cancel window closed in 2035. An engine can be cancelled only before it is ready, and this one has been ready since 2036. - launch and launch if selected need a live airframe not yet in service, and none exists. - Joint Venture with RR: hold only. Withdraw is legal only before formation, and the Joint Venture formed in 2035. - So no Board item exists. A round of holds never reaches the Board's review, which is why the record goes in our sealed rationale. - Miss a cycle does not apply: both cycles are taken. OBJECTIVE STATUS (brief §2) - Restore credibility: MET. The Joint Venture engine is in service on NGSA and fps. - Capitalise on the GTF: MET, ΔPV +8.88 ≥ 0. - PV given up this round: $0. - Credibility holds only while the time-on-wing record holds. We do not claim it in public. BOARD GUIDANCE (2050) - Nothing to approve, and the would-veto list is empty. - It wants: - hold/hold; - a final whole-programme account; - fleet data to the Governance and Public Policy Committee; - capital in its order; - Joint Venture governance that keeps our modules ours; - our answer to Boeing's 'one source' line, with no concession; - 'learned our lesson' restated as a commitment; - the remaining risk carried into the Audit Committee's top enterprise risks. - Risk appetite 3.5. Its balance-sheet stance may ease toward 3 as debt reaches pre-ASR levels.

Options to test.

  • A. GTF2 Solo: hold, Joint Venture with RR: hold (row 'GTF2: hold'). This is the only plan on the grid. - S1: +8.88 (108.1%). The worst column and the best column are both S1. - Expected PV +8.88 at S1 = 1.00, and the booked number is +8.88: all of it is on the public record. - No Board item. Premium $0, and the ledger stays at $0.26B of the $1B cap. - This is my lean. Test it for the record only: Neil's four grounds and Shane's two grounds on the exact orders.
  • Struck as not legal, listed so the record shows why: - GTF2 Solo: cancel: the engine has been ready since 2036, and the window closed in 2035; - Joint Venture with RR: withdraw: illegal after the 2035 formation; - GTF2 Solo: launch or launch if selected: no live airframe is waiting to enter service; - Joint Venture with RR: commit: the Joint Venture has already formed. The Board's standing tests (Premature exit, Committed airframe) have nothing to bite on.
  • Other moves to test against the red lines and the vetoes: (i) Hot Section kit insertion continues, charged, on standard terms (public) [PX-0088][PX-0106][PX-0100]. (ii) Fleet ring-fence and weekly pacing-parts review [PX-0131] (private). - AOG recovery keeps first call on parts. - New capacity is qualified before it ships. - The 2040 capacity look-back result is reported, or reported as not yet available. (iii) Standing durability report (private): weekly to ExCo, quarterly to the Governance and Public Policy Committee, and at once on any escape [PG-0050]. (iv) NEW (private). Carry three items into the annual top enterprise risks reported to the Audit Committee and the full Board [PG-0034]: - the Joint Venture engine's in-service durability; - the 2040 capacity step; - the concentration of P&W's NB share on one engine. (v) Fleet data shared with Airbus and Boeing as it is flown, with no claim beyond the hours flown and on standard terms. NEW: publish the fact of the cadence, not the data, as our answer to the 'one source' line. Neil to test it under ground 4, Shane under ground 1. (vi) Joint Venture governance (public). One engine and one support chain. The gear, the core and the GTF2 technology stay P&W modules under P&W design authority [P-1233][P-1744][P-1240][P-2004][P-1875]. (vii) Capital-order note to Finance (private): dividend, then debt, then buybacks. Lifecycle value is not cash. (viii) Whole-programme close-out to the Board (private), in the sealed rationale and board_response. Red lines.

  • Safety and durability first [PX-0035][PX-0073]. - In-service durability on NGSA and fps is a fleet-safety matter, not a capital question. - Shane's two technical grounds bind me. - No time-on-wing claim beyond the hours flown, and no 'proven' before the fleet data shows it. The benchmark is about 1M fleet hours [P-0847], and it surfaces problems; it does not prove durability.
  • The fleet beats a new engine [PX-0080]. - Neither the 1,460-a-year rate nor any Joint Venture engineering may draw castings, forgings, powder-metal disks or engineers from GTF fleet AOG recovery or from kit insertion. - New capacity is qualified before it ships. - If the fleet is short, Shane's ground 2 binds and the rate waits. - Contain first on any escape.
  • Joint Venture: share risk and investment, never our core technology [P-1233]. - The gear, the core and the GTF2 technology stay P&W modules under P&W design authority. - P&W keeps the gear team and the gear data [P-2004]. - One engine [P-1875]. - No UltraFan NB content and no merged derivative without a new appropriation and its own durability programme.
  • Capital order: dividend first [PX-0081], then debt back to and held at pre-ASR levels [P-0686], then buybacks [P-0669]. - The dividend never funds an engine. - Any P&W cash beyond GTF2's $2B goes through Neil's gate and the Finance Committee to the Board, with a return case against hold and a buyback. - Lifecycle value is never presented as cash or free cash flow.
  • Value, not share [PX-0055][PX-0100]. - Standard commercial terms, and the kit is charged. - No concession, discount, free upgrade or discounted spares to either airframer, including in answer to Boeing's 'one source' or 'third source' remarks. - A rival's price never moves the answer.
  • We never speak for an airframer's dates, rates or sourcing decisions [PX-0062], and never for Rolls-Royce. Whether Boeing wants a third source is Boeing's to say.
  • No widebody engine move [PX-0027].

The acceptable alternative in every case is hold.
  • Red lines are never traded for PV. Premiums are declared in $B inside the team's $1B cap. This round: $0, and the ledger stays at $0.26B.

Initial lean. LEAN: GTF2 Solo: hold, Joint Venture with RR: hold. This is the brief's only plan: +8.88 $B (108.1%) in S1. - predictions S1 = 1.00, which is also the expected column; - expected ΔPV +8.88; - premium 0, with the ledger at $0.26B of the $1B cap. Both objectives are met, with $0 of PV given up. NO BOARD ITEM, AND WHY (rationale) - The cancel window closed in 2035. - A withdraw is illegal after the 2035 formation. - No airframe is waiting to enter service. WHAT I WILL PUT ON THE RECORD - The close-out for 2030, 2035, 2045 and 2050: expected against booked, the 5.4x return, and payback in 2040 nominal and 2041 discounted on lifecycle value, on Neil's numbers. - What I own: - the upside came in the column we weighted lowest, so the order was right because it was weakly dominant, not because we read Rolls-Royce well; - the 2030 S5 figure of +22.00 was never the plan; - the pre-EIS Committee reporting cannot be evidenced; - we still have no fleet data on the board. BIAS CHECK - Optimism on dates: I state none. - Architecture loyalty: the test now is time on wing, not the gear. - Value capture: the kit stays charged, and we answer Boeing with no concession. OTHER MOVES - Public: (i) kit, charged; (vi) Joint Venture governance; and the fact of the fleet-data cadence, if Neil and Shane pass it. - Private: (ii) ring-fence and look-back; (iii) Committee report; (iv) top enterprise risks to the Audit Committee; (vii) capital note; (viii) close-out. PROPOSED DISCLOSURE (public; it carries no figures, so Neil's ranges are not needed): "Bad news first. Our new engine's durability record on the new single-aisle aircraft is still being earned, one flight hour at a time. Our dates have slipped before, and the GTF fleet taught us what it costs to say more than the data shows. We said we had learned our lesson from the prior iterations of the GTF. Take that as a commitment, and measure us on the fleet data, not on this statement. An engine joins an aircraft and stays on it on proven durability. That is the test our customers have set, and we accept it. We answer it with the engine and with the data, not with price. Time on wing, removals and fixes are shared with both airframers as the fleet flies, and we claim nothing beyond the hours flown. Our terms stay standard: no discounts, no concessions, no free upgrades. Which engines go on an aircraft is our customers' decision, and theirs to announce. What is on the record: the Joint Venture with Rolls-Royce formed in 2035. Its engine is built on GTF2, has been ready since 2036, and is on both new single-aisle aircraft alongside the other engine makers. The Joint Venture shares risk and investment, not technology. The gear, the core and the GTF2 technology stay Pratt & Whitney modules, under our design authority. It is one engine, and any change to its configuration would have to earn its own durability record first. The fleet still comes first. We keep inserting the Hot Section durability kit across the GTF fleet, on standard commercial terms. We review the pacing parts every week. Our rule is that new-engine production may not take parts or engineers from fleet recovery, and new capacity is qualified before it ships a part. If we find a problem, you will hear it from us first, with the plan to contain and fix it. We control what we can control. On capital, our order of priority does not change: the dividend first, then debt back to pre-ASR levels, then buybacks. There is no new engine programme from us this year. Any further investment would come to our Board on its own return case. We do not speak for our airframer customers' plans, dates, rates or sourcing, or for Rolls-Royce." If Shane cannot evidence a fleet-data point, the statement says less, not more.

I asked for a date on it in 2045, and the order went out without one. I can't tell you what the quarterly Committee report showed. That's on us. What is on the record: the engine was ready in 2036, a year ahead of NGSA and four ahead of fps. Both airframers fitted it on their own durability test. My parts passes in 2030, 2035, 2045 and today rest on the board, not on data. Boeing's line is fair. The answer is the data Boeing's safety committee already reviews: reliability, durability and LLP status split by environment, removals against plan, and every fix campaign with a date to finish it. Not price. Publishing that we share the data passes ground 1, if we write it as our rule and attach no claim. Restating 'learned our lesson' as a commitment measured by fleet data clears my flag. Chris Calio decides

Orders. Do Nothing

Rationale. CONTROL WHAT YOU CAN CONTROL. Orders: GTF2 Solo: hold, Joint Venture with RR: hold. These are the brief's only legal values (§3). The grid row 'GTF2: hold' is +8.88 $B (108.1%) in S1, its only column: engine value +10.88 less R&D 2.00. predictions S1 = 1.00, expected ΔPV +8.88, premium 0, and the cumulative ledger stays at $0.26B of the $1B cap. NO BOARD ITEM IS LEGAL, AND WHY - The cancel window closed in 2035. GTF2 folded into the Joint Venture that year, the engine has been ready since 2036, and an engine can be cancelled only before it is ready. - A withdraw is not legal: the Joint Venture formed in 2035, and a withdraw is legal only before formation. - launch and launch if selected cannot be ordered: no airframe is waiting to enter service (NGSA since 2037, fps since 2040). - So the Board's standing tests (Premature exit, Committed airframe) have nothing to bite on, and Miss a cycle does not apply: both cycles were taken. DECISION BY THE TEAM RULE - I start from Eddy's proposal, hold/hold. Mitchill recommends the same. - Binding vetoes: none stands. Mitchill invokes none of his four grounds: no new cash; the engine is fitted on both airframes, so it is not unselected; there is no terms order; the booked +8.88 is all on the public record. Eddy invokes neither technical ground: the engine was ready in 2036, against EIS dates of 2037 and 2040, and the brief shows no live fleet problem. - Conditional vetoes, all respected in the moves and the statement: - Mitchill ground 4: no 'proven', no time-on-wing claim, no published fleet figure, no objective claim, no lifecycle value as cash, no derivative value. - Mitchill ground 3: the kit is charged and the answer to Boeing carries no concession. - Eddy ground 1: no configuration change without its own durability programme. - Eddy ground 2: the ring-fence; the rate waits if the fleet is short. - Safety and durability constraint first [PX-0035][PX-0073]. On this board it binds through the other moves, not the orders. The fleet beats a new engine [PX-0080]. - Overrides: none. ANSWER TO BOEING'S 'ONE SOURCE' LINE - It is fair, and it is the right test. Eddy calls it common-mode risk: one engine, one configuration, one LLP set and one casting, forging and powder-metal supply serve both airframes. One finding touches both fleets at once. - We answer with product and data, not price [PX-0055][P-0768][PX-0100]: - a public rule that fleet data goes to both airframers as flown; - a private data pack that matches what Boeing's safety committee reviews, split by environment with hot-and-harsh shown separately. - No concession, discount, free upgrade, discounted spares or time-on-wing guarantee. Mitchill confirms that ground 3 passes. - Whether Boeing wants a third source is Boeing's to say [PX-0062]. WHOLE-PROGRAMME CLOSE-OUT AGAINST PLAN [P-1191] (Mitchill's numbers, which I trust over my own) - 2030: launch if selected fired on code 7. Expected +0.23 (mine) and -1.72 (his); booked 0.00. Against Do Nothing it was worth +16.20 (mine) and +13.69 (his). The +22.00 S5 column assumed no Rolls-Royce NB engine and was never the plan. - 2035 grid: - hold: +3.37 / -17.95 / -8.44 / +3.37; - hold + commit: +3.37 / -17.95 / -8.44 / +8.88. - Expected: +0.39 (mine) and +0.07 (his). Booked: +3.37, with the commit at $0. The outcome was S4, +8.88, so the commit realised +5.51 over hold. The cancel he advised against would have written off $1.67B to save $0.33B, against rows of -32.79 to -11.47. - 2045 and 2050: expected = booked = +8.88. That is +8.81 over his 2035 expected and +10.60 over his 2030 expected. - Return: $10.88B of PV engine value on $2.00B of R&D, 5.44x on the board's basis. It beats a buyback at about $0 NPV at the 10% grid rate. - It is a value multiple gross of production cost, not a cash return. - Against the PV of the phased R&D it is about 10x; we do not book that figure. - Payback on lifecycle value: 2040 nominal (cumulative +4.4 against 2.00) and 2041 discounted (+2.15). Cash payback is later and not on the board. - Cost: GTF2 cost its plan, $2.00B, about $0.33B a year in 2030-35 (5.6% of the envelope, on his phasing). The fold write-off was $0. There has been no R&D or write-off since 2035, no Joint Venture cash beyond $2B, and no use of the stretch. - Value split, on my arithmetic confirmed by Mitchill: about +8.43 from deliveries through 2050 and +2.39 from 2051-56 (total +10.82 against the brief's +10.88; the gap is rounding). WHAT I OWN (1) The upside came in the column we weighted lowest: S4 at 0.10 (mine) and 0.08 (his). In a sealed round, Rolls-Royce's conditional commit was as free for it as ours was for us. The order was right because it was weakly dominant (0 / 0 / 0 / +5.51), not because we read Rolls-Royce well. (2) The 2030 S5 figure of +22.00 was never the plan. (3) The Board's 2035 statement tightening was not taken up. The 2036 date held on the board, which is counter-evidence to my date optimism, not a licence; I state no date this year. (4) The pre-EIS reporting to the Governance and Public Policy Committee cannot be evidenced. (5) The 2045 look-back went out undated, against Eddy's advice. It is dated now: the Committee's next quarterly meeting, and at once on any finding. (6) We still have no fleet data on the board. Eddy says plainly "I don't have it" on hours, removals, campaigns, AOG, pacing parts and kit insertion. His parts passes in every round rested on the board. So we disclose rules and commitments, not claims, and log the gap as a control gap for the Audit Committee. CAPITAL: dividend, then debt, then buybacks. - The analyst context runs to 2030E only: the dividend is covered 2.3-2.4x and net debt is 0.76-0.94x EBITDA. Past 2030 the line rests on the board alone, so it is written as an order of priority, not as a 2050 status. - The $14.7B against $9.7B (2050, nominal) is lifecycle value at engine price x 1.6, not free cash flow. BIAS CHECK - Optimism on dates: none stated. The look-back date is a reporting date. - Architecture loyalty: the test now is time on wing, not the gear. - Value capture: the kit stays charged, and Boeing gets no concession. DOCTRINE, NOT MY RECORD My record has no Joint Venture evidence (Low). The following are company doctrine and Eddy's seat inference: - the Joint Venture governance [P-1233][P-1744][P-1240][P-2004]; - the Committee cadence; - the Audit Committee entries. Applying 'miss a cycle' [PX-0071] and demand visibility [PX-0109] to engines was inference throughout. READ BACKWARDS, MY QUESTIONS - Was the demand visible? Yes: two airframers put us on the record. - Was durability mature at EIS? The board says ready. The data has not shown it yet, and I won't claim it. - Was it a responsible bet with a responsible payback [PX-0010]? On the board, yes: 5.4x, and payback in 2040-41 on lifecycle value. - Is the dividend safe [PX-0081]? Nothing on this board touches it; past 2030 that rests on the board alone.

Weighing the CFO. Weighted heavily. His cash numbers carry the close-out, and I trust them over my own dates. Taken up in full: - his ground-by-ground pass on both holds; - the booked +8.88, all of it on the record; - no new money and no fold write-off; - the reconciliation (+10.82 against +10.88, rounding); - the close-out: 5.44x, payback 2040 nominal and 2041 discounted, +5.51 realised by the commit, and against Do Nothing in 2030 +13.69 at his weights; - the value-at-stake split (+8.43 / +2.39) and what the board does not count; - the cash read of lifecycle value: about $3.1B price and $1.9B aftermarket, $0 of FCF, likely negative engine margin first; - his statement that past 2030 the capital line rests on the board alone. His two conditional binding vetoes (ground 4 on claims and figures, ground 3 on terms) are respected as drafted. His non-binding advice: - Taken: 'will' or rule wording for the data cadence, written as our rule; dropping 'first' from 'hear it from us first'; saying less about Rolls-Royce's side, so 'built on GTF2' is cut from the statement; the Board's ease toward 3 waits until debt is shown held. - Kept, as my call: 'the Joint Venture shares risk and investment, not technology' in the governance move. It is our red line [P-1233], not a statement for Rolls-Royce. We share the S4 lesson. No disagreement to record.

Weighing the operating head. Weighted on doctrine, with care, and valued most for its candour. Eddy's own record is one event, the June 2023 investor day before the recall, so his Joint Venture, capacity, Committee and data-sharing views are seat doctrine and inference. He says so. Adopted: - His proposal, hold/hold. His readiness check passes: ready 2036, a 1-year margin on NGSA and 4 years on fps. He invokes neither ground. - His plain 'I don't have it' on every fleet figure. It sets the statement: rules and commitments, no numbers. - His caveat that the board's 'ready' is a schedule rule. Severe-environment validation and full-life LLPs at each EIS are not evidenced, and I say so to the Board. - His common-mode read of Boeing's line, and his six-item data pack (a)-(f), split by environment. - Dating the look-back to the Committee's next quarterly meeting. He asked for this in 2045 and we did not do it; that is owned. - Taking the geared-IP clause out of public text. - Writing the data cadence as a rule. - 'with containment and a dated recovery' in place of 'first'. - Naming the missing fleet data as a control gap, and hot-and-harsh operation, in the Audit Committee entry. His restatement test passes: 'learned our lesson' now reads as a commitment measured by fleet data, which clears his 2045 flag. His standing conditional vetoes (ground 1 on configuration change and claims; ground 2 on the rate drawing from the fleet) are written into the other moves.

The gear, the core and the GTF2 technology stay P&W modules under P&W design authority, and design teams mirror module ownership. - Any derivative, UltraFan NB content, top-up or cash beyond $2B is a new appropriation through Mitchill's gate and Finance to the Board, with its own return case and durability programme. Objective. Both parts of the objective are met on the board (brief §2), and $0 of PV is given up this round. - Restore credibility: a new P&W engine is in service on a new airframe by 2050. The Joint Venture engine, GTF2 by the 2035 fold, has been on NGSA since 2037 and on fps since 2040, under code 7. - Capitalise on the GTF: ΔPV +8.88 $B, which is ≥ 0, a 5.4x value return on $2.00B of R&D. Off the board, credibility lasts only as long as the time-on-wing record does, and we have no fleet data on the record. We do not claim the objective in public; the fleet data has to carry it.

Predictions. S1 = 1.00 (rivals hold). It is the only column on the 2050 grid and the expected column. Mitchill also has S1 = 1.00.

Expected ΔPV. +8.88 $B (GM valuation after the round: +8.88 $B)

Other moves.

  • GTF Hot Section durability kit insertion continues across the fleet, charged (public): Insertion continues across the GTF fleet on standard commercial terms. The kit is charged, not given away, and there are no discounted spares and no concessions [PX-0088][PX-0106][PX-0100]. The fleet comes first [PX-0080], and AOG recovery keeps first call on parts. This respects Mitchill's conditional ground-3 veto. We publish no insertion percentage, because Eddy has no 2050 figure. No effect on the game board.
  • Joint Venture governance: one engine, P&W modules, P&W design authority (public): The Joint Venture formed in 2035 and shares risk and investment, not technology [P-1233]. The gear, the core and the GTF2 technology stay Pratt & Whitney modules under P&W design authority [P-1744], and design teams mirror module ownership [P-1240]. It is one engine and one support chain [P-1875]. Any configuration change to the in-service engine is not on this board, whether UltraFan NB content or a merged derivative. It would be a new capital appropriation through Mitchill's gate and the Finance Committee to the Board, with its own return case against hold and a buyback and its own durability programme under Eddy's ground 1. We do not speak for Rolls-Royce. Change from 2045, on Eddy's advice: the geared-IP clause [P-2004] is taken out of public text and kept in the private governance move below.
  • Fleet-data rule toward Airbus and Boeing (the fact of the rule only) (public): This is our answer to the 'one source' line, given with product and data and not with price [PX-0055][P-0768]. We publish the rule, not the data and not what the data shows. Time-on-wing, removal and fix-campaign data on the Joint Venture engine go to both airframers as the fleet flies, with no claim beyond the hours flown. It is written as a rule because the board cannot evidence that the 2045 cadence ran (Eddy; Mitchill's advice). It carries no figures and no characterisation such as 'on plan' or 'mature'. Standard commercial terms, with no concession, free upgrade, discounted spares or time-on-wing guarantee (Mitchill ground 3). It passes Eddy's ground 1 and Mitchill's ground 4. Whether Boeing wants a third source is Boeing's to say [PX-0062].
  • Data pack to both airframers' in-service reviews (private): Following Eddy, the private content under the public rule: (a) reliability, durability and LLP status, the three items Boeing's safety committee reviews; (b) hours and removals split by environment, with hot-and-harsh operation shown separately, because the fleet average hid the GTF's shortfall [PX-0122]; (c) shop-visit rate and time on wing against plan; (d) every fix campaign, with its containment and a dated completion [PX-0121]; (e) AOG and pacing-parts counts; (f) the 2040 capacity look-back result. Shared on standard terms with nothing attached. No figure from it is published by P&W.
  • Fleet ring-fence, weekly pacing-parts review and a DATED records look-back on the 2040 capacity step (private): The weekly pacing-parts review [PX-0131] ring-fences the 1,460-a-year rate. Neither the Joint Venture rate nor any Joint Venture engineering may take castings, forgings, powder-metal disks or engineers from GTF fleet AOG recovery or from kit insertion. New capacity is qualified before it ships. The records look-back covers every part made on the capacity added for the 2040 step (990 to 1,460 a year, +47.5% in one year). It now carries a date: its result goes to the Governance and Public Policy Committee's next quarterly meeting, and at once on any finding. If it cannot close by then, we say so plainly and give a new date. Our last escape came from ramp capacity [P-1040][P-1062], and the powder-metal cause was found only after a records review [PX-0039]. Contain first. If the review or the look-back shows the fleet short, Eddy's ground 2 binds and the rate waits.
  • Standing durability and parts report to the Governance and Public Policy Committee (private): Weekly to ExCo, quarterly to the Committee, and at once on any escape [PG-0050][P-1360]. The first 2050 report must state in writing what earlier reports showed. Where nothing can be evidenced, it says 'not available' instead of filling the gap. Contents: - Joint Venture engine fleet hours by airframe and by environment [PX-0122], against the ~1M-hour benchmark [P-0847]. The benchmark surfaces problems; it does not prove durability. - Removals and time on wing against plan, LLP status, and fix campaigns. - AOG on both fleets and the GTF fleet. - The pacing-parts count at the 1,460 rate (the last count was about 30, in 2023 [PX-0123]). - Kit insertion as a % of the GTF fleet [PX-0116]. - Capacity qualification status and the look-back result.
  • Top enterprise risks to the Audit Committee and the full Board (private): Three entries go into the annual top enterprise risks [PG-0034]: (1) The Joint Venture engine's in-service durability, with hot-and-harsh operation named. (2) The capacity added for the 2040 step to 1,460 engines a year. (3) The concentration of all P&W new NB share (36.5%) on one engine, one configuration, one LLP set and one casting, forging and powder-metal supply. This is common-mode risk across both airframes. On Eddy's advice, the lack of fleet data on the record is logged as a control gap. Value at stake, on Mitchill's numbers: - +2.39 $B in 2026 PV from deliveries in 2051-56 is still to be earned on the board. - The board does not count deliveries after 2056 (about $1.1B in 2026 PV), share loss from a durability finding (codes are locked at EIS), an in-service charge (the last one was a $5.4B sales charge), negative engine margin or partner shares. We book nothing either way.
  • Joint Venture technical governance, private clauses (private): P&W keeps the gear team and the gear data, which keeps Rolls-Royce's geared-IP claim closed [P-2004]. This is kept out of public text on Eddy's advice, because in public it reads as a point scored off our partner. Any pressure for UltraFan NB content or a merged derivative is reported to ExCo at once and treated as a new appropriation with its own durability programme. Eddy sees none on the 2050 record.
  • Capital-order note to the Finance Committee (private): Written as an order of priority, not as a 2050 status: the dividend first [PX-0081], then debt back to and held at pre-ASR levels [P-0686], then buybacks as the fill-in [P-0669]. The dividend never funds an engine. The analyst baseline runs to 2030E only: - dividend $5.0-5.6B, covered 2.3-2.4x by FCF; - net debt 0.76-0.94x EBITDA, back below Mitchill's pre-ASR approximation by about 2028E (inference); - buybacks $4.0-5.0B. From 2031 to 2050 the line rests on the board alone, and the note says so. Lifecycle value is not cash. The 2050 figure is $14.7B against $9.7B nominal, +$5.0B. Of that, about $3.1B is engine price (sales value, not margin) and about $1.9B is aftermarket collected later. Free cash flow from it this year: $0. The extra 500 engines a year likely cost cash first, at a negative engine margin (inference). The 5.4x is a value multiple gross of production cost, not a cash return. Mitchill's advice is recorded: the Board's ease toward 3 should wait until debt is shown to be held at pre-ASR levels, not just reached. Any P&W cash beyond GTF2's $2B needs a new appropriation through his gate and Finance, with a return case against hold and a buyback.
  • Whole-programme close-out against plan, reported to the Board (private): Reported in the sealed rationale and board_response for 2030, 2035, 2045 and 2050 [P-1191], on Mitchill's numbers: expected against booked, the 5.4x return, and payback on lifecycle value in 2040 nominal and 2041 discounted. It also records what we got wrong: - the S4 weighting; - the 2030 S5 figure; - the 2035 statement tightening we did not take up; - pre-EIS Committee reporting we cannot evidence; - the undated 2045 look-back; - no fleet data on the record.

Board guidance before the ExCo met

Priorities.

  • Product safety in service is our absolute priority. The Joint Venture engine has been ready since 2036. It has flown on NGSA since 2037 and on fps since 2040, at 36.5% of the narrowbody market: 1,460 engines a year and about 17,533 in our share by end-2049 (brief year table). Boeing now says in public that the Joint Venture engine is one of exactly two fps sources: 'If the Joint Venture engine stumbles, the fps is back on CFM alone.' Pratt & Whitney says the engine's durability record is 'still being earned'. So the fleet comes first: durability, life-limited parts at full life, and partner-shop capacity ahead of the first shop-visit wave. If durability bites, we fix the fleet first and anything new waits. The Trent 1000 is the precedent we will not repeat. [RG-0027, RG-0025, RG-0068, RX-0283, RX-0284, RX-0287, RX-0296, R-1476]
  • Protect the widebody cash cow. No widebody programme goes beside the Joint Venture. 'UltraFan NB: hold' (+32.35 / +32.35 / +32.70 in S1-S3) is the best grid plan in every column. Against it, the Trent 1000 upgrade is -6.72 / -6.72 / -6.62 and UltraFan WB is -9.00 / -8.67 / -8.32. Trent widebody share in 2050 is 55.2% (58.0% in S3), above our 50% line, and strain stays at $0. Time on wing inside the existing budget is the defence. [RG-0019, R-0929, R-1127, RX-0214, RX-0246, RX-0285, R-1574]
  • The balance sheet and returns stay intact. No new development money this round. Narrowbody ramp and early-unit costs are met from free cash flow and shared with Pratt & Whitney. If they run over, buybacks give way first. No equity, leverage below about 1.5x, no borrowing for distributions. [RX-0242, RG-0041, RG-0059, RG-0060, R-0900, R-0547]
  • Make the partnership work. Last round we asked for a Joint Venture governance note before 2050, and it is now due. Pratt & Whitney's public terms are unchanged: the venture shares risk and investment, not technology, under its design authority. Any configuration change, such as UltraFan NB content, would need its own return case and its own durability record. No Rolls-Royce money beyond our $4B share goes in without the board. [R-0318, R-0916, R-0920, R-1010, RX-0072]
  • Close the game on Control's terms, stated plainly. Narrowbody entry is met (36.5% in 2045 and 2050) and widebody dominance is met (worst year 55.2%). Our own narrowbody money is $5.71B against $4B: not met, and final. The strain line stays at $0 to the end. Any widebody launch in this last round would put a permanent $5B on the record. [RG-0033, R-1561, RX-0124, RG-0019]
