Recommendations.

  • The installed fleet comes first. Boeing now says in public that the Joint Venture engine is one of exactly two fps sources, and that any durability finding is a live problem that would make it want a third source. Our position on both new narrowbodies therefore rests on durability in service, not on the next programme. Watson should keep his quarterly report to the Safety, Energy Transition & Tech Committee. It should cover: - durability in severe-environment operation; - life-limited parts at full declared life; - partner-shop induction slots and spares ahead of the first shop-visit wave from the 2037-40 cohorts; - spare engines for severe-environment operators. If durability bites, the Committee hears first, the fleet is protected and retrofitted at shop visit, as with the Trent 1000 package, and anything new waits. Product safety is and always must be our most important priority.
  • Bring the Joint Venture governance note in this package. It was due before the 2050 round. It should state plainly that on the record Pratt & Whitney holds design authority over the gear, the core and GTF2, and that we bring risk, investment and the support network. It should also ask for: - hot-section and life-limited-part data in proportion to the risk we carry; - cost on any retrofit to follow design authority, or a joint say in the fix; - work and revenue share against the equal 36.5% shares. If our content per engine is below half, McCabe should say what that does to the board's engine value. Pratt & Whitney has said in public that UltraFan NB content or a merged derivative would be a new appropriation with its own durability record. Any such proposal from us comes to this board as a new programme, on its own return case. No Rolls-Royce money beyond our $4B share goes in without the board. We left IAE for want of alignment, and we will not drift there again.
  • Defend the widebody core inside the existing budget, and hold both widebody orders in this last round. Continue Trent time on wing as an unpriced other move: HP turbine blades on the Trent 1000 and Trent 7000, life-limited-part life extension, and Trent XWB shop-visit cost down. Airbus says it will take a further A350 step only when 'the technology, the engine and the business case are all ready'. Our part is to keep the Trent XWB ready commercially and technically, on standard terms, without a programme order. We power the A350 alone, so watch that exposure. If a Re-engine goes on the record this round, record in rationale how we would answer it after the game: an airframe on the record first, the strain shown, and the case made on its own return. We are a long-term business with very long investment cycles. Long-term widebody presence is earned through the fleet we have.
  • Funding discipline. McCabe should keep reporting each quarter on our share of narrowbody ramp and early-unit costs, shared with Pratt & Whitney, against her base of about $1.9-4.3B and her reasonable worst case of about $7.5B ($9B if we carry a retrofit alone). The report should also cover the net LTSA balance, time on wing and any onerous-contract provision. Our order holds: the balance sheet first, then the 30-40% dividend, then investment and further distributions. If the ramp or a fleet fix runs over, buybacks give way first, as in 2015, and a fleet fix is never re-phased for cash. Any need for equity, leverage above about 1.5x or borrowing for distributions comes to the board before it arises. Gross R&D stays broadly flat.
  • Close the game on Control's terms, stated plainly in objective_note: - narrowbody entry: met (36.5% in 2045 and 2050); - widebody dominance: met (worst year 55.2%); - strain: met at $0, held there to the end by the two widebody holds; - own narrowbody money: not met, and final, at $5.71B against $4B. That is the $4B share plus $1.71B written off at the 2035 fold, caused by the 2030 double selection. We never cancel or fold for a metric. When we commit, we deliver, and we did. Keep the internal metric out of the public statement.
  • Public statement and other moves. Repeat what is on the record: the Joint Venture formed, its engine is in service on both new narrowbodies, and the fleet comes first. Say: - no date for any new programme, retrofit, kit or growth engine; - nothing on Re-engines or any airframer's dates or rates; - no Joint Venture terms beyond the record; - no claim of Rolls-Royce module technology in the in-service engine, which would contradict our partner's public line. Keep both airframers on standard commercial terms through the Investment Committee, with no concessions to hold a position. On widebody, the line stays 'no new widebody programme beside the narrowbody, and Trent time on wing keeps improving'. We won't do anything not profitable.

Tufan Erginbilgic frames the round

Question. So, 2050. This is the last round. There is nothing left to launch on the narrowbody, and the question is cash and quality of earnings, not share [RX-0054]. Where we stand: - The Joint Venture formed in 2035. Its engine has been ready since 2036, on NGSA since 2037 and on fps since 2040. - We hold 36.5% of narrowbody engines, 1,460 a year: about 17,533 in our share by end-2049 and 18,993 by end-2050 (brief year table). - Widebody share is 55.2% in 2050 (58.0% in S3). - Hold is worth +32.35 / +32.35 / +32.70 in S1-S3. The question has three parts. (1) Does the installed fleet turn into durable, profitable aftermarket cash? - Boeing now says in public that the Joint Venture engine is one of exactly two fps sources, and that any durability finding would make it want a third. - P&W says the engine's durability record is 'still being earned'. - So our narrowbody position rests on durability in service, not on a next programme. - The Trent 1000 is the movie I have seen before [RX-0087, RX-0114]. (2) Does any widebody spend earn its keep beside the narrowbody in the last round? Frankly, no. - The Trent 1000 upgrade is -6.72 / -6.72 / -6.62 against hold, and UltraFan WB is -9.00 / -8.67 / -8.32. - Each loses more than its own bill in every column, with a permanent $5B of strain stacked on it. (3) Is the partnership aligned on terms that protect our cash? The governance note is due now. It covers: - design authority; - data on the hot section and life-limited parts; - retrofit liability; - work and revenue share against equal 36.5% shares; - our cash staying within the $4B share. 'I worry about tomorrow's financials' [RX-0125]. We close the game on cash, not on a launch.

Situation. PUBLIC RECORD (round 4 bulletin) Airframes: - NGSA (Airbus, launched 2030) has been in service since 2037. - fps (Boeing, 10-year ramp-up, launched 2030) has been in service since 2040. - Both carry code 7, with CFM, P&W and RR fitted on both. Airbus says the NGSA code was locked at entry into service. - Boeing counts the Joint Venture engine as one source, which leaves the fps on exactly two. Its words: 'If the Joint Venture engine stumbles, the fps is back on CFM alone.' It reviews both engine sources at each meeting of its Aerospace Safety Committee. Engines: - The P&W-RR Joint Venture formed in 2035. Its engine has been ready since 2036 (the date inherited from the folded GTF2). - Our UltraFan NB Solo and P&W's GTF2 Solo both folded into it in 2035. - CFM's ducted engine has been ready since 2036 and is in service on both new narrowbodies. The CFM-Embraer partnership has been ready since 2037. - The GEnx upgrade has been ready since 2033. It counted from 2042 and took our widebody share from 58.0% to 55.2%. - CFM keeps RISE funded as technology, with no date and no new programmes. Its narrowbody share is 27%. P&W's public Joint Venture terms, unchanged: - The venture shares risk and investment, not technology. - The gear, the core and the GTF2 technology stay P&W modules under its design authority. It is one engine and one support chain. - Any configuration change, such as UltraFan NB content or a merged derivative, would be a new capital appropriation with its own return case and its own durability programme. - P&W is still inserting its Hot Section durability kit across the GTF fleet. Re-engines: neither is on the record. No 787 or A350 Re-engine has been launched, and none was announced for this round in an earlier public statement. - Boeing: 'On the 787, we're not starting a new development this year.' It grows the 787 out of Charleston capacity, 'When there's a business case for the next step on the widebody, we'll bring it, and not before.' - Airbus: the A350 Re-engine is held 'until the technology, the engine and the business case are all ready'. OUR POSITION (private brief) - Hold is worth +32.35 (yield 129.4%). Engine value +38.07, R&D -4.00, write-offs -1.71. - Narrowbody engine share: 24.1-24.8% in 2037-39, then 36.5% from 2040. Other moves.

  • Fleet first on the Joint Venture engine in service (public): The Joint Venture engine is in service on NGSA and fps. Rolls-Royce puts the installed fleet first: durability in service, life-limited parts at full declared life, and support through the joint partner-shop network. If durability bites, the fleet is fixed first and anything new waits. We report what the fleet data shows and claim nothing beyond it. No dates, no retrofit or kit timing, and no Joint Venture terms beyond the public record.
  • Quarterly fleet report to the Safety, Energy Transition & Tech Committee (Watson) (private): Covers our share of the fleet: about 17,533 engines by end-2049 and 18,993 by end-2050, at 1,460 a year since 2040. The first shop-visit wave is the 2037-40 cohorts: 965 + 978 + 990 + 1,460 = 4,393 engines in our share. Each quarter Watson reports: - durability in severe-environment operation; - life-limited parts at full declared life; - partner-shop induction slots ahead of the first shop-visit wave; - life-limited-part and hot-section spares (P&W holds design authority and controls that supply); - spare engines for severe-environment operators; - what we can and cannot see: hot-section and life-limited-part data sit with P&W until the governance note opens them to us. Retrofit rule if durability bites, on the Trent 1000 model: (1) the Committee hears first, before anything is said in public; (2) protect the fleet with inspection intervals and a spare-engine pool; (3) the design authority issues the kit, inserted at shop visit through the joint partner shops; (4) anything new waits; (5) the cost split follows the governance note, and McCabe brings a fresh number to the Board. New-engine production does not take parts from fleet recovery. Watson claims no data, shop count or slot number the record cannot show.
  • Joint Venture governance note to the Board, delivered now (Watson and McCabe) (private): The note the Board asked for before 2050. Company doctrine (the IAE lesson) and inference: my record is Low on Joint Venture terms. OPERATING SIDE (Watson): (1) Design authority, stated plainly. On the record P&W holds the gear, the core and GTF2 as its modules under its design authority. It is one engine and one support chain. In this engine we bring risk, investment and the support network. We hold no module design authority. (2) Our technology role. UltraFan stays ours and feeds the Trent fleet. 'We are actually bringing a technology' [RX-0072] belongs to a later engine under our own design authority, not this one. (3) Data. Hot-section, life-limited-part and severe-environment fleet data through the joint support agreement, in proportion to our equal 36.5% share of the risk. Without it Watson cannot report durability to the Committee beyond the public record. (4) Support network. Our Singapore-model partner shops plus P&W's in-service shops. Induction slots, spares and a spare-engine pool planned jointly ahead of the 2037-40 wave. Any kit goes in at shop visit through these shops. MONEY SIDE (McCabe): (5) Work share and revenue share at 36.5% each, matching the equal engine shares. The board credits our 1,460 engines a year at full value, which matches our cash only at about half the content and revenue of each Joint Venture engine. Each 10 points of content below half takes about $7.7B off the narrowbody value: at 40% content engine value is about +30.3 and hold about +24.6; at 30%, about +22.6 and +16.9. Service revenue counts as much as build work share. (6) Retrofit liability. Cost follows design authority, or we get a joint say in the fix. Planning figure: half a Trent 1000-type bill, about £1.1bn; worst case about £2.2bn. That anchor comes from a smaller widebody fleet, so it is a planning figure, not a ceiling. Any finding comes to the Board with a fresh number before anything is public. (7) Cash. Our money stays within the $4B share. No Rolls-Royce money beyond it without the Board. (8) Configuration. Any UltraFan NB content or merged derivative is a new programme: it comes to the Board on its own return case and its own durability record, as P&W's public terms also require. (9) Alignment. Who books the service contracts on our 36.5% is to be settled in the note, so the narrowbody float is proven, not assumed. We left IAE for want of alignment; we will not drift there again.
  • Funding discipline and quarterly report to the Board (McCabe) (private): Our share of narrowbody ramp and early-unit costs, shared with P&W, held at the top of the base range until actuals exist: about $4.3B (£3.1bn) against a base of about $1.9-4.3B (£1.4-3.1bn). Reasonable worst case about $7.5B (£5.5bn) with a retrofit shared 50/50, or about $9B (£6.7bn) if we carry a retrofit alone. The window rolls forward to the first shop-visit wave from the 2037-40 cohorts. Also each quarter: the net LTSA balance (no narrowbody float booked until the governance note settles who holds the service contracts), time on wing (no upside booked before it is delivered), and any onerous-contract provision, booked plainly if a Joint Venture contract turns loss-making. Order: the balance sheet, then the 30-40% dividend, then investment and further distributions. If the ramp or a fleet fix runs over, buybacks give way first, and a fleet fix is never re-phased for cash. No equity, leverage below about 1.5x, no borrowing for distributions. Gross R&D stays broadly flat. No balance-sheet trigger stands.
  • Trent time on wing and fleet support inside the existing budget (Watson) (public): Longer-life HP turbine blades on the Trent 1000 and Trent 7000, life extension for life-limited parts, UltraFan technology fed into the Trent fleet, and Trent XWB shop-visit cost down. Funded inside the existing fleet budget. This is not the Trent 1000 upgrade order and not a new programme, and it carries no strain. We keep the Trent XWB ready commercially and technically for the A350 family on standard terms, and watch our sole-source exposure there. No dates disclosed.
  • Commercial terms with Airbus and Boeing (public): Standard commercial terms with both airframers on NGSA, fps and the widebody fleets: value remunerated, win-win. No launch-style concession, discount or free upgrade to hold a position. Every new contract goes through the Investment Committee [RX-0081, RX-0097, R-1582]. We do not speak for any airframer's dates or rates.

One order differs.
  • Boeing's fps engine selection: CFM alone (code 3) in the previous game, all three makers (code 7) here. Ortberg's lean was code 3 in both games; the enabler moved it.
  • Every other order in all 20 company-rounds is the same, including Boeing's 10-year ramp, both Joint Venture commitments and every hold.
Same orders, different reasons.
  • Boeing's ramp: in the previous game the $0.46B was a doctrine premium and the Board's 7-year advice was "Not taken". Here the Board offered the 10-year as an approved alternative for the stress-case debt line, and Ortberg split the premium into doctrine and objective parts.
  • Airbus's code 7: previously "supply certainty and customer choice"; here "the enabler trap".
  • Rolls-Royce's 2030 launch: the same order, now with the $4B breach priced and stated.
The engine makers' values move with one selection.
  • P&W +$11.81B and Rolls-Royce +$11.80B: from 2040 fps is split among all three makers, with the Joint Venture engine beside CFM, where before it was all CFM. CFM/GE −$31.40B.
  • The three engine makers together are $7.79B worse off, so the change is not a pure transfer (inference: the makers' discount rates and lifecycle values differ).
  • The airframers' values are identical to the cent.
On Control's yardstick, the previous game's orders score one objective lower.
  • Boeing's first enabler line fails there (fps on CFM alone, one source); every other added objective scores the same, including Rolls-Royce's $5.71B breach and Boeing's repaired balance sheet.
  • Among the base objectives, CFM/GE's narrowbody dominance flips: met there (51.1% at worst), missed here (27.0%). P&W's ΔPV objective flips the other way: missed there (−$2.93B), met here (+$8.88B).

The analyst models: prediction against the game

Before this game each company's profile gained a note on the July-August 2026 analyst models: Morgan Stanley and Goldman Sachs company models, and S&P Capital IQ consensus where the files had it. The notes are real-world context; the dashboard's numbers still set every payoff. Two things come from them directly: Boeing's net-debt tracker (start, free cash flow, historical level) and the stress case, set from the spread of estimates and Boeing's record. Below, what the models say, and how their implications for each company's decisions compare with what the agents then did.

Money is nominal in the reporting currency. The tracker's validation: with base cash flow only it gives Boeing net debt of $16.49B at end-2027 and $6.70B at end-2028 in 2026 dollars, against consensus $16.57B and $6.90B.

Boeing: the analysts' cash flow decided the debt objective before the game did.
  • The tracker reproduces consensus net debt within $0.2B and reaches zero in 2029 with no new programme. The fps then competes with returns to owners, not with debt repair, as the note predicted: "Under debt first, programme money after 2029 comes out of what would otherwise go to owners." (GS models $42B of buybacks in 2027-2030.)
  • "A launch in the 2030 round mostly tests the hold years", the note said, and it did: the 7-year ramp failed the stress case at the 2035 hold year, not the 2030 deadline. The 10-year's later, lower spending passed.
  • The note flagged engine selection as "a supply-risk choice the models do not price". Boeing took it as one, on the enabler.
Airbus: money was not the limit, as the note said, but its own cash line was.
  • The banks show net cash above EUR 31bn in 2030E. Airbus's agents measured NGSA against one year's free cash flow instead: $5.07B a year against a $5.2B line, 97% used. That line, with its other rules, kept the A350 Re-engine and Delay Tactics out in 2030 and 2035.
  • "Keep two sources if the board allows it": NGSA flies two.
CFM/GE: the note named its biggest risk, and half of it came true: Boeing's slot was shared, not lost.
  • "Losing a new Boeing narrowbody to a rival, including a Pratt & Whitney and Rolls-Royce Joint Venture, costs more than losing an Airbus slot." Sharing fps cost CFM/GE $31.40B against the previous game.
  • "A Ducted launch is the defence if a rival engine is selected": it was launched in 2030 and is worth 10 points before re-normalising, but it could not undo selections sealed in the same round.
P&amp;W: launch against a committed airframer, and share the risk.
  • The note's advice, prefer "launch only if an airframer selects P&W" and a Joint Venture to share new-engine losses, is exactly what P&W did.
  • Its durability precedent ($5.4bn of sales in 2023) is the risk Boeing now names in public. P&W answered "with product and data, not price".
Rolls-Royce: the note's two warnings split.
  • "Do not stack projects in the 2030 round": kept. No widebody programme was ever on the record.
  • "An UltraFan narrowbody Solo launch repeats the Trent ramp at bigger volume" and "The Joint Venture fits the R&D budget better": the conditional Solo it chose cost $1.71B more than its Joint Venture share.

Method

How the game was run

  • A replay. The previous ExCo-and-Board game (run dash-2050-exco) replayed from the start in a fresh run, dash-2050-obj: the same dashboard, agents, rules and decision years. Three things were added to the companies' files before 2030, and nothing else changed.
    • Control's objectives (listed under Control's objectives), in each company's private brief with its metrics for every plan on the payoff grid. Boeing's brief also carried its net-debt path, base and stress, and a table of the engine sources each engine code would give.
    • The GM's balance-sheet tracker for Boeing (below).
    • The analyst notes: a note per company on the July-August 2026 Morgan Stanley and Goldman Sachs models and, for Boeing, Capital IQ consensus, each checked against the extracted model files. The notes are context; the dashboard sets every payoff.
  • Dashboard. Your combined_dash.py, run headless (never in Streamlit) at the Game_v3.txt snapshot. Solved by the game master (GM), it reproduces the snapshot: airframers 4 Pure Nash and 12 Near-Nash, engines 1 Pure Nash and 11 Near-Nash.
  • Players. 20 AI agents. In each company, the CEO, CFO and operating head of the default 2026 executive committee, each profiled from that person's own public words, and the Board, profiled from transcripts, filings and web search, with a culture score. Where an executive's record was thin, the seat's tests were derived from the role or company doctrine and labelled low confidence (Pope, Toepfer, Wagner). They are AI agents, not the people.
  • Each round, in each company. The Board gives guidance; the CEO frames the choice; the CFO and operating head test it independently; the CEO decides; the CFO and operating head run a veto check, and the CEO revises once if a binding veto or red-line flag stands; each Board item goes to Board review, with one more revision and a reversion to the default if a Board veto stands. Each company's chain ran as its own workflow, in parallel; nothing passed between companies.
  • Information. The public bulletin plus a private brief per company. Only the GM saw the dashboard and the other companies' briefs. The isolation hook denies other companies' files and briefs, the dashboard, the snapshot, GM code, earlier reports and runs, and the GM's scratch files. An audit of every tool call found all 20 company-rounds clean.
  • Rounds. Four sealed, simultaneous rounds: 2030, 2035, 2045, 2050. Each round's value is the GM valuation of the state after that round, assuming nobody moves again. The final round's value is the game outcome.

How Control's objectives are scored

  • They never change a payoff. The dashboard's ΔPV, including its own debt penalty on $45B of debt, is untouched. A company could give up value for an objective only within its premium cap, and had to log it.
  • Boeing's net debt (total debt less cash and short-term investments) at year end, in 2026 dollars. Start: $22.53B at end-2026, the consensus mean. Base free cash flow: consensus for 2027-2030 ($5.67B, $9.86B, $13.03B, $15.04B nominal), deflated at the dashboard's 2.2% CPI, then flat at $13.79B; the stress case is one-third lower. Each year: free cash flow = base + 79% of (the game's profit change against its baseline − programme cash) − 3% real interest on any debt the game adds; net debt = last year's in today's money − free cash flow, never below the historical level once there (surplus goes to owners). Programme cash: each bill spread over its development years on a standard curve (5% in year 1 of 10, peaking at 14% in year 7), plus the two-front strain over the fps and 787 Re-engine overlap; the 737 rate increase spent evenly to 2032. Profits count from the first decision year, as played. Historical level $0, rounded from the 2010-2018 average of −$0.6B.
  • Engine sources. The independent engine sources fitted to a new narrowbody in production in 2040, 2045 and 2050: CFM, P&W's GTF2, Rolls-Royce's UltraFan NB, or the P&W-Rolls-Royce Joint Venture engine, which counts as one. Engine makers in the market: those with narrowbody share above zero in 2045 and 2050.
  • Rolls-Royce's own narrowbody money: $8B for UltraFan NB Solo, $4B for its Joint Venture share; a Solo cancelled or folded counts its spend to date. Strain: the dashboard's one-off $5B whenever a narrowbody and a widebody engine programme are both on the record.

Rules the GM added to the static dashboard (as in the previous game)

  • Time. A programme enters service, or an engine is ready, after its development time from the decision year: fps 7 or 10 years, fps via Embraer 10, NGSA 7, Re-engines 5; ducted 6, GTF2 6, UltraFan NB 7, UltraFan WB 6, Trent and GEnx upgrades 3, the Embraer partnership 7, the Joint Venture 6 or an inherited schedule; Open Fan 10, never before 2045.
  • Cancellations write off the bill × years elapsed ÷ development years. Delay Tactics are covert; none was ordered.
  • Engines. The dashboard's engine game is applied year by year, splitting each airframer's narrowbody share equally among the engines fitted to it. Each narrowbody engine move counts from the later of its ready year and the first new narrowbody's entry into service (2037 here); widebody engine upgrades count from the first Re-engine's entry into service, or 2042.
  • Joint Venture. It forms when both makers commit. It folds in solo programmes, writing off spend beyond each maker's share, and inherits the most advanced folded schedule. A Joint Venture formed after an airframe's entry into service does not rewrite the engines fitted before it (a check added for this game).
  • Tests. Dashboard reproduction, the engine move combinations and the snapshot equilibria; both games replay exactly, and no played year changes; the isolation tests.

What the numbers are

  • ΔPV and yield. ΔPV is the change in present value at 2026 against the status quo (nobody launches anything), at each company's dashboard WACC. Yield = 100 + 100 × ΔPV ÷ enterprise value.
  • Dashboard conventions. Airframe programme spend is charged in full at entry into service. Engine R&D is undiscounted. Engine value is the lifetime value per engine delivered.
  • Regret. The final ΔPV a company would have had with its best alternative orders in that round, holding every other order in the game as played (later rounds re-run), minus its actual final ΔPV.
  • S1, S2, …. The scenario columns of each company's own payoff grid in that round's brief; they differ by company and round. Ids in brackets, such as [BX-1239], are the agents' evidence citations. "(inference)" marks a reading of the record that no single number states.
  • Your dashboard alone. The table below sets each final value next to your dashboard alone. The airframers match exactly. For the engine makers the dashboard fixes a 50/50 airframer split and locks P&W to GTF2 Solo; the GM's Joint Venture and year-by-year split account for the difference.
